history.meaning: name (of a thing, place, or book), title

назвать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic назьвати ('to call by name, summon'), formed from the prefix на- and звать ('to call', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati, cognate with Sanskrit hváyati 'calls, invokes').

назначить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix на- and значить ('to mark, signify, mean'), derived from знак ('sign, mark', from Proto-Slavic *znakъ, built on *znati 'to know'). Literally, 'to put a mark on, designate for a role or time', whence 'to appoint (to a post), set (a date/meeting), or prescribe (treatment)'.

history.meaning: to appoint, designate, set (a time), prescribe

называть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic называти (Proto-Slavic *nazyvati), the imperfective of назвать ('to call by name, name'), formed from на- + звать ('to call', Proto-Slavic *zъvati) with lengthened root vowel *ъ -> *y.

называться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/passive verb formed from называть ('to call, name', imperfective of назвать, with lengthened root vowel -ы- from Proto-Slavic *nazyvati, built on *zъvati 'to call'). Means 'to be called, have the name/title of'.

rootFamily.gloss: name, title (of an object, book, restaurant)

найти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наити ('to come upon, walk onto, find'), from Proto-Slavic *naiti, formed from the prefix *na- ('onto, upon') + *iti ('to walk, go', modern Russian идти). Literally 'to walk right onto something, come across it', which became the standard Slavic verb 'to find' (parallel to Latin invenīre 'to come upon').

history.meaning: to walk upon, come across → to find

найтись.etymology: Perfective reflexive/passive form of найти ('to find', literally 'to come upon by walking', from на- 'onto, upon' + йти / идти 'to go', Old East Slavic наити, Proto-Slavic *najьti). With -сь, найтись means 'to be found, turn up' (and figuratively 'to find the right words, not be at a loss').

rootFamily.gloss: to be located; to be found (impf.)

наказать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наказати ('to instruct, admonish, teach a lesson'), formed from the prefix на- and казати ('to show, point out, speak', Proto-Slavic *kazati). Up to the 18th century, наказать meant 'to instruct, give orders' (preserved in наказ 'mandate, instruction to a deputy'); from 'teaching someone a stern lesson', it shifted in modern Russian to 'to punish'.

наклейка.etymology: Deverbal object noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from наклеить ('to glue on, stick on'), built from на- ('onto') + клеить ('to glue', from клей 'glue', Proto-Slavic *klejь).

history.meaning: to stick on -> sticker, pasted label

наклонить.etymology: Formed with the prefix на- ('downward, toward') + клонить ('to incline, bend, tilt'), inherited from Old East Slavic клонити and Proto-Slavic *kloniti.

наклониться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of наклонить ('to tilt, bend down'), formed with prefix на- ('onto, downward') + клонить ('to incline, bend, bow', from Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

history.meaning: to tilt → to lean down, bend over

наклонять.etymology: Derived as the imperfective of наклонить ('to tilt, incline, bend downward'), formed from на- ('toward, down') + клонить ('to incline, bow', Proto-Slavic *kloniti).

наконец.etymology: Formed in Russian by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на конец ('to the end, at the end'), from на ('to, at') + конец ('end', Proto-Slavic *konьcь).

накопить.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('amass a quantity of') + копить ('to save up, hoard, accumulate', derived from копа 'heap, stack, threescore', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kopa).

history.meaning: heap, stack -> to heap up, amass

накосячить.etymology: Colloquial slang perfective verb formed with на- from косячить ('to botch, blunder, mess up'), derived from косяк ('something skewed or awry; a blunder', built on косой 'crooked, askew, slanted', Proto-Slavic *kosъ).

history.meaning: askew -> blunder -> to mess up, screw up

накричать.etymology: Formed from the prefix на- ('upon, at', governing на + accusative) + кричать ('to shout, yell', inherited from Proto-Slavic *kričati).

history.meaning: to yell at, scold loudly (накричать на кого-либо)

наладиться.etymology: Reflexive-intransitive derivative of наладить ('to put in order, adjust, set right', formed from на- + ладить 'to arrange harmoniously', built on лад 'harmony, order', Proto-Slavic *ladъ) + -ся.

history.meaning: order, harmony -> to put in order
to set right -> to work out, come right, improve

налаживаться.etymology: Imperfective of наладиться ('to work out, get sorted'), formed from налаживать ('to set right, adjust', from на- + ладить 'to put in order', with regular д -> ж palatalization) + -ся.

history.meaning: to get sorted out, start going well (Жизнь налаживается!)

morphemes.meaning: order, harmony (from лад with д -> ж)

налево.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на лево ('to the left'), combining the directional preposition на with the short neuter accusative of левый ('left', from Old East Slavic лѣвыи, Proto-Slavic *lěvъ, continuing PIE *leh₂iwós 'left, curved'; directly cognate with Latin laevus and Ancient Greek λαιός 'left').

history.meaning: to the left, on the left

наливать.etymology: Imperfective partner of налить ('to pour, fill by pouring'), formed from prefix на- ('in, onto') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', from Old East Slavic лити, Proto-Slavic *liti, cognate with Lithuanian lìeti 'to pour').

налить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic налити (future налью, past налил), formed from prefix на- ('into, onto') + лить ('to pour', from Proto-Slavic *liti, continuing Balto-Slavic *lei- 'to pour, flow'; cognate with Lithuanian lìeti 'to pour' and lytùs 'rain').

наличные.etymology: Substantivized plural of наличный (as in наличные деньги 'cash money'), formed from the phrase на лицо ('present in person, physically before one's face/eyes', built on на + лицо 'face, presence'): originally 'goods or coins physically on hand for inspection', as opposed to credit or bills of exchange.

history.meaning: present before one's eyes → ready money on hand, cash

налогоплательщик.etymology: Compound noun formed in Russian (calquing German Steuerzahler) from налог ('tax, assessment', originally 'that which is laid upon', deverbal from наложить) + linking vowel -о- + плательщик ('payer', from платить 'to pay').

намного.etymology: Formed by fusing the preposition на ('by [a margin]') with много ('much, a lot'): literally 'by a lot, much (+ comparative)'.
намного.notes: Used before comparatives: намного лучше ('much better'), намного проще ('far simpler').

намокнуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prefix на- ('to a resulting state') + мокнуть ('to get wet', built on the root of мокрый 'wet', Proto-Slavic *mokrъ).
намокнуть.notes: Past tense drops the suffix -ну-: он намок, она промокла.

нанести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нанести ('to bring upon, lay on'), formed from prefix на- ('onto, upon a surface') + нести ('to carry, bring', from Proto-Slavic *nesti). Used for brushing on glaze/paint, plotting marks on a map, or paying a visit.

history.meaning: to apply, brush on (glaze, paint), mark (on a map)

нанимать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наимати and Proto-Slavic *najьmati ('to hire, rent', imperfective of нанять < *najęti), formed from на- + имать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *jьmati): literally 'to take on (a worker or lodging for pay)'.

history.meaning: to take on -> to hire, rent

наносить.etymology: Imperfective of нанести, formed from на- ('onto, upon') + носить ('to carry, bring', iterative of нести, from Proto-Slavic *nositi).

history.meaning: to apply (a layer of cream or paint); to inflict (a blow, damage, or insult); to pay (a visit)

наоборот.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на оборот ('onto the reverse turn/side'), combining на with оборот ('turn, rotation, reverse side', native East Slavic pleophonic form from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortъ, built on *vьrtěti 'to turn').

history.meaning: on the contrary, the other way round, vice versa

наотрез.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на отрез ('as if cutting clean off'), from на + отрез ('a clean cut-off', deverbal from отрезать 'to cut off', Proto-Slavic *otrězati).

history.meaning: to cut off -> clean cut -> flatly, point-blank (especially in отказаться наотрез 'to refuse point-blank')

нападающий.etymology: Substantivized present active participle of нападать ('to attack', from на- 'upon' + падать 'to fall', Proto-Slavic *padati); adopted in twentieth-century sporting terminology as a semantic calque of English forward / attacker.

напарник.etymology: Formed in Russian from на паре ('in a pair, working as a pair') — from на- + пара ('pair', borrowed via German Paar / Polish para from Latin paria 'equal things, pair') + the person suffix -ник: 'one who works in a pair with another, work partner, teammate'.

напасть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic напасти and Proto-Slavic *napasti ('to fall upon, attack'), formed from на- ('upon, against') + пасть ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *pasti).

напевать.etymology: Formed in Russian from на- ('lightly, in a low or casual way') + певать (iterative of петь 'to sing', Proto-Slavic *pěti): 'to hum, croon, sing softly to oneself'.

напечатать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix на- from печатать ('to stamp with a seal, print, type'), derived from печать ('seal, stamp, printing press', Old East Slavic печать, Proto-Slavic *pečatь).

написать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic написати ('to write, paint'), formed as the standard perfective of писать ('to write') by adding the prefix на- ('on a surface, to completion').

history.meaning: to write down, paint on a surface

напиток.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic напитокъ, formed with the noun suffix -ок from напить / напиться ('to drink one's fill', passive participle напитый), built from the prefix на- and пить ('to drink', Proto-Slavic *piti).

напоить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic напоити and Proto-Slavic *napojiti ('to give to drink'), formed from completive на- + поить ('to give to drink, water', Proto-Slavic *pojiti, the o-grade causative of *piti 'to drink').

history.meaning: to drink -> to cause to drink -> to give a drink
to give someone a drink (e.g. tea); to get someone drunk

наполовину.etymology: Formed by fusing the preposition на ('to the extent of') with the accusative singular половину of половина ('half', derived from пол 'half', Proto-Slavic *polъ).

напомнить.etymology: Formed in Russian from на- ('onto, into awareness') + помнить ('to remember', Proto-Slavic *pomьniti, from *mьněti 'to think, keep in mind'): 'to bring back to someone's memory, remind'.

направить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic направити (Proto-Slavic *napraviti 'to make straight, guide, direct'), formed from на- ('toward') + править ('to direct, steer, make straight', from правый 'straight, right').

направление.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from направить ('to direct, guide, refer'), built from на- + править ('to steer, direct, make straight', derived from правый 'straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.meaning: to direct, refer -> direction, trend; medical or official referral slip

направо.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the directional preposition на ('to') with the short neuter accusative право of правый ('right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.meaning: to the right, on the right

например.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на пример ('for an example, after the model of'), formed from the preposition на ('for, onto') + пример ('example, model'), which is derived from примерить ('to try on, measure against', from при- + мерить 'to measure', built on мера 'measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

напролёт.etymology: Adverb formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на пролёт ('straight through in a single flight'), from на + пролёт ('flight straight through', from пролететь 'to fly through', built on лететь 'to fly', Proto-Slavic *letěti).

history.meaning: straight through -> all through without stopping, on end (всю ночь напролёт 'all night long')

напряжённый.etymology: Past passive participle / verbal adjective of напрячь ('to strain, tense, stretch tight'), formed from на- + прячь ('to harness, draw tight, stretch', from Proto-Slavic *pręťi, seen in упряжка 'team harness').

history.meaning: to stretch tight, draw a bow
to strain, tense -> tense, strained, intense

напугать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of пугать ('to scare, frighten'), formed with the prefix на- and the expressive East Slavic verb пугать (compare dialectal пуга 'whip; owl' and Ukrainian пугач 'eagle owl', from an onomatopoeic cry *pug- used to startle birds or animals).

нарезать.etymology: Formed from the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity, into pieces') and резать ('to cut, slice'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати and Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, carve', cognate with Lithuanian rė́žti 'to cut, incise'). Note that stress distinguishes aspect: perfective **наре́зать** ('to slice up') vs. imperfective **нареза́ть**.

нарезка.etymology: Formed in Russian as an action and result noun from нарезать ('to slice up, cut into pieces', from на- + резать 'to cut') with the suffix -ка.

history.meaning: slicing; platter of sliced food (cold cuts, cheese)

нарисовать.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix на- ('onto a surface, to completion') to рисовать ('to draw').

наркоз.etymology: Borrowed via German Narkose from Ancient Greek νάρκωσις (nárkōsis, 'numbing, stupor, torpor'), derived from ναρκόω ('to benumb, deaden', from νάρκη 'numbness, torpor').

народ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic народъ ('people, multitude, lineage'), from Proto-Slavic *narodъ, a deverbal noun formed from *naroditi ('to give birth to in numbers, beget, produce'), from *na- + *roditi ('to give birth', Russian родить). Literally, 'that which has been born or grown up together, a generation or people'.

народный.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic народьныи, formed from народ ('people, nation', from Proto-Slavic *narodъ) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

наружу.etymology: Formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на ружу ('to the outside, into open view'), from Old East Slavic ружь ('outward appearance, open air, outside', related to обнаружить 'to uncover, detect').
наружу.notes: Indicates motion outward (выйти наружу 'to come out'), whereas снаружи indicates location ('on the outside').

нарушать.etymology: Imperfective of нарушить ('to violate, break, disturb'), borrowed/adapted from Old Church Slavonic нарушати / нарушити ('to break down, destroy, transgress'), formed from на- + рушить ('to pull down, demolish, break', Proto-Slavic *rušiti).

history.meaning: to violate, break (a law, rule, silence, or peace)

нарушение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from нарушить ('to break, violate, disturb'), built from на- + рушить ('to break down, tear down, shatter', from Proto-Slavic *rušiti). Just as English speaks of 'breaking' a law or rule, Russian uses нарушить / нарушение for the 'breach or violation' of a rule, law, or order.

history.meaning: to break (a rule/peace) → violation, breach, infringement

нарываться.etymology: Imperfective of нарваться ('to dash oneself onto a sharp obstacle or ambush; colloquially to ask for trouble, provoke a fight'), formed from на- ('onto, against') + рываться (iterative of рваться 'to rush, lunge, tear forward', from рвать 'to tear', Proto-Slavic *rъvati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to run into an ambush -> (colloquial) to ask for trouble, push one's luck

нарываться.notes: Often heard in the colloquial warning Ты нарываешься! ('You're asking for trouble! / You're pushing it!').

насквозь.etymology: Adverb formed in Russian from prefix на- + сквозь ('through, right through'), inherited from Old East Slavic сквозѣ and Proto-Slavic *skvozě ('through an opening or gap').

history.meaning: right through, all the way through

насколько.etymology: Adverb and conjunction formed by univerbation of the prepositional phrase на сколько ('to how much, by how much'), from на + сколько ('how much, how many', Proto-Slavic *kolьko).

history.meaning: to what extent, how much; as far as (насколько я знаю 'as far as I know')

наследие.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic наслѣдие ('inheritance, heritage'), built on на- + слѣдъ ('track, footprint', Proto-Slavic *slědъ): literally 'that which follows in a predecessor's footsteps'.

наставник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic наставьникъ ('guide, teacher, preceptor, spiritual mentor', calquing Ancient Greek ἐπιστάτης and καθηγητής), formed with the agent suffix -ник from наставити ('to set on the right path, instruct', from на- + ставить 'to set, place').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

настойчиво.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from настойчивый ('persistent, insistent'), derived from настоять / настаивать ('to insist, stand firm upon', from на- 'upon' + стоять 'to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati).

history.meaning: to stand firm on -> insistent -> persistently, insistently

настольный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the prepositional phrase на столе ('on the table'), combining prefix на- ('on') + стол ('table, desk', from Proto-Slavic *stolъ) + adjectival suffix -ный: 'meant to stand or be used on a table or desk' (настольная лампа 'desk lamp', настольная игра 'board game').

настоящий.etymology: Borrowed in its Church Slavonic participial form настоящии (with -щ- from *tj), the present active participle of настояти ('to stand upon, be present at hand', built on на- + стоять 'to stand'). First meant 'currently standing before us, present' (настоящее время 'present tense'), and from 'actually present' developed the everyday sense 'real, genuine, authentic'.

настраивать.etymology: Imperfective of настроить ('to tune a musical instrument, configure equipment, put someone in a mood'), formed from на- + строить ('to build, arrange, put in order', from строй 'order, harmony, tuning', Proto-Slavic *strojiti) + -ивать.

history.meaning: to tune (an instrument); to adjust, configure; to predispose emotionally

morphemes.meaning: order, tune (from строить with о -> а)

настроение.etymology: Verbal noun from настроить ('to tune a musical instrument; to attune, put in a frame of mind'), built from на- + строить ('to arrange, order, build', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti). Just as German Stimmung ('mood') comes from stimmen ('to tune an instrument'), Russian настроение shifted from 'the tuning of strings' to a person's emotional 'mood, frame of mind'.

history.meaning: tuning of a musical instrument → emotional attunement, mood

настроить.etymology: Formed from на- ('into proper order') + строить ('to build, arrange, order', Proto-Slavic *strojiti, from *strojь 'order, array, tuning'): 'to put an instrument into tune' or 'to configure, set up'.

history.meaning: to tune (an instrument); to set up, configure

cognates.meaning: to tune (an instrument); put in a mood

настройка.etymology: Derived in Russian from настроить ('to tune; to set up, configure') with the action/object noun suffix -ка.

history.meaning: tuning (of a piano or violin); adjustment, setting

наступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic наступити ('to step upon, advance; to come upon'), formed from the prefix на- ('on, onto') and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). Has two primary uses in modern Russian: physical ('to step on something', наступить на ногу) and temporal ('to come, set in, arrive', of seasons, times of day, or events: наступила зима).

history.meaning: to step on; to set in
to step on (+ на); to come, arrive (of time/events)

насчёт.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase на счёт ('onto the account of'), combining the preposition на with счёт ('count, reckoning, account', from Proto-Slavic *sъčьtъ, related to считать 'to count'). Grammaticalized as a conversational preposition (+ genitive) meaning 'about, regarding, concerning'.

насыпать.etymology: Formed from на- ('into, onto, filling') + сыпать ('to pour or strew dry, granular substances such as flour, sugar, or sand', Proto-Slavic *sypati).
насыпать.notes: Russian distinguishes налить ('to pour liquids') from насыпать ('to pour dry goods like flour, salt, or sugar'). Also note the stress pair: насыпа́ть (imperfective) vs. насы́пать (perfective).

натворить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the cumulative prefix на- ('in a quantity') and творить ('to create, make, do'), inherited from Old East Slavic творити and Proto-Slavic *tvoriti ('to form, shape, make', related to тварь 'creature'). In modern colloquial Russian, натворить specialized in a negative or ironic sense: 'to do something bad, cause a mess or trouble' (Что ты натворил? 'What have you done?!').

history.meaning: to do/make (especially mischief, trouble, or a mess)

натирать.etymology: Imperfective of натереть ('to rub on, polish, grate, chafe'), formed from на- + тирать (the iterative stem of тереть 'to rub, grate', inherited from Proto-Slavic *terti / *tirati).

history.meaning: to rub with ointment, polish (a floor), grate (cheese), chafe (a blister)

наткнуться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed from на- ('onto, against') + ткнуть ('to poke, thrust, jab', semelfactive of тыкать, from Proto-Slavic *tъknǫti) + -ся: literally 'to strike or impale oneself upon something unexpectedly', hence 'to stumble across, bump into'.

history.meaning: to strike against; to stumble upon, run into by chance

натуральный.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish naturalny or German natural from Latin nātūrālis ('by birth, natural, genuine'), derived from nātūra ('nature', from nāscī 'to be born').

научить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic научити, formed from the perfective prefix на- and учить ('to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed, learn').

history.meaning: to teach (someone: acc. + чему: dat. or infinitive)

научиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся ('oneself') to научить ('to teach'), from Old East Slavic научити, built from на- + учить ('to teach', Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative of the PIE root *h₁ewk- 'to become accustomed'). Literally, 'to teach oneself, acquire a skill'.

научный.etymology: Relational adjective formed in Russian with the suffix -ный (and regular к -> ч palatalization) from наука ('science, scholarship, learning', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nauka, built on the root *uk- / *uč- of учить 'to teach, learn').

нахвататься.etymology: Formed with the cumulative prefix на- ('in quantity, a lot of') + хватать ('to grab, snatch, catch', Proto-Slavic *xvatati) + reflexive -ся, meaning 'to pick up or accumulate (habits, words, or superficial knowledge)'.

находиться.etymology: Reflexive of находить ('to come upon, find', imperfective of найти, built from на- 'upon' + ходить 'to walk, go'). Literally 'to be found (in a place)' — compare French se trouver — which became the standard Russian verb 'to be located, be situated'.

history.meaning: to be found → to be located, be situated

находка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ка from находить ('to find, come across', built on на- + ходить). Denotes a found object, a lucky discovery, or a lost-and-found item (бюро находок 'lost-and-found office').

history.meaning: something found, lucky find, lost property

находчивый.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -чивый from находить / находка ('to find, hit upon a solution / a clever find'), built on на- ('upon') + ходить ('to go, walk'): 'quick at finding a solution, resourceful'.

history.meaning: to find / a find → resourceful, quick-witted

начало.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начало and Proto-Slavic *načęlo ('beginning, origin'), formed with the neuter noun suffix *-lo from *načęti (Russian начать 'to begin').

начальник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начальникъ (and Old Church Slavonic начѧльникъ 'founder, leader, chief'), formed from начало ('beginning, command, authority', from начать 'to begin', Proto-Slavic *načęti) + the agent suffix -ник.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

начатое.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of начатый ('begun, started'), the past passive participle of начать ('to begin, start', inherited from Old East Slavic начати, Proto-Slavic *načęti).

history.meaning: started -> that which has been started (довести начатое до конца 'to finish what one started')

начать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начати (future начну, past начал; Old Church Slavonic начѧти), from Proto-Slavic *načęti ('to begin, start'), formed from prefix *na- + *čęti ('to begin, initiate', from PIE *kʷen- / *ken- 'to arise, begin anew'; related to конец 'end', originally 'extremity, tip', and искони 'from the beginning').
начать.notes: The historical nasal vowel *ę* appears as **-а-** in the infinitive and past (**начать, начал**) and as **-н-** before a vowel in the future (**начну, начнёшь, начнут**).

начаться.etymology: Perfective intransitive/reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to начать ('to begin, start'), inherited from Old East Slavic начати, from Proto-Slavic *načęti ('to begin', from *na- + *čęti, related to конец 'end').

начинать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic начинати and Proto-Slavic *načinati ('to begin'), the imperfective counterpart of начать (*načęti), showing the ancient Indo-European ablaut alternation between nasal *-čę- (in начать) and lengthened *-čin- (in начинать). The root *čęti is cognate with конец ('end'), originally denoting either extremity of a span.

начинка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from начинить ('to fill, stuff [a pie, dumpling, or pastry]'), built from на- + чинить ('to arrange, prepare, fill', from чин 'order, arrangement', Proto-Slavic *činiti).

history.meaning: to stuff, fill -> pie or dumpling filling, stuffing

наш.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нашь (f. наша, n. наше), from Proto-Slavic *našь ('our, ours'), formed from the first-person plural pronoun stem *na- / *no- (seen in oblique нас, нам; compare Latin nōs) + possessive suffix *-sjь (with *sj > ш).

не.etymology: The negative particle не is inherited from older Slavic, rather than being a recent borrowing. Vasmer compares negative forms across the Indo-European languages, including Latin ne- and Baltic ne. The Russian particle also appears in word formation, but a prefixed word may develop a meaning of its own.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: не

небо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic небо and Proto-Slavic *nebo ('sky, heaven'), an ancient Proto-Indo-European neuter *-es-stem (*nébʰos 'cloud, mist, sky'), cognate with Ancient Greek néphos ('cloud'), Latin nebula ('mist'), and Sanskrit nábhas ('cloud, sky').
небо.notes: Preserves its ancient *-es-stem in the plural небеса ('the heavens, skies').

небольшой.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing negative не- ('not, un-') to большой ('big, large', from Old East Slavic большии 'bigger, greater'), yielding a litotes meaning 'small, modest-sized'.

неважно.etymology: Formed with negative не- ('not') + важно ('importantly; it is important'), from важный ('weighty, important', borrowed via Polish ważny from Old High German wāga 'weight, scales').

history.meaning: not important → never mind, it does not matter; (colloquial) poorly

невероятно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of невероятный ('incredible, improbable'), formed with negative не- + вероятный ('probable, likely', literally 'capable of being taken on trust', a Church Slavonic-modelled compound of вера 'faith, belief' + яти 'to take', calquing German wahrscheinlich / Latin vērīsimilis).

невероятный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not') + вероятный ('probable, believable'), which was borrowed from Old Church Slavonic вѣроѩтьнъ ('credible, worthy of belief', a compound of вѣра 'faith, belief' + ѩти 'to take', calquing Ancient Greek πιθανός): literally 'not able to be taken on faith, unbelievable'.

невеста.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic невѣста and Proto-Slavic *nevěsta ('bride, newlywed daughter-in-law'), most widely explained by etymologists as *ne- ('not') + *věsta ('known', verbal adjective from *věděti 'to know'): a protective taboo name ('the unknown woman') for a bride entering her husband's household from another clan so as not to expose her to hostile spirits.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: невеста

невозможно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from невозможный ('impossible'), built with the negative prefix не- on возможный ('possible'), which derives from Old Church Slavonic възмощи / возмочь ('to be able, have the power to', from въз- + мощи / мочь 'to be able, can', Proto-Slavic *moťi).

невыезд.etymology: Formed with the negative prefix не- ('non-') from выезд ('departure, exit by vehicle, trip out'), a deverbal noun from выехать ('to drive out, depart', from вы- + ехать 'to go by vehicle', Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Used almost exclusively in the legal formula **подписка о невыезде** ('signed undertaking not to leave town pending trial or investigation').

невыносимый.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + выносимый ('bearable', present passive participle of выносить 'to bear, endure, tolerate', from вы- + носить 'to carry').

неделя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic недѣля ('Sunday, day of rest; seven-day week'), from Proto-Slavic *nedělja, a compound of *ne ('not') + *dělati ('to do, work'): literally 'no-working day' (Sunday). In Russian, the church word воскресение ('Resurrection') took over the meaning 'Sunday', while неделя shifted to name the whole seven-day week.

недооценить.etymology: Formed in Russian with the compound prefix недо- ('insufficiently, under-') + оценить ('to value, appraise, assess', built on цена 'price, value', Proto-Slavic *cěna).

history.meaning: to assess, value -> to underestimate, undervalue

нежнее.etymology: Comparative degree of нежный ('tender, gentle, delicate') and нежно ('tenderly'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *něžьnъ (derived from *něga 'pampering, tenderness, comfort').

нежность.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ость from нежный ('tender, gentle, delicate'), which is derived from нега ('blissful comfort, pampered ease, softness', inherited from Proto-Slavic *něga).

нежный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣжьныи and Proto-Slavic *něžьnъ ('tender, delicate, pampered'), derived from нега ('bliss, comfort, tender care', Proto-Slavic *něga).

незабываемый.etymology: Formed with negative prefix не- ('un-') + забываемый (present passive participle of забывать 'to forget', built on за- + бывать / быть 'to be'). Literally 'not able to be forgotten, unforgettable'.

незаконно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from незаконный ('illegal, unlawful'), formed from negative не- ('not, il-') + законный ('legal, lawful', from закон 'law', Proto-Slavic *zakonъ).

history.meaning: lawful -> unlawful -> illegally; it is illegal

незаметно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from незаметный ('inconspicuous, imperceptible'), formed from negative не- ('not') + заметный ('noticeable', from заметить 'to notice').

незнакомец.etymology: Built transparently from не- 'un-, not' + знакомец 'acquaintance' (from знакомый 'familiar, known' + person suffix -ец, ultimately from знать 'to know').

неизбежный.etymology: Borrowed/adapted from Church Slavonic неизбѣжьнъ ('inescapable, unavoidable'), formed from negative не- ('not') + избежать ('to escape, flee out of, avoid', from из- 'out' + бежать 'to run, flee', Proto-Slavic *běžati) + -ный.

неизвестный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + известный ('known, well-known', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic извѣстьнъ, built on вѣсть 'news, knowledge').
неизвестный.notes: The middle -т- is silent in standard pronunciation: [неизвесный].

неисправимый.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, in-') + исправимый ('corrigible, reparable', present passive participle of исправить 'to correct, reform', built on правый 'right, straight').

некогда.etymology: Formed from the negative predicative prefix не́- ('there is no...') + когда ('when', Proto-Slavic *kъgda): with stressed не́когда it means 'there is no time (to do something)'; with unstressed некогда́ it means 'once upon a time, formerly'.
некогда.notes: Takes a dative logical subject + infinitive: Мне некогда ждать ('I have no time to wait').

некого.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun (stressed on the prefix: не́кого, lacking a nominative case), formed by univerbation of Old East Slavic не (ѥсть) кого ('there is not [anyone] whom [to...]'), combining negative не with кого, the genitive/accusative of кто ('who', Proto-Slavic *kъto).

history.meaning: there is nobody to (with infinitive: некого послать 'there is nobody to send')

некого.notes: Prepositions are placed between не and the pronoun: не с кем поговорить ('there is nobody to talk to'), не у кого спросить ('there is nobody to ask').

некультурно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from некультурный ('uncultured, ill-mannered'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + культурный ('cultured, polite', derived from культура 'culture', Latin cultūra).

history.meaning: cultured -> uncultured -> in an uncultured way; it is bad manners

неласковый.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + ласковый ('affectionate, gentle, tender'), derived from ласка ('caress, affection', inherited from Proto-Slavic *laska).

нелепый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нелѣпыи and Old Church Slavonic нелѣпъ ('unseemly, unfitting, absurd'), formed from negative не- ('not') + archaic лепый (*lěpъ 'handsome, fitting, fair', preserved in великолепный 'magnificent' and Czech lepý 'comely'): originally 'unbecoming, ill-fitting', later 'absurd, ridiculous'.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: лепый

неловкий.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + ловкий ('deft, agile, adroit', derived from лов / ловить 'to catch, hunt', Proto-Slavic *lovъ): literally 'not deft at catching', hence both physically 'clumsy' and socially 'awkward, embarrassing'.

нельзя.etymology: Univerbation of Old East Slavic не льзѣ ('it is not possible, there is no freedom/ease'), combining the negative particle не with льзѣ, the dative-locative singular of an old noun льга ('ease, freedom, benefit', from Proto-Slavic *lьga, related to лёгкий 'light, easy' and preserved in льгота 'privilege, exemption').

history.meaning: it is not permitted / not possible

немедленно.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective немедленный ('immediate, unhesitating'), built with the negative prefix не- on медленный ('slow'), historically a participle related to медлить ('to delay, tarry', from Proto-Slavic *mьdьlъ 'slow, sluggish').

немец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмьць and Proto-Slavic *němьcь ('foreigner speaking an unintelligible tongue; specifically a German'), formed with the personal suffix -ец from немой (*němъ 'mute, dumb, unable to speak intelligibly [i.e., in Slavic]', in contrast to *slověne 'those who speak clearly, Slavs').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: немец

немецкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нѣмьчьскыи ('foreign, Western European, German'), formed from нѣмьць / немец ('German; in medieval Rus', any foreigner speaking an unintelligible Western tongue'), derived with the suffix *-ьcь from нѣмъ / немой ('mute, dumb, unable to speak intelligibly', Proto-Slavic *němъ). Early Slavs contrasted themselves — словене, 'people of the intelligible word (слово)' — with their western neighbors, *němьci ('those who cannot speak [our language]').

history.meaning: mute → speaker of an unintelligible tongue, Germanic neighbor

немного.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing не- ('not') to много ('much, a lot'): literally 'not much', i.e. 'a little, some, slightly'.

ненавидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ненавидѣти (and Old Church Slavonic ненавидѣти 'to hate'), from Proto-Slavic *nenaviděti, formed with the negative prefix *ne- on *naviděti ('to look gladly upon, favor'), itself from *na- ('upon') + *viděti ('to see, look at', Russian видеть). Literally, 'not to bear looking at someone' (compare Latin invidia 'envy', from in- + vidēre).

history.meaning: to be unable to look upon → to hate

ненормальный.etymology: Formed with the negative prefix не- ('non-, un-') + нормальный ('normal', borrowed via French normal / German normal from Latin normalis 'made according to a carpenter's square, regular', from norma 'rule, norm').

необходимость.etymology: Formed in Russian with the abstract noun suffix -ость from необходимый ('necessary, essential, indispensable').

необходимый.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('not') + обходимый ('bypassable', present passive participle of обходить 'to walk around, bypass, do without'): literally 'that which cannot be bypassed or dispensed with'.

history.meaning: to bypass -> impossible to bypass, indispensable, necessary

необычно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from необычный ('unusual'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + обычный ('usual, customary', derived from обычай 'custom', Proto-Slavic *obyčajь).

history.meaning: usual -> unusual -> unusually; it is unusual

неожиданно.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from неожиданный ('unexpected'), built from negative не- ('not, un-') + ожиданный (passive participle of ожидать 'to expect, await', from ждать 'to wait', Proto-Slavic *žьdati).

неправда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправьда ('injustice, falsehood, untruth'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правда ('truth, justice', derived from правый 'right, true, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

неправильно.etymology: Adverb formed with the negative prefix не- from правильно ('correctly, rightly'), derived from правильный ('correct, right') and правило ('rule'), ultimately from правый ('straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

неправый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic неправыи ('unjust, crooked, wrong'), formed with the negative prefix не- and правый ('right, straight, just', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). In modern Russian, it is used almost exclusively in the short predicate forms **неправ / неправа / неправы** ('wrong, mistaken': ты неправ 'you are wrong').

нервничать.etymology: Formed in 19th-century Russian with the colloquial behavioral verb suffix -ничать from нервный ('nervous'), itself derived from нерв ('nerve'), borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus ('sinew, tendon, nerve').

history.meaning: nervous → to act nervously, fret, worry

morphemes.meaning: to behave in a certain manner

неровно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate in -о from неровный ('uneven, crooked'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + ровный ('even, flat, straight', inherited from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ).

несерьёзный.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + серьёзный ('serious'), which was borrowed in the eighteenth century from French sérieux (from Late Latin sēriōsus, built on Latin sērius 'earnest, grave').

несуществующий.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('non-, not') + существующий ('existing', present active participle of существовать 'to exist', derived from существо 'being, creature, essence', built on the Old Church Slavonic present participle сѫщь 'being' of быти 'to be').

несчастье.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('lack of, bad') + счастье ('happiness, good fortune', from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje, built on *sъ- 'good, with' + *čęstь 'part, share, lot').

нет.etymology: Contracted from Old East Slavic нѣту / нѣтъ ('there is not'), itself a fusion of the Proto-Slavic negative phrase *ne je tu ('is not here': negative particle *ne + *jestь 'is' + locative *tu 'there/here'). Because it originally contained the verb 'is', нет means both 'no' in replies and 'there is no' (+ genitive).

неудачно.etymology: Adverb in -о formed from неудачный ('unsuccessful, unlucky, ill-chosen'), built from negative не- ('un-') + удачный ('successful', from удача 'success, good luck', derived from удаться 'to turn out well').

неудобство.etymology: Formed with the abstract noun suffix -ство from неудобный ('inconvenient, uncomfortable'), built from negative не- ('in-, un-') + удобный ('convenient, comfortable', derived from Proto-Slavic *udobь 'at a fitting time or manner', built on *doba 'fitting time').

неужели.etymology: Formed in Russian by fusing не ('not') + уже ('already', older уж / уже) + the interrogative particle ли: literally 'is it not already so that...?', expressing surprise or disbelief ('really?, can it really be?').

неуместный.etymology: Formed from the negative prefix не- ('in-, not') + уместный ('appropriate, fitting, in its proper place', derived from the prepositional phrase у места 'at the right place', built on место 'place', Proto-Slavic *město).

history.meaning: in place -> appropriate -> inappropriate, out of place

неуместный.notes: The middle -т- is silent in standard pronunciation: [неумесный].

неумеха.etymology: Colloquial common-gender noun formed with the expressive person suffix -ха from не уметь ('not to know how', from не + уметь 'to know how, be able', inherited from Proto-Slavic *uměti).

history.meaning: not to know how -> bungler, all-thumbs person

нехороший.etymology: Formed in Russian from the negative prefix не- ('not, un-') + хороший ('good').

нечаянно.etymology: Adverb in -о from нечаянный ('unintended, accidental, unexpected'), formed from negative не- ('not, un-') + чаянный, the past passive participle of archaic чаять ('to expect, hope for, wait for', from Old East Slavic чаяти, Proto-Slavic *čajati): literally 'unlooked-for, unforeseen'.

нечего.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun (stressed on the first syllable: **не́чего**, literally 'there is nothing [to do]') inherited from Old East Slavic нечего, contracted from *не есть чего ('there is not of what', where не is fused with the lost present copula *е / есть and чего is the genitive of что 'what', Proto-Slavic *čьto). Distinct in stress and meaning from **нечего́ / ничего́** ('nothing').

history.meaning: there is nothing (to); no point in (+ infinitive)

нечего.notes: Followed by an infinitive (with an optional dative subject): **Мне не́чего сказать** ('I have nothing to say'), **Не́чего делать** ('There's nothing to do').

нечем.etymology: Negative predicative pronoun in the instrumental case (stressed on the prefix: не́чем, corresponding to genitive не́чего), formed by univerbation of не (есть) чем ('there is nothing with which [to...]'), from negative не + чем, the instrumental singular of что ('what', Proto-Slavic *čьto).

history.meaning: nothing (to do something with: мне нечем платить 'I have nothing to pay with')

ни.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ни ('not even, neither, nor'), from Proto-Slavic *ni, formed by combining the Indo-European negative particle *ne ('not') with the emphatic/connective particle *i ('even, also'): literally 'not even'.

нигде.etymology: Negative locative adverb inherited from Old East Slavic никъдѣ, formed from the negative prefix ни- and где ('where', Old East Slavic къдѣ, from Proto-Slavic *kъde).

ниже.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ниже and Proto-Slavic *niže ('lower, below'), the comparative of низкий ('low') and низко, built on *nizъ ('bottom, down', with z + j -> ž).

нижний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нижьнии (Proto-Slavic *nižьnьjь), the relational positional adjective formed from низ ('bottom, lower part') with the soft adjectival suffix -ний (with з -> ж).

низ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic низъ ('down, bottom, low ground'), from Proto-Slavic *nizъ ('bottom, downward'), continuing a Proto-Indo-European spatial stem *ni- ('down, below', cognate with English beneath and German nieder).

низко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic низько, the short neuter and adverbial form of низкий ('low', Proto-Slavic *nizъkъ, derived from *nizъ 'down, bottom').

никак.etymology: Negative adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and как ('how', from Old East Slavic како, Proto-Slavic *kako).

history.meaning: in no way, by no means, not at all

никакой.etymology: Formed by adding the negative prefix ни- ('not even one, no') to какой ('what kind of, which'): 'no ... whatsoever, none at all'.

history.meaning: none at all, no kind of

никакой.notes: When used with a preposition, ни splits off in front of the preposition: ни в коем случае / ни по какой причине ('for no reason at all').

никогда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic никъгда ('never'), from Proto-Slavic *nikъgda, formed by prefixing the negative particle *ni ('not even') to *kъgda ('when', modern Russian когда).

никто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic никъто ('nobody, no one'), from Proto-Slavic *nikъto, compounded from the negative particle *ni ('not even') + the interrogative pronoun *kъto ('who').
никто.notes: With a preposition, the word splits in three: **ни у кого** ('nobody has'), **ни с кем** ('with nobody').

никуда.etymology: Negative directional adverb formed from the negative prefix ни- and куда ('where to, whither', from Old East Slavic кудѣ / куда, Proto-Slavic *kǫdě).
никуда.notes: Russian distinguishes location (**нигде** 'nowhere, in no place') from direction of motion (**никуда** 'to nowhere': *я никуда не пойду*).

ничто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ничьто ('nothing'), from Proto-Slavic *ničьto, compounded from the negative particle *ni ('not even') + the interrogative pronoun *čьto ('what').
ничто.notes: Most often encountered in its genitive/accusative form **ничего** (pronounced *ничево*).

ничья.etymology: Substantivized feminine singular of the negative possessive pronoun ничей ('nobody's, belonging to neither side', formed from ни- + чей 'whose', Proto-Slavic *čьjь), originally modifying игра ('nobody's game') or партия ('nobody's match').
ничья.notes: Declines like the feminine pronoun чья: сыграть вничью ('to play to a draw'), закончиться ничьей ('to end in a tie').

ниша.etymology: Borrowed as an architectural term from French niche ('wall recess'), from Old French nichier 'to make a nest', going back to Latin nidus 'nest' (distant Indo-European cousin of Russian гнездо and English nest).

но.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нъ / но ('but'), from Proto-Slavic *nъ, which Vasmer traces to an old Indo-European adversative and temporal particle *nu ('now, well, on the other hand').

новый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic новъ, from Proto-Slavic *novъ, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos ('new'), cognate with English new, German neu, French neuf/nouveau, Latin novus, and Ancient Greek νέος.

нога.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нога and Proto-Slavic *noga ('foot, leg'). Outside Slavic, its exact cognate is Lithuanian nagas ('fingernail, claw, hoof', Russian ноготь 'nail'), showing an ancient semantic shift within Slavic from 'claw/hoof' to the whole leg and foot.
нога.notes: Covers both 'leg' and 'foot' in Russian. Accusative singular shifts stress to the stem: но́гу; nominative plural is но́ги.

нож.etymology: Нож is an inherited Slavic word, recorded as ножь in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer connects its historical root with заноза, вонзить and пронзить: words involving a splinter, piercing or thrusting into something. That connection gives the knife word a history associated with a pointed or piercing object.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: нож

ножка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of нога ('foot, leg', with regular velar palatalization г → ж before -к-), inherited from Old East Slavic ножька and Proto-Slavic *nožьka. Used both for a small foot and for the supporting leg or stem of a chair, table, or glass.

history.meaning: foot, leg → little foot; furniture leg

ноль.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Null ('zero') from Italian nulla / Medieval Latin nulla (figura) ('no figure, cipher'), feminine of Latin nūllus ('not any, none'); Russian uses both ноль (in everyday speech and sports scores) and нуль (in technical and mathematical idioms like с нуля 'from scratch').

номер.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (via German Nummer or Dutch nummer) from Latin numerus / Italian numero ('number'). In 19th-century Russian inns and hotels, номер ('a numbered room') became the standard everyday word for a hotel room.

норма.etymology: Borrowed via German Norm or Polish norma from Latin norma ('carpenter's square, rule, pattern, standard').

нормально.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of нормальный ('normal, standard'), derived from норма ('norm, standard, rule'), borrowed via German Norm / Polish norma from Latin norma ('carpenter's square, rule, standard'). In everyday spoken Russian, нормально commonly means 'fine, OK, doing well'.

нос.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic носъ and Proto-Slavic *nosъ ('nose; beak; prow'), from the o-grade of Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s- ('nose'), cognate with English nose, Latin nāsus, and Sanskrit nā́sā.

history.meaning: nose; spout of a kettle; bow of a ship

нос.notes: Takes the stressed locative -у after в and на: на носу ('on the nose; just around the corner').

носик.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ик from нос ('nose; prow, beak, spout'), inherited from Old East Slavic носъ and Proto-Slavic *nosъ (cognate with English nose and Latin nāsus).

history.meaning: nose → little nose; pouring spout (of a kettle or teapot)

носить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic носити ('to carry repeatedly, bear, wear'), from Proto-Slavic *nositi, the o-grade iterative/multidirectional counterpart of нести (*nesti 'to carry in one direction', from PIE *h₁neḱ-). Just like English wear / bear or French porter, carrying clothes on the body became the standard verb 'to wear'.

history.meaning: to carry (one way) → to carry habitually, wear

нотный.etymology: Formed in Russian from нота ('musical note') with the adjectival suffix -ный; нота was borrowed via Polish nota from Latin nota ('written mark, sign, musical note').
нотный.notes: Used in collocations like нотная тетрадь ('music manuscript notebook') and нотный лист ('sheet of music').

ноутбук.etymology: Borrowed in the 1990s from English notebook (computer) ('portable folding personal computer the size of a paper notebook').
ноутбук.notes: In Russian, ноутбук (often shortened colloquially to ноут) is the universal word for any laptop computer, while a paper notebook is блокнот or тетрадь.

ночлежка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from ночлежный дом ('night-lodging house, doss-house'), derived from ночлег ('overnight lodging', an East Slavic compound of ночь 'night' + лечь / лежать 'to lie down', Proto-Slavic *noťьlěgъ).

history.meaning: night + lying down -> place to sleep for the night

ночной.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночьныи (Proto-Slavic *noktьnъ), the relational adjective derived from ночь ('night', Proto-Slavic *noktь) with the suffix -ной.

ночь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ночь (Old Church Slavonic нощь), from Proto-Slavic *noktь, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts ('night'), cognate with English night, German Nacht, French nuit, Latin nox, and Lithuanian naktìs.

нравиться.etymology: Formed in Russian as the reflexive of нравить ('to please, suit someone's disposition'), derived from нрав ('character, disposition, temper', borrowed in its Church Slavonic non-pleophonic form нравъ alongside native East Slavic норовъ, from Proto-Slavic *norvъ): literally 'to match someone's disposition or taste'.

history.meaning: to suit one's taste, please, be liked

нравиться.notes: The person who likes something stands in the dative case, while the thing liked is the grammatical subject: **Мне нравится эта комната** ('This room pleases me / I like this room').

нравоучение.etymology: Compound noun coined in eighteenth-century literary Russian (calquing German Sittenlehre and Latin doctrīna mōrum) from нравы ('morals, customs, character', plural of Church Slavonic нравъ, corresponding to native East Slavic норов from Proto-Slavic *norvъ) + linking vowel -о- + учение ('teaching, instruction').

history.meaning: moralizing lecture, sermon, moral of a fable

ну.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ну ('well!, now then!, come on!'), from Proto-Slavic *nu, an ancient Indo-European discourse and prompting particle related to *nyně ('now'; compare English now, German nun, Latin nunc, and Lithuanian nù 'well!').

ну-ка.etymology: Colloquial hortatory particle formed from the interjection/particle ну ('well, come on', inherited from Proto-Slavic *nu, cognate with English now and Latin nunc) + the enclitic particle -ка (shortened from тка / тако, used with imperatives to soften or urge an immediate action).

history.meaning: come on, let's see, go on

нужно.etymology: Neuter short-form predicate and adverbial form of нужный ('necessary, needed'), derived from нужда / нужа ('need, necessity, compulsion', from Old East Slavic нужа / Old Church Slavonic нѫжда and Proto-Slavic *nǫdja).

history.meaning: needed → (it is) necessary, one needs to

нужный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic нужьныи ('necessary, urgent, pressing'), derived from нужа / нужда ('need, necessity, compulsion'), from Proto-Slavic *nudja, related to нудить ('to compel, urge').
нужный.notes: Most often heard in its short neuter forms **нужно** ('one needs to') and **нужен / нужна / нужны** ('is needed').

о.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic о / объ and Proto-Slavic *o(b) ('around, against, concerning'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂mbʰi ('around, on both sides'), cognate with Ancient Greek amphí and Latin ob.
о.notes: Uses the variant об before words beginning with a vowel sound (а, о, у, э, и): думать о работе, but думать об осени.

обвести.etymology: Formed from об- ('around') + вести ('to lead, draw a line', Proto-Slavic *vesti): 'to lead or draw a line around something, to circle or outline'.
обвести.notes: Conjugates with the dental stem вед-: я обведу, ты обведёшь; past tense обвёл, обвела.

обед.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обѣдъ and Proto-Slavic *obědъ ('midday meal, dinner'), a prefixal derivative of *ob- ('around, at') + *ěsti ('to eat', Russian есть). Originally it denoted both the main meal of the day and the midday time around which it was eaten.

обеспечить.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- + без- (spelled обес- before voiceless п) + the root of archaic печа ('care, worry, anxiety, trouble', Old East Slavic печа, Proto-Slavic *peča, also seen in беспечный 'carefree' and опека 'guardianship'): originally 'to free someone from material worry or want', whence 'to provide for, secure, ensure'.

history.meaning: to free from material worry -> to provide for, supply, ensure

обеспечить.notes: Although modern speakers often mentally associate обеспечить with печь ('stove'), its historical root is печа ('care, worry', related to печаль 'sorrow' and печься 'to care about').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: беспечный

обещание.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic обѣщаниѥ ('promise, vow'), a verbal noun from обѣщати (modern обещать 'to promise'), showing the South Slavic reflex -щ- from Proto-Slavic *tj in *ob-větjati, built on *ob- + *větъ ('solemn word, declaration, counsel'; compare обет 'vow' and ответ 'answer').

обещать.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic обѣщати ('to promise, vow'), derived from обѣтъ ('vow, solemn promise', Proto-Slavic *obvětъ, built on *ob- + *větъ 'speech, counsel, pact', as in совет 'advice, council' and ответ 'answer').

morphemes.meaning: speak, vow (*vět- + *-j- -> щ in Church Slavonic)

обещать.notes: Notice the Church Slavonic sound change *tj -> щ in обещать (from обет 'vow').

обжиматься.etymology: Colloquial reciprocal-reflexive verb formed from обжимать ('to squeeze or press all around', imperfective of обжать, built from об- 'around' + жимать / жать 'to press, squeeze', Proto-Slavic *žęti / *žimati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to squeeze around -> (colloquial) to hug tightly, cuddle, neck in corners

обидеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти ('to wrong, injure, offend'), from Proto-Slavic *obiděti, reduced by haplology/dissimilation from *ob-viděti ('to look past, overlook, slight', from *ob- 'around, past' + *viděti 'to see', Russian видеть). From 'looking past someone with disregard', the meaning developed into 'to wrong, hurt, offend'.

history.meaning: to look past, slight → to wrong, offend

обидеться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed by adding -ся to обидеть ('to offend, hurt'), inherited from Old East Slavic обидѣти, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

обидно.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate continuing the short neuter singular of обидный ('hurtful, offensive, disappointing'), derived from обида ('offence, hurt, wrong', inherited from Old East Slavic обида, Proto-Slavic *obida, contracted from *ob-viděti 'to look past, overlook, slight').

history.meaning: to look past, slight -> offence, injury
offence -> hurtful -> it is hurtful, it's a shame

обижать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обидеть ('to offend, hurt, wrong'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати (with East Slavic ж from Proto-Slavic *dj; compare Church Slavonic обиждати), formed from *ob- ('around, past') + *viděti ('to see', Russian видеть). Originally *ob-viděti meant 'to look past someone, overlook, slight, treat with disregard', which developed into 'to wrong, offend, hurt'.

history.meaning: to overlook, slight → to wrong, offend

обижаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from обижать ('to offend, hurt'), continuing Old East Slavic обижати, from Proto-Slavic *obiděti / *obidjati (reduced from *ob-viděti 'to look past, slight').

область.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область ('power, authority, domain, province'), reflecting Proto-Slavic *ob-vold-tь with South Slavic liquid metathesis (-ла-), whereas native East Slavic pleophony produced волость ('rural district; old princely authority'), built on *volděti ('to rule, possess').

history.meaning: administrative region (oblast); field or sphere of knowledge

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: область

облизать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic облизати and Proto-Slavic *oblizati, formed from the prefix об- ('all around, all over') + лизать ('to lick', Proto-Slavic *lizati, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- 'to lick', cognate with English lick and Latin lingere).

history.meaning: to lick -> to lick all over
to lick clean, lick all over

облизать.notes: Famous in the culinary praise Пальчики оближешь! ('You'll lick your fingers! / Finger-licking good!').

обложка.etymology: Formed in Russian from обложить ('to lay around, wrap, cover') + -ка: literally the protective outer wrap laid around the pages of a book or notebook.

обман.etymology: Deverbal noun from обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and the Proto-Slavic root *man- ('to beckon, lure, delude', as in манить 'to lure, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'delusion, sorcery').

обмануть.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- ('around') on the Proto-Slavic root *maniti ('to beckon, lure, delude, trick'; compare манить 'to beckon, entice' and Lithuanian monai 'witchcraft, delusion'). The consonant cluster -бм- simplified from *об-мануть, literally 'to lure around, delude with false appearances'.

обманщик.etymology: Agent noun formed in Russian with the suffix -щик from обман ('deceit, trickery') / обмануть ('to deceive, cheat', built on the Proto-Slavic root *man- 'to lure, delude').

обманывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of обмануть ('to deceive, cheat'), formed with the imperfectivizing suffix -ыва- on the stem обман- (from об- 'around' + Proto-Slavic *maniti 'to lure, delude, trick').

обмен.etymology: Deverbal noun from обменять ('to exchange, swap'), formed from prefix об- + мена / менять ('exchange / to change, swap', from Old East Slavic мѣна and Proto-Slavic *měna).

обнаглеть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix об- from наглеть ('to grow insolent'), from наглый ('impudent, brazen'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *naglъ ('sudden, impetuous, bold').

обновить.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- from новить ('to make new'), derived from новый ('new'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *novъ (from Proto-Indo-European *néwos).

обнять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обьяти / обняти ('to embrace, clasp around'), formed from the prefix об- ('around') and яти ('to take, grasp', Proto-Slavic *obъjęti, with epenthetic -н- generalized from nasal prefixes into the infinitive обнять and present обниму, while the past tense обнял preserves the older nasal-free stem).

обогреватель.etymology: Agent/instrument noun in -тель formed from обогревать ('to warm up, heat'), prefixed with обо- from греть ('to warm'), from Proto-Slavic *grěti ('to warm, heat').

обожать.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic обожати ('to deify, worship as a god', used as a calque of French adorer 'to adore'), formed from о- + бог ('god', with г -> ж) + -ать.

обойти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic обити / обоити ('to walk around'), formed with the prefix об- / обо- ('around') + йти / идти ('to go on foot, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti).

history.meaning: to walk around, bypass, make the rounds of

оборот.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic оборотъ ('turn, rotation, reverse side'), showing native East Slavic pleophony (-оро-) from Proto-Slavic *obvortъ (from *ob- 'around' + *vortiti 'to turn', Russian воротить / вертеть).

morphemes.meaning: turn (from *vort- with East Slavic -оро- and loss of v after b)

rootFamily.gloss: on the contrary, the other way round

оборотный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from оборот ('turn, rotation, reverse side'), built on prefix об- + ворот ('turning', native East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *vortъ, from *vьrtěti 'to turn').

history.meaning: turn, reverse → reverse, back (оборотная сторона 'reverse/back side')

morphemes.meaning: turn (ворот, with simplification of бв → б)

оборудование.etymology: Verbal noun formed from оборудовать ('to equip, fit out with tools and machinery'), built with the prefix об- on the archaic noun орудие / орудъ ('tool, instrument, implement, affair', from Proto-Slavic *orǫdьje 'tool, business, gear'; compare Polish orędzie and Old High German arunti 'errand').

history.meaning: to fit out with tools → equipment, machinery

обрадоваться.etymology: Formed in Russian from об- (perfectivizing prefix) + радоваться ('to rejoice, be glad', derived from рад 'glad', Proto-Slavic *radъ).
обрадоваться.notes: Takes the dative case for what delights you: обрадоваться подарку ('to be delighted with the gift').

образец.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ец from образ ('form, image, pattern'), inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic образъ ('carved figure, form, manner'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-razъ (from *ob- + *raziti 'to strike, carve').

образование.etymology: Verbal noun from образовать ('to form, shape, educate'), a calque on German Bildung ('formation, education') built on образ ('form, image'), from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ.

образцовый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from образец ('sample, model'), itself derived from образ ('form, image, pattern', from Proto-Slavic *obrazъ).

обратно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of обратный ('reverse, return'), borrowed from Church Slavonic обратьныи (with South Slavic -ра- instead of East Slavic -оро- as in оборот), formed from обратити ('to turn back, turn around', from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti, built on *vьrtěti 'to turn').

rootFamily.gloss: on the contrary, the other way round

обращать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обращати ('to turn, convert'), imperfective of обратити, from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti ('to turn around', with South Slavic metathesis *vort- > врат-/вращ-), from *vьrtěti ('to turn').

обращаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of обращать ('to turn, direct'), from Old Church Slavonic обращати (Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti 'to turn around'), developing the senses 'to turn toward someone, address' and 'to handle, treat'.

history.meaning: to address, turn to; to treat, handle

обращение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from обращать / обратиться ('to turn, address, treat'), from Old Church Slavonic обращение ('turning, conversion'), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ob-vortiti.

обстоятельство.etymology: Coined in the 18th century (featured in Trediakovsky and Lomonosov, on the model of Old Church Slavonic обстояние) as a structural calque of Latin circumstantia / French circonstance ('that which stands around an event: a circumstance'), formed from об- ('around', Latin circum-) + стоять ('to stand', Latin stāre) + -тельство.

обсуждать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обсѫждати (imperfective of обсѫдити / обсудить 'to judge from all sides, deliberate upon, discuss'), showing the Old Church Slavonic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic осужать), formed from об- ('around, from all sides') + судить ('to judge', from суд 'judgment, court', Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ).

обсуждаться.etymology: Reflexive/passive form in -ся of обсуждать ('to discuss, deliberate'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обсуждати ('to judge, examine'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-sǫditi, from *sǫdъ ('judgment').

обходительный.etymology: Adjective in -тельный formed from обходиться ('to treat, deal with people, behave toward'), itself from обходить ('to go around'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-xoditi.

общаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/reciprocal verb formed from общать (Old Church Slavonic обьщати 'to make common, share, associate with'), derived from общий ('common, shared', from Proto-Slavic *obьťь, built on *ob 'around'). Literally, 'to share company or conversation with others'.

history.meaning: to communicate, talk with, socialize, hang out

общественный.etymology: Adjective in -енный formed from общество ('society, community'), derived from общий ('common, shared'), an Old Church Slavonicism from Proto-Slavic *obьťь ('common, around').

общий.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic обьщь ('common, shared, general'), where -щ- is the South Slavic reflex of Proto-Slavic *tj (compare native East Slavic вобче / вообще). Derived from Proto-Slavic *obьťь ('around, shared by those around'), formed from the preposition/prefix *ob ('around, about').

общительный.etymology: Adjective in -тельный formed from общаться ('to communicate, associate') / общить ('to make common, unite'), from общий ('common, shared'), via Old Church Slavonic from Proto-Slavic *obьťь.

объект.etymology: Borrowed via German Objekt or Polish obiekt from Medieval Latin obiectum ('something thrown before the mind, object'), neuter past participle of Latin obicere ('to throw before, present'), from ob- + iacere ('to throw').

history.meaning: thing presented to the mind or senses

объективный.etymology: Borrowed via German objektiv or French objectif from Medieval Latin obiectivus ('relating to an object'), formed with Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

объявлять.etymology: Imperfective of объявить ('to declare, announce'), formed with prefix об- and stem явить ('to show, manifest'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *aviti ('to reveal, make known').

обыграть.etymology: Formed with the prefix об- ('around, out-') from играть ('to play'), inherited from Old East Slavic играти, from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati ('to play, dance').

обычно.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of обычный ('usual, customary'), derived from обычай ('custom, habit', Old East Slavic обычаи, from *ob- + *vyknǫti 'to get used to, learn by habit', as in привыкнуть).

обязанный.etymology: Adjectival passive participle of обязать ('to bind around; to oblige, place under a duty'), borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic prefixal form об-язати (where East Slavic had обвязать), from *ob- ('around') + *vęzati ('to tie, bind', Russian вязать). Literally, 'bound by obligation' (paralleling Latin obligātus from ligāre 'to bind').

обязательно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of обязательный ('obligatory, binding, without fail'), derived from обязать ('to bind by duty, oblige'), historically formed with Church Slavonic об- (for обв-) + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati): literally 'in a binding way'.

овощ.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic овощь ('fruit, garden produce', compare native Old East Slavic овочь) from Proto-Slavic *ovoktь ('growing fruit or crop'), often connected by Vasmer with the Indo-European root *h₂weg- ('to grow, increase', as in Latin augēre and English wax).
овощ.notes: A classic Slavic 'false friend': in Polish (owoc) and Czech (ovoce) the word still means 'fruit', whereas in Russian овощи narrowed to 'vegetables'.

овца.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic овьца, from Proto-Slavic *ovьca ('sheep'), a diminutive of *ovь, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ówis ('sheep'; compare Latin ovis, Sanskrit ávi-, English ewe).

ого.etymology: Expressive Slavic interjection ого! (compare Ukrainian ого, Polish oho, German oho), formed by reduplicating the vocalic exclamation о! with an intervocalic breathy [ɣ] or [h] sound to express surprise, admiration, or impression at size or scale ('whoa!', 'oh my!').

огонь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic огнь and Proto-Slavic *ognjь ('fire'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ngʷnis ('fire'), a famous ancient sacred word cognate with Sanskrit agní ('fire; the fire god Agni'), Latin ignis ('fire', whence English ignite), and Lithuanian ugnis.
огонь.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: огонь -> огня, на огне ('on the stove heat').

ограбить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix о- from грабить ('to rob, plunder'), originally 'to seize, rake away', from Proto-Slavic *grabiti ('to seize, snatch, rake').

оградка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of ограда ('fence, enclosure'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic ограда (compare East Slavic огорода), from Proto-Slavic *ob-gorda, from *gorditi ('to enclose, fence').

ограничить.etymology: Formed with prefix о- and verbal suffix -ить from граница ('border, boundary'), itself derived from грань ('edge, boundary, landmark'), from Proto-Slavic *granь.

огромный.etymology: Derived from the Slavic root гром- ('thunder', as in гром 'thunder' and громить 'to smash, crash'). Originally meaning 'thunderous, stunning, awe-inspiring in scale' (compare Polish ogromny 'huge, vast'), the meaning shifted from auditory force to visual and physical immensity.

огрызок.etymology: Formed with suffix -ок from огрызть ('to gnaw around'), from о- ('around') + грызть ('to gnaw, bite'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *gryzti ('to gnaw').

одеваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of одевать ('to dress, clothe'), imperfective of одеть, from Proto-Slavic *ob-děti ('to put around, clothe'), from *děti ('to put, place').

history.meaning: to get dressed, to dress oneself

одежда.etymology: Borrowed in its Old Church Slavonic form одежда ('clothing, garment, attire'), showing the South Slavic reflex -жд- for Proto-Slavic *dj (compare native East Slavic одёжа), from Proto-Slavic *odedja, derived from *oděti ('to clothe, wrap around', Russian одеть), formed from *o(b)- ('around') + *děti ('to put, place', PIE *dʰeh₁-).

morphemes.meaning: put, clothe (Church Slavonic stem of одеть)

rootFamily.gloss: to put on (an item of clothing)

один.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одинъ (alongside Church Slavonic единъ), from Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *odinъ ('one, alone'), compounded from an intensifying particle *ed- / *od- plus *inъ ('one, single, another', from Proto-Indo-European *óynos, cognate with English one, German ein, and Latin ūnus).

одинаково.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of одинаковый ('identical, the same'), built on один ('one', Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *odinъ) with the suffixes -ак- and -овый.

history.meaning: identically, in the same way, equally

одинаковый.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the adjectival suffix -овый from одинакий ('single, identical, of one kind'), built on один ('one', from Proto-Slavic *odinъ / *edinъ) + the qualitative suffix -ак- (compare двоякий 'twofold').

history.meaning: one → of one and the same kind, identical

одиннадцать.etymology: Inherited via contraction from the Old East Slavic phrase одинъ на десяте ('one on [top of] ten', Proto-Slavic *jedinъ na desęte). The unstressed second element на десяте wore down in pronunciation to the suffix -надцать used in all Russian teen numerals (11–19).
одиннадцать.notes: Spelled with double -нн- because the final -н of один meets the initial н- of на десяте.

одинокий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic одиногии / одинокыи, formed with suffix -окий from один ('one, alone'), from Proto-Slavic *edinъ / *odinъ ('one').

однажды.etymology: Formed in Russian from the feminine/archaic stem одна- of один ('one', Old Church Slavonic единажды) with the multiplicative adverbial suffix -жды (from Old Church Slavonic шьды, related to шествие 'going, step'): literally 'one time, once, one day'.

одноклассник.etymology: Compound noun formed from одно- (from один 'one, same') + класс ('class, school grade', from Latin classis via French/German) + agent suffix -ник.

одобрить.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic одобрити ('to approve, deem good'), a denominal verb built from о- + добрый ('good', Proto-Slavic *dobrъ) + -ить: literally 'to declare good, give one's approval to'.

одобрять.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with одобрить ('to approve, endorse'), formed with prefix о- from добрый ('good, kind', from Proto-Slavic *dobrъ): literally 'to deem good, pronounce favourable'.

ознакомиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix о- and -ся from знакомить ('to acquaint'), derived from знакомый ('familiar, acquainted'), from знать ('to know', Proto-Slavic *znati).

ой.etymology: An inherited Slavic primary interjection (Proto-Slavic *ojь), attested across East, West, and South Slavic as a natural vocalic exclamation of sudden surprise, alarm, pain, or mild dismay ('oh!', 'oops!').

ой-ой.etymology: Formed by expressive reduplication of the primary Slavic interjection ой ('oh!, ouch!'), conveying mild alarm, sympathy, or sudden discomfort.

ой-ой-ой.etymology: Formed by triple reduplication of the interjection ой ('oh!, ouch!'), expressing heightened dismay, concern, or playful reproach ('oh dear!, oh no!').

оказаться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from оказать ('to show, render'), built from the prefix о- and казать ('to show, appear', Old East Slavic казати, Proto-Slavic *kazati). With the reflexive suffix -ся, оказаться literally means 'to show oneself to be', whence 'to turn out to be' or 'to find oneself in a place'.

history.meaning: to turn out to be; to find oneself (somewhere)

оказываться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of оказывать ('to show, render'), imperfective of оказать, formed from о- + казать ('to show'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kazati ('to show, point out').

history.meaning: to turn out to be, prove to be

океан.etymology: Borrowed via Old East Slavic окиянъ / океанъ from Byzantine Greek ὠκεανός (ōkeanós, 'the great outer sea, ocean'), personified in antiquity as the Titan Oceanus.

окей.etymology: 20th-century borrowing from English okay / OK, originating in 1839 American newspaper slang (initialism for 'oll korrect', a humorous spelling of 'all correct').

окно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic окно, from Proto-Slavic *okъno, derived from *oko ('eye', from PIE *h₃ekʷ-). Like English window (from Old Norse vindauga, 'wind-eye'), Slavic named a window as the 'eye' of a house wall.

окончить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix о- from кончить ('to finish, end'), derived from конец ('end'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *konьcь ('end, limit').

окошко.etymology: Affectionate/everyday diminutive in -ко of окно ('window', via earlier/dialectal оконо / окошно), inherited from Proto-Slavic *okno, which was derived from *oko ('eye') because early windows were round 'eye-holes' in a timber wall.

октава.etymology: Borrowed via Italian ottava or Polish oktawa from Medieval Latin octāva ('interval of an eighth'), feminine of Latin octāvus ('eighth', from octō 'eight', distant Indo-European cognate of Russian восемь).

history.meaning: eighth (musical interval spanning eight scale degrees)

оливковый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from оливка ('olive'), borrowed via Polish oliwka or German Olive from Latin olīva ('olive, olive tree'), itself an early borrowing from Greek ἐλαία (elaía).

омерзительно.etymology: Adverb formed from омерзительный ('revolting, disgusting'), derived from омерзить / омерзеть ('to disgust, become loathsome'), from Proto-Slavic *mьrzěti ('to be loathsome, freeze/shudder'; compare мерзкий).

омлет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French omelette ('omelette'), altered in Middle French from earlier alemette / alumelle ('thin metal blade, flat pancake'), ultimately from Latin lāmella ('thin plate', diminutive of lāmina).

он.etymology: An inherited Slavic pronoun, recorded in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic as онъ. Its older demonstrative sense connects “he” with “that one”; Vasmer compares other Slavic forms and Lithuanian anas, meaning that one or he.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: он

он.notes: Many simple prepositions require an initial н- in the third-person oblique forms: у него, к нему, с ним, о нём. Check the construction rather than adding н- after every preposition.

она.etymology: Она belongs to the inherited Slavic demonstrative-pronoun family also seen in он and оно. Vasmer records the feminine form она in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic and compares feminine forms in the other Slavic languages. The older connection with pointing to that person survives behind its everyday meaning she.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: он (including она)

они.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic они (masculine plural; feminine plural онѣ > оне merged into они in modern Russian), from the Proto-Slavic distal demonstrative pronoun *onъ ('that one, he'; plural *oni 'those ones, they').

опа-на.etymology: Expressive colloquial interjection formed from оп / опа (an exclamation accompanying a sudden jump, catch, or surprise, compare гоп) + the demonstrative/emphatic particle -на ('there, take that!').

history.meaning: exclamation of sudden action or surprise
