опаздывать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of опоздать ('to be late, arrive late'), formed with root vowel lengthening (о > а) and the imperfective suffix -ыва- from поздно / поздний ('late', Old East Slavic поздо, Proto-Slavic *pozdъ).

history.meaning: to be running late, be late (imperfective)

опасно.etymology: Adverb formed from опасный ('dangerous'), originally 'cautious, watchful', derived from опасать ('to guard, beware'), from о- + пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over'), from Proto-Slavic *pasti.

опасный.etymology: Derived from опасаться ('to beware, be on one's guard, fear') and archaic опасъ ('caution, guard, protection'), built from о- ('around') + пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over', from Proto-Slavic *pasti, PIE *peh₂- 'to protect, tend'). Originally опасный meant 'watchful, cautious, circumspect'; by the 18th century it shifted from the person exercising caution to the situation requiring caution ('fraught with danger, dangerous').

rootFamily.gloss: thank you (from спаси Бог, same root пас-)

оператор.etymology: Borrowed via German Operator or French opérateur from Late Latin operātor ('worker, performer'), agent noun from Latin operārī ('to work, operate'), from opus ('work').

операция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (early 18th century) via Polish operacja or German Operation from Latin operātiō ('work, performance, activity'), derived from operārī ('to work, labor') and opus ('work').

оперировать.etymology: Borrowed via German operieren from Latin operārī ('to work, labor; perform an operation'), from opus, operis ('work'), adapted with the Russian verbal suffix -овать.

history.meaning: to operate on, to perform surgery

оплата.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from оплатить ('to pay for'), from о- + платить ('to pay'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *platiti ('to pay', originally with pieces of cloth, *platъ).

оплатить.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- ('around, completely') + платить ('to pay', Proto-Slavic *platiti): 'to pay for (a bill, fare, or purchase)'.
оплатить.notes: Usage contrast: оплатить takes a direct object in the accusative without a preposition (оплатить проезд, оплатить счёт), whereas заплатить takes за + accusative (заплатить за кофе).

опоздать.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- + поздно ('late', Proto-Slavic *pozdьno, built on *pozdъ 'late', related to по- / после 'after'): 'to arrive or act too late, miss'.
опоздать.notes: Takes на + accusative for an event or transport: опоздать на поезд ('to miss / be late for the train'), опоздать на работу ('to be late for work').

оптовик.etymology: Derived with suffix -ик from оптовый ('wholesale'), from опт ('wholesale trade', as in оптом 'in bulk'), generally connected with общий ('common, shared') or Old East Slavic оpath/объть ('together, in full').

опускать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of опустить ('to lower, let down, drop into'), from о- + пускать ('to let go, release', Proto-Slavic *puskati).

history.meaning: to lower, put down, drop in

опустить.etymology: Formed from о- + пустить ('to let go, release', Proto-Slavic *pustiti): 'to let something down, lower (one's hands, a lid, or a blind), or drop (a letter into a postbox)'.

history.meaning: to lower, put down, drop in

опустить.notes: First-person singular has ст -> щ mutation: я опущу, ты опустишь.

опыт.etymology: Deverbal noun formed in East Slavic from опытать ('to test, examine, try out all around'), built on prefix о- + пытать ('to inquire, test, try', from Proto-Slavic *pytati). Covers both accumulated 'experience' and a scientific or culinary 'experiment, trial'.

опытный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from опыт ('experience, experiment, trial'), a deverbal noun from опытать ('to test, try out, assay'), built from о- + пытать ('to test, inquire, probe', from Proto-Slavic *pytati). Literally, 'tested by trial, possessing practical experience'.

орать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic орати ('to shout, bellow'), from Proto-Slavic *orati / *orti ('to shout, roar'), of expressive/onomatopoeic origin (distinct from archaic орать 'to plow' < *orati).

организация.etymology: Borrowed via French organisation or German Organisation from Medieval Latin organisatio, derived from Greek ὄργανον (órganon, 'instrument, tool, organ').

организм.etymology: Borrowed from French organisme or German Organismus, formed in modern scientific Latin/French from Ancient Greek ὄργανον (órganon, 'instrument, bodily organ').

организовать.etymology: Borrowed via German organisieren or French organiser (ultimately from Medieval Latinizare / Greek ὄργανον 'instrument, organ'), adapted with the Russian verbal suffix -овать.

ордер.etymology: Borrowed via German Order or Dutch order from French ordre ('order, command, warrant'), ultimately from Latin ōrdō, ōrdinis ('row, rank, order').

орех.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic орѣхъ and Proto-Slavic *orěxъ ('nut, hazelnut, walnut'), with close Baltic cognates in Lithuanian riešutas and Latvian rieksts ('nut').

ореховый.etymology: Derived in Russian from орех ('nut; walnut') with the adjectival suffix -овый: 'made with nuts' or 'made of walnut wood / walnut-coloured'.

оригинал.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Original / Polish oryginał from Medieval Latin originale ('original document or work'), substantivized neuter of Latin originalis ('from the beginning, original', from origo 'origin, source').

оружие.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic оружие (influenced by Old Church Slavonic оружие), from Proto-Slavic *orǫžьje ('implement, weapon'), related to *orǫdьje ('tool, business').

освежать.etymology: Imperfective verb paired with освежить ('to refresh, freshen up'), formed with prefix о- from свежий ('fresh, cool', from Old East Slavic свѣжии and Proto-Slavic *svěžь).

history.meaning: to make fresh → to refresh, brighten

освободить.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic освобoдити ('to set free, emancipate'), formed with the prefix о- from свобода ('freedom, liberty', from Proto-Slavic *svoboda, related to свой 'one's own').

освободиться.etymology: Reflexive of освободить ('to free, liberate'), inherited via Old Church Slavonic освободити (from prefix о- + свобода 'freedom, liberty', Proto-Slavic *svoboda) + -ся.

освобождаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of освобождать ('to free, clear, release'), imperfective counterpart of освободить, showing the Church Slavonic alternation д → жд built on свобода ('freedom', from Proto-Slavic *svoboda).

history.meaning: to free → to become free, be excused, clear up

осень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic осень and Proto-Slavic *esenь / *osenь ('autumn, harvest season'), cognate with Old Prussian assanis ('autumn') and Gothic asans ('harvest, summer work season').
осень.notes: A feminine third-declension noun ending in -ь (поздняя осень 'late autumn').

осетровый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from осётр ('sturgeon'), inherited from Old East Slavic осетръ, from Proto-Slavic *jesetrъ ('sturgeon', literally 'the sharp-scaled one', related to *ostrъ 'sharp').

оскорблять.etymology: Imperfective of оскорбить ('to insult, offend, grieve'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оскръбити ('to afflict, sadden'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-skъrbiti, from *skъrbь ('grief, sorrow', Russian скорбь).

ослабить.etymology: Formed from о- + слабый ('weak, loose, slack', Proto-Slavic *slabъ, cognate with German schlaff 'slack') + -ить: 'to weaken, loosen, slacken (a screw, tension, or grip)'.

осмотреть.etymology: Formed with prefix о- ('around, over') from смотреть ('to look, watch'), inherited from Old East Slavic съмотрити, from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti.

осмотреться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of осмотреть ('to inspect, look around'), from о- ('around') + смотреть ('to look', Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

основа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic основа ('warp threads stretched on a loom; foundation'), a deverbal noun from основати ('to set up the warp, lay a foundation', from Proto-Slavic *osnova / *snovati).

history.meaning: warp of a loom; foundation, base

основание.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic основаниѥ ('foundation, base, groundwork'), a verbal noun from основати ('to set up the warp threads on a loom, lay a foundation', built on о- + сновать 'to warp threads', from Proto-Slavic *snovati).

особенно.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of особенный ('special, particular'), derived from особа ('individual person, apart') and the reflexive pronoun себе ('to oneself', as in особняком 'apart by oneself').

особенный.etymology: Extended adjectival form of особый ('special, separate, particular'), formed with the suffix -енный from особа / особь ('individual, person apart'), which goes back to the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase о собѣ ('by oneself, apart, separately', from о + собѣ, the dative/locative of the reflexive pronoun себя 'oneself').

особый.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic особыи ('separate, distinct, special'), formed from the archaic adverb особь ('apart, separately'), which originated from the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase о собѣ ('by oneself', where собѣ is the older East Slavic dative/locative of the reflexive pronoun себя 'oneself', Proto-Slavic *o sobě; compare Polish osobny 'separate').

оставаться.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of остаться ('to stay, remain'), from о- ('around, behind') + ставать (imperfective stem of стать 'to stand, become', Proto-Slavic *stati) + -ся.
оставаться.notes: Present tense drops the -ва- syllable and takes stressed -ю́, -ёшь: я остаю́сь, ты остаёшься.

оставить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic оставити ('to leave behind, let remain'), from Proto-Slavic *ostaviti, formed from the prefix *o(b)- + *staviti ('to set, place, make stand', causative of *stati 'to stand').

остановить.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from о- + становить ('to set upright, place in a standing position', causative of стать 'to stand', from стан 'camp, station, stature', Proto-Slavic *stanъ): 'to bring to a standstill, stop'.

history.meaning: to set up, bring to a stand

остановиться.etymology: Formed by adding the reflexive-intransitive postfix -ся to остановить ('to bring to a standstill'): 'to come to a halt, stop moving, or stay at an inn/hotel'.

history.meaning: to stop, come to a halt (intransitive)

осторожнее.etymology: Formed with the comparative suffix -ее from осторожный ('careful, cautious, watchful'), derived from Old East Slavic осторого ('guarding, watchfulness around oneself'), built on о- ('around') + сторожить ('to guard, watch over', Proto-Slavic *storžiti, cognate with стража).
осторожнее.notes: Frequently used as a polite warning: Пожалуйста, осторожнее! ('Please be more careful!').

осторожно.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of осторожный ('careful, cautious, wary'), built on Old Russian осторога ('watchfulness, guard, caution'), from the native East Slavic root сторож- (Proto-Slavic *storžь 'watchman, guard', from *stergti 'to guard, watch over', modern Russian стеречь).

осторожность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость from осторожный ('cautious, careful'), derived from остеречь / сторожить ('to guard, watch over'), from Proto-Slavic *storgti ('to guard, watch').

осторожный.etymology: Formed with prefix о- and adjectival suffix -ный from сторож ('guard, watchman') / сторожить ('to watch over, guard'), from Proto-Slavic *storgti ('to watch, guard', showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-): literally 'keeping watch all around, circumspect, careful'.

острый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic острыи ('sharp, pointed, keen'), from Proto-Slavic *ostrъ, continuing the ancient Proto-Indo-European root *h₂eḱ- ('sharp, pointed'), cognate with Latin ācer ('sharp, keen'), Ancient Greek ἄκρος ('topmost, pointed'), and English edge.

остывать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective of остыть / остынуть ('to cool down, lose heat'), from о- + стыть ('to grow cold, congeal', Proto-Slavic *styti, from the same root as студёный 'icy cold' and стужа 'hard frost').

от.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъ ('away from, from'), from Proto-Slavic *otъ, cognate with Lithuanian at- / ata- ('away, back') and Sanskrit áti ('beyond, past').
от.notes: Always governs the genitive case: ключ от комнаты ('key to/from the room'), далеко от вокзала ('far from the station').

отвалить.etymology: Formed with prefix от- ('away') from валить ('to roll, topple, throng'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *valiti ('to roll, tumble'); in colloquial speech 'to move away, back off'.

history.meaning: to roll away; (colloq.) to back off

отведать.etymology: Formed with prefix от- from ведать ('to know, experience'), inherited from Old East Slavic вѣдати, from Proto-Slavic *vědati ('to know'), shifting from 'to find out by trying' to 'to taste, sample'.

отвергать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic отъвръгати ('to cast away, reject'), imperfective of отъврѣщи, from Proto-Slavic *otъ-vьrgti ('to throw away'), from *vьrgti ('to throw').

отвернуться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of отвернуть ('to turn away, unscrew'), formed with prefix от- ('away') from вернуть ('to turn'), from Proto-Slavic *vьrtěti ('to turn').

отвести.etymology: Formed with prefix от- ('away') from вести ('to lead'), inherited from Old East Slavic вести (веду), from Proto-Slavic *vesti ('to lead').

ответ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъвѣтъ ('answer, reply, counsel, account'), from Proto-Slavic *otъvětъ, formed from *otъ- ('back, in return') + *větъ ('speech, counsel, declaration'; compare совет 'advice, council' and привет 'greeting').

ответить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъвѣтити, from Proto-Slavic *otъvětiti ('to answer, reply'), formed from the prefix *otъ- ('back, in return') and *větiti ('to speak solemnly, counsel, address', from *větъ 'counsel, pact', preserved in совет 'advice, council' and привет 'greeting').

ответственность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from ответственный ('responsible, accountable, answerable'), derived from ответ ('answer, reply; account', from ответить 'to answer', Proto-Slavic *otъvětъ). Coined in the late 18th century (recorded from 1789 by Karamzin) as a semantic calque of French responsabilité and German Verantwortung ('being answerable for').

ответственный.etymology: Adjective formed from ответственность / ответствовать ('to answer for, be responsible'), derived from ответ ('answer, reply'), from Proto-Slavic *otъ-větъ ('reply, counsel').

отвечать.etymology: Imperfective partner of ответить ('to answer, reply'), inherited (with Church Slavonic ч < *tj) from Old East Slavic отъвѣчати / отъвѣщати, formed from prefix от- ('back, in return') + вѣтъ ('counsel, speech, pact', from Proto-Slavic *větъ, preserved in совет 'advice, council' and привет 'greeting').

history.meaning: to answer, reply; to be responsible for

отвод.etymology: Deverbal noun from отводить / отвести ('to lead away, divert, reject'), formed from prefix от- ('away') + водить ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

отвратительно.etymology: Adverb from отвратительный ('disgusting, repulsive'), derived from отвратить ('to turn away, avert, repel'), an Old Church Slavonicism from Proto-Slavic *otъ-vortiti ('to turn away').

отговорка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from отговориться ('to talk one's way out of, make an excuse') / отговорить, from от- ('away') + говорить ('to speak', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

отдавать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of отдать ('to give back, return, hand over'), formed from the prefix от- ('away, back') and давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati, PIE *deh₃- 'to give').

history.meaning: to hand over, give back, return

отдел.etymology: Formed as a prefixal-stem noun from отделить ('to separate off, allocate a section', from от- 'off, from' + делить 'to divide, share', Proto-Slavic *děliti): 'a distinct section, division, or department'.

отделаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of отделать ('to finish off'), formed with prefix от- ('away, off') from делать ('to do, make'), from Proto-Slavic *dělati, acquiring the sense 'to rid oneself of, get off lightly'.

history.meaning: to get off, get away with

отдельно.etymology: Adverb formed from отдельный ('separate'), derived from отделить ('to separate, divide off'), from от- ('away') + делить ('to divide', from Proto-Slavic *děliti).

отдельный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from отделить / отдел ('separation, division'), from prefix от- ('away') + делить ('to divide, part'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *děliti.

отдохнуть.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic отъдъхнути, formed from от- ('off, back') + дохнуть ('to draw breath', Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti, from the root of дух 'breath, spirit' and дышать 'to breathe'): literally 'to catch one's breath after exertion', hence 'to rest'.

history.meaning: to rest, take a break, holiday

отель.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French hôtel ('mansion, hotel'), from Old French hostel ('lodging, inn'), which goes back to Medieval Latin hospitāle ('guest house'), from Latin hospes ('host, guest').

отец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отьць (and Old Church Slavonic отьць, vocative отче), from Proto-Slavic *otьcь ('father'), formed with the affectionate/diminutive suffix *-ьcь from *otъ ('father'), from Proto-Indo-European nursery word *átta ('daddy, father'; compare Ancient Greek ἄττα, Latin atta, Gothic atta, and Hittite attas).

отказываться.etymology: Formed as the imperfective reflexive of отказаться ('to refuse, decline, give up'), from от- ('away from') + казать ('to show, declare, speak', Proto-Slavic *kazati) + -ся: literally 'to speak oneself away from an offer or claim'.
отказываться.notes: Takes от + genitive for a noun (отказываться от помощи 'to decline help') or an infinitive.

отклеить.etymology: Formed with prefix от- ('away, off') from клеить ('to glue, stick'), derived from клей ('glue'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъlejь ('gum, resin, glue').

отключить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix от- ('off, away, disconnecting') and ключить (built on ключ 'key, switch', from Proto-Slavic *kľučь 'hook, key, bolt'), on the model of включить ('to switch on') and выключить ('to switch off'). Means 'to disconnect, cut off (power, water, or a phone), switch off'.

history.meaning: to disconnect, cut off, switch off

открываться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive counterpart of открывать ('to open'), formed from открыть ('to uncover, open') + imperfective suffix -ва- + reflexive marker -ся.

history.meaning: to open (by itself), come open, open for business

открытие.etymology: Formed with the verbal-noun suffix -ие from открыть ('to open, uncover, discover', from от- 'away, off' + крыть 'to cover'): both 'an opening ceremony' and 'a discovery' (parallel to French découverte and English discovery, literally 'an uncovering').

открытка.etymology: Coined in late nineteenth-century Russian as a colloquial ellipsis of открытое письмо ('open, unsealed letter', calquing German offener Brief / Postkarte) with the suffix -ка.

открыто.etymology: Adverb formed from открытый ('open, frank'), past passive participle of открыть ('to open, uncover'), from от- ('away, un-') + крыть ('to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti).

открытый.etymology: Originally the past passive participle of открыть ('to uncover, open', from от- 'off' + крыть 'to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti), fully lexicalized as the everyday adjective meaning 'open, uncovered, public'.

открыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъкрыти ('to uncover, reveal, open'), formed from the privative/separative prefix от- ('away, off') + крыть ('to cover', from Proto-Slavic *kryti): literally 'to take the cover off', which became the general Russian verb 'to open' (a door, window, bottle, or book) and 'to discover'.

откуда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъкуда, formed from the ablative prefix от- ('from') + куда ('where, whither', Proto-Slavic *kǫda, built on the interrogative stem *k-): 'from where?, whence?, how come?'.

отличиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of отличить ('to distinguish, single out'), derived from отличный / сличить, built on лик / лицо ('face, appearance, mark'), from Proto-Slavic *likъ.

отличный.etymology: Derived from отличить ('to distinguish, set apart by face or mark', built on от- 'apart from' + лик / лицо 'face, appearance') with the suffix -ный: originally 'distinct, standing out from the rest', which developed into 'outstanding, excellent'.

отложить.etymology: Formed with prefix от- ('aside, away') from ложить ('to lay, put'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ložiti (causative of *ležati 'to lie').

history.meaning: to put aside, to put down; to postpone

отменить.etymology: Formed from от- ('away, back') + менить ('to change, exchange', Proto-Slavic *měniti, from мена 'exchange, change'): literally 'to change back, revoke', hence 'to cancel, abolish, call off'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

отмерить.etymology: Formed with the prefix от- ('off from a whole') + мерить ('to measure'), derived from мера ('measure', from Old East Slavic мѣра and Proto-Slavic *měra).

отнести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отънести ('to carry away, take to a place'), formed from the prefix от- ('away, to a destination') + нести ('to carry on foot', from Proto-Slavic *nesti, PIE *h₁neḱ-).

отнестись.etymology: Reflexive form in -сь of отнести ('to carry away, refer, attribute'), formed with prefix от- from нести ('to carry'), from Proto-Slavic *nesti; the sense 'to relate to, treat' is a semantic calque on German sich verhalten / sich beziehen.

отношение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from относить / отнести ('to carry away; to refer, relate') and относиться ('to relate to, treat'), a compound of от- ('from, away') + носить ('to carry'). In the 18th century it calqued French relation and German Verhältnis ('relation, attitude; in plural, interpersonal relationships').

отогнать.etymology: Formed with prefix ото- ('away') from гнать ('to drive, chase'), inherited from Old East Slavic гънати, from Proto-Slavic *gъnati ('to drive, pursue').

отойти.etymology: Formed from ото- (variant of от- 'away from' before clusters) + идти ('to go, walk', Proto-Slavic *iti): 'to walk away, step back, move a short distance off'.

history.meaning: to step away, move back, come loose

отойти.notes: Past tense uses the suppletive root шед-/шл-: отошёл, отошла, отошли.

отомстить.etymology: Perfective counterpart of мстить ('to take vengeance, avenge'), inherited from Old East Slavic отъмьстити, formed from the prefix от- / ото- ('back, in return') and мьстити ('to avenge'), a denominative verb from мьсть / месть ('vengeance, retribution'), from Proto-Slavic *mьstь (originally 'recompense, exchange, return payment', cognate with Sanskrit mithás 'mutually, alternately' and Gothic maipms 'gift').

history.meaning: retribution, payback → to pay back, avenge
to take revenge, get back at (+ dat.)

отопление.etymology: Verbal noun formed from отопить ('to heat a building or room'), built from prefix о- ('around, throughout') + топить ('to stoke a stove, heat', the o-grade causative *topiti of the Proto-Slavic heat root *tep-, seen in тёплый 'warm' and тепло 'warmth').

history.meaning: to make warm, heat a stove
to heat a building → heating system, heating

оторванный.etymology: Past passive participle of оторвать ('to tear off, rip away'), formed from prefix от- / ото- ('off, away') + рвать ('to tear', from Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

оторвать.etymology: Formed with prefix ото- ('away, off') from рвать ('to tear, pluck'), inherited from Old East Slavic ръвати, from Proto-Slavic *rъvati ('to tear, pull out').

отправитель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from отправить ('to send off, dispatch'), built on prefix от- ('away, off') + править ('to direct, steer, send', from Proto-Slavic *praviti).

history.meaning: to dispatch, send → sender (on a letter or parcel)

отпустить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic отъпустити ('to let go, release, remit'), formed from the prefix от- ('away, off') and пустить ('to let go, allow, release', from Proto-Slavic *pustiti, originally 'to make empty/free', from *pustъ 'empty, free', Russian пустой).

отравиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from отравить ('to poison'), built from о- + травить ('to poison; originally to graze cattle on grass, consume with herbs/potions'), a denominative verb from трава ('grass, herb, medicinal or poisonous plant', inherited from Old East Slavic трава, Proto-Slavic *trava, from *truti 'to consume, wear away').

history.meaning: grass, herb → to feed on herbs / treat with herbal poison
to get poisoned, suffer food poisoning

отрезать.etymology: Formed from the prefix от- ('off, away') and резать ('to cut, slice', from Old East Slavic рѣзати, Proto-Slavic *rězati). Stress distinguishes aspect: perfective **отре́зать** ('to cut off, slice off') vs. imperfective **отреза́ть**.

отставать.etymology: Imperfective of отстать ('to fall behind, come off'), formed with prefix от- ('away, behind') from ставать / стать ('to stand, become'), from Proto-Slavic *stati.

отсчитать.etymology: Formed with the prefix от- ('off, away from a whole') + считать ('to count'), built on Proto-Slavic *čitati: 'to count off, measure out by counting'.

отсюда.etymology: Formed in Russian from the ablative prefix от- ('from') + сюда ('here, hither', Old East Slavic сюда / сюды, built on the proximal demonstrative stem *sь 'this'): 'from here'.

оттенок.etymology: Formed with prefix от- and diminutive/nominal suffix -ок from тень ('shadow, shade'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *těnь ('shadow, shade'), as a semantic calque on French nuance.

оттуда.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from the ablative preposition от ('from') + туда ('thither, there', from Old East Slavic туду / туда, built on the distal demonstrative stem *t- 'that').

отходить.etymology: Formed with prefix от- ('away') from ходить ('to walk, go'), inherited from Old East Slavic ходити, from Proto-Slavic *xoditi.

отходы.etymology: Plural noun derived from отходить ('to move away, separate off during processing'), from prefix от- + ходить ('to go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi), denoting residual material or waste.

отыграться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix от- ('back, in return') and -ся from играть ('to play'), from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati ('to play'), meaning 'to win back what was lost in play'.

history.meaning: to tie the score, recoup, fight back

отыгрываться.etymology: Imperfective of отыграться ('to win back, get even'), formed with suffix -ыва- from от- ('back') + играть ('to play', Proto-Slavic *jьgrati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to win back, to get even

официально.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of официальный ('official'), borrowed via German offiziell / French officiel or Polish oficjalny from Late Latin officiālis ('belonging to duty or office', from Latin officium 'service, duty, office').

официант.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century via German Offiziant or Polish oficjant ('subordinate official, functionary, attendant') from Medieval Latin officiāns (genitive officiantis), present participle of officiāre ('to perform a duty or service'), from Latin officium ('service, duty, office'). In Russian, the word narrowed from a minor civil or church attendant to a restaurant waiter.

охотник.etymology: Agent noun in -ник derived from охота ('wish, eagerness; hunting'), from хотеть ('to want, desire'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *xotěti ('to want').

охрана.etymology: Derived from охранить ('to guard, protect'), showing the South Slavic / Church Slavonic root vocalism -хран- (compare native East Slavic -хорон- in хоронить) from Proto-Slavic *xorniti ('to guard, keep safe') with the prefix о-.

оценка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the noun suffix -ка from оценить ('to set a price on, appraise, evaluate'), built on о- + цена ('price, value', Proto-Slavic *cěna): 'an appraisal, school grade, or rating'.

history.meaning: to value, rate -> valuation, rating, grade

очень.etymology: Developed in Middle Russian (replacing older вельми and гораздо in the sense 'very') from dialectal очунь ('very, truly'), which Vasmer links to очнуться / очутиться ('to come to one's senses, wake up fully', built on око 'eye' or чуять 'to feel'): originally 'wide awake, sensibly, acutely', then generalized as the intensifier 'very'.

очередник.etymology: Formed with agent suffix -ник from очередной / очередь ('turn, line, waiting list'), inherited from East Slavic очередь (compare Old Church Slavonic чрѣда), from Proto-Slavic *čerda ('herd, row, turn, order').

очередь.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic очередь ('succession, turn in rotation'), showing native East Slavic pleophony (-ере-) from Proto-Slavic *očerdь, built on *ob- + *čerda ('herd, row, regular succession, turn', compare Old Church Slavonic чрѣда and Russian череда).

очкарик.etymology: Colloquial expressive noun formed in 20th-century Russian with the compound suffix -арик (on the pattern of words like сухарик, комарик) from очки ('glasses, spectacles'), itself the plural diminutive of archaic око ('eye', Old East Slavic око, Proto-Slavic *oko, PIE *h₃ekʷ-).

очки.etymology: Plural of очко, the diminutive of archaic Russian око ('eye', from Proto-Slavic *oko, PIE *h₃ekʷ-). Attested from the 16th–17th centuries in the plural sense 'little eyepieces, spectacles'.

очнуться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic очьнутисѧ ('to wake up, come to'), formed with prefix об-/о- from *čьnǫti / *čuti ('to feel, perceive, be awake'), from Proto-Slavic *čuti.

history.meaning: to come to one's senses, to wake up

ошеломлённый.etymology: Past passive participle of ошеломить ('to stun, daze'), literally 'to strike on the helmet', formed from о- + шелом ('helmet', archaic East Slavic form of шлем), from Proto-Slavic *šelmъ.

ошибаться.etymology: Imperfective of ошибиться ('to make a mistake'), literally 'to strike past the mark, miss in hitting', formed with prefix о- ('around, past') + шибить ('to strike, throw') + -ся, from Proto-Slavic *šibati.

history.meaning: to make a mistake, be mistaken

ошибиться.etymology: Formed in Russian from о- ('past the mark, amiss') + Old Russian шибить ('to strike, hurl, fling', Proto-Slavic *šibiti) + -ся: originally a physical metaphor meaning 'to strike past the target, miss one's blow', which became 'to make a mistake, be wrong'.

history.meaning: to miss a blow, miss the mark -> to make a mistake

ошибиться.notes: Past tense drops the -и- in the masculine singular: он ошибся, она ошиблась.

ошибка.etymology: Formed in Russian from ошибиться ('to make a mistake', originally 'to miss one's mark in striking or throwing'), built from prefix о- ('around, past the mark') + dialectal/older шибить ('to strike, hurl, fling', from Proto-Slavic *šibiti) + noun suffix -ка.

history.meaning: to strike past the mark, miss → to err

ошибочка.etymology: Diminutive in -очка of ошибка ('mistake, error'), deverbal noun from ошибиться ('to miss the mark, err'), from о- + шибить ('to hit, strike').

ошибочно.etymology: Adverb formed from ошибочный ('erroneous, mistaken'), adjective from ошибка ('mistake'), derived from ошибиться ('to miss the mark, err', from о- + шибить).

оштрафовать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix о- from штрафовать ('to fine'), derived from штраф ('fine, penalty'), borrowed in the Petrine era from German Strafe ('punishment, fine').

ощипывать.etymology: Imperfective of ощипать ('to pluck all around'), formed with prefix о- ('around') from щипать ('to pinch, pluck'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ščipati ('to pinch, nip, pluck').

ощущение.etymology: Verbal noun from ощутить / ощущать ('to feel, sense, perceive'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оштутити (with щ < *tj), from Proto-Slavic *ob-čutiti, built on *čuti ('to feel, perceive').

падать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic падати and Proto-Slavic *padati ('to fall'), the imperfective-iterative counterpart of пасть (*pasti 'to fall', preserved in упасть and попасть), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- ('to step, stumble, fall').

пакет.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Paket or French paquet ('small bundle, parcel, packet'), a diminutive of Middle Dutch or Middle French pac ('bundle, pack', cognate with English pack and packet).

history.meaning: bag (paper or plastic carrier bag); packet, parcel

пакет.notes: In everyday Russian, пакет is the standard word for a paper or plastic shopping bag.

пакетик.etymology: Diminutive in -ик of пакет ('packet, bag'), borrowed via German Paket or French paquet from Middle Dutch pak ('bundle, pack').

палец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пальць and Proto-Slavic *palьcь, formed with the diminutive suffix *-ьcь from *palъ ('thumb, thick digit', often compared by etymologists with Latin pollex 'thumb'). In East Slavic, палец expanded from 'thumb' to mean any finger or toe.
палец.notes: Notice how Czech palec still means specifically 'thumb', whereas Russian палец means any finger (and 'thumb' is большой палец). Drops the fleeting е in oblique cases: палец -> пальца.

палка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic палъка, derived from палица ('club, staff, cudgel'), from Proto-Slavic *palica / *pala ('stick, staff, club').

палочка.etymology: Diminutive in -очка of палка ('stick, rod'), from Proto-Slavic *palica / *pala ('staff, stick').

пальто.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French paletot ('overcoat'), from Middle French paltoke ('short cloak or tunic'), widely traced via Middle English paltok or Spanish palletoque to Latin palla ('long outer cloak'). Like other French borrowings in -о, it is indeclinable in Russian.
пальто.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun: в тёплом пальто, без пальто.

пальчик.etymology: Diminutive in -чик of палец ('finger, toe'), inherited from Old East Slavic пальць ('thumb; finger'), from Proto-Slavic *palьcь ('thumb, big toe').

памятник.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic памятникъ and Old Church Slavonic памѧтьникъ ('memorial, monument, record'), formed from память ('memory') + the suffix -ник: 'that which preserves memory, a monument'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

памятник.notes: Takes the dative case for the person commemorated: памятник Пушкину ('monument to Pushkin').

память.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic память (Old Church Slavonic памѧть) and Proto-Slavic *pamętь ('memory, remembrance'), a nominal compound of the archaic nominal prefix *pa- + *mętь ('thought, mind', from Proto-Indo-European *men- 'to think, remember', cognate with Latin mēns and English mind).

панда.etymology: Borrowed via French panda (introduced by Georges Cuvier in 1825 for the red panda), likely from Nepali पोंया (põyā) / Newar निल्या पोंया ('bamboo-eater').

панель.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via German Paneel or French panneau (Old French panel) from Vulgar Latin *pannellum ('rectangular piece of cloth or wooden wainscoting'), diminutive of Latin pannus ('piece of cloth, pane').

паника.etymology: Borrowed via French panique or German Panik from Ancient Greek panikón (deîma) ('sudden, groundless terror sent by the woodland god Pan'), who was believed to startle travellers and herds in lonely mountain glens.

history.meaning: of the god Pan; sudden terror in the wild

папа.etymology: International nursery kinship word formed by reduplicating the bilabial syllable па- (pa-pa); reinforced in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Russian family speech by French papa.
папа.notes: Masculine noun in Russian (мой папа 'my dad'), while declining with feminine -а endings.

папин.etymology: Possessive adjective in -ин formed from папа ('dad, father'), borrowed in the 18th–19th centuries from French papa (or nursery Lallwort *papa).

папка.etymology: Borrowed into Russian (with the feminine suffix -ка) from German Pappe ('pasteboard, cardboard'), so called because a document folder was traditionally made of stiff pasteboard covers.

парашют.etymology: Borrowed from French parachute, coined in 1785 by Jean-Pierre Blanchard from Italian/Greek-style para- ('defense against', from Italian parare 'to ward off') + French chute ('fall').

history.meaning: device to slow a fall, parachute

пардон.etymology: Borrowed from French pardon ('forgiveness, excuse me'), deverbal noun from pardonner ('to forgive'), from Vulgar Latin *perdonare (from per- + donare 'to give').

парень.etymology: Attested in Russian from the 17th century. Most etymologists (following Sobolevsky and Vasmer) derive парень from dialectal парь ('lad') or directly from Old East Slavic паробокъ / паробьць ('servant lad, youth', compare Polish parobek and Ukrainian парубок), formed with the archaic prefix па- and робъ ('servant, child, worker') and reshaped with the suffix -ень.
парень.notes: In modern colloquial Russian, парень means both 'guy, lad' and 'boyfriend' (мой парень). Its plural is irregular in everyday speech: **ребята** (or **парни**).

пари.etymology: Borrowed from French pari ('bet, wager'), deverbal noun from parier ('to bet'), from Latin pariāre ('to make equal, match stakes'), from par ('equal').

париться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of парить ('to steam, beat with a birch besom in a steam bath'), derived from пар ('steam, vapor'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *parъ ('steam, heat').

history.meaning: to steam oneself in a bathhouse; (slang) to sweat over

пармезан.etymology: Borrowed from French parmesan ('of Parma; Parmesan cheese'), from Italian parmigiano ('from Parma, a city in Emilia-Romagna, Italy').

паровозик.etymology: Formed with the diminutive suffix -ик from паровоз ('steam locomotive'), a nineteenth-century Russian compound coined by N. I. Grech from пар ('steam', Proto-Slavic *parъ) + linking vowel -о- + воз ('hauler, vehicle', from возить 'to haul, transport'): literally 'steam-hauler'.

пароль.etymology: Borrowed via German Parole from French parole ('word, watchword, password'), from Late Latin parabola ('comparison, speech, word'), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ).

партизанить.etymology: Denominative verb in -ить formed from партизан ('partisan, guerrilla fighter'), borrowed via French partisan from Italian partigiano ('member of a party or faction', from parte 'part, side').

history.meaning: supporter of a party; irregular fighter

партия.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish partia / German Partie from French partie ('part, share, batch of goods, match/game, political party'), originally the feminine past participle of partir ('to divide, share', from Latin partīrī, built on pars, partis 'part').

history.meaning: batch (of goods or baking); game (of chess); party

паршивый.etymology: Adjective formed with -ивый from парша ('scab, favus, mange'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pьrša / *parša ('scaly skin disease, scab'), developing the figurative sense 'scabby, wretched, lousy'.

пас.etymology: Two converged homonyms: in card games ('я пас' = 'I pass'), from French je passe (from passer 'to pass'); in ball sports ('a pass'), borrowed in the 20th century from English pass (ultimately from the same French verb).

пассажир.etymology: Borrowed via German Passagier or Dutch passagier from French passager ('traveler, passenger'), derived from passage ('passage, journey').

паста.etymology: Borrowed via German Paste ('paste, ointment') and Italian pasta ('dough, pasta'), from Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste'), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, 'barley porridge').

пасха.etymology: Borrowed in the Old East Slavic period via Old Church Slavonic пасха from Byzantine Greek πάσχα (páskha, 'Passover; Easter'), from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā) and Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ, 'Passover', from pāsaḥ 'to pass over, spare'). In Russian, Пасха denotes both the Christian holiday of Easter and the traditional pyramid-shaped sweetened quark/curd cheese dish prepared for Easter.

пауза.etymology: Borrowed via German Pause from Latin pausa ('halt, stop, cessation'), itself from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis, 'stopping, ceasing'), from παύω (paúō, 'to stop').

паутина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic паучина / паутина, derived with suffix -ина from паук ('spider'), from Proto-Slavic *paǫkъ ('spider') / *paǫtina ('spiderweb').

пачка.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via Polish paczka ('parcel, packet') from German Pack ('pack, bundle', related to English pack), adapted with the feminine diminutive/noun suffix -ка.

паштет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Pastete ('pâté, meat pie, pastry'), from Medieval Latin pastāta / Old Italian pastata, derived from Late Latin pasta ('dough, paste'), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, 'barley porridge, salted mess of food').

history.meaning: dough, paste → dish baked in pastry

паяльник.etymology: Instrument noun in -ник formed from паять ('to solder'), of uncertain origin; Vasmer links it via *паяти ('to join, give to drink/quench metal') to поить ('to water') or спаять.

паясничать.etymology: Derived with verbal suffix -ничать from паяц ('buffoon, clown'), borrowed via French paillasse or German Bajazzo from Italian pagliaccio ('clown', literally 'straw mattress', from paglia 'straw', after the mattress-ticking costume of comic actors).

history.meaning: to clown around, to play the fool

педаль.etymology: Borrowed via French pédale (and Italian pedale) from Latin pedālis ('pertaining to the foot'), derived from pēs, stem ped- ('foot', Indo-European cognate of Russian пешком 'on foot').

history.meaning: pedal (of a piano, bicycle, or car)

rootFamily.gloss: on foot (native Slavic cousin of Latin ped-)

пекарня.etymology: Built in Russian from пекарь 'baker' + the place suffix -ня, from the Slavic verb печь 'to bake, roast'.
пекарня.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: пекарен.

пекарь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пекарь (and reinforced by Polish piekarz), formed from the verbal root of печь ('to bake', stem пек-, Proto-Slavic *pekti) with the agent suffix -арь (from Proto-Slavic *-arь, an early borrowing from Latin -ārius).

пена.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣна, from Proto-Slavic *pěna ('foam, froth'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poymneh₂ (cognate with Latin spūma, Sanskrit phéna, Old English fām 'foam').

пенсионер.etymology: Borrowed from French pensionnaire or German Pensionär ('recipient of a pension'), derived from pension (from Latin pēnsiō 'payment, weight').

первый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пьрвыи ('first'), from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *pŕ̥h₂wos ('foremost, first', built on *per- 'forward, in front'), directly cognate with Sanskrit pū́rva ('first, former'), Lithuanian pìrmas, and English first / fore.

перебивать.etymology: Imperfective of перебить ('to break across, interrupt'), formed with prefix пере- ('across, through') + бивать, iterative of бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

перебить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, over') from бить ('to beat, strike'), inherited from Old East Slavic бити, from Proto-Slavic *biti.

перебор.etymology: Deverbal noun from перебрать / перебирать ('to take too much, exceed the limit, sort through'), from пере- ('over, excess') + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

перевезти.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, over') from везти ('to convey by vehicle, transport'), inherited from Old East Slavic везти, from Proto-Slavic *vezti.

history.meaning: to transport, carry in a vehicle

перевернуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from пере- ('over, from one side to the other') + вернуть ('to turn', Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti, related to вертеть 'to turn, spin'): 'to turn over, flip upside down or to the other side'.

перевести.etymology: Formed from пере- ('across, from one side or language to another') + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti): 'to lead across (a street), transfer, translate (from one language to another), or catch one's breath (перевести дух)'.

history.meaning: to translate; to transfer; to lead across

перевести.notes: Notice how перевести ('to lead across -> translate') exactly parallels Latin trādūcere (trans 'across' + dūcere 'to lead' -> French traduire 'to translate').

переводить.etymology: Imperfective of перевести ('to lead across, transfer; to translate'), formed from пере- ('across') + водить ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *voditi); the sense 'to translate' is a calque on Latin trānsferre / trādūcere.

history.meaning: to transfer, to move; to translate

переворот.etymology: Deverbal noun from переворотить ('to turn upside down, overturn'), formed from пере- ('over') + воротить ('to turn', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *vortiti).

перевязать.etymology: Formed with the prefix пере- ('across, around, anew') + вязать ('to tie, bind'), from Old East Slavic вязати and Proto-Slavic *vęzati ('to tie, bind').

history.meaning: to tie up, bind across with string; to bandage

перевязочная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from перевязочный ('bandaging, dressing'), derived from перевязка ('bandaging') / перевязать ('to bandage, bind around'), from пере- + вязать ('to tie, bind', Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

history.meaning: dressing room (in a clinic or hospital)

перегибать.etymology: Imperfective of перегнуть ('to bend over, bend too far'), formed with prefix пере- ('over, too much') from сгибать / гнуть ('to bend'), from Proto-Slavic *gъbnǫti ('to bend').

history.meaning: to overdo it (перегибать палку = to go too far)

передавать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix пере- ('across, from one to another') + давать ('to give', iterative of дать, from Proto-Slavic *davati).

history.meaning: to hand over, pass along, transmit

передать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic передати ('to hand over, pass across, transmit'), formed from the native East Slavic prefix пере- ('across, over', Proto-Slavic *per-) + дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati). Used both physically ('pass the salt, hand over a key') and communicatively ('pass on a message, send regards: передать привет').

history.meaning: to pass on, hand over, convey (perfective)

morphemes.meaning: across, over from one to another

передача.etymology: Derived with suffix -ча from передать ('to hand over, transmit, broadcast'), formed from пере- ('across, over') + дать ('to give', from Proto-Slavic *dati).

переделать.etymology: Formed in Russian from пере- ('over again, anew, differently') + делать ('to do, make'): 'to redo, remake, remodel, or convert'.

переделка.etymology: Derived in Russian from переделать ('to redo, remodel, alter') with the action/result noun suffix -ка.

передний.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic передьнии, showing native East Slavic pleophony (-ере-) from Proto-Slavic *perdьnьjь ('situated in front'), derived from перед ('front; before') with the soft positional suffix -ний.

передумать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix пере- (indicating redoing or altering a previous state) and думать ('to think', from Old East Slavic думати, Proto-Slavic *dumati). Literally, 'to think over again in a different way', i.e., 'to change one's mind'.

переезд.etymology: Formed as a prefixal-stem noun from переехать ('to move, travel across, relocate', from пере- 'across, to a new place' + ехать / ездить 'to ride, drive'): both 'moving house, relocation' and 'a railway level crossing'.

переехать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix пере- ('across, from one place to another') and ехать ('to go by vehicle, travel', from Old East Slavic ѣхати, Proto-Slavic *ěxati). Means 'to cross by vehicle, run over' or 'to move to a new home, apartment, or city'.

history.meaning: to ride across, move to another place

morphemes.meaning: across, from one place to another

пережарить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('over, excessively') from жарить ('to fry, roast'), derived from жар ('heat, embers'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *žarъ ('glowing heat').

перейти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic переити (Proto-Slavic *perjьti 'to walk across'), formed from пере- ('across, over to') + идти ('to walk, go'): 'to cross (a street or bridge)' or 'to switch over to'.
перейти.notes: Future tense: я перейду, ты перейдёшь; past tense: перешёл, перешла.

переключиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of переключить ('to switch over'), formed with prefix пере- from включить / ключ ('key, switch'), from Proto-Slavic *kľučь ('hook, key, bolt').

history.meaning: to switch over, to shift focus

перекрыть.etymology: Formed from пере- ('across, blocking') + крыть ('to cover', Proto-Slavic *kryti): 'to cover over completely, roof over' and hence 'to dam, block off, or shut off (water, gas, or a road)'.

history.meaning: to shut off (water, gas), block, roof over

перекрыть.notes: Conjugates like крыть: я перекрою, ты перекроешь ('I will shut off').

перекурить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('in an interval, briefly') from курить ('to smoke'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kuriti ('to make smoke, kindle').

history.meaning: to smoke, have a smoke break

перекусить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across; briefly in between') from кусить ('to bite'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti ('to bite, taste a piece').

history.meaning: to bite through; to have a bite to eat, grab a snack

переложить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, from one place to another') from ложить ('to lay, put'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ložiti ('to lay, place').

перемешивать.etymology: Imperfective of перемешать ('to mix thoroughly, stir up'), formed with prefix пере- from мешать ('to mix, stir'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *měšati ('to mix, knead').

перенести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перенести (Proto-Slavic *pernesti), formed from пере- ('across, to another place or time') + нести ('to carry', Proto-Slavic *nesti): 'to carry across, move, or reschedule/postpone to another date'.

history.meaning: to move, carry over; to reschedule; to endure

переодеться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of переодеть ('to change clothes'), formed with prefix пере- ('anew, differently') from одеть ('to dress'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-děti.

перепел.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перепелъ, from Proto-Slavic *perpelъ ('quail'), a reduplicated onomatopoeic formation imitating the bird's call or fluttering wings (compare *pьrpati).

переперчить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, too much') from перчить ('to pepper'), derived from перец ('pepper'), from Old East Slavic пьпьрь (via Greek πέπερι from Sanskrit pippalī).

history.meaning: to over-pepper, put too much pepper

переписать.etymology: Formed with the prefix пере- ('over again, anew, from one sheet to another') + писать ('to write', from Old East Slavic писати and Proto-Slavic *pьsati).

переплёт.etymology: Deverbal noun from переплести ('to interweave, bind a book by sewing and lacing the gatherings onto cords'), formed from prefix пере- ('across, together') + плести ('to plait, weave, braid', from Proto-Slavic *plesti).

history.meaning: to lace and bind book pages → bookbinding, hard cover

перепутанный.etymology: Formed as the past passive participle and adjective of перепутать ('to tangle up, mix up, confuse'), built from пере- + путать ('to tangle, fetter, confuse', derived from путо 'hobble, tether, fetter', Proto-Slavic *pǫto).

перепутать.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix пере- from путать ('to tangle, confuse'), derived from путо ('fetters, hobble, cord'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pǫto ('bond, fetter').

перерыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from перервать / перерывать ('to tear across, interrupt, pause'), formed from пере- ('across') + рвать ('to tear', Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

пересмотр.etymology: Deverbal noun from пересмотреть ('to look over again, review, revise'), formed from пере- ('anew') + смотреть ('to look, examine', Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

пересолить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('excessively, too much') from солить ('to salt'), derived from соль ('salt'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *solь ('salt').

history.meaning: oversalt, put too much salt in

переставить.etymology: Formed with the prefix пере- ('across, to another place, anew') + ставить ('to put, set, stand', from Proto-Slavic *staviti).

history.meaning: to move, shift to another spot, rearrange

переставлять.etymology: Imperfective of переставить ('to move to another place, rearrange'), formed from пере- ('across, over') + ставить ('to place, set upright', from Proto-Slavic *staviti).

перестать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перестати ('to stop, cease'), formed from the prefix пере- ('across, over, through') and стать ('to stand, come to a halt', from Proto-Slavic *stati).

history.meaning: to come to a stop, cease

переть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перети (пьру, 'to press, push, prop'), from Proto-Slavic *perti ('to press, push, carry forcefully'), from Proto-Indo-European *per-.

переулок.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from пере- ('across, connecting between') + улка / улица ('street', originally 'narrow passage, opening'): a short side street or lane running across between two main streets.
переулок.notes: Drops the fleeting -о- in all oblique forms: переулок -> в переулке ('in the side street').

перехватить.etymology: Formed with prefix пере- ('across, intercepting') from хватить ('to seize, grab'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatiti ('to snatch, grasp').

history.meaning: to intercept, to grab, to take over

переход.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic переходъ (Proto-Slavic *perxodъ), a prefixal-stem noun derived from переходить / перейти ('to walk across, pass over', from пере- 'across' + ход 'going, walk').

переходить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic переходити (Proto-Slavic *perxoditi), formed from пере- ('across, over') + ходить ('to walk, go'): the imperfective of перейти ('to cross a street; to move on or switch to').

перец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перьць ('pepper'), formed with the Slavic noun suffix *-ьcь from early Slavic *pьpьrь, borrowed via Latin piper or Byzantine Greek πέπερι (péperi) ultimately from Sanskrit पिप्पली (pippalī, 'long pepper').

history.meaning: pepper (spice or bell/chili pepper); (slang) guy, fellow

перечить.etymology: Derived from перек / поперёк ('across, athwart'), inherited from Old East Slavic перекы ('across, against'), from Proto-Slavic *perkъ ('transverse, contrary', compare Old Church Slavonic прѣкъ).

перила.etymology: Plural-only derivative built on the Slavic root of переть / опереться ('to press, lean, support oneself') with the instrument suffix -ило: literally 'the bars one leans on for support' along stairs or a bridge.
перила.notes: Always plural in modern standard Russian: держаться за перила ('to hold on to the railing').

перо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic перо ('feather, wing, quill'), from Proto-Slavic *pero, built on the Proto-Indo-European root *per- / *pet- ('to fly, wing'; cognate with Ancient Greek πτερόν 'feather, wing' and English feather). Because goose quills were for centuries the standard writing instrument, перо also came to mean a metal pen nib.

персонаж.etymology: Borrowed from French personnage ('character in a play or novel, personage'), derived from personne ('person'), from Latin persōna ('actor's mask, character, person').

перспективный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from перспектива ('perspective, future prospect'), borrowed via French perspective / German Perspektive from Medieval Latin perspectiva (ars) ('optical science, view through'), from Latin perspicere ('to look through').

перьевой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -евой from the collective/plural stem перья ('feathers, nibs', singular перо, from Proto-Slavic *pero 'feather'). Used especially in перьевая ручка ('fountain pen, nib pen').

history.meaning: feather, nib → feather, nib (перьевая ручка 'fountain pen')

песня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣснь / пѣсня and Proto-Slavic *pěsnь ('song'), formed with the archaic Slavic action-noun suffix *-snь from the verbal root of петь ('to sing', Proto-Slavic *pěti).
песня.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: много песен ('many songs').

песок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣсъкъ and Proto-Slavic *pěsъkъ 'sand', related to Indo-European words for crushed grit and dust (compare Sanskrit pamsu 'crumbling soil, sand').
песок.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel -о- in all oblique forms: песок -> песка, на песке.

петербург.etymology: Everyday shortened form of Санкт-Петербург (Saint Petersburg), founded by Tsar Peter the Great in May 1703 and named in Dutch/German style (Sankt-Pieterburch / Sankt-Petersburg) after his patron saint, the Apostle Peter (from Greek Πέτρος 'rock, stone') + Germanic -burg ('fortress, city').

петля.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic петля ('noose, loop, snare, buttonhole') and Proto-Slavic *pętlja, generally connected by Vasmer and Trubachev with the nasal root *pęti ('to stretch, pull taut, fasten', compare распять and путо), or with early Germanic *fatilaz ('strap, band'). From a cord loop it extended to a metal door hinge.

history.meaning: loop, buttonhole; door or cabinet hinge

петля.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: дверных петель ('of door hinges').

петрушка.etymology: Borrowed via Polish pietruszka (adapted from Czech petrzel and Middle High German petersilje), ultimately from Latin petroselinum and Ancient Greek petroselinon, literally 'rock celery' (petra 'rock' + selinon 'celery'). Reshaped in Russian to match familiar -ушка nouns.

петь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пѣти and Proto-Slavic *pěti (present tense *pojǫ 'I sing'), originally meaning 'to celebrate in song, chant, praise'.

morphemes.meaning: sing (alternating with поj- in present tense)

cognates.meaning: to crow (of a rooster; archaic 'to sing')

петь.notes: Present tense uses the o-grade stem поj-: я пою, ты поёшь, они поют.

печатный.etymology: Derived in Russian from печать ('seal, stamp; printing press, print', Proto-Slavic *pečatь) with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'printed (as opposed to handwritten), press'.
печатный.notes: Used in писать печатными буквами ('to write in block / printed letters').

печать.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *pečatь, originally meaning a heated branding iron used to stamp livestock or wax, derived from the same root as печь 'to bake, burn, scorch'. From 'brand, seal' it expanded to 'printing press' and 'print'.

печенье.etymology: Formed as a verbal noun in -енье from печь ('to bake', passive participle печёный 'baked', Proto-Slavic *pekti): originally 'the act of baking' or 'baked goods', which specialized to 'biscuits, cookies, small pastries'.
печенье.notes: Usually used as an uncountable collective singular in Russian: домашнее печенье ('homemade cookies').

печка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of печь ('stove, oven'), inherited from Old East Slavic печь, from Proto-Slavic *pečь ('oven, stove, cave'), derived from *pekti ('to bake, roast').

печь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic печь, where both the feminine noun печь ('oven, masonry stove', from Proto-Slavic *pektь) and the verb печь ('to bake', from *pekti) continue Proto-Indo-European *pekʷ- ('to cook, bake', cognate with Latin coquō).

печёночный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from печёнка / печень ('liver'), inherited from Old East Slavic печень, from Proto-Slavic *pečenь ('liver', originally 'that which is roasted', from *pekti 'to roast').

пианино.etymology: Borrowed from Italian pianino, a diminutive of piano with the suffix -ino, so literally 'a little piano'. Russian uses it for the upright piano found in homes; the grand piano is рояль. Like other borrowed nouns in -о, it never changes its ending.
пианино.notes: Indeclinable: играть на пианино, у пианино, с пианино.

пиво.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пиво ('drink, beverage; beer, ale'), from Proto-Slavic *pivo, formed from *piti ('to drink', Russian пить) with the neuter noun suffix *-vo. Originally meaning any 'drink, potion', across most Slavic languages *pivo specialized to mean 'beer'.

пиджак.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English pea jacket (originally a sailor's heavy short coat, itself from Dutch pijjekker 'coat of coarse wool'). In Russian the word shifted to mean an ordinary suit jacket or blazer.

пинцет.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French pincette ('small tongs, tweezers'), diminutive of pince ('plier, grip'), from pincer ('to pinch, grip between two points').

пирамида.etymology: Borrowed via German Pyramide or Latin pyramis, pyramidis from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís, 'Egyptian pyramid'), itself from Egyptian pꜣ-mr ('the pyramid, tomb') or folk-etymologized in Greek from πυραμίς ('wheat cake').

пирог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пирогъ, from Proto-Slavic *pirogъ, formed from *pirъ ('feast, banquet', itself derived from пить 'to drink'). Originally пирог named special festive stuffed bread baked for guests at a celebration.

писатель.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -тель from писать ('to write', originally 'to paint, decorate with marks', from Old East Slavic писати, Proto-Slavic *pьsati, from PIE *peys- / *pik- 'to carve, mark, paint').

писать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic писати (present пишу, пишеши; Old Church Slavonic пьсати), from Proto-Slavic *pьsati (originally 'to paint, trace designs, adorn with colour', then 'to write'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *peyk̂- ('to mark, incise, paint'; cognate with Latin pingō / pictūra, whence English picture and paint).

history.meaning: to write (also 'to paint' in писать картину)

писать.notes: In artistic usage, Russian still says **писать картину маслом** ('to paint a picture in oils'), preserving the ancient meaning 'to paint'.

письмо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic письмо, from Proto-Slavic *pisьmo ('writing, inscription, letter'), derived from писать (*pьsati, originally 'to paint, trace designs, write', cognate with Latin pingō 'to paint').

питание.etymology: Verbal noun from питать ('to nourish, feed'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic питати ('to nourish, rear'), from Proto-Slavic *pitati ('to feed, nourish', related to *piťa 'food').

пить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пити, from Proto-Slavic *piti ('to drink'), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃(i)- ('to drink'; compare Ancient Greek πίνω, Sanskrit píbati, and Latin bibō / pōtus).

rootFamily.gloss: to drink up; to have a drink

пищевой.etymology: Adjective in -евой formed from пища ('food, nourishment'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пища (with щ < *tj, compare native East Slavic пича), from Proto-Slavic *pitja ('food, nourishment').

плавать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плавати, iterative-durative of плыть ('to swim, float, sail'), from Proto-Slavic *plavati (lengthened grade of *pluti, from Proto-Indo-European *plew- 'to flow, float').

плавочки.etymology: Diminutive plural of плавки ('swimming briefs/trunks'), formed in the 20th century from плавать ('to swim', from Proto-Slavic *plavati).

плакат.etymology: Borrowed from German Plakat ('poster, placard'), from Dutch plakkaat / Middle French placard ('notice posted on a wall'), from plaquer ('to plate, stick flat on').

плакать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плакати and Proto-Slavic *plakati ('to weep, lament; originally to beat one's breast in mourning'), from Proto-Indo-European *plāk- ('to strike flat, beat the chest in grief'), cognate with Latin plangere ('to beat the breast, lament', whence French plaindre and English plaintive) and Lithuanian plakti ('to beat, whip').

history.meaning: to strike, beat the breast in grief

плакать.notes: Present tense shows к -> ч palatalization throughout: я плачу, ты плачешь, они плачут (stress on the first syllable: я пла́чу 'I cry' vs. я плачу́ 'I pay').

пламенный.etymology: Adjective formed from пламя (stem пламен-, 'flame'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пламѩ (compare native East Slavic полымя), from Proto-Slavic *polmę ('flame').

пламя.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic liquid metathesis плам- (compare native Old East Slavic поломя) from Proto-Slavic *polmę ('flame, blaze'), an ancient neuter *-men-stem built on the same root as палить ('to burn, scorch') and пепел ('ash').
пламя.notes: Belongs to the small neuter -мя declension (alongside имя, время, семя): genitive/dative/prepositional пламени, instrumental пламенем.

план.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via French plan and German Plan ('flat drawing, ground plan, scheme'), where architectural plan ('ground-floor projection') blended Latin plānus ('flat, level surface') with planta ('sole of the foot; footprint of a building').

планировать.etymology: Derived in Russian from план ('plan') with the borrowed verbal suffix -ировать (after German planen / French planifier): 'to draw up a plan, schedule, or design'.
планировать.notes: A homonym плани́ровать ('to glide in the air', from French planer) has fixed stress on -и́-, whereas плани́ровать ('to make a plan') is stressed on the same syllable in modern standard Russian.

планшет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French planchette ('small flat board, surveyor's plane-table'), diminutive of planche ('plank, board', from Late Latin planca). First used in Russian for a cartographer's drawing board or officer's map-case, and in the 21st century adopted (via планшетный компьютер) for a touchscreen tablet.

платить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic платити ('to pay'), from Proto-Slavic *platiti, a denominative verb built on *platъ ('piece of cloth, linen'). In early medieval Slavic trade, standardized pieces of woven linen cloth served as a medium of exchange and currency (compare Czech platit 'to pay' and plátno 'linen').

history.meaning: piece of linen cloth (used as currency) → to pay

платный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from плата ('pay, fee') / платить ('to pay'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *platiti ('to pay').

платье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic платие (originally a collective neuter noun meaning 'garments, clothes in general', a sense preserved in верхнее платье 'outerwear' and платяной шкаф 'wardrobe'), derived from платъ ('piece of woven cloth, kerchief', from Proto-Slavic *platъ). Narrowed in modern everyday usage to 'a woman's dress'.

плевать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пльвати (present плюю), from Proto-Slavic *pľьvati ('to spit'), an ancient onomatopoeic Indo-European verb (*spjew- / *pjew-; compare Lithuanian spiáuti, Latin spuō, Gothic speiwan, and English spew). In colloquial Russian, мне плевать (на что-то) means 'I couldn't care less, I don't give a spit about it'.

пленник.etymology: Derived with suffix -ник from плен ('captivity'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic плѣнъ ('booty, captivity', compare native East Slavic полон), from Proto-Slavic *pelnъ.

плескаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of плескать ('to splash, lap, slosh'), inherited from Old East Slavic плескати and Proto-Slavic *pleskati, an onomatopoeic root imitating the sound of slapping water or clapping hands.

history.meaning: to splash → to splash about, lap (of water)

плечо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плече and Proto-Slavic *pleťe ('shoulder, upper back'), formed from *plet-je ('broad, flat shoulder blade area'), from Proto-Indo-European *plat- / *pleth₂- ('flat, broad', cognate with Ancient Greek platýs 'broad, flat' and English flat / plate).
плечо.notes: Notice how *tj gave ч in East Slavic плечо (compare Old Church Slavonic плеще with щ). Nominative plural is пле́чи, genitive plural плеч.

плита.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic плита ('flat stone slab, paving flag, brick') from Byzantine Greek plítha / Ancient Greek plínthos ('fired brick, squared stone slab, plinth'). In modern Russian it denotes both a heavy stone or concrete slab and a kitchen cooking stove (originally a cast-iron top plate set over a brick hearth).

cognates.meaning: squared base slab of a column (from Greek plinthos)

плитка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of плита ('flat stone slab, flagstone, cooker range'), borrowed early into Old East Slavic плита from Byzantine and Ancient Greek πλίνθος ('fired brick, squared tile, flat slab'). Used for a ceramic tile, a small hotplate, or a moulded bar of chocolate.

плод.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плодъ and Old Church Slavonic плодъ ('fruit, offspring, produce'), from Proto-Slavic *plodъ ('fruit, yield'), related to племя ('tribe, seed') and расплодиться ('to multiply').

пломба.etymology: Borrowed via German Plombe ('lead seal; dental filling') from French plomb ('lead, lead seal'), from Latin plumbum ('lead').

плоский.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плоскыи and Proto-Slavic *ploskъ ('flat, level, broad'), built with the suffix *-skъ on the root *plo- / *plat- ('broad, flat', also seen in плечо 'shoulder' and пласт 'flat layer').

плоско.etymology: Formed as the short neuter and adverbial form in -о of плоский ('flat', Proto-Slavic *ploskъ).

плот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плотъ ('wattle fence, raft'), from Proto-Slavic *plotъ ('wattled structure, fence, raft bound together'), ablaut-grade noun from *plesti ('to plait, weave, bind').

плотно.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of плотный ('dense, tight, snug'), from Old East Slavic плътьныи.

плотный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плътьныи ('compact, stout, corporeal'), derived from плъть ('flesh, body; compact woven fence', from Proto-Slavic *plъtь, related to плести 'to plait, weave tightly together').

history.meaning: closely woven structure, flesh → compact, dense

плохо.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed from плохой ('bad'), originally the neuter short form of the adjective. Inherited from Old East Slavic плохъ ('simple, poor, weak, bad'), from Proto-Slavic *ploxъ, whose deeper Indo-European connections remain uncertain (Vasmer compares possible links to words for 'timid, startled' or 'flat, bare').
плохо.notes: Used both as a manner adverb (он плохо готовит) and as an impersonal predicate with a dative experiencer (мне плохо 'I feel unwell').

площадь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic площадь ('open town square, level space'), borrowed or adapted from Old Church Slavonic площадь, a derivative of плоскъ ('flat, level', with sk + j -> šč): originally 'a broad, flat open space in a town'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

плыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плыти (present плыву, older плову), from Proto-Slavic *plyti / *pluti ('to float, swim, sail'), from Proto-Indo-European *plew- ('to flow, float, swim'; compare Ancient Greek πλέω 'to sail', Sanskrit plávate 'floats, swims', Latin pluere 'to rain', and English flow / float).

history.meaning: to swim, float, sail (in one direction)

плюс.etymology: Borrowed via German Plus / French plus from Latin plūs ('more'), used in European arithmetic since the Renaissance for addition ('+') and extended in everyday Russian to mean 'an advantage' or 'plus, in addition to'.

плющ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic плющь and Proto-Slavic *pljuščь ('ivy'). Etymologists debate its deeper source: Vasmer notes connections with *pljuti ('to spit, ooze') after the plant's bitter sap, or with root-clusters meaning 'to creep, entwine, cling'.

по.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic по ('along, over, after, according to'), from Proto-Slavic *po, continuing Proto-Indo-European *po / *pos ('after, along, by'; compare Lithuanian põ 'after, under, through' and Latin po- in pōnō).
по.notes: Takes the dative in its most common spatial and communicative uses: идти по улице ('walk along the street'), говорить по телефону ('talk on the phone').

по-братски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from братский ('brotherly, fraternal'), derived from брат ('brother'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *bratrъ / *bratъ (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr).

по-бретонски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from бретонский ('Breton'), from French breton ('of Brittany, France').

history.meaning: Breton, in the Breton culinary style

по-быстрому.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -omu from быстрый ('fast, quick'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *bystrъ ('swift, clear-flowing').

по-вашему.etymology: Adverb formed from preposition по- and the dative neuter singular of ваш ('your'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *vašь ('your').

по-моему.etymology: Parenthetical adverbial phrase formed from the preposition по ('according to, in the manner of') + моему, the dative singular masculine/neuter of мой ('my, mine', Old East Slavic мои, Proto-Slavic *mojь), with ellipsis of мнению ('according to my opinion').

history.meaning: according to my (opinion) → in my opinion; my way

по-настоящему.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ему from настоящий ('present, real, genuine'), originally present active participle of настоять ('to stand firm, be present'), from Proto-Slavic *stojati.

по-новому.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ому from новый ('new'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *novъ ('new').

по-русски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from русский ('Russian'), inherited from Old East Slavic русьскыи ('pertaining to Rus'').

по-соседски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from соседский ('neighborly'), derived from сосед ('neighbor'), from Proto-Slavic *sǫsědъ ('one who sits/dwells together', from *sǫ- + *sěděti).

по-старому.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ому from старый ('old'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *starъ ('old').

history.meaning: as before, in the old way

по-флорентийски.etymology: Adverb formed with circumfix по-...-ски from флорентийский ('Florentine', of Florence / Firenze, Italy), calquing culinary French à la florentine (typically prepared with spinach and Mornay sauce).

по-честному.etymology: Adverb formed with prefix по- and dative ending -ому from честный ('honest, fair'), derived from честь ('honor'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *čьstь ('honor, respect').

побегать.etymology: Delimitative verb formed with prefix по- ('for a while') from бегать ('to run around'), iterative of бежать ('to run'), from Proto-Slavic *běgati.

победа.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic побѣда ('victory, conquest'), a deverbal noun from побѣдити / победить ('to vanquish, overcome, defeat'), built on бѣда ('distress, compulsion, calamity', Russian беда, Proto-Slavic *běda). Originally 'the overcoming or subjugation of an adversary by force'.

победитель.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic побѣдитель ('victor, conqueror, winner'), formed with the agent suffix -тель from побѣдити (modern победить 'to conquer, win'), built on по- + бѣда (modern беда 'calamity, distress', originally 'compulsion, overcoming by force', from Proto-Slavic *běda).

победить.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic побѣдити ('to conquer, vanquish, defeat'), formed from по- and бѣдити ('to compel, force, overcome'), a denominative verb from бѣда ('calamity, distress, compulsion', modern Russian беда, from Proto-Slavic *běda 'necessity, distress', cognate with Gothic baidjan 'to compel' and Latin fīdō).
победить.notes: Famous in Russian grammar for lacking a standard 1st-person singular future form (*побежу / *победю are avoided in standard speech in favor of **я одержу победу** or **я смогу победить**).

побеждать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic побѣждати (imperfective of побѣдити 'to conquer, vanquish', with жд < *dj), derived from бѣда ('trouble, compulsion, plight', Proto-Slavic *běda), originally meaning 'to overcome by force'.

побитый.etymology: Past passive participle of побить ('to beat, batter, strike down'), formed with prefix по- from бить ('to beat, hit'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *biti.

поблагодарить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from благодарить ('to thank'), derived from Old Church Slavonic благодарити, a calque on Greek εὐχαριστεῖν (from благо 'good' + дарить 'to give, grant').

побледнеть.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from бледнеть ('to grow pale'), derived from бледный ('pale'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *blědъ ('pale, wan').

поближе.etymology: Formed by adding the attenuative prefix по- ('a little more, somewhat') to ближе ('closer, nearer', comparative of близкий / близко, from Proto-Slavic *blizъ).

побольше.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the attenuative/distributive prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat, as much as possible') to больше ('more, bigger', comparative of большой and много).

history.meaning: a bit more, a bit bigger, plenty

повар.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поваръ ('cook'), formed from prefix по- + the root вар- of варить ('to boil, cook', from Proto-Slavic *variti, causative of *vьrěti 'to boil, bubble', built on *varъ 'boiling heat, boiling water').

повезти.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the inceptive prefix по- and везти ('to convey, carry by vehicle, pull a cart or sleigh', inherited from Old East Slavic везти, Proto-Slavic *vezti, from PIE *weǵʰ- 'to convey in a vehicle', cognate with Latin vehō and English wagon / way). From the image of a horse or fortune 'pulling one's cart smoothly along', the impersonal dative construction мне повезло ('it carried me well') became the standard Russian expression for 'I got lucky'.

history.meaning: to take by vehicle; (impersonal + dat. повезло) to be lucky

rootFamily.gloss: to carry by vehicle; to be lucky (impf.)

поверить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + верить ('to believe, trust', Proto-Slavic *věriti, derived from вера 'faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra, cognate with Latin vērus 'true').
поверить.notes: Takes the dative case for the person or thing believed: поверить другу ('to believe a friend'), поверить своим глазам ('to believe one's eyes').

повернуть.etymology: Formed from по- + вернуть ('to turn, twist', Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti, built on the same Indo-European root *wert- 'to turn' as вертеть and поворот): 'to turn (a key, a handle, or around a corner)'.

повести.etymology: Formed with the perfective/inchoative prefix по- ('setting off') + вести ('to lead, conduct', inherited from Old East Slavic вести and Proto-Slavic *vesti).

history.meaning: to lead, take along; to start leading

rootFamily.gloss: to lead in; to wind up
to spend time; to lead through

повод.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поводъ ('rein, bridle, lead-rope; guidance, cause'), a deverbal noun from поводить / повести ('to lead along', built from по- + водить / вести 'to lead', Proto-Slavic *povodъ). From the literal 'bridle rein' by which a horse is led (still used in на поводу у кого-то), the word developed the figurative meaning 'that which leads to an action: a pretext, occasion, or reason'.

поворачивать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of повернуть ('to turn'), built from по- + -ворач- (lengthened East Slavic pleophonic stem of воротить 'to turn', from Proto-Slavic *vortiti, with т -> ч) + -ивать.

поворачиваться.etymology: Formed by adding the reflexive-intransitive postfix -ся to поворачивать ('to turn'): 'to turn oneself around, turn one's body or head'.
