повредить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix по- from вредить ('to harm, injure'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic врѣдити (compare native East Slavic вередить), from Proto-Slavic *verdъ ('harm, sore, injury').

повторить.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic повторити ('to do a second time, repeat'), a denominal verb built from по- + вторый ('second', modern Russian второй, Proto-Slavic *vъtorъ): literally 'to second, do a second time'.

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic
history.meaning: to do a second time, repeat

повторять.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of повторить ('to repeat', built on второй 'second') by replacing -ить with the imperfective suffix -ять.

повыше.etymology: Attenuative comparative formed with prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') from выше ('higher'), comparative of высокий ('high'), from Proto-Slavic *vyše.

погаснуть.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + гаснуть ('to go out, be extinguished', Proto-Slavic *gasnǫti, inchoative of *gasiti 'to extinguish', cognate with Lithuanian gesiti 'to put out a fire').

history.meaning: to go out, die down (of a light or flame)

погаснуть.notes: Past tense drops the suffix -ну-: свет погас ('the light went out'), свеча погасла ('the candle went out').

погладить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + гладить ('to make smooth, stroke, iron', Proto-Slavic *gladiti, derived from гладкий 'smooth', Proto-Slavic *gladъkъ).
погладить.notes: Means both 'to stroke/pet' (погладить кошку) and 'to iron' (погладить рубашку), because both actions smooth a surface.

погнуть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix по- + гнуть ('to bend, curve'), inherited from Old East Slavic гънути and Proto-Slavic *gъbnǫti (with loss of *b before *n; compare сгиб 'crease, fold').

history.meaning: to bend (slightly or out of shape)

поговорить.etymology: Formed from the delimitative/perfective prefix по- ('for a while') + говорить ('to speak, talk', originally 'to chatter, make noise', from говор 'talk, murmur', Proto-Slavic *govorъ): 'to have a talk, chat for a while'.

погода.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic погода and Proto-Slavic *pogoda ('favourable weather, seasonable time; weather'), formed from по- + год ('suitable time, right season; year', Proto-Slavic *godъ, related to годный 'fit, suitable' and ждать / погодить 'to wait'). Originally погода meant specifically 'good, fair weather' (contrasted with непогода 'bad weather'), before generalizing in Russian to any weather.

пограничник.etymology: Agent noun in -ник formed from пограничный ('border, frontier'), derived from по- ('along') + граница ('border'), from Proto-Slavic *granь ('boundary mark, edge').

погреться.etymology: Delimitative reflexive formed with prefix по- ('a little, for a while') and -ся from греть ('to warm, heat'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti.

под.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic подъ ('under, beneath'), from Proto-Slavic *podъ (originally also a noun meaning 'bottom, floor, hearthstone', still used as под in печной под 'oven floor'), continuing a Proto-Indo-European formation built on *ped- / *pod- ('foot, ground underneath').
под.notes: Takes the instrumental case for static position (под столом 'under the table') and the accusative for motion (под стол 'under the table').

подальше.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the attenuative prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') to дальше ('further, farther', comparative of далёкий and далеко).

history.meaning: a bit further away, well away

подарить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and дарить ('to give as a gift, bestow'), a denominative verb from дар ('gift'), inherited from Old East Slavic даръ and Proto-Slavic *darъ ('gift', from the PIE root *deh₃- 'to give', as in дать 'to give' and Greek δῶρον 'gift').

history.meaning: to bestow, grant as a gift

подарок.etymology: Derived in East Slavic with the noun suffix -ок from подарить ('to give as a gift, present'), itself built from по- + дарить ('to bestow', from дар 'gift', Proto-Slavic *darъ, from *dati 'to give').
подарок.notes: Drops the fleeting -о- in all oblique forms: подарок -> подарка, подарки.

подать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic подати and Proto-Slavic *podati ('to hand over, reach out, serve'), formed from по- + дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati).

history.meaning: to serve (food); to hand, pass; to submit

подать.notes: Conjugates with the archaic reduplicated stem of дать: я подам, ты подашь, он подаст, они подадут.

подвернуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from под- ('under') + вернуть ('to turn, twist', Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti): 'to tuck or roll up from underneath (sleeves or trouser hems)' or 'to twist/sprain (one's ankle or foot: подвернуть ногу)'.

history.meaning: to tuck, roll up; to twist (an ankle)

подвинуться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of подвинуть ('to move slightly, shift'), formed with prefix по- from двинуть ('to move'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *dvignǫti ('to lift, move').

подглядывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix под- ('from under, secretly on the sly') + глядывать (iterative of глядеть 'to look, gaze', from Proto-Slavic *ględati).

подготовиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of подготовить ('to prepare'), formed with prefix под- from готовить ('to prepare, make ready'), derived from готовый ('ready'), from Proto-Slavic *gotovъ.

поддерживать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from поддержать ('to hold up from underneath, support'), built on prefix под- ('under') + держать ('to hold', from Old East Slavic дьржати and Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

history.meaning: to hold up from below → to support, back up, maintain

поддержка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from поддержать / поддерживать ('to hold up from underneath, support'), built from под- ('under') + держать ('to hold'). In the 18th–19th centuries it also absorbed the figurative sense of French soutenir / support ('moral, political, or financial backing').

поддеть.etymology: Formed with the prefix под- ('under, from beneath') + деть ('to put, place, catch', from Old East Slavic дѣти and Proto-Slavic *děti): literally 'to slip or hook something underneath in order to lift or pry it up'.

поддон.etymology: Formed with prefix под- ('under') from дно (stem дон-, 'bottom'), inherited from Old East Slavic дъно, from Proto-Slavic *dъno ('bottom').

поделиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix по- and -ся from делить ('to divide, share'), inherited from Old East Slavic дѣлити, from Proto-Slavic *děliti.

поделка.etymology: Noun in -ка derived from поделать ('to make, craft'), formed with prefix по- from делать ('to do, make'), from Proto-Slavic *dělati.

подержать.etymology: Formed from the delimitative prefix по- ('for a little while') + держать ('to hold, keep', Old East Slavic дьржати, Proto-Slavic *dьržati): 'to hold for a moment or a while'.
подержать.notes: Do not confuse подержать ('to hold for a while', prefix по-, single -д-) with поддержать ('to support, back up', prefix под-, double -дд-).

поджаренный.etymology: Past passive participle of поджарить ('to fry or toast lightly, brown'), formed from attenuative/bottom prefix под- ('slightly; from underneath') + жарить ('to fry, roast, toast', derived from жар 'heat, glowing coals', Proto-Slavic *žarъ).

history.meaning: to toast, brown → toasted, lightly browned

поджать.etymology: Formed with prefix под- ('under, inward') from жать (жму, 'to press, squeeze'), inherited from Old East Slavic жати (жьму), from Proto-Slavic *žęti ('to press, squeeze').

подкаблучник.etymology: Colloquial noun formed with prefix под- ('under'), каблук ('shoe heel', borrowed via Turkic kabluq 'heel'), and agent suffix -ник, from the phrase быть под каблуком ('to be under one's wife's heel').

history.meaning: heel of a boot or shoe

подкашиваться.etymology: Formed as the imperfective reflexive of подкоситься ('to be cut from underneath, buckle, give way'), built from под- ('under, at the base') + косить ('to mow, cut down with a scythe', from коса 'scythe', Proto-Slavic *kosa): a vivid metaphor comparing knees or legs giving way from exhaustion or shock to grass cut at the stem by a scythe (ноги подкашиваются).

history.meaning: to cut from underneath -> to buckle, give way (of legs)

morphemes.meaning: mow, cut down (косить, о -> а and с -> ш)

подкашиваться.notes: Almost always used of legs or knees: от усталости ноги подкашиваются ('one's legs are buckling from tiredness').

подлизываться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective formed with prefix под- ('up to') and -ся from лизать ('to lick'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *lizati ('to lick'), comparing a fawning person to a dog licking its master.

подложить.etymology: Formed with prefix под- ('under') from ложить ('to lay, put'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ložiti ('to lay, place').

history.meaning: to put under, to slip under

подмести.etymology: Formed from под- ('under, along the floor') + мести ('to sweep, fling', Proto-Slavic *mesti, present stem мет-): 'to sweep the floor clean with a broom'.
подмести.notes: Conjugates with the dental stem мет-: я подмету, ты подметёшь; past tense подмёл, подмела.

поднести.etymology: Formed with the prefix под- ('up to, close to') + нести ('to carry, bring', inherited from Old East Slavic нести and Proto-Slavic *nesti).

history.meaning: to bring close, hold up to

поднимать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic подъимати (Proto-Slavic *podъjimati), formed from под- ('from under, upward') + -нимать (the imperfective stem of ять / взять 'to take', Proto-Slavic *jęti / *imati, with an epenthetic н- generalized from prefixes originally ending in a nasal, such as сън-имати -> снимать): literally 'to take from underneath', hence 'to lift, raise'.

подниматься.etymology: Formed by adding the reflexive-intransitive postfix -ся to поднимать ('to lift, raise'): 'to raise oneself, rise, climb, or go upstairs'.

поднос.etymology: Formed in Russian as a prefixal-stem instrument noun from подносить / поднести ('to carry up to, present, serve to guests', from под- 'up to, under' + носить / нести 'to carry'): 'a flat tray used to carry and serve food or drinks'.

подобный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic подобьнъ ('fitting, similar'), derived from подоба ('likeness, suitability, manner'), from по- + доба ('fitting time, proper way', Proto-Slavic *doba).

подобрать.etymology: Formed with prefix подо- ('from under, up') from брать ('to take, gather'), inherited from Old East Slavic бърати, from Proto-Slavic *bьrati.

history.meaning: to pick up; to select, to find a match

подогнуть.etymology: Formed with prefix подо- ('under') from гнуть ('to bend'), inherited from Old East Slavic гънути, from Proto-Slavic *gъbnǫti ('to bend, fold').

history.meaning: to tuck in, hem, bend under

подождать.etymology: Formed in Russian as the standard perfective of ждать ('to wait') by prefixing подо- (the prevocalic/cluster variant of под-). The base verb comes from Old East Slavic жьдати (Proto-Slavic *žьdati); the lost weak yer ь in жьдати triggered the vowel o in the prefix подо-.

подозреваться.etymology: Passive/reflexive form in -ся of подозревать ('to suspect'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic подозрѣвати ('to look askance/from under at, suspect'), from под- ('under') + зрѣти ('to look', Proto-Slavic *zьrěti).

подозрительно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of подозрительный ('suspicious'), derived from подозревать / подозрение ('to suspect / suspicion'), an Old Church Slavonic-modelled formation built on под- ('under, from beneath') + зрѣти ('to look, peer', from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti, calquing Latin suspicere 'to look up at from beneath, suspect').

подойти.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix под- / подо- ('under, up to, near') and идти ('to go, walk'), continuing Old East Slavic подъити and Proto-Slavic *podъjьti ('to approach, walk up to').

history.meaning: to walk under or up to
to approach, come up to; to suit

подоконник.etymology: Transparent Russian spatial compound built from под- ('under, at the base of') + окно ('window') + -ник: the sill or ledge set directly beneath the window frame.

подорвать.etymology: Formed with prefix подо- ('from under') from рвать ('to tear, blast'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *rъvati ('to tear, rend').

подпереть.etymology: Formed with the prefix под- ('under, from beneath') + переть ('to press, push, prop', from Old East Slavic перети and Proto-Slavic *perti).

history.meaning: to prop up, brace, shore up

подписать.etymology: Formed from под- ('under, at the bottom of') + писать ('to write', Proto-Slavic *pisati): 'to write one's name underneath a document, to sign' (parallel to Latin subscribere and German unterschreiben).

rootFamily.gloss: to sign one's name (in a register)

подписаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of подписать ('to sign, write underneath'), formed from под- ('under') + писать ('to write', from Proto-Slavic *pisati).

history.meaning: to sign, put one's signature; subscribe

подписка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from подписать ('to sign underneath, subscribe'), built from под- ('under') + писать ('to write', Proto-Slavic *pьsati). Like Latin subscriptiō ('writing underneath'), подписка means both a periodical 'subscription' and a 'signed legal undertaking' (most famously in подписка о невыезде 'a signed undertaking not to leave town while under investigation').

подписывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ывать from подписать ('to sign, write underneath'), built on prefix под- ('under, at the bottom of a document') + писать ('to write', from Proto-Slavic *pьsati).

подпись.etymology: Deverbal feminine noun formed from подписать ('to sign, write underneath'), built from prefix под- ('under') + писать ('to write'): literally 'an under-writing' (a structural parallel to Latin subscriptiō and German Unterschrift).

подробно.etymology: Adverb formed from подробный ('detailed'), originally 'divided into small pieces/particles', derived from по- + дробь ('small piece, fraction'), from Proto-Slavic *drobъ ('small fragment, crumb').

подробность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from подробный ('detailed, minute'), derived from по- + дробь ('small particle, fragment', from Proto-Slavic *drobъ).

подросток.etymology: Derived in Russian from подрасти / подросток ('one who is growing up', formed from prefix под- 'up from under, somewhat' + расти / рост 'to grow, growth', Proto-Slavic *orsti) + noun suffix -ок.

history.meaning: to grow up somewhat; young growth

подряд.etymology: Adverbialized prepositional phrase formed from под ('under, along') + ряд ('row, order, sequence'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *rędъ ('row, order').

подсказка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from подсказать ('to prompt, whisper an answer, give a hint'), built on под- ('under, quietly on the side') + сказать ('to say, tell', from Proto-Slavic *sъkazati).

history.meaning: to prompt, hint → clue, hint, prompt

morphemes.meaning: quietly from below / on the side

подставка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the object suffix -ка from подставить ('to set or place underneath as a support', from под- 'under' + ставить 'to stand, place'): 'a stand, base, coaster, or holder'.

подсудимый.etymology: Substantivized adjective formed from под ('under [the jurisdiction of]') + суд ('court, trial', from Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ) + participial/adjectival suffix -имый.

подсунуть.etymology: Formed with prefix под- ('under, surreptitiously') from сунуть ('to shove, thrust, slip'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *sunǫti ('to push, thrust').

history.meaning: to slip under, to palm off on someone

подумать.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing/delimitative prefix по- + думать ('to think', Old East Slavic думати, from дума 'thought, counsel', an early Proto-Slavic borrowing from Proto-Germanic *dōmaz 'judgment, thought', cognate with English doom and deem).

history.meaning: to think, give some thought to

подушка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic подушька (Proto-Slavic *podušьka, from *poduxa). Etymologists trace it to *duxъ 'breath, air' via the idea of something puffed up or stuffed with down, though popular tradition has long reinterpreted it as под ухо ('under the ear').

подходить.etymology: Formed from prefix под- ('up to, close to') + ходить ('to walk, go'). Means both literally 'to walk up to, approach' (подходить к окну) and figuratively 'to fit, suit, be right for' (этот ключ подходит 'this key fits').

history.meaning: to walk up to, approach; to suit, fit

подходящий.etymology: Present active participle of подходить ('to approach; to fit, suit'), formed from под- ('up to') + ходить ('to go', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

подчинение.etymology: Verbal noun from подчинить ('to subordinate, place under someone's rank'), formed from под- ('under') + чин ('rank, order'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *činъ ('order, rank, arrangement').

подшутить.etymology: Formed with prefix под- ('slightly, slyly') from шутить ('to joke, jest'), derived from шут ('jester, fool'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *šutъ.

history.meaning: to play a prank, to tease

подъезд.etymology: Deverbal noun from подъехать / подъезжать ('to drive up to'), formed from под- ('up to') + езд (from ехать / ездить 'to ride, drive', Proto-Slavic *ězdъ), originally 'carriage approach to a building entrance'.

подъезжать.etymology: Imperfective of подъехать ('to drive up to, approach'), formed with prefix под- ('up to') from езжать / ездить ('to ride, drive'), from Proto-Slavic *ězditi.

поезд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поѣздъ ('a riding out, wedding or princely cortege'), a deverbal noun from поехать / ездить ('to ride, travel'). In the 19th century it was adopted for a railway train, parallel to French train and German Zug.

поездка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the action-noun suffix -ка from поездить / поехать ('to travel, take a ride'), built on ездить / ехать ('to ride, travel by vehicle', from Proto-Slavic *ězditi / *ěxati).

поезжать.etymology: Formed with prefix по- ('setting off') from езжать, iterative of ездить ('to ride, go by vehicle'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *ězditi (used in modern Russian primarily in the imperative поезжай).

history.meaning: to go, to drive, to set off

поехать.etymology: Perfective verb formed by adding the inceptive prefix по- ('setting off, starting an action') to ехать ('to go by vehicle, ride'), inherited from Old East Slavic ѣхати, from Proto-Slavic *ěxati ('to ride, travel').

history.meaning: to go by vehicle, set off

пожалеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and жалеть ('to feel sorry for, pity; to regret, spare'), derived from жаль ('pity, sorrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic жаль ('grief, sorrow, compassion; grave mound') and Proto-Slavic *žalь ('sharp pain, grief', cognate with Lithuanian gė́la 'sharp pain').

history.meaning: to take pity on; to regret

rootFamily.gloss: it's a pity; feel sorry for

пожаловать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пожаловати ('to show favour, grant, deign to visit'), formed from по- + жаловать ('to favour, hold dear, reward', related to жаль 'pity, affection'). Today used chiefly in the traditional hospitality greeting Добро пожаловать! ('Welcome!', literally 'deign to come in kindness!') and in пожалуйста ('please').

history.meaning: to grant favour, deign to visit
to come as an honoured guest, welcome

пожалуй.etymology: Fossilized 2nd-person singular imperative (пожалуй 'be so gracious as to grant!') of пожаловать ('to grant, bestow favor, show mercy'), formed from по- + жаловать ('to favor, feel affection/pity for', from Proto-Slavic *žalovati, related to жаль). Just as пожалуй + ста ('be so kind, sir') fused into пожалуйста ('please'), bare пожалуй grammaticalized as a parenthetical discourse particle meaning 'if you please → I suppose, perhaps, probably'.

history.meaning: be so gracious as to grant!

пожалуйста.etymology: Formed by fusing older пожалуй (imperative of пожаловать, 'be so kind, grant a favour', related to жаловать) with the old deferential enclitic particle -ста. While the first half clearly asks for gracious favour, Vasmer notes that the exact origin of the particle -ста (linked variously to сударь or old forms of стать/быть) remains debated.
пожалуйста.notes: Covers 'please', 'you're welcome', and 'here you go' when handing something over.

пожертвовать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from жертвовать ('to sacrifice, donate'), derived from жертва ('sacrifice, offering'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic жрьтва (from Proto-Slavic *žьrtva 'sacrifice, praise').

history.meaning: to sacrifice, to give up; to donate

позаботиться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from заботиться ('to care for, worry about'), derived from забота ('care, concern, anxiety'), related to зобать ('to peck, eat, gnaw at').

history.meaning: to take care of, look after

позади.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from the prefix/preposition по- + зади (locative singular of задъ 'back, rear part', from Proto-Slavic *zadъ): literally 'along/at the back of, behind'.

позапрошлый.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing поза- ('behind, beyond the immediately preceding one', from по- + за) to прошлый ('past, last'): 'the one before last' (позапрошлый год 'the year before last', позапрошлая неделя 'the week before last').

позвать.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + звать ('to call, invite', Old East Slavic зъвати, Proto-Slavic *zъvati, cognate with Sanskrit hváyati 'calls, invokes').
позвать.notes: Future tense inserts a fleeting -о- in the root: я позову, ты позовёшь, они позовут.

позволять.etymology: Imperfective of позволить ('to allow, permit'), borrowed in the 17th century via Polish pozwolić ('to permit, consent'), formed from po- + wolić (from wola 'will', Proto-Slavic *voľa).

позвонить.etymology: Formed as the perfective counterpart of звонить ('to ring, call by phone') with the prefix по-. The base verb comes from Old East Slavic звонити ('to ring a bell, resound'), built on звон ('ringing sound', from Proto-Slavic *zvonъ).

history.meaning: to ring, make a phone call (perfective)

поздравить.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic stem здрав- (compare native East Slavic здоров- in здоровый) from поздравити, originally meaning 'to wish someone good health (здравие)', built on по- + здравый ('healthy, sound', Proto-Slavic *sъdorvъ): from wishing health on a feast day or birthday, it generalized to 'to congratulate'.

history.meaning: to wish good health -> to congratulate

поздравить.notes: Takes the accusative of the person and с + instrumental for the occasion: поздравить друга с днём рождения ('to wish a friend a happy birthday').

поздравлять.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of поздравить ('to congratulate', literally 'to wish good health') with the suffix -лять (including labial epenthesis в -> вл).

позже.etymology: Comparative degree ('later') of поздний / поздно ('late'), formed from the stem позд- (Old East Slavic поздо / поздьнъ, Proto-Slavic *pozdъ, built on *po- 'after') with palatalization before the comparative suffix *-je.

позлить.etymology: Formed with prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') from злить ('to anger, make mad'), derived from злой ('angry, evil, wicked'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ.

history.meaning: to anger, to tease, to annoy

познакомиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed with the prefix по- from знакомиться ('to get acquainted'), derived from знакомый ('familiar, acquainted'), originally a passive participle in -м- from Old East Slavic знакъ ('sign, mark') and знати / знать ('to know', from Proto-Slavic *znati, PIE *ǵneh₃-).

поймать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поимати ('to take, seize, catch'), formed from the perfective prefix по- and имати ('to take, grasp, catch', from Proto-Slavic *jьmati, iterative of *jęti 'to take', with initial *jь- coalescing after the vowel of по- into пой-).

morphemes.meaning: take, seize (from Old East Slavic имати)

поймать.notes: Forms an aspectual pair with **ловить** (impf. 'to try to catch, be catching') / **поймать** (pf. 'to catch').

пока.etymology: Shortened in East Slavic from older покамѣстъ ('for the time being, while, until'), formed from the distributive preposition по + the pronominal stem ка- ('which, what': originally 'up to what point / while'). The colloquial farewell Пока! ('Bye! / See you for now!') developed in the 20th century as an ellipsis of Пока до свидания ('Goodbye for now').

history.meaning: up to what point, while, for now

показать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic показати and Proto-Slavic *pokazati ('to show, point out, instruct'), formed from по- + казать ('to show, declare', Proto-Slavic *kazati).
показать.notes: Future tense shows з -> ж palatalization: я покажу, ты покажешь.

показывать.etymology: Formed in Russian as the imperfective counterpart of показать ('to show') with the productive imperfective suffix -ывать.

покер.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or 20th century from English poker (the American card game attested from the 1830s, probably influenced by French poque and German Poch, bluffing card games).

поклониться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поклонитися and Proto-Slavic *pokloniti sę ('to bend oneself down, bow in greeting or reverence'), formed from по- + клонить ('to incline, bend', Proto-Slavic *kloniti) + -ся.

покой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic покои and Proto-Slavic *pokojь ('rest, peace, quiet'), a prefixal noun built on *po- + *kojь / *počiti ('to rest, lie still', from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey- 'to rest, be quiet', cognate with Latin quiēs and English quiet).
покой.notes: Notice how in Polish (pokój) and Czech (pokoj) the sense 'resting chamber' became the everyday word for 'room', a sense preserved in older Russian царские покои ('royal apartments').

поколение.etymology: Derived in Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic поколѣние ('generation, tribe, lineage') from по- + колѣно ('knee; joint, node of a stem; degree of kinship, generation'), from Proto-Slavic *kolěno.

покормить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix по- from кормить ('to feed, nourish'), derived from корм ('fodder, food'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kъrmъ ('food, fodder').

покрасить.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix по- to красить ('to paint, dye', Proto-Slavic *krasiti).

покраска.etymology: Derived in Russian from покрасить ('to paint') with the action-noun suffix -ка: 'the act or process of painting, a coat/job of paint'.

покупатель.etymology: Formed in Russian from покупать ('to buy') with the agent-noun suffix -тель: 'one who buys, a buyer, customer, or shopper'.

покупать.etymology: Formed in East Slavic as the imperfective counterpart of купить ('to buy'), from по- + купать (iterative of купить, Proto-Slavic *kupiti, an early Proto-Slavic borrowing from Gothic kaupōn 'to trade, traffic', itself from Latin caupō 'merchant, innkeeper', the same source as German kaufen and English cheap).

покупка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from покупать ('to buy'), derived with prefix по- from купать / купить ('to buy'), an early Proto-Slavic *kupiti borrowing from Gothic kaupōn ('to trade, traffic', ultimately from Latin caupō 'innkeeper, peddler').

пол.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic полъ ('half, one side; plank floor made of split logs'), from Proto-Slavic *polъ ('half, side', from PIE *(s)pólH-o- 'split piece, half, board', because traditional floors were laid with tree trunks split in half). The same historical word meaning 'one of two halves of humanity' gives the homonym пол ('biological sex, gender') and the compounding prefix пол- ('half-').
пол.notes: In the meaning 'floor', takes the stressed ending **-у́** in the locative (**на полу́**) and moves stress to the preposition in **на́ пол** ('onto the floor').

полдень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic полудьнь / полъдьне ('midday, noon; south'), a compound of пол- ('half, mid-', from Proto-Slavic *polъ) + день ('day', from Proto-Slavic *dьnь): literally 'half-day, mid-day'.

history.meaning: half of the day, midday, noon

полегче.etymology: Attenuative comparative formed with prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') from легче ('lighter, easier'), comparative of лёгкий ('light, easy'), from Proto-Slavic *lьgъkъ.

полежать.etymology: Delimitative verb formed with prefix по- ('for a while') from лежать ('to lie, recline'), inherited from Old East Slavic лежати, from Proto-Slavic *ležati.

полезно.etymology: Adverb formed from полезный ('useful, beneficial'), derived from польза (dialectal/older полеза, 'benefit, use, advantage'), from Proto-Slavic *polьga ('relief, benefit', related to *lьgъkъ 'light, easy').

полезный.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic полѣзьнъ / пользьнъ ('beneficial, useful, profitable'), formed from польза ('benefit, use, advantage', Old East Slavic польга / Old Church Slavonic польза, from Proto-Slavic *polьga, built on *lьg- 'light, easy', as in лёгкий). Literally, 'bringing ease or benefit'.

полениться.etymology: Formed with prefix по- from лениться ('to be lazy'), derived from лень ('laziness, sloth'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *lěnь ('laziness, slow').

history.meaning: to be too lazy, hesitate to make an effort

полететь.etymology: Inceptive perfective formed with prefix по- ('setting off') from лететь ('to fly'), inherited from Old East Slavic летѣти, from Proto-Slavic *letěti ('to fly').

полицай.etymology: Borrowed during World War II directly from the phonetic pronunciation of German Polizei ('police', [poliˈtsaɪ]), specifically designating a local auxiliary policeman serving in the German occupation forces on occupied Soviet territory (Hilfspolizei).

полиция.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great in the early 18th century via German Polizei (older Policey) and Polish policja from Late Latin polītīa ('civil administration, public order'), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, 'citizenship, government, administration of a polis'), from πόλις (pólis, 'city-state').

полк.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пълкъ ('host, campaign, armed band, people'), from Proto-Slavic *pъlkъ ('crowd, armed host'), an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *fulką ('people, troop, folk'; compare English folk, German Volk).

полкило.etymology: Compound formed from пол- ('half', from половина / полъ, Proto-Slavic *polъ 'side, half') + кило (clipping of килограмм 'kilogram', from French kilogramme).

полмиллиона.etymology: Compound formed from пол- ('half', from Proto-Slavic *polъ) + миллиона (genitive singular of миллион 'million', borrowed via French million from Italian milione, augmentative of mille 'thousand').

полминуты.etymology: Formed in Russian by combining the compounding stem пол- ('half', reduced from полъ / половина, Proto-Slavic *polъ) with the genitive singular минуты of минута ('minute', from Medieval Latin minūta): literally 'half of a minute'.

morphemes.meaning: of a minute (genitive singular of минута)

полностью.etymology: Lexicalized instrumental singular of полночь/полность (abstract noun from полный 'full', from Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ): literally 'in its fullness', hence the adverb 'completely, fully, in full'.

полночь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic полуночь / пълночь and Proto-Slavic *polъnoktь ('midnight'), a compound of *polъ ('half, middle') + *noktь ('night', Russian ночь): literally 'half-night, middle of the night'.
полночь.notes: In oblique cases the first element often expands to полу-: около полуночи ('around midnight'), за полночь ('past midnight').

полный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пълнъ / пълныи ('full'), from Proto-Slavic *pъlnъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós ('full', passive participle of *pleh₁- 'to fill'), directly cognate with English full, German voll, Latin plēnus, Lithuanian pìlnas, and Sanskrit pūrṇá.

половина.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic половина ('one of two equal sides, half'), from Proto-Slavic *polovina, derived from *polъ ('side, half', preserved in Russian пол 'floor; sex', полдень 'midday', and полцены 'half price').

половинка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of половина ('half'), inherited from Old East Slavic половина and Proto-Slavic *polovina, built on *polъ ('half, side').

половник.etymology: Derived with the utensil suffix -ник from dialectal and older Russian половой / ополовник (connected by Vasmer either with пол 'half' — a ladle holding half a measure or skimming the surface — or with полоть / полый 'hollow, open scoop').

положительный.etymology: Adjective formed from положить ('to lay down, establish, affirm'), calquing Latin positivus (from pōnere, positum 'to put, lay down, posit'), built on Proto-Slavic *ložiti.

положить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic положити ('to lay down, place, put'), from Proto-Slavic *položiti, formed from prefix *po- + *ložiti ('to lay', causative of *legti 'to lie down', from PIE *legʰ-). In standard modern Russian, положить serves as the suppletive perfective partner of imperfective класть ('to put, lay').
положить.notes: In standard Russian, the root **-лож-** is never used without a prefix (always say **положить**, and use **класть** for the imperfective).

полоса.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic полоса ('strip of ploughed land, furrow, streak, band'), showing regular East Slavic pleophony (-оло-) from Proto-Slavic *polsa ('ploughed strip, band'), related to вспахать / пашня and Czech plasa ('strip of land').
полоса.notes: Accusative singular shifts stress to the first syllable: по́лосу; nominative plural is по́лосы.

полоска.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of полоса ('stripe, strip, band, furrow'), inherited from Old East Slavic полоса (showing East Slavic pleophony -оло-) and Proto-Slavic *polsa ('furrow, strip of land or cloth').

полотенце.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьnьce, a diminutive in -це of полотно 'linen cloth' — originally 'a small piece of linen' for drying one's hands or face.
полотенце.notes: Genitive plural inserts a fleeting е: полотенец.

полотно.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *poltьno 'woven linen cloth', showing regular East Slavic pleophony (-оло- from *-ol- between consonants; compare the Church Slavonic doublet платно and Polish plotno).

history.meaning: linen fabric; painter's canvas; railway roadbed

полсантиметра.etymology: Formed in Russian by combining the compounding stem пол- ('half', from Proto-Slavic *polъ) with the genitive singular сантиметра of сантиметр ('centimetre'): literally 'half of a centimetre'.

полседьмого.etymology: Colloquial Russian compound time expression contracted from половина седьмого (часа) ('half of the seventh hour', i.e. 6:30), combining пол- ('half', from полъ) + седьмого (genitive singular of седьмой 'seventh').

history.meaning: half of the seventh (hour) → half past six (6:30)

полседьмого.notes: Russian clock expressions count forward into the upcoming hour: *полседьмого* ('half of the seventh') is 6:30.

полуденный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from полдень (genitive полудня 'midday, noon'), a compound of полу- ('half', old genitive/locative of полъ) + день ('day', from Proto-Slavic *dьnь).

получать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of получить ('to receive, get, obtain'), formed from the prefix по- and лучать / лучить ('to hit a mark, obtain by lot', from Proto-Slavic *lučiti; compare случай 'chance, occasion' and благополучный 'fortunate').

history.meaning: to hit the mark, come by lot

получаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive/intransitive verb formed from получать ('to receive, obtain', imperfective of получить). The root луч- goes back to Proto-Slavic *lučiti ('to hit the mark, happen upon, receive by lot or fortune'; compare случай 'case, chance' and благополучный 'prosperous'). With -ся, получаться means 'to turn out, work out, succeed'.

history.meaning: to hit a target, happen by lot
to turn out, work out, come out

получение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from получить ('to receive, obtain'), formed with prefix по- from лучить ('to hit the mark, obtain, reach'), from Proto-Slavic *lučiti ('to hit, find, happen').

history.meaning: to hit a target, reach, obtain

получить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic получити ('to hit the mark, attain, receive'), from Proto-Slavic *polučiti, built on по- + *lučiti ('to aim at, hit a target, reach by lot'; compare случиться 'to happen').

history.meaning: to hit the mark, obtain, receive

получиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of получить ('to receive, obtain', from Proto-Slavic *polučiti 'to hit the mark, come about'). In the reflexive it means 'to turn out, work out, succeed'.

history.meaning: to obtain → to turn out, work out, come out well

полцены.etymology: Compound formed in Russian by fusing пол- ('half', from Proto-Slavic *polъ) with цены, the genitive singular of цена ('price, value', from Old East Slavic цѣна, Proto-Slavic *cěna): literally 'half of the price' (за полцены 'for half price').

morphemes.meaning: genitive singular ending governed by пол-

полшага.etymology: Compound noun formed from пол- ('half', from Old East Slavic полъ) + шага (genitive singular of шаг 'step, pace').

history.meaning: half + of a step → half a pace, half a step

польза.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic польза (earlier польга, with dialectal/analogical shift г > з from the dative/locative пользѣ), from Proto-Slavic *polьga ('easing, relief, benefit'), from *po- + *lьga (related to лёгкий 'light, easy' and льгота).

пользоваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of пользовать ('to benefit, treat'), derived from польза ('benefit, use'), from Proto-Slavic *polьga ('relief, benefit').

history.meaning: to use, to take advantage of

полюбить.etymology: Formed from the inchoative/perfective prefix по- ('to begin to, come to') + любить ('to love', Proto-Slavic *ljubiti, from *ljubъ 'dear, beloved', cognate with English love and German lieb): 'to come to love, grow fond of, fall in love with'.

history.meaning: to come to love, grow fond of

cognates.meaning: to grow fond of, come to like

полюбоваться.etymology: Formed with the delimitative/perfective prefix по- ('for a while') + любоваться ('to admire, gaze with pleasure at'), built on любый ('dear, pleasing') and любить ('to love', from Proto-Slavic *ľubiti).

history.meaning: pleasing → to take visual delight in
to admire for a moment (takes instrumental case)

полюбоваться.notes: Takes the instrumental case for what is being admired: *полюбоваться видом* ('to admire the view').

полярник.etymology: Formed in Russian with agent suffix -ник from полярный ('polar'), borrowed via German polar / French polaire from Medieval Latin polaris (from Latin polus, Ancient Greek πόλος 'axis, pole').

помазать.etymology: Formed with prefix по- from мазать ('to smear, oil, anoint'), inherited from Old East Slavic мазати, from Proto-Slavic *mazati ('to smear, daub').

history.meaning: to apply ointment, to dab on

помахать.etymology: Formed from the delimitative/perfective prefix по- + махать ('to wave, brandish, flap', Old East Slavic махати, Proto-Slavic *maxati): 'to wave (one's hand, a handkerchief) a few times'.
помахать.notes: Takes the instrumental of what is waved and dative of the person waved to: помахать рукой другу ('to wave one's hand to a friend').

поменять.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + менять ('to change, exchange, swap', Old East Slavic мѣняти, Proto-Slavic *měnjati, built on *měna 'exchange, change').

померить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix по- from мерить ('to measure, try on'), derived from мера ('measure'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *měra ('measure').

поместиться.etymology: Formed from по- + местить ('to place, locate', derived from место 'place, room, space', Proto-Slavic *město) + -ся: 'to find room for oneself, fit into a space'.

history.meaning: to place -> to fit into a space

помешать.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing/delimitative prefix по- + мешать ('to stir, mix; to disturb, hinder', Proto-Slavic *měšati). Just like its base verb, it has two distinct meanings depending on case government: 'to stir for a little while' (+ accusative) and 'to hinder, get in the way of, disturb' (+ dative).

history.meaning: to stir (for a while); to hinder, disturb

cognates.meaning: to stir for a while; mix up

помешать.notes: Compare: помешать суп ложкой ('to give the soup a stir with a spoon', accusative) vs. помешать разговору ('to interrupt / hinder a conversation', dative).

помещаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of помещать ('to place, locate, accommodate'), imperfective of поместить, derived from место ('place, room, space'), from Proto-Slavic *město ('place').

history.meaning: to fit in, to find room; to be located

помирить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix по- from мирить ('to reconcile, make peace'), derived from мир ('peace'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *mirъ ('peace, concord').

помириться.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + мириться ('to make peace with one another', from мирить 'to reconcile', built on мир 'peace', Proto-Slavic *mirъ) + -ся.

history.meaning: to make peace, make up, reconcile

помнить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic помьнити and Proto-Slavic *pomьniti ('to keep in mind, remember'), formed from по- + мнить ('to think, hold in mind', Old East Slavic мьнѣти, Proto-Slavic *mьněti, from Proto-Indo-European *men- 'to think, remember', cognate with память and English mind).

помогать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic помогати and Proto-Slavic *pomagati ('to help, assist'), the imperfective counterpart of помочь (*pomogti), showing the regular Slavic lengthened imperfective root vowel *-mag- from *-mog- (мочь 'to be able, have power').
помогать.notes: Takes the dative case of the person helped: помогать маме ('to help mum').

помоложе.etymology: Attenuated comparative formed by adding the prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') to моложе ('younger'), the comparative degree of молодой ('young', Old East Slavic молодыи, from Proto-Slavic *moldъ, comparative *moldje, with East Slavic ж from *dj).

помолчать.etymology: Delimitative verb formed with prefix по- ('for a while') from молчать ('to be silent'), inherited from Old East Slavic мълчати, from Proto-Slavic *mъlčati ('to keep silent').

помочь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic помочи and Proto-Slavic *pomogti ('to help, lend one's strength to'), formed from по- + мочь ('to be able, have power or might', Proto-Slavic *mogti, cognate with English may and might).

morphemes.meaning: be able, have strength (мочь, stem мог-)

помочь.notes: Conjugates like мочь with г -> ж alternation: я помогу, ты поможешь, они помогут; past tense помог, помогла. Takes the dative case.

помощник.etymology: Derived with the agent suffix -ник from помощь ('help, aid'), which preserves the Old Church Slavonic sound change *gt -> щ (compare native Old East Slavic помочь as a noun) from Proto-Slavic *pomogtь ('help, power').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

помощник.notes: In traditional Moscow pronunciation, щн in помощник is pronounced [шн] ([памо́шник]), though spelling pronunciation is also heard.

помощь.etymology: Adopted with the Old Church Slavonic reflex -щ- (compare native East Slavic помочь in dialectal/idiomatic бог в помочь) from Old Church Slavonic помощь ('help, aid, assistance'), from Proto-Slavic *pomoťь, formed from *po- and *moťь ('power, might', from *moťi 'to be able', Russian мочь).

помыть.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + мыть ('to wash', Proto-Slavic *myti).
помыть.notes: Future tense alternates ы -> о: я помою, ты помоешь.

понадобиться.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix по- from надобиться ('to be needed'), derived from надобный ('necessary') and Old East Slavic надобѣ ('it is needful', originally the locative phrase на добѣ 'at the right time/fit occasion', from доба 'fitting time, season').

history.meaning: at a fitting time → it is needed
to be needed → to come to be needed, come in handy

понарошку.etymology: Colloquial adverb formed with prefix по- from нарочно / нароком ('on purpose, expressly, in jest'), derived from Old East Slavic нарокъ ('appointed word, purpose, name'), from Proto-Slavic *narokъ (from *rekti 'to speak').

понедельник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic понедѣльникъ (Proto-Slavic *ponedělьnikъ), a compound built on the prepositional phrase по недѣли ('after Sunday') + -ник. In Old East Slavic (and still in all other Slavic languages), недѣля meant 'Sunday' — literally the 'no-work day' (не дѣлати). Thus понедельник literally means 'the day after Sunday (the no-work day)'.

morphemes.meaning: Sunday ('no-work day', older sense of неделя)

понести.etymology: Formed with prefix по- ('setting off; undergoing') from нести ('to carry, bear'), inherited from Old East Slavic нести, from Proto-Slavic *nesti.

понизить.etymology: Formed with prefix по- from низить ('to lower'), derived from низ ('bottom, low place') / низкий ('low'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *nizъ ('down, low').

понимать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic понимати ('to grasp, seize, comprehend'), imperfective of понять ('to understand'), formed from prefix по- + -нимать / ять ('to take, grasp', from Proto-Slavic *jьmati / *jęti, with epenthetic н after a vowel/originally nasal prefix). Like English grasp or Latin comprehendere, its literal root sense is 'to take hold of mentally'.

понт.etymology: From Russian criminal/card-playing argot понт ('bluff, flashy display to impress or deceive'), borrowed from French ponte ('punter in basset, faro, or trente-et-quarante') or point ('point in cards'); compare понтировать ('to punt, bet against the bank').

history.meaning: player betting against the bank, punter

понятие.etymology: Verbal noun from понять ('to understand, grasp'), inherited from Old East Slavic поняти ('to seize, grasp, comprehend'), from Proto-Slavic *po-jęti ('to take, grasp', from *jęti 'to take').

понятный.etymology: Derived in Russian from понять ('to grasp, understand', passive participle понятый) with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'capable of being grasped, clear, understandable'.

понять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пояти / поняти and Proto-Slavic *pojęti ('to take, grasp, seize; to comprehend'), formed from по- + ять (*jęti 'to take, grasp', with an epenthetic н carried over from prefixes ending in a nasal): the universal metaphor of 'grasping' an idea with the mind (compare Latin comprehendere and German begreifen).

history.meaning: to take hold of, grasp, understand

понять.notes: Future tense uses the -йм- stem (direct reflex of *po-jьm-): я пойму, ты поймёшь, они поймут; past tense по́нял, поняла́, по́няли.

пообедать.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix по- from обедать ('to dine, have midday meal'), derived from обед ('dinner, midday meal'), from Proto-Slavic *ob-ědъ ('meal, time around eating', from *ěsti 'to eat').

попадать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of попасть ('to fall into, hit a target, end up'), from по- + падать ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *padati).

history.meaning: to hit (a target), land; to get somewhere

попасть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic попасти (Proto-Slavic *popasti), formed from по- + пасть ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *pasti, stem пад-): originally 'to fall right onto or into a spot', hence 'to hit a mark' or 'to find oneself in / get into a place or situation'.

history.meaning: to fall onto, hit, end up in
to hit (a target); to end up, get into

попасть.notes: Conjugates with the dental stem пад-: я попаду, ты попадёшь; past tense попал, попала.

попасться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of попасть ('to hit a mark, fall into, end up'), formed from prefix по- + пасть ('to fall', from Proto-Slavic *pasti). Adding -ся gives the sense 'to get caught in a trap; to happen to cross one's path, turn up'.

history.meaning: to land in → to get caught; to turn up, come across

поплакать.etymology: Delimitative verb formed with prefix по- ('for a while, a little') from плакать ('to weep, cry'), inherited from Old East Slavic плакати, from Proto-Slavic *plakati ('to beat one's breast, lament, weep').

пополам.etymology: Fused adverbial phrase from the preposition по ('by, into') + полам (old dative plural of полъ 'half, side', from Proto-Slavic *polъ): literally 'by halves, into two equal halves'.

поправить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поправити (Proto-Slavic *popraviti 'to set straight, mend, correct'), formed from по- + править ('to make straight, direct', from правый 'right, straight').

попробовать.etymology: Formed by adding the perfectivizing prefix по- to пробовать ('to try, test, taste').

попросить.etymology: Formed as the perfective of просить ('to ask for, request') with the prefix по-. The base verb comes from Old East Slavic просити, from Proto-Slavic *prositi ('to ask, beg, request'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *proḱ-éye- (from *preḱ- 'to ask, entreat'; cognate with Latin precor 'to pray, beg' and German fragen 'to ask').
попросить.notes: Use **попросить** for asking a favour or requesting an object (*попросить чашку чая*), and **спросить** for asking a question for information.

попрощаться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from прощаться ('to ask mutual forgiveness at parting, bid farewell'), derived from простить ('to forgive, pardon', from Proto-Slavic *prostiti, from *prostъ 'free, simple').

history.meaning: to say goodbye, to bid farewell

популярность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from популярный ('popular'), borrowed via French populaire / German populär from Latin populāris ('belonging to the people', from populus 'people').

популярный.etymology: Borrowed via Polish popularny, German populär, or French populaire from Latin populāris ('of the people, well-liked by the public'), from populus ('people').

попытка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from попытаться ('to try, attempt'), built on prefix по- + пытаться ('to try, endeavour', from Proto-Slavic *pytati 'to ask, investigate, test').

пора.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пора ('time, season, vigour, mature strength'), from Proto-Slavic *pora ('effort, push, fitting time, season'), related by o-grade ablaut to переть ('to press, push'). In the set phrase до сих пор ('up to these times', with genitive plural сиx of сей 'this'), it means 'still, up to now'.

history.meaning: time, season; it is time to (пора + infinitive)

пора.notes: **Пора́** as a predicate means 'it is time (to go/do something)'; **до сих пор** literally means 'until these times' ('still, up to now').

поработать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') and работать ('to work', from работа 'work', Proto-Slavic *orbota).

history.meaning: to work for a while, do some work

порадоваться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix по- and -ся from радоваться ('to rejoice, be glad'), derived from рад ('glad, happy'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *radъ.

history.meaning: to rejoice, to be happy, to be glad

поранить.etymology: Formed with perfective prefix по- from ранить ('to wound, injure'), derived from рана ('wound'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *rana ('wound, gash').

порваться.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + рвать ('to tear, rip, pluck', Proto-Slavic *rъvati) + the intransitive postfix -ся: 'to tear, rip, or snap apart'.

порезать.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + резать ('to cut, slice', Proto-Slavic *rězati): 'to slice up, cut into pieces' or 'to cut slightly (e.g. one's finger)'.
порезать.notes: Future tense shows з -> ж palatalization: я порежу, ты порежешь.

поровну.etymology: Adverb formed in East Slavic from the distributive preposition по + ровну (old dative singular of ровный 'even, equal', from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ).

порог.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic порогъ ('doorstep, threshold; river rapid'), showing regular East Slavic pleophony (-оро-) from Proto-Slavic *porgъ ('threshold, raised sill or rocky ledge', compare Old Church Slavonic прагъ, Polish próg, and Czech práh).

порода.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from породить ('to give birth to, generate, breed'), built from the prefix по- and родить ('to give birth, bear', from род 'kin, lineage, birth', Proto-Slavic *rodъ). Denotes lineage, stock, animal breed, or geological rock formation.

history.meaning: to beget, breed → lineage, breed, species

порождать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic порождати (imperfective of породити 'to give birth to, generate', with жд < *dj), from по- + родити ('to bear, give birth', Proto-Slavic *roditi).

history.meaning: to breed, to give rise to

порошок.etymology: Diminutive in -ок of порох ('dust, powder; gunpowder'), inherited from Old East Slavic порохъ ('dust, ash'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *porxъ ('dust, fine particles'; compare Old Church Slavonic прахъ).

портрет.etymology: Borrowed via German Porträt from French portrait ('likeness, portrait'), originally the past participle of Old French portraire 'to draw forth, depict', from Latin protrahere ('to draw out, bring to light').

порыв.etymology: Deverbal noun from порывать / порвать ('to tear, burst forth'), formed from prefix по- + the root рыв- (lengthened iterative grade of рвать 'to tear, pluck, lunge', from Proto-Slavic *rъvati / *ryvati). Denotes a sudden burst — whether a 'gust' of wind or an emotional 'impulse'.

порядок.etymology: Formed in East Slavic (compare Polish porządek) from по ряду ('in a row, in proper sequence', built on ряд 'row, order', from Proto-Slavic *rędъ) + suffix -ок: 'proper sequence, tidy arrangement, order'.

history.meaning: arrangement in a row → order, proper state

порядок.notes: Takes the locative in **-е**: **всё в порядке** ('everything is in order / all right').

порядочность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость from порядочный ('orderly, decent, honorable'), derived from порядок ('order, sequence'), from по- + ряд ('row, order', Proto-Slavic *rędъ).

посадить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic посадити, formed from the perfective prefix по- and садить ('to make sit, seat, plant'), the Proto-Slavic causative *saditi ('to cause to sit, set') built on the o-grade of *sěděti / *sěsti ('to sit', PIE *sod-éye-ti, exact cognate with English set).

history.meaning: to seat; to plant; to imprison

rootFamily.gloss: to sit; to be in prison

посидеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') and сидеть ('to sit'), inherited from Old East Slavic сидѣти and Proto-Slavic *ěděti / *sěděti (from PIE *sed- 'to sit').

history.meaning: to sit for a while; to spend time together

последний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic послѣдьнии ('following behind, last'), formed from по слѣду ('along the track, following after', built on след 'footprint, track', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ) + adjectival suffix -ний.

history.meaning: coming at the end of the trail, last

последствие.etymology: Derived in Old Church Slavonic / bookish Russian послѣдьствие ('following after, result, consequence') from послѣдь ('afterward'), built on слѣдъ ('track, footprint', Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

послезавтра.etymology: Compound adverb formed from после ('after', from Proto-Slavic *poslě) + завтра ('tomorrow', from *za utra 'in the morning').

послужной.etymology: Adjective formed from послуга / послужить ('service, tenure of service'), derived from служить ('to serve'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *služiti ('to serve', from *sluga 'servant').

послушать.etymology: Formed as the perfective counterpart of слушать ('to listen') with the prefix по-. The base verb comes from Old East Slavic слушати ('to listen, obey'), from Proto-Slavic *slušati, built on the same Indo-European root *ḱlew- ('to hear') as слышать.

посметь.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and сметь ('to dare, venture'), inherited from Old East Slavic съмѣти (and Old Church Slavonic съмѣти), from Proto-Slavic *sъměti ('to dare').

посмеяться.etymology: Delimitative/perfective verb formed with prefix по- from смеяться ('to laugh'), inherited from Old East Slavic смѣятисѧ, from Proto-Slavic *smějati sę ('to laugh').

посмотреть.etymology: Formed in Russian as the perfective counterpart of смотреть ('to look, watch') by adding the bounding prefix по-. The base verb comes from Old East Slavic съмотрити ('to look closely, consider'), originally a prefixed derivative of Proto-Slavic *motriti ('to gaze, observe'; compare Lithuanian matýti 'to see').

посоветоваться.etymology: Perfective reflexive formed with prefix по- and -ся from советовать ('to advise, take counsel'), derived from совет ('counsel, advice'), from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтъ (Proto-Slavic *sъvětъ).

посолить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from солить ('to salt'), derived from соль ('salt'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *solь ('salt').

посольство.etymology: Derived from посол ('ambassador, envoy', from Old East Slavic посълъ, deverbal from посълати 'to send forth', from по- + Proto-Slavic *sъlati 'to send') + abstract/institutional suffix -ство.

посреди.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing по- ('along, in') to среди ('in the middle of, among', originally the locative singular of среда / середа 'middle', Proto-Slavic *serda).
посреди.notes: Takes the genitive case: посреди комнаты ('right in the middle of the room').

поссориться.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + ссориться ('to quarrel, fall out'), built on ссора ('quarrel, discord', Old East Slavic съсора, traditionally analyzed as съ- 'together' + a root related to свара 'quarrel, wrangling', or сор 'litter, trouble').

пост.etymology: In the sense 'station, guard post, office', borrowed via French poste or German Posten from Italian posto ('station, place'), from Vulgar Latin *positum (from Latin pōnere 'to place'). (Distinct from religious пост 'fast', an early Germanic loan.)

поставленный.etymology: Past passive participle of поставить ('to put, place, establish'), formed from perfective prefix по- + ставить ('to place, set upright', from Proto-Slavic *staviti, causative of *stati 'to stand').

поставлять.etymology: Imperfective of поставить ('to place, set up; to supply, deliver'), formed with prefix по- from ставить ('to set, place'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *staviti.

поставщик.etymology: Agent noun formed with suffix -щик from поставка / поставлять ('to supply, deliver'), derived from по- + ставить ('to set, place, furnish', Proto-Slavic *staviti).

постановить.etymology: Formed with prefix по- from становить ('to set up, establish, decide'), derived from стан ('stand, camp, frame') / стать ('to stand'), from Proto-Slavic *stanoviti.

постареть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + стареть ('to grow old, age'), derived from старый ('old', inherited from Proto-Slavic *starъ).

постель.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic постеля ('bed, bedding'), derived from постлать / постелю ('to spread out, make a bed'), formed from по- + Proto-Slavic *stьlati ('to spread, strew').

постельный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from постель ('bed, bedding'), inherited from Old East Slavic постеля ('bedding, spread'), derived from по- + стлать (стелю, 'to spread, lay out'), from Proto-Slavic *postelja.

постепенно.etymology: Adverb derived from постепенный ('gradual'), formed from the preposition/prefix по- ('by, according to') + степень ('step, degree, grade', from Old Church Slavonic степень, Proto-Slavic *stepenь).

постирать.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + стирать ('to wash laundry; originally to rub off, wipe away', iterative of стереть, from с- + Proto-Slavic *terti 'to rub').

history.meaning: to wipe off; to wash laundry

постичь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic постичи / Old Church Slavonic постигнути ('to reach, overtake, grasp, comprehend'), formed from по- + Proto-Slavic *stigti ('to stride, reach, overtake').

посторожить.etymology: Formed with the delimitative/perfective prefix по- ('for a while') + сторожить ('to guard, watch over'), derived from сторож ('watchman, guard', from Proto-Slavic *storgъ with East Slavic pleophony -оро-).

history.meaning: to guard, keep watch over for a while

посторонний.etymology: Adjective formed from по стороне ('off to the side, outside'), derived from сторона ('side, region'), East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *storna ('side, direction').

постоялец.etymology: Derived from постоялый ('staying temporarily, lodging', from постоять 'to stand or stay for a while', from по- + Proto-Slavic *stojati 'to stand') + agent noun suffix -ец.

history.meaning: lodger, guest at an inn or hotel

постоянно.etymology: Adverb formed from постоянный ('constant, permanent, steady'), derived from постоять ('to stand firm, abide'), built from по- + стоять ('to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati; compare Latin cōnstāns 'standing firm, constant').

постоянный.etymology: Derived from постоять ('to stand for a while, stand firm', from по- + стоять 'to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati) with the adjectival suffix -нный: originally 'standing firm, steadfast', which developed into 'constant, permanent, regular'.

постоять.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the delimitative prefix по- ('for a while') and стоять ('to stand'), inherited from Old East Slavic постояти, from Proto-Slavic *postojati (from PIE *stā- / *steh₂- 'to stand'). With за + accusative (постоять за себя), it means 'to stand up for, defend'.

history.meaning: to stand for a while; to defend
to stand for a while; to stand up for

пострадать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from страдать ('to suffer, endure hardship'), inherited from Old East Slavic страдати ('to labor hard, suffer'), from Proto-Slavic *stradati.

постричь.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from стричь ('to shear, cut hair'), inherited from Old East Slavic стричи (стригу), from Proto-Slavic *strigti ('to shear, clip').

построже.etymology: Attenuative comparative form derived from prefix по- ('a little, somewhat') + строже ('stricter', comparative of строгий 'strict, severe', from Proto-Slavic *strogъ).

построить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix по- and строить ('to build, construct; to arrange'), inherited from Old East Slavic строити ('to arrange, order, prepare, build'), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti, causative/denominative from *strojь ('order, arrangement, structure').

постройка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from построить ('to build, construct'), derived with prefix по- from строить ('to arrange, build'), from строй ('order, array'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *strojiti.

постскриптум.etymology: Borrowed from Latin post scriptum ('written afterward'), from post ('after') + scriptum, neuter past passive participle of scribere ('to write').

поступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic поступити ('to step forward, proceed, act'), formed from the prefix по- and ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti). From 'stepping forward', it developed both the sense 'to act, behave' (поступить правильно) and 'to enter, enroll in an institution' (поступить в университет).

history.meaning: to act, behave; to enroll, enter

rootFamily.gloss: to step on; to arrive (of time)

поступиться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from поступить ('to step, act, yield', from по- + ступить 'to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to step back from, give up, sacrifice').

постучать.etymology: Formed with the perfective/delimitative prefix по- ('a little, for a moment') + стучать ('to knock, tap, rap'), built on the Slavic sound-symbolic root *stuk- ('knock, thud').

посуда.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic посуда, originally a collective noun formed from по- + судъ ('vessel, pot, container', Old East Slavic судъ, Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ, preserved in сосуд 'vessel' and судно 'ship, vessel'): 'household vessels and dishes collectively, crockery, cookware'.
посуда.notes: Always singular in Russian (мыть посуду 'to wash the dishes', чистая посуда 'clean dishes').

посудить.etymology: Formed from prefix по- + судить ('to judge, reason, consider', inherited from Old East Slavic судити, from Proto-Slavic *sǫditi, derived from *sǫdъ 'judgment, court').

посчастливиться.etymology: Impersonal reflexive verb formed from perfective prefix по- + счастливиться (from счастливый 'lucky, fortunate', derived from счастье 'good fortune, happiness', from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje) + -ся.

посчитать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from считать ('to count, consider'), inherited from Old East Slavic съчитати ('to read/count together'), from Proto-Slavic *sъ-čitati.

посылать.etymology: Imperfective of послать ('to send'), formed with prefix по- and lengthened-grade iterative stem -сылать from слать (шлю, 'to send'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъlati.

посылка.etymology: Derived from посылать ('to send, dispatch', imperfective of послать, from по- + Proto-Slavic *sъlati 'to send') + noun suffix -ка, denoting first the act of sending and then a dispatched parcel.

пот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic потъ ('sweat, toil'), from Proto-Slavic *potъ ('sweat'), from Proto-Indo-European *pokʷ-to- ('cooked, heated'), from *pekʷ- ('to cook, heat').

потанцевать.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('for a while') + танцевать ('to dance', borrowed via Polish tańcować from Middle High German tanzen, from Old French dancier).

потащить.etymology: Formed from perfective/inchoative prefix по- + тащить ('to drag, pull, haul', related to Old East Slavic тъщити and таскати).

потемнеть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + темнеть ('to grow dark, darken'), derived from тёмный ('dark', from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnъ, from *tьma 'darkness').

потенциал.etymology: Borrowed via German Potential or French potentiel from Late Latin potentialis ('powerful, potential'), derived from Latin potentia ('power, capacity'), from potens ('able, mighty').

потереть.etymology: Formed from perfective/delimitative prefix по- ('a little, for a while') + тереть ('to rub, grate', inherited from Old East Slavic терети, from Proto-Slavic *terti 'to rub').

потерпевшая.etymology: Substantivized feminine past active participle of потерпеть ('to suffer, undergo, endure'), formed from prefix по- + терпеть ('to suffer, endure', from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti).

потеря.etymology: Deverbal noun from потерять ('to lose'), formed from perfective prefix по- + терять ('to lose; in Old East Slavic теряти to ruin, waste, pillage', related to Proto-Slavic *terti 'to rub, wear away').

потерянный.etymology: Past passive participle of потерять ('to lose'), formed with perfective prefix по- + терять ('to lose, waste, shed', from Old East Slavic теряти, related to тереть 'to rub away, wear down').

потерять.etymology: Formed by adding the perfectivizing prefix по- to терять ('to lose', originally 'to rub away, wear out, waste', derived from the same Indo-European root as тереть 'to rub, wipe', Proto-Slavic *terti).

потечь.etymology: Formed from the inchoative/perfective prefix по- ('to begin to') + течь ('to flow, run, leak', Old East Slavic течи, Proto-Slavic *tekti, from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- 'to run, flow'): 'to start flowing, begin to leak'.

history.meaning: to flow -> to begin to flow
to start flowing, begin to leak

потечь.notes: Conjugates with к -> ч alternation: он потечёт, они потекут; past tense потёк, потекла.

потешить.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + тешить ('to amuse, comfort, gratify', inherited from Old East Slavic тѣшити, from Proto-Slavic *těšiti 'to console, please, amuse').

потихонечку.etymology: Affectionate/diminutive adverb formed with prefix по- and double diminutive suffix -оньк-/-ечк- from тихо ('quietly, slowly'), from тихий ('quiet, still', Proto-Slavic *tixъ).

потише.etymology: Attenuative comparative formed with prefix по- ('a little') from тише ('quieter'), comparative of тихий ('quiet, soft'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *tixъ.

поток.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic потокъ ('stream, torrent'), formed from по- + ток ('flow, current'), o-grade noun from течь ('to flow, run', Proto-Slavic *tokъ / *tekti).

потолок.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with the prefix по- from толока / толочь ('to tread down, stamp earth, pack tight', Proto-Slavic *tolkti): in traditional timber houses, the ceiling (потолок) was made of wooden planks covered on top with a thick insulating layer of stamped clay and earth to keep heat inside the room.
потолок.notes: Drops the fleeting -о- in all oblique forms: потолок -> под потолком ('under the ceiling'), на потолке ('on the ceiling').

потом.etymology: Univerbation of the Old East Slavic prepositional phrase по томь ('after that'), combining the preposition по ('after') with томь, the locative singular of the demonstrative pronoun то ('that', from Proto-Slavic *to).

потому.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase по тому ('by that, on account of that'), combining the preposition по ('along, by, because of') with тому, the dative singular of то ('that'). Most frequently used in the compound conjunction потому что ('because', literally 'on account of that which').

history.meaning: by that, on account of that

потонуть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + тонуть ('to sink, drown', inherited from Old East Slavic тонути, from Proto-Slavic *topnǫti, inchoative of *topiti 'to sink, submerge').

потоп.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic потопъ ('flood, deluge'), from Proto-Slavic *potopъ, deverbal from *potopiti ('to flood, submerge', from *po- + *topiti).

поторапливаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb derived from поторопиться ('to hurry up'), formed from prefix по- + торопиться ('to hurry, rush', from Proto-Slavic *torpiti) with imperfectivizing suffix -ива- and -ся.

history.meaning: to hurry along, get a move on

поторговаться.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') + торговаться ('to bargain, haggle', from торговать 'to trade', derived from торг 'market, trade', from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ).

поторопить.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + торопить ('to hurry, rush someone', inherited from Old East Slavic торопити, from Proto-Slavic *torpiti).

потравить.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + травить ('to poison, exterminate; originally to graze down or consume', from Old East Slavic травити, from Proto-Slavic *traviti).

потратить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from тратить ('to spend, expend, waste'), inherited from Old East Slavic тратити ('to consume, destroy, spend'), from Proto-Slavic *tratiti.

history.meaning: to spend, to waste, to use up

потребовать.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + требовать ('to demand, require', from Old East Slavic трѣбовати 'to need, require', from Proto-Slavic *trěbovati, derived from *trěba 'need, requirement').

потревожить.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from тревожить ('to disturb, alarm'), derived from тревога ('alarm, anxiety, commotion'), likely connected with отвага or older тривога.

потренироваться.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('for a while, a bit') + тренироваться ('to train, practice', from тренировать + -ся, borrowed via German trainieren or French entraîner from English train).

потрудиться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from трудиться ('to labor, take pains'), derived from труд ('labor, toil, effort'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *trudъ ('toil, hardship').

history.meaning: to take the trouble, to bother

потрясти.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + трясти ('to shake, jolt', inherited from Old East Slavic трясти, from Proto-Slavic *tręsti 'to shake, tremble').

history.meaning: to shake; to stun, deeply move

потухнуть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + тухнуть ('to go out, be extinguished', from Proto-Slavic *tuxnǫti 'to subside, die down', related to *tušiti 'to extinguish, quench').

history.meaning: to go out (of fire or light)

потянуть.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing/delimitative prefix по- + тянуть ('to pull, draw, stretch', Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti, with simplification of *gn -> н): 'to pull, give a tug'.

потянуться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed from потянуть ('to pull, stretch', from по- + тянуть 'to pull, draw', from Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti) + reflexive suffix -ся.

history.meaning: to stretch; to reach out, be drawn to

поужинать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from ужинать ('to have supper/dinner'), derived from ужин ('evening meal', originally 'midday/south meal'), from Old East Slavic ужинъ, derived from югъ / угъ ('south, midday sun', Proto-Slavic *jugъ).

поумнеть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + умнеть ('to grow smarter, become wiser'), derived from умный ('smart, wise', from ум 'mind, intellect', from Proto-Slavic *umъ).

поухаживать.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('for a while') + ухаживать ('to look after, tend; to court, woo', iterative derived from у- + ходить 'to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

history.meaning: to court or look after for a while

поучительный.etymology: Derived from поучить / поучать ('to instruct, teach, edify', from по- + учить 'to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti) + adjectival suffix -тельн-ый.

поучиться.etymology: Delimitative/perfective verb formed with prefix по- from учиться ('to learn, study'), reflexive of учить ('to teach'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *učiti.

пофантазировать.etymology: Formed from delimitative prefix по- ('a bit, for a while') + фантазировать ('to fantasize, daydream', borrowed via German phantasieren from Late Latin phantasiare, from Ancient Greek φαντασία 'imagination').

history.meaning: to fantasize, daydream for a while

похвала.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic похвала ('praise, laudation'), deverbal from похвалити ('to praise', from по- + Proto-Slavic *xvaliti, from *xvala 'praise').

похвалить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic похвалити (Proto-Slavic *poxvaliti), formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + хвалить ('to praise', from хвала 'praise', Proto-Slavic *xvala).

похвастаться.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from хвастаться ('to boast, brag'), derived from хвастать, from Proto-Slavic *xvastati ('to babble, brag', of expressive/onomatopoeic origin).

похитить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic похитити ('to snatch away, seize, abduct', corresponding to East Slavic похватить), formed from по- + Proto-Slavic *xytiti ('to snatch, catch, seize').

похищать.etymology: Imperfective of похитить, borrowed from Old Church Slavonic похищати ('to snatch away, abduct'), with the Church Slavonic reflex -щ- (*tj) from Proto-Slavic *poxytjati (*po- + *xytiti 'to seize').

похмелье.etymology: Prepositional-suffixal derivative formed from по ('after') + хмель ('hops; intoxication', from Old East Slavic хмѣль, Proto-Slavic *xъmelь) + neuter suffix -ье, literally 'the condition after intoxication'.

походу.etymology: Colloquial adverbialization of the prepositional phrase по ходу ('along the course [of events], by the look of things'), from по ('along, by') + ход ('course, movement', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

похоже.etymology: Neuter short form and adverb of похожий ('similar, resembling'), derived from походить ('to take after, resemble', from по- + ходить 'to walk, go'). Used both as a predicate ('it looks like, it is similar') and as a parenthetical discourse marker ('it seems, apparently').

history.meaning: similar → alike; it seems, looks like

похожий.etymology: Derived from походить ('to resemble, take after, go along someone's path'), built from the prefix по- ('along, after') and ходить ('to walk, go', Proto-Slavic *xoditi), with the alternation д > ж before the adjectival suffix -ий. Literally, 'walking in the same way, taking after'.

history.meaning: taking after in gait/manner → similar, resembling

похороны.etymology: Plural-only noun derived from похоронить ('to bury, inter'), from по- + хоронить ('to bury; originally to guard, keep safe, hide', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *xorniti).

похудеть.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix по- + худеть ('to grow thin, lose weight'), derived from худой ('thin, lean; bad', inherited from Proto-Slavic *xudъ 'thin, meager, poor').

похуже.etymology: Attenuative comparative form derived from prefix по- ('a bit, somewhat') + хуже ('worse', comparative of худой 'bad', from Proto-Slavic *xudje).

поцеловать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of целовать ('to kiss'), formed with the prefix по- from Old East Slavic цѣловати ('to greet, wish good health; to kiss'), derived from цѣлъ / целый ('whole, hale, healthy', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

history.meaning: whole, hale → to wish health in greeting, kiss

поцелуй.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from the imperative stem of поцеловать ('to kiss'), from по- + целовать ('to kiss, greet', originally 'to wish someone whole/healthy'), derived from целый ('whole, intact', Proto-Slavic *cělъ).

почва.etymology: Developed from earlier Russian подчва / почва ('sole of footwear; ground underfoot, underlying layer'), formed from prefix под- ('under') + root *čьva (related to чобот 'boot, shoe').

почему.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase по чему ('along/by what?, on account of what?'), combining the preposition по with чему, the dative singular of что ('what', from Old East Slavic чьто).

почесать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix по- from чесать ('to scratch, comb'), inherited from Old East Slavic чесати, from Proto-Slavic *česati ('to comb, scratch, strip').

починить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + чинить ('to repair, mend, put in order', derived from чин 'order, rank, proper arrangement', Proto-Slavic *činъ): 'to fix, mend, repair'.

history.meaning: order -> to arrange, put in order

почистить.etymology: Formed from the perfectivizing prefix по- + чистить ('to clean, brush, peel', Proto-Slavic *čistiti, derived from чистый 'clean, pure', Proto-Slavic *čistъ).
почистить.notes: First-person singular shows ст -> щ mutation: я почищу, ты почистишь.

почитать.etymology: Delimitative perfective formed with prefix по- ('for a while, a little') from читать ('to read'), inherited from Old East Slavic читати, iterative of чьсти ('to read, count, honor', Proto-Slavic *čitati).

почка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пъчька / почка ('bud, swelling; kidney'), diminutive of archaic *пъка ('swelling, bulge'), from Proto-Slavic *pъkati ('to swell, burst open, bud').

почта.etymology: Borrowed in the late seventeenth century via Polish poczta from Italian posta ('relay station where fresh horses are stationed; mail service'), originally the feminine past participle of Latin pōnere (posita 'placed, stationed').
почта.notes: Takes на for both 'at the post office' (на почте) and 'by mail / email' (отправить по почте).

почтальон.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French postillon (and Italian postiglione 'post-rider, mail coachman'), reshaped in Russian under the influence of почта ('mail, post').
