продолжаться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of продолжать ('to continue, prolong'), derived from продолжить, built on долгий ('long'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *dьlgъ ('long').

продолжение.etymology: Verbal noun from продолжить ('to continue, prolong, lengthen', formed from prefix про- + должить, derived from долгий 'long', from Proto-Slavic *dъlgъ) + suffix -ение.

продохнуть.etymology: Formed from prefix про- + дохнуть ('to breathe, take a breath', from Proto-Slavic *dъxnǫti, from the root of дух 'breath, spirit').

продуктовый.etymology: Adjective formed with -овый from продукты ('foodstuffs, groceries'), plural of продукт ('product, produce'), borrowed via German Produkt from Latin prōductum ('something brought forth', from prōdūcere).

history.meaning: that which is produced, brought forth

продумать.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') from думать ('to think'), inherited from Old East Slavic думати ('to take counsel, think'), from Proto-Slavic *dumati (from *duma 'thought, counsel').

history.meaning: to think through, to plan out

продуть.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('through') from дуть ('to blow'), inherited from Old East Slavic дути (дую), from Proto-Slavic *duti ('to blow').

history.meaning: to blow through; catch a chill/draft; (colloq.) lose a game

продюсер.etymology: Borrowed in the 20th century from English producer ('film, theatrical, or music producer'), derived from produce, from Latin producere ('to lead or bring forth', from pro- 'forth' + ducere 'to lead').

history.meaning: person overseeing film or stage production

проезд.etymology: Deverbal noun from проехать / проезжать ('to drive or ride through'), formed from prefix про- ('through, past') + езд (from ездить / ехать 'to ride, travel', from Proto-Slavic *ězdъ).

проездом.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of проезд ('passage, journey through', from про- + езд, Proto-Slavic *ězdъ), literally 'by way of passing through'.

проект.etymology: Borrowed under Peter the Great (early 18th century, often spelled прожект from French before settling on проект after German Projekt) from Latin prōiectum ('something thrown forth, plan, design'), neuter past participle of prōicere ('to throw forward, stretch out', from prō- 'forth' + iacere 'to throw').

проектировать.etymology: Formed in Russian from проект ('project, engineering design', borrowed via German Projekt from Latin prōiectum 'something thrown forward, plan') with the verbal suffix -ировать.

history.meaning: design, project -> to design, engineer, plan

проехать.etymology: Formed from про- ('past, through, covering a distance') + ехать ('to go by vehicle, drive, ride', Proto-Slavic *jěxati): 'to drive past, drive through, or travel a certain distance'.
проехать.notes: Conjugates with the suppletive present/future stem ед-: я проеду, ты проедешь.

проехаться.etymology: Formed from prefix про- + ехать ('to ride, drive', from Proto-Slavic *ěxati) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to go for a short ride; colloquially to run over a topic or person, take a dig at').

history.meaning: to take a ride; to have a dig at

прожаренный.etymology: Past passive participle of прожарить ('to fry or roast thoroughly'), formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + жарить ('to fry, roast', from жар 'heat, embers', Proto-Slavic *žarъ).

прожарить.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + жарить ('to fry, roast, broil', derived from жар 'heat, glowing embers', from Proto-Slavic *žarъ, related to *gorěti 'to burn').

прожевать.etymology: Formed with the completive prefix про- ('thoroughly, all the way through') + жевать ('to chew'), inherited from Old East Slavic жевати / жьвати and Proto-Slavic *žьvati ('to chew', directly cognate with English chew and German kauen).

прожечь.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through') + жечь ('to burn', inherited from Old East Slavic жечи, from Proto-Slavic *žeťi 'to burn').

history.meaning: to burn through, burn a hole in

проживать.etymology: Imperfective of прожить ('to live through, reside; to spend'), formed from prefix про- + живать (iterative of жить 'to live', from Proto-Slavic *žiti).

прожить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прожити ('to live through a period; to spend'), formed from perdurative prefix про- + жить ('to live', from Proto-Slavic *žiti).

history.meaning: to live (for a time); to get by

прожорливый.etymology: Derived from прожора ('glutton') / прожрать ('to devour, eat away', from prefix про- + жрать 'to devour, gorge', from Proto-Slavic *žьrati 'to swallow, devour') + adjectival suffix -ливый.

прозвенеть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix про- + звенеть ('to ring, jingle, clink'), inherited from Old East Slavic звьнѣти and Proto-Slavic *zvьněti, related by ablaut to звон ('ringing, peal') and звук ('sound').

прозвище.etymology: Derived with suffix -ище from прозвать ('to call by a byname, nickname'), formed from про- + звать ('to call, name', inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъvati).

прозрачно.etymology: Adverb formed from прозрачный ('transparent, pellucid, clear'), borrowed with Old Church Slavonic vocalism -зрач- from *prozračьnъ ('looking through'), built on про- ('through') + зракъ ('sight, look', from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti 'to see, look').

прозрачный.etymology: Borrowed from Church Slavonic прозрачьнъ ('transparent, seeing through'), formed from prefix про- ('through') + зракъ ('sight, look, vision', non-pleophonic Church Slavonic reflex of Proto-Slavic *zorkъ, from *zьrěti 'to see, look') + -ный.

проигранный.etymology: Past passive participle of проиграть ('to lose in a game or contest'), formed with prefix про- (indicating loss) from играть ('to play', from Proto-Slavic *jьgrati).

проиграть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix про- (in the sense of loss, forfeiture, or spending through an action) and играть ('to play'), from Old East Slavic играти and Proto-Slavic *jьgrati.

history.meaning: to lose (in a game, bet, or contest)

проиграться.etymology: Formed from prefix про- (indicating loss or exhaustion) + играть ('to play, gamble', from игра 'game, play', from Proto-Slavic *jьgra) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to gamble away all one's money').

произведение.etymology: Verbal noun from произвести ('to bring forth, produce, create'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic произведение ('bringing forth, creation'), from про- + из- + вести ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *vesti), calquing Latin prōductiō.

производительность.etymology: Abstract noun derived from производительный ('productive', from производить 'to produce, bring forth', from про- + из- + водить 'to lead', calquing Latin producere) + suffix -ость.

производственный.etymology: Adjective formed from производство ('production, manufacture, industry'), derived from производить ('to produce, bring forth'), from про- + из- + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi).

произвол.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic произволъ ('free will, choice, pleasure'), deverbal from произволити ('to choose, prefer, will', from про- + из- + волити 'to will, wish', from воля 'will, freedom', Proto-Slavic *voľa); shifted in Russian to 'unchecked self-will, arbitrary rule'.

произносить.etymology: Imperfective of произнести ('to pronounce, utter, deliver [a speech]', a Church Slavonic calque of Latin pronuntiare / Ancient Greek προφέρω), formed from про- + из- ('forth, out') + носить ('to carry, bear', Proto-Slavic *nositi).

произойти.etymology: Perfective counterpart of происходить ('to happen, occur; to originate from'), formed from про- ('forth, through') + из- / изо- ('out of') + йти / идти ('to go', Proto-Slavic *iti). Literally, 'to come forth out of', whence 'to come to pass, happen, occur'.

history.meaning: to come forth, issue → to happen, take place

проинспектировать.etymology: Perfective formed with prefix про- from инспектировать ('to inspect'), borrowed via German inspizieren from Latin īnspectāre / īnspicere, īnspectum ('to look into, examine').

происходить.etymology: Imperfective verb borrowed from or modeled on Old Church Slavonic происходити ('to go forth, issue from, originate'), formed from про- ('forth, through') + ис- / из- ('out of') + ходити ('to go, walk'). From 'coming forth, originating', it developed the modern meaning 'to happen, take place'.

history.meaning: to happen, occur; to originate from

происшествие.etymology: Derived with Church Slavonic vocalism and consonantism from происшедший (past active participle of произойти 'to happen, take place, come forth', from про- + из- + ити 'to go', Proto-Slavic *jьti) + suffix -ствие.

пройтись.etymology: Formed from пройти ('to walk through, pass, go over', from про- + идти 'to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to take a short walk, stroll; to go over').

history.meaning: to take a stroll; to go over

прокатить.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through, past, for a distance') + катить ('to roll, wheel, drive', inherited from Old East Slavic катити, from Proto-Slavic *katiti 'to roll').

history.meaning: to take for a ride; (colloquial) to pass muster, work

прокатиться.etymology: Reflexive of прокатить ('to roll past; to take for a ride', from про- + катить 'to roll', from Proto-Slavic *katiti) + -ся ('to roll along; to go for a ride').

history.meaning: to roll; to give a ride
to roll past; to go for a ride

проклясть.etymology: Formed with prefix про- from клясть (кляну, 'to curse, swear'), inherited from Old East Slavic прокляти, from Proto-Slavic *pro-klęti ('to curse, execrate', from *klęti 'to swear, curse').

проклятие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проклятиѥ ('curse, malediction, anathema'), verbal noun from прокляти ('to curse, damn', from про- + кляти 'to swear, curse', from Proto-Slavic *klęti).

проклятый.etymology: Past passive participle of проклясть ('to curse, damn'), inherited from Old East Slavic проклятыи, from про- + клясть ('to curse, swear', from Proto-Slavic *klęti).

проклятье.etymology: Colloquial and poetic variant of проклятие ('curse; damn!'), with East Slavic contraction -ье for Church Slavonic -ие, derived from проклясть ('to curse', from про- + Proto-Slavic *klęti).

пролежать.etymology: Formed with the perdurative prefix про- ('through a whole span of time') + лежать ('to lie', inherited from Old East Slavic лежати and Proto-Slavic *ležati).

history.meaning: to lie (somewhere for a specified period of time)

пролететь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пролетѣти ('to fly through or past'), formed from prefix про- ('through, past') + лететь ('to fly', from Proto-Slavic *letěti).

пролить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пролити (Proto-Slavic *proliti), formed from про- ('out, forth, accidentally') + лить ('to pour', Proto-Slavic *liti): 'to spill, shed (liquid)'.
пролить.notes: Future tense uses the -ль- stem: я пролью, ты прольёшь; past tense про́лил, пролила́.

промах.etymology: Deverbal noun from промахнуть / промахнуться ('to swing past the mark, miss'), formed from про- ('past, by') + махать / махнуть ('to wave, swing', inherited from Proto-Slavic *maxati).

промилле.etymology: Borrowed via German Promille from Medieval/Modern Latin pro mille ('per thousand, for each thousand'), modeled on pro cento ('per hundred') from Latin pro ('for, per') + mille ('thousand').

промокнуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from про- ('all the way through') + мокнуть ('to get wet', from мокрый 'wet', Proto-Slavic *mokrъ): 'to get soaked right through, get drenched'.

history.meaning: to get soaked through, get drenched

промокнуть.notes: In the sense 'to get soaked through', past tense drops -ну-: он промок до нитки ('he got soaked to the skin').

промолчать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic промълчати ('to keep silent'), formed from prefix про- + молчать ('to be silent', from Proto-Slavic *mьlčati).

промывать.etymology: Imperfective of промыть ('to wash out, rinse thoroughly'), formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + мывать (iterative of мыть 'to wash', from Proto-Slavic *myti).

промыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic промыти ('to wash through, rinse'), formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + мыть ('to wash', from Proto-Slavic *myti).

пронести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пронести ('to carry through or past'), formed from prefix про- ('through, past') + нести ('to carry, bear', from Proto-Slavic *nesti); impersonally пронесло means 'danger passed by without hitting'.

history.meaning: to carry past; (impersonal) to blow over, dodge trouble

пронзить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic проньзити ('to pierce through, stab'), formed with prefix про- ('through') from ньзити / нъзити ('to pierce, thrust in', Proto-Slavic *nьziti, with Proto-Slavic third palatalization *g > *z from the root of нож 'knife' and заноза 'splinter').

проникать.etymology: Imperfective of проникнуть ('to penetrate, get through'), borrowed from or influenced by Old Church Slavonic проникати / проникнути ('to bend forward, peer into, penetrate', from про- + никнути 'to bend down, bow, sprout', from Proto-Slavic *niknǫti).

пропавший.etymology: Past active participle of пропасть ('to fall through, disappear, be lost'), formed with prefix про- ('through, away') from пасть ('to fall', inherited from Proto-Slavic *pasti).

пропадать.etymology: Imperfective of пропасть ('to fall through, disappear, be lost, perish'), formed from prefix про- ('through, away') + падать ('to fall', iterative of пасть, from Proto-Slavic *padati / *pasti).

history.meaning: to disappear, go missing, go to waste

пропасть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пропасти (Proto-Slavic *propasti), formed from про- ('through, away into nowhere') + пасть ('to fall', Proto-Slavic *pasti, stem пад-): literally 'to fall through out of sight', hence 'to vanish, go missing, get lost'.
пропасть.notes: Conjugates with the dental stem пад-: я пропаду, он пропадёт; past tense пропал, пропала. (A noun homonym про́пасть 'precipice, abyss' is stressed on the first syllable.)

прописать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прописати ('to write out, depict, register'), formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + писать ('to write', from Proto-Slavic *pisati).

history.meaning: to prescribe (medicine); to register officially at an address

пропить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пропити ('to squander on drink'), formed from prefix про- (indicating spending or loss) + пить ('to drink', from Proto-Slavic *piti).

history.meaning: to spend or lose by drinking
to drink away, squander on drink

пропуск.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from пропустить / пропускать ('to let pass through; to omit, skip', from prefix про- 'through' + пустить 'to let go', Proto-Slavic *pustiti).

пропускать.etymology: Imperfective of пропустить ('to let through; to omit, skip, miss'), formed from prefix про- ('through, past') + пускать ('to let go, allow', from Proto-Slavic *pustiti / *puskati).

history.meaning: to let pass; to skip, miss
to let through; to miss, skip

пропустить.etymology: Formed with the prefix про- ('through, past') + пустить ('to let go, allow to pass', from Old East Slavic пустити and Proto-Slavic *pustiti). Depending on context, 'letting something pass by' means either 'to let someone through' or 'to miss, skip'.

history.meaning: to let pass; to miss, skip

проработать.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('for a certain duration; thoroughly') from работать ('to work'), derived from работа ('work'), from Proto-Slavic *orbota.

history.meaning: to work (for a time); to work through thoroughly

прорвать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic проръвати ('to tear through, breach'), formed from prefix про- ('through') + рвать ('to tear, rend', from Proto-Slavic *rъvati).

прорваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of прорвать ('to tear through, breach'), formed with prefix про- ('through') from рвать ('to tear, rend'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *rъvati.

history.meaning: to break through, to pull through

пророк.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пророкъ ('prophet', a calque of Ancient Greek προφήτης 'one who speaks forth, prophet'), formed from про- ('forth, fore-') + *rokъ (ablaut noun from рещи 'to speak, say', Proto-Slavic *reťi).

пророчество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пророчьство ('prophecy', calquing Ancient Greek προφητεία), derived from пророкъ ('prophet', from про- + *rokъ 'speech') + abstract suffix -ьство.

просечь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic просѣчи ('to cut or hew through'), formed from prefix про- ('through') + сечь ('to cut, chop, hew', from Proto-Slavic *sěťi); in modern colloquial Russian figuratively 'to cut to the heart of a matter, figure out'.

history.meaning: to cut through; (colloquial) to figure out, see through

просить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic просити ('to ask, beg, request'), from Proto-Slavic *prositi, continuing the Proto-Indo-European root *preḱ- ('to ask, entreat'), cognate with Latin precārī ('to pray, entreat'), German fragen ('to ask'), and Lithuanian prašyti ('to ask').

проследить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') and следить ('to track, watch, keep an eye on'), derived from след ('footprint, track', from Proto-Slavic *slědъ).

history.meaning: to track down; to see to it, make sure

просмотреть.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through; past, overlooking') + смотреть ('to look, watch', from Proto-Slavic *sъmotriti).

history.meaning: to look through, review; to overlook

проспаться.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('thoroughly, to completion') + спать ('to sleep', from Proto-Slavic *sъpati) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to sleep until fully rested or sober').

history.meaning: to sleep off drunkenness, sober up by sleeping

проспект.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century (originally during the laying out of the long straight avenues of Saint Petersburg, such as Nevsky Prospekt, first called першпектива) from Latin prōspectus ('distant view, vista, straight avenue opening a long perspective'), from prōspicere ('to look forward into the distance').

history.meaning: broad straight city avenue; printed prospectus

проспорить.etymology: Formed from prefix про- (indicating loss, as in проиграть) + спорить ('to argue, bet, dispute', derived from спор 'dispute, argument', from Proto-Slavic *sъporъ).

history.meaning: to lose a bet or argument

просроченный.etymology: Past passive participle of просрочить ('to let a deadline or term expire, miss a due date'), formed from prefix про- ('past, beyond') + срок ('fixed time, deadline, term', from Old Church Slavonic сърокъ 'agreement, appointed time', from съ- + рещи 'to speak, stipulate').

history.meaning: to miss a deadline, let expire

просрочиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive of просрочить ('to let a deadline pass, expire', derived from prefix про- 'past' + срок 'term, expiration date', from Old Church Slavonic сърокъ 'appointed time') + -ся.

history.meaning: to let a deadline or term pass

простить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic простити ('to set free, release from debt or guilt, forgive'), from Proto-Slavic *prostiti, a denominative verb from *prostъ ('free, straight, unencumbered, simple', modern Russian простой). Literally 'to make someone free of an obligation'.
простить.notes: The imperative **Простите!** ('Forgive me! / Excuse me!') is slightly weightier and more deferential than **Извините!**.

просто.etymology: Adverb and particle formed from the short neuter singular of простой ('simple, plain, straight'), from Old East Slavic простъ ('straight, upright, simple, free'), from Proto-Slavic *prostъ (literally 'standing forward, straight', from *pro- 'forward' + *stati 'to stand').

просто-напросто.etymology: Reduplicated intensive adverb formed from просто ('simply', from простой 'simple, plain', from Proto-Slavic *prostъ 'straight, simple, free') + напросто ('out and out, simply', from на- + просто).

простоватый.etymology: Attenuative adjective formed with suffix -оватый ('somewhat, rather') from простой ('simple, plain'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *prostъ ('straight, simple, free').

простой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic простыи and Proto-Slavic *prostъ ('straight, upright, unbent; plain, simple, ordinary; free'), originally a compound of *pro- ('forward') + *-st- (the root of стоять / стать 'to stand'): literally 'standing straight forward, unbent, uncomplicated'.
простой.notes: Notice how Polish prosty still means both 'straight' (idź prosto 'go straight') and 'simple', whereas in Russian простой specialized to 'simple, plain'.

просторно.etymology: Adverb formed from просторный ('spacious, roomy'), derived from простор ('open space, expanse'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pro-storъ ('wide open space', from *sterti 'to spread, extend').

пространство.etymology: Derived from пространный ('spacious, vast, expansive', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic пространьнъ, from про- + страна 'side, land, expanse', from Proto-Slavic *storna, related to *prosterti 'to stretch out') + suffix -ство.

простудиться.etymology: Reflexive of простудить ('to chill thoroughly, cause to catch cold'), formed from prefix про- ('through') + студить ('to cool, chill', from студа / стужа 'cold, frost', from Proto-Slavic *studiti) + -ся.

простыня.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic простыня ('plain unsewn length of linen cloth, bedsheet'), derived from простой ('simple, plain, unornamented', from Proto-Slavic *prostъ) with the feminine noun suffix -ыня: originally 'a plain, simple sheet of linen cloth' as opposed to tailored or embroidered garments.

просыпать.etymology: Formed from prefix про- (indicating an accidental slip or spilling past the edge) + сыпать ('to pour, strew [dry, granular substances]', inherited from Proto-Slavic *sypati).

просыпаться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of проснуться ('to wake up'), formed from the prefix про- ('through, out of') and the iterative stem -сыпать (with lengthened zero-grade vowel ы < *ū from the root of спать 'to sleep', Old East Slavic съпати, Proto-Slavic *sъpati, from PIE *swep- 'to sleep').

протереть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic протерети (Proto-Slavic *proterti), formed from про- ('across a surface; or right through') + тереть ('to rub, wipe', Proto-Slavic *terti): both 'to wipe clean with a cloth' and 'to rub/wear a hole through'.

history.meaning: to wipe off, wipe clean; to wear through

протереть.notes: Future tense uses the zero-grade stem -тр-: я протру, ты протрёшь; past tense протёр, протёрла.

протест.etymology: Borrowed via German Protest or French protêt / protestation from Italian protesto, deverbal from protestare, from Late Latin protestari ('to declare publicly, testify, protest', from pro- 'forth, before' + testari 'to bear witness', from testis 'witness').

протестовать.etymology: Borrowed via Polish protestować or German protestieren from French protester, from Late Latin protestari ('to declare publicly, protest', from pro- 'before' + testari 'to testify').

протечь.etymology: Formed from про- ('through') + течь ('to flow, run', Proto-Slavic *tekti): 'to leak through (of water, a roof, or a pipe)'.
протечь.notes: Conjugates: он протечёт, они протекут; past tense протёк, протекла.

против.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic противу / противъ ('against, opposite, facing'), from Proto-Slavic *protivъ, derived from the prefix *proti / *proty ('towards, facing, against'; compare Ancient Greek προτί / πρός and Sanskrit práti).

противень.etymology: A folk-etymological reshaping of German Bratpfanne 'roasting pan' (braten 'to roast' + Pfanne 'pan'). Because Bratpfanne was unfamiliar to Russian ears, speakers adapted its beginning toward the native word против.
противень.notes: Drops the fleeting vowel е in oblique cases: противень -> на противне.

противник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic противьникъ ('adversary, enemy'), formed with agent suffix -ник from противный ('opposite, opposing'), from против ('against, opposite', Proto-Slavic *protivъ).

противный.etymology: Derived from против ('against, opposite', from Old East Slavic противу, from Proto-Slavic *protivъ, related to *prostъ) + adjectival suffix -ный; shifted from 'opposite, contrary, opposing' to 'repugnant, nasty, unpleasant'.

противопоказанный.etymology: Medical calque of New Latin contraindicatus / French contre-indiqué, formed from противо- ('against, contra-', from против) + показанный ('indicated, prescribed', past passive participle of показать 'to show, indicate', from по- + казать, Proto-Slavic *kazati).

протирать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of протереть ('to wipe clean; wear through'), showing the regular Slavic lengthened imperfective root vowel -тир- from -тер- (тереть 'to rub').

протрезветь.etymology: Formed from perfective prefix про- + трезветь ('to become sober', derived from трезвый 'sober', borrowed from Old Church Slavonic трѣзвъ 'sober', corresponding to East Slavic тверезый, from Proto-Slavic *terzvъ).

протухнуть.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('thoroughly') + тухнуть ('to rot, go bad, spoil', from Proto-Slavic *tuxnǫti, related to *tuxlъ 'rotten, putrid' and *duxъ 'smell, breath').

протухший.etymology: Past active participle of протухнуть ('to go bad, rot', formed from prefix про- + тухнуть 'to spoil, become putrid', from Proto-Slavic *tuxnǫti).

проучить.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('thoroughly') + учить ('to teach, instruct; in older usage also to flog or punish for instruction', inherited from Old East Slavic учити, from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

проучиться.etymology: Formed from perdurative prefix про- ('through a period of time') + учиться ('to study, learn', reflexive of учить 'to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

профессионал.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century via French professionnel / English professional, derived from Medieval Latin professiōnālis and Classical Latin professiō ('public declaration, occupation, profession', from profitērī 'to declare openly').

профессиональный.etymology: Borrowed via French professionnel or German professionell, or formed from профессия ('profession, occupation', from Latin professio 'public declaration, occupation') + adjectival suffix -альн-ый.

профессия.etymology: Borrowed via German Profession, Polish profesja, or French profession from Latin professiō ('public declaration, occupation, profession'), from profitērī ('to declare openly, profess').

профессор.etymology: Borrowed via German Professor from Latin professor ('public teacher, one who professes an art or science'), an agent noun from profitērī ('to declare openly, profess', from pro- 'forth' + fatērī 'to acknowledge, speak').

профи.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial clipping of профессионал ('professional', via German Profi or directly shortened in Russian from профессионал, ultimately from Latin professio).

профилактика.etymology: Learned medical/technical borrowing via German Prophylaktik / French prophylactique from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, 'precautionary, guarding beforehand'), from προφυλάσσω ('to keep guard before').

профильный.etymology: Derived from профиль ('profile, side view; specialized field or specialization', borrowed via French profil and German Profil from Italian profilo 'outline, side view', from profilare 'to draw in outline') + adjectival suffix -ный.

history.meaning: profile; specialized, relevant to a field

прохладный.etymology: Formed with the prefix про- ('moderately, refreshingly') and suffix -ный from the South Slavic / Church Slavonic root хлад- ('coolness, cold', compare native East Slavic холод in холодный, from Proto-Slavic *xoldъ).

morphemes.meaning: cool, cold (Church Slavonic counterpart of холод)

прохладный.notes: Notice how Russian uses the Church Slavonic root хлад- for 'pleasantly cool' (прохладный) and the native East Slavic pleophonic root холод- for 'cold' (холодный).

прохлаждаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of прохлаждать ('to cool, refresh'), borrowed with Old Church Slavonic non-pleophonic -хлад- (compare native прохолодиться) from про- + хладъ ('coolness', Proto-Slavic *xoldъ), shifting from 'to take one's ease in the cool shade' to 'to idle, loaf'.

history.meaning: to cool oneself, refresh oneself, take leisure

проход.etymology: Deverbal noun from проходить ('to walk through, pass'), formed from prefix про- ('through') + ход ('going, passage', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

проходить.etymology: Formed from the prefix про- ('through, past') + ходить ('to walk, go', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi). Means both 'to walk through, pass by' and, in hospitality (Проходите, пожалуйста!), 'to come on in (through the doorway)'.

history.meaning: to come in, pass through, elapse

прохождение.etymology: Verbal noun from проходить ('to pass through, undergo'), with the Church Slavonic stem alternation -жд- (*dj) from прохожденииѥ, derived from про- + ходить ('to go, walk', Proto-Slavic *xoditi).

прохожий.etymology: Substantivized adjective inherited from Old East Slavic прохожии ('passing by, transient'), formed from проходить ('to walk past, pass by', from про- + ходить, Proto-Slavic *xoditi, with East Slavic ж from *dj).

процедить.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through') + цедить ('to strain, filter, draw off liquid', inherited from Old East Slavic цѣдити, from Proto-Slavic *cěditi 'to strain, filter', related to *čistъ 'clean, pure').

history.meaning: to strain, filter; to mutter through clenched teeth

процедура.etymology: Borrowed via German Prozedur and French procédure ('procedure, course of action'), derived from Old/Middle French proceder ('to proceed'), from Latin procedere ('to go forward, advance', from pro- 'forward' + cedere 'to go').

процедурная.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from процедурный ('relating to medical procedures', from процедура 'procedure, treatment', ultimately from French procédure / Latin procedere), standing for процедурная комната ('treatment room').

history.meaning: treatment room (in a clinic or hospital)

процент.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Prozent (or Dutch procent) from Italian per cento and Medieval Latin per centum ('by the hundred, per hundred', from centum 'hundred', Indo-European cognate of Russian сто).

rootFamily.gloss: hundred (native Slavic cognate of Latin centum)

прочесать.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + чесать ('to comb, scratch, card wool', inherited from Old East Slavic чесати, from Proto-Slavic *česati 'to comb, scrape').

history.meaning: to comb through; (figurative) to search an area thoroughly

прочий.etymology: Borrowed via Old Church Slavonic прочии ('remaining, other'), derived from the archaic adverb прочь / проче ('away, beyond, further on'), from Proto-Slavic *pročь, formed from the Indo-European root *pro- ('forward, forth, away'; compare Latin procul 'far off' and Russian про-). Originally meaning 'that which lies further on, the rest', it became the adjective for 'other, remaining'.

history.meaning: other, remaining (esp. in и прочее 'et cetera')

прочитать.etymology: Formed as the perfective of читать ('to read') by adding the prefix про- ('through from start to finish'). The base verb читать comes from Old East Slavic читати (iterative of чисти / чьту, Proto-Slavic *čьtǫ, *čisti 'to count, reckon, read, honour').

прочность.etymology: Abstract noun in -ость formed from прочный ('durable, solid, lasting'), derived from прок ('benefit, reserve for the future, durability', originally 'what remains over/ahead', from Proto-Slavic *prokъ).

прочный.etymology: Derived with suffix -ный from прок ('lasting use, benefit for the future', as in впрок), inherited from Old East Slavic прокъ ('remainder, future'), from Proto-Slavic *prokъ ('remaining, further', from *pro).

прочь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прочь ('away, off, aside') and Proto-Slavic *pročь, an adverbial formation built on *prokъ ('remaining, other, further away', itself from *pro 'forward, away').
прочь.notes: Also used in the idiom не прочь (+ infinitive): я не прочь выпить чаю ('I wouldn't mind having some tea').

прошлое.etymology: Substantivized neuter singular of прошлый ('past, bygone'), contracted from прошедший / прошъдъшии, past active participle of пройти ('to pass, go by'), from про- + идти (stem шьд-, Proto-Slavic *pro-šьdlъ).

прощай.etymology: Fossilized second-person singular imperative of прощать ('to forgive, pardon', borrowed from or influenced by Old Church Slavonic прощати, imperfective of простити 'to forgive, release', from простъ 'free, simple', Proto-Slavic *prostъ); literally 'forgive me!' spoken at parting.

прощальный.etymology: Derived from прощаться ('to say goodbye, bid farewell', originally 'to ask mutual forgiveness at parting', from прощать 'to forgive') + adjectival suffix -ный.

прощать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прощати (imperfective of простити 'to pardon, forgive, set free', with щ < *stj; compare native East Slavic простить), from Proto-Slavic *prostiti (from *prostъ 'free, straight, simple').

прощаться.etymology: Reflexive/reciprocal form of прощать ('to forgive', from Old Church Slavonic прощати, derived from простъ 'free, simple', Proto-Slavic *prostъ), because traditional Russian parting involved asking one another's forgiveness ('прости / прощай').

history.meaning: to ask mutual forgiveness at parting -> to say goodbye

проще.etymology: Comparative of простой ('simple, plain, easy', inherited from Old East Slavic простыи, from Proto-Slavic *prostъ 'straight, simple'), with the Church Slavonic / literary palatalized comparative reflex -щ- (*stj).

прощение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic прощение ('release, pardon, forgiveness'), the verbal noun of простити / простить ('to forgive, release, set free'), derived from простъ ('simple, straight, free', Russian простой). The -щ- reflects the Old Church Slavonic outcome of Proto-Slavic *stj.

history.meaning: free, simple → to set free, pardon

прощение.notes: Common in the polite apology **Прошу прощения** ('I beg your pardon / excuse me').

проявить.etymology: Formed with prefix про- ('forth, out') from явить ('to show, reveal, manifest'), inherited from Old East Slavic явити, from Proto-Slavic *aviti ('to make clear, reveal').

history.meaning: to show, display, manifest; to develop (film)

проявление.etymology: Verbal noun from проявить ('to show, manifest, reveal; to develop photographic film', formed from prefix про- + явить 'to show, reveal', from Proto-Slavic *javiti) + suffix -ение.

проявлять.etymology: Imperfective of проявить ('to show, manifest, display'), formed from prefix про- + являть (from Proto-Slavic *javľati, iterative of *javiti 'to show, reveal', related to *javь 'wakefulness, reality').

прояснить.etymology: Formed from prefix про- ('through, thoroughly') + яснить ('to make clear', derived from ясный 'clear, bright', from Proto-Slavic *jasnъ).

пружинить.etymology: Derived in Russian from пружина ('spring'), which was formed with the suffix -ина from older Russian пругий ('elastic, taut, resilient', preserved in упругий 'elastic, springy', from Proto-Slavic *prǫgъ 'taut, springing', related to прясть / напрячь 'to stretch, strain').

history.meaning: spring -> to spring back, be springy

прыгнуть.etymology: Formed with the semelfactive suffix -нуть ('once') from прыгать ('to jump, leap'), an expressive East Slavic verb allied to the Proto-Slavic root *pręg- / *prǫg- ('to spring, snap, stretch taut', as in пружина 'spring' and пряжка).

прямо.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of прямой ('straight, direct'), from Old East Slavic прямъ ('straight, upright, frank'), from Proto-Slavic *prěmъ. Used both spatially ('straight ahead') and as an emphatic particle ('right, directly').

прямой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прямыи ('straight, direct, upright, frank'), from Proto-Slavic *prěmъ ('straight, direct').

прятать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic прятати ('to put away, tidy, bury, hide'), from Proto-Slavic *prętati ('to gather up, stow away, conceal'; compare Czech zpřátat 'to tidy away' and Slovene sprátati 'to clear away, store'). From 'clearing things away into storage', in Russian it became the standard verb for 'to hide, conceal'.

history.meaning: to stow away, put in order
to stow away, prepare for burial, conceal

прятаться.etymology: Formed by adding the reflexive postfix -ся to прятать ('to hide, put away'), inherited from Old East Slavic прятати and Proto-Slavic *prętati ('to put in order, tidy away, stow, bury'), which shifted in Russian from 'to stow safely away' to 'to hide, conceal'.

history.meaning: to stow away, put in order

прятаться.notes: Notice the striking semantic comparison with Polish sprzątać ('to tidy up, put things away in their places') vs. Russian прятать ('to hide away'). Present tense shows т -> ч: я прячусь, ты прячешься.

прятки.etymology: Plural noun derived from прятать ('to hide, conceal'), inherited from Old East Slavic прятати ('to put away, tidy, bury, hide'), from Proto-Slavic *prętati.

псевдоаллергический.etymology: Modern medical compound formed from prefixoid псевдо- ('pseudo-, false', from Ancient Greek ψευδο-, from ψεῦδος 'falsehood') + аллергический ('allergic', from аллергия 'allergy', coined by Clemens von Pirquet in 1906 from Greek ἄλλος 'other' + ἔργον 'work, reaction').

псих.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial back-formation / clipping from психопат ('psychopath') and психически больной ('mentally ill person'), ultimately from Ancient Greek ψυχή ('soul, mind, breath').

психануть.etymology: Colloquial semelfactive verb formed from психовать ('to freak out, lose one's temper', derived from псих 'psycho, nervous person', from Greek ψυχή 'soul, mind') + perfective semelfactive suffix -ануть.

history.meaning: to freak out, lose one's cool

психиатр.etymology: Borrowed via German Psychiater or French psychiatre (coined by Johann Christian Reil in 1808 with психиатрия / Psychiatrie), from Ancient Greek ψυχή ('soul, mind') + ἰατρός ('physician, healer').

психика.etymology: Borrowed via German Psychik from Ancient Greek ψυχική (sc. τέχνη or φύσις), feminine of ψυχικός ('of the soul or mind, mental'), from ψυχή ('soul, mind, breath').

history.meaning: pertaining to the soul or mind

психический.etymology: Derived via German psychisch or French psychique from Ancient Greek ψυχικός ('of the soul, mental'), from ψυχή ('soul, mind, life-breath') + Russian adjectival suffix -еский.

психовать.etymology: 20th-century colloquial verb formed with suffix -овать from псих ('hothead, neurotic person; fit of temper'), a back-formation/clipping from психопат or психический (from Ancient Greek ψυχή psukhḗ 'soul, mind').

психологический.etymology: Derived from психология ('psychology', borrowed from New Latin psychologia, from Ancient Greek ψυχή 'soul, mind' + -λογία 'study of') + adjectival suffix -ический (after German涵 psychologisch / French psychologique).

history.meaning: study of the mind or soul

психология.etymology: Borrowed via German Psychologie / French psychologie from New Latin psychologia, coined in the 16th century from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, 'soul, mind') + -λογία (-logía, 'study, discourse').

психопат.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from German Psychopath, coined from Ancient Greek ψυχή ('soul, mind') + πάθος ('suffering, ailment, passion').

психушка.etymology: Twentieth-century colloquial condensation of психиатрическая больница ('psychiatric hospital'), formed from the stem псих- (from Ancient Greek ψυχή 'mind, soul') + colloquial suffix -ушка.

птица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пьтица and Proto-Slavic *pъtica ('bird'), originally a diminutive in *-ica of *pъta ('bird', preserved in Russian птаха / пташка), from an Indo-European root for 'little one, chick' or 'flying creature' (compare Latin putus 'little boy', pullus 'chick', and Sanskrit putrá).

публика.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish publika or German Publikum / French public from Latin pūblica (rēs) / pūblicus ('pertaining to the people, public', from populus 'people').

публиковать.etymology: Borrowed in the early 18th century via Polish publikować (and German publizieren) from Latin publicare ('to make public, publish'), derived from publicus ('of the people, public', from populus 'people').

публично.etymology: Adverb derived from публичный ('public', borrowed via Polish publiczny from Latin publicus 'belonging to the people, public') + -о.

пугать.etymology: Imperfective verb (paired with напугать / испугать 'to frighten, scare'). Attested in East Slavic (compare dialectal пуга 'whip; owl', Ukrainian пугач 'eagle owl'), generally considered by Vasmer to be of expressive or onomatopoeic origin (from the hooting or sudden cry *pug- used to startle birds or animals, or from the crack of a whip).

пугаться.etymology: Reflexive of пугать ('to frighten, scare', iterative related to dialectal пужать, of uncertain ultimate origin; Vasmer connects it with Old Russian пуга 'whip, lash' or an expressive root *pug-) + -ся.

пуговица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пугъвица ('round button, knob'), formed with suffix -овица from Proto-Slavic *pǫgy (genitive *pǫgъve 'knob, swelling, globule, button'), from PIE *pew- / *poug- ('to swell, puff up', cognate with пухнуть).

пудра.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Puder from French poudre ('fine powder, cosmetic powder, powdered sugar'), which evolved from Old French poldre (with epenthetic d) from Latin pulvis, stem pulver- ('dust, fine powder').

пуля.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish kula (dissimilated or blended in East Slavic to пуля) or directly via Middle Low German / French boule ('ball, sphere'), ultimately from Latin bulla ('bubble, round boss, knob').

пункт.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Punkt or Polish punkt from Medieval Latin pūnctum ('point, dot, item or clause in a document'), originally the neuter past participle of Latin pungere ('to prick, pierce', because a point on parchment was made by pricking with a stylus).

cognates.meaning: point (from the same Latin source via French)

пускать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пускати and Proto-Slavic *puskati ('to let go, release, allow'), the imperfective counterpart of пустить (*pustiti), built on the same root as пустой ('empty, left free/deserted').

пусто.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пусто, the short neuter and adverbial form of пустой ('empty, deserted, hollow', Proto-Slavic *pustъ, cognate with Old Prussian pausto 'wild').

пустой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пустъ / пустыи ('empty, deserted, uninhabited'), from Proto-Slavic *pustъ, closely cognate with Old Prussian pausto ('wild').

пустота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пустота ('emptiness, desolation, vanity'), formed from пустой ('empty, deserted, hollow', from Proto-Slavic *pustъ) + abstract noun suffix -ота.

пусть.etymology: Formed in Russian by apocope (loss of finalunstressed -и) from пусти, the second-person singular imperative of пустить ('to let, allow', Proto-Slavic *pustiti): literally 'let!, allow!', grammaticalized into the optative/hortative particle 'let (him/her/them)...'.
пусть.notes: Followed by a third-person present or future tense verb: пусть он войдёт ('let him come in'), пусть будет так ('let it be so').

пустяк.etymology: Formed in Russian with the expressive noun suffix -як from пустой ('empty, hollow, vain, trivial', from Old East Slavic пустыи and Proto-Slavic *pustъ): literally 'an empty, inconsequential thing, a trifle'.
пустяк.notes: In the plural, *Пустяки!* means 'It's nothing!, Don't mention it!, A mere trifle!'.

путать.etymology: Derived from путо / пута ('fetters, hobbles for a horse's legs, bonds'), inherited from Old East Slavic путо, from Proto-Slavic *pǫto ('fetter, snare, cord', related to пнуть / пядь).

history.meaning: to tangle; to confuse, mix up

путеводитель.etymology: A native compound of путь 'way, road' and водитель 'one who leads', joined by the linking vowel -е-: literally 'a way-leader'. It names a guidebook, and in older usage also a guide.

путь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic путь and Proto-Slavic *pǫtь 'way, road, journey', from Proto-Indo-European *pontohs 'crossing, path', cognate with Latin pons ('bridge') and Sanskrit pantha ('road, path').
путь.notes: Unique masculine noun in Russian: it is masculine (добрый путь!), yet declines like a feminine -ь noun except in the instrumental singular (путём).

путёвка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from путёвый / путевой ('relating to a road, journey, or dispatch'), derived from путь ('way, road, journey'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *pǫtь ('path, way').

пух.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пухъ ('down, fluff, puff'), from Proto-Slavic *puxъ ('breath, puff, fluff, swelling'), of onomatopoeic/expressive origin from Proto-Indo-European *pew- / *pux- ('to blow, puff, swell', cognate with пухнуть 'to swell').

пушистый.etymology: Adjective formed with suffix -истый from пух ('down, fluff, soft fur'), inherited from Old East Slavic пухъ, from Proto-Slavic *puxъ ('breath, puff, soft down', of onomatopoeic origin).

пчелиный.etymology: Possessive/relational adjective formed with the animal suffix -иный from пчела ('bee'), inherited from Old East Slavic бъчела and Proto-Slavic *bъčela ('bee', an expressive root connected with buzzing).

пыль.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic пыль ('fine floating dust'), derived from the Proto-Slavic root *pyl- / *pux- ('to blow, billow, puff up into the air', related to пылать 'to blaze' and пух 'down, fluff', or cognate with Latin pulvis 'dust').
пыль.notes: Takes the stressed locative -и́ after в: весь в пыли́ ('covered in dust').

пыльный.etymology: Derived in Russian from пыль ('dust') with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'dusty, covered with dust'.

пытать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пытати ('to ask, inquire, investigate, test; to interrogate under torture'), from Proto-Slavic *pytati ('to inquire, search into, probe'). While its reflexive derivative пытаться kept the mild sense 'to try, attempt' (and Ukrainian питати means simply 'to ask'), non-reflexive пытать in Russian specialized in legal history (from judicial interrogation on the rack) to mean 'to torture'.

history.meaning: to ask, investigate; to question under torture

пытаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of пытать ('to test, try, question'), inherited from Old East Slavic пытати ('to ask, investigate, strive') and Proto-Slavic *pytati.

history.meaning: to test → to try, attempt, endeavour

пьющий.etymology: Present active participle of пить ('to drink; to drink alcohol habitually', inherited from Old East Slavic пити, from Proto-Slavic *piti, from PIE *peh₃(y)- 'to drink').

пьянка.etymology: Colloquial noun in -ка formed from пьяный ('drunk, intoxicated'), inherited from Old East Slavic пияныи / пьяныи, from Proto-Slavic *pьjanъ ('drunk', old participle from *piti 'to drink').

пьянство.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пияньство, formed with abstract suffix -ство from пьяный ('drunk'), from Proto-Slavic *pьjanъ (from *piti 'to drink').

пьяный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пияныи ('drunk, intoxicated'), from Proto-Slavic *pьjanъ, historically an archaic passive/stative participle in *-nъ formed from *piti ('to drink', Russian пить; compare Sanskrit pīyáte 'is drunk'), meaning 'having drunk deeply'.

пюре.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French purée ('mashed vegetables or pulse, purée'), feminine past participle of Old French purer ('to purify, strain, squeeze through a sieve'), from Late Latin purare ('to purify'), from purus ('pure').

пятеро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пятеро, from Proto-Slavic collective numeral *pętero ('group of five'), derived from *pętь ('five', Russian пять) + collective numeral suffix *-ero (from PIE *-ero-).

пятка.etymology: Formed as the diminutive (now standard everyday form) of пята ('heel', Old East Slavic пята, Proto-Slavic *pęta 'heel'), derived from the nasal root *pęti ('to stretch, brace, kick', compare Lithuanian pentis 'heel; back of an axe blade').

rootFamily.gloss: heel (archaic/idiomatic, as in с головы до пят 'from head to toe')

пятнашка.etymology: Colloquial noun derived from пятнадцать ('fifteen', from Old East Slavic пять на десяте 'five on ten') + colloquial suffix -шка, denoting fifteen units (such as 15 rubles, 15 thousand, or the 15-puzzle).

пятница.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пятница (Old Church Slavonic пѧтьница), formed from пятый / пять ('fifth / five'). Slavic weekday names count cleanly from Monday: вторник (2nd), среда (middle), четверг (4th), пятница (5th).

пятничный.etymology: Formed in Russian from пятница ('Friday', derived from пятый 'fifth' — the fifth day of the week after Sunday, with ц -> ч before -ный) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

пятно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пятно ('brand mark, scar, spot'), from Proto-Slavic *pętьno ('mark, stamp, spot'), connected by Vasmer either with *pęta ('heel, footprint impression') or *pęti ('to stretch, strike, brand').

пяточка.etymology: Affectionate double diminutive derived from пятка ('heel', diminutive of пята 'heel', inherited from Old East Slavic пята, from Proto-Slavic *pęta 'heel, spur') + suffix -очка.

пять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic пять (Old Church Slavonic пѧть), from Proto-Slavic *pętь ('five', originally a feminine abstract noun 'a group of five'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe ('five'), cognate with English five, German fünf, Ancient Greek πέντε, and Sanskrit páñca.

пятьдесят.etymology: Compound numeral inherited from Old East Slavic пять десятъ ('five tens, fifty'), from Proto-Slavic *pętь desętъ, where пять ('five') governed the archaic genitive plural десятъ ('of tens', from десять 'ten').

пёсик.etymology: Diminutive in -ик of пёс ('dog, hound'), inherited from Old East Slavic пьсъ, from Proto-Slavic *pьsъ ('dog').

раб.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic рабъ ('slave, servant', corresponding to native East Slavic робъ with initial ро- from *or-), from Proto-Slavic *orbъ ('orphan, servant, slave'), from PIE *h₃órbʰos ('orphan; person deprived of free status', cognate with Latin orbus and German Arbeit).

работа.etymology: The older Russian form робота could mean work, servitude or bondage. Vasmer connects it with the same historical family as раб, a slave. The everyday modern meaning is work; the older senses explain a history of compelled labour.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: работа

работа.notes:
- Collocations: *найти работу* (find a job), *уйти с работы* (leave work), *на работе* (at work).
- *За работу!* is an idiomatic call to get started.

работать.etymology: Denominative verb built on работа ('work, labour'), generalizing the South Slavic / Church Slavonic initial ра- (compare Old East Slavic роботати and Czech pracovat / robotovat), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *orbota ('hard labour').

работаться.etymology: Impersonal reflexive verb derived from работать ('to work', from работа 'work', inherited from Old East Slavic робота / Old Church Slavonic работа, from Proto-Slavic *orbota) + -ся, expressing one's disposition or ease in working.

history.meaning: to feel like working, for work to go well/poorly

работающий.etymology: Present active participle of работать ('to work, function, operate', derived from работа 'work', from Proto-Slavic *orbota).

работодатель.etymology: Nineteenth-century compound calque of German Arbeitgeber ('employer', literally 'work-giver'), formed from работа ('work', from Proto-Slavic *orbota) + linking vowel -о- + датель ('giver', from дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati).

работящий.etymology: Colloquial adjective formed on the participial pattern -ящий from работать ('to work'), derived from работа ('work, labor'), from Proto-Slavic *orbota.

рабочий.etymology: Derived from работа ('work, labor', Old Russian робота) with palatalization of т > ч before the adjectival suffix -ий (compare Old Church Slavonic работии / рабочии). Functions both as an relational adjective ('working, work-related') and as a substantivized noun ('worker, laborer').

равиоли.etymology: Borrowed from Italian ravioli (plural of raviolo 'stuffed pasta parcel'), from Northern Italian dialectal raviöl, usually traced to Medieval Latin rabiola / rapa ('turnip, herb filling') or Italian riavvolgere ('to wrap up').

равно.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic initial ра- (compare native East Slavic ро- in ровный 'even, straight') from Old Church Slavonic равьно ('equally, alike'), from Proto-Slavic *orvьno.

history.meaning: equally, equals; all the same (всё равно)

morphemes.meaning: equal, even (Church Slavonic doublet of ровн-)

равно.notes: Used constantly in the idiom мне всё равно ('it's all the same to me / I don't mind') and in arithmetic: два плюс два равно четыре ('two plus two equals four').

равнодушный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic равьнодушьнъ (originally 'unanimous, of like mind', calquing Greek ἰσόψυχος, from равный 'equal, even' + душа 'soul'; later reinterpreted after French indifférent / German gleichgültig as 'even-minded, unmoved, indifferent').

history.meaning: of equal spirit; later unmoved, indifferent

равномерно.etymology: Adverb formed from равномерный ('uniform, even-measured'), compound of равный ('equal', Old Church Slavonic равьнъ) + мера ('measure', Proto-Slavic *měra).

равный.etymology: Borrowed with Old Church Slavonic initial ра- (compare native East Slavic ровный 'flat, even') from равьнъ ('flat, level, equal'), from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ ('level, even').

рагу.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French ragoût ('savory stew'), deverbal from ragoûter ('to revive the taste, whet the appetite'), from re- + à + goût ('taste', from Latin gustus).

ради.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ради and Old Church Slavonic ради ('for the sake of, on account of'), from Proto-Slavic *radi, an old locative/instrumental case form connected with *radъ ('glad, willing, caring for', modern рад) and Old Persian rādiy ('on account of, for the sake of').

history.meaning: for the sake of, because of
for the sake of (governs the genitive case)

радовать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic радовати ('to gladden, make joyful'), derived from рад ('glad, joyful', from Old East Slavic радъ, from Proto-Slavic *radъ) + verbal suffix -овать.

радоваться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic радоватися and Proto-Slavic *radovati sę ('to rejoice, be glad'), a denominal verb built on рад ('glad, joyful', Proto-Slavic *radъ) with the suffix -ова- and reflexive -ся.
радоваться.notes: Takes the dative case for the cause of joy: радоваться весне ('to rejoice at the spring'), радоваться успехам ('to be glad at successes').

радостный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic радостьныи, formed with suffix -ный from радость ('joy, gladness'), derived from рад ('glad'), from Proto-Slavic *radostь.

радость.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic радость and Proto-Slavic *radostь ('joy, gladness'), formed from рад ('glad, joyful', Proto-Slavic *radъ) with the feminine abstract-noun suffix -ость.

раз.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic разъ ('stroke, blow; one time, occasion'), from Proto-Slavic *razъ, an o-grade noun derived from *rězati ('to cut, strike', modern Russian резать). Just as French coup and German Schlag shifted from 'a strike' to 'one time', a single stroke of counting became Russian раз ('time, occasion; one!').

разбивать.etymology: Imperfective of разбить ('to smash, break to pieces'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart, into pieces') from бивать / бить ('to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti).

разбиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of разбиться ('to break into pieces, shatter, crash'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, into pieces') + биваться (iterative of бить 'to strike, beat', from Proto-Slavic *biti) + -ся.

разбирать.etymology: Imperfective of разобрать ('to take apart, sort out, take one by one'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart') and lengthened-grade iterative stem -бирать from брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

history.meaning: to take apart; to take, grab (one each); to sort out

разбитый.etymology: Originally the past passive participle of разбить ('to smash, shatter, break into pieces', from раз- 'apart, in pieces' + бить 'to beat, strike', Proto-Slavic *biti), used as an adjective meaning 'broken, shattered, smashed'.
разбитый.notes: In Russian, разбить / разбитый is used for brittle things that shatter into pieces (a cup, plate, window, or mirror), whereas сломать / сломанный is used for mechanisms, furniture, or bones.

разбить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic разбитии, formed from the prefix раз- ('apart, into pieces') and бить ('to beat, strike', Old East Slavic бити, Proto-Slavic *biti). Literally, 'to strike into pieces, smash, shatter'.

history.meaning: to break, smash, shatter; to wreck (a car)

разбиться.etymology: Reflexive of разбить ('to smash, break into pieces', inherited from Old East Slavic розбити / разбити, from prefix раз- 'apart' + бить 'to beat, strike', from Proto-Slavic *biti) + -ся.

разбогатеть.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- (indicating full development or intensity of a state) + богатеть ('to grow rich', derived from богатый 'rich, wealthy', from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ, derived from *bogъ 'share, fortune, wealth').

разболеться.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- (indicating an action gaining intensity) + болеть ('to hurt, ache, be ill', from боль 'pain', from Proto-Slavic *bolěti) + reflexive suffix -ся ('to start hurting badly or fall seriously ill').

history.meaning: to start aching badly; to fall thoroughly ill

разбрасывать.etymology: Imperfective of разбросать ('to scatter, throw about'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, in different directions') + брасывать (iterative of бросать 'to throw, cast', from Proto-Slavic *brъsati).

разбрасываться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective formed with prefix раз- ('in all directions, wastefully') and -ся from брасывать / бросать ('to throw, fling'), from Proto-Slavic *brosati.

разбудить.etymology: Formed from раз- ('out of a state, stirring up') + будить ('to wake someone up', Old East Slavic будити, Proto-Slavic *buditi, the ancient Indo-European o-grade causative of *bʰewdʰ- 'to be awake, aware', cognate with бодрый and Sanskrit bodhati).
разбудить.notes: Transitive ('to wake someone else up'); to wake up on one's own is проснуться.

разваливаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective of развалиться ('to collapse, fall apart, sprawl'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart') and -ся from валить ('to topple, tumble'), from Proto-Slavic *valiti.

развалиться.etymology: Reflexive of развалить ('to pull down, demolish', formed from prefix раз- 'apart' + валить 'to topple, tumble, roll', from Proto-Slavic *valiti) + -ся ('to fall apart, collapse; to sprawl').

развалюха.etymology: Colloquial noun derived from развалиться / разваливаться ('to fall apart, crumble', from раз- + валить 'to topple', Proto-Slavic *valiti) + expressive colloquial noun suffix -юха.

разведка.etymology: Noun in -ка formed from разведать ('to find out, explore, reconnoiter'), derived from раз- + ведать ('to know, inquire'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *vědati ('to know').

разведённый.etymology: Past passive participle of развести ('to lead apart, separate, divorce; to dilute'), formed from раз- ('apart') + вести ('to lead', from Proto-Slavic *vesti).

развернуть.etymology: Formed with the prefix раз- ('apart, un-') + вернуть ('to turn, roll', from Proto-Slavic *vьrnǫti / *vьrtěti 'to turn'): 'to unroll, unfold, unwrap'.

развернуться.etymology: Formed from раз- ('apart, un-, all the way around') + вернуться ('to turn', from вертеть / вернуть) + -ся: both 'to unwrap/unfold' and 'to turn right around (180 degrees) to face or go the opposite way'.

развесить.etymology: Formed with the distributive prefix раз- ('around, in various places') + весить ('to hang', causative of висеть 'to be hanging', from Proto-Slavic *věsiti).

history.meaning: to hang up around, string out

развешивать.etymology: Imperfective of развешать ('to hang up in various places'), formed from prefix раз- ('around, in various places') + вешать ('to hang', iterative of весить, from Proto-Slavic *věšati).

развеяться.etymology: Reflexive of развеять ('to scatter in the wind, dispel', formed from prefix раз- 'apart, away' + веять 'to blow, winnow', from Proto-Slavic *vějati) + -ся ('to disperse; figuratively to clear one's head, unwind').

history.meaning: to dispel, scatter in the wind
to disperse; to clear one's head, unwind

развиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of развиться ('to untwist, unroll; to develop, evolve', a semantic calque of French se développer / German sich entwickeln), formed from prefix раз- ('un-, out') + вивать (iterative of вить 'to twist, wind', from Proto-Slavic *viti) + -ся.

развитие.etymology: Verbal noun from развить / развиться ('to unroll, unwind; to develop', calquing French développement and German Entwicklung), formed from раз- ('un-, out') + вить ('to wind, twist', Proto-Slavic *viti) + -тие.

развитый.etymology: Past passive participle of развить ('to unwind; to develop', calquing French développé / German entwickelt), formed from prefix раз- + вить ('to twist, wind', from Proto-Slavic *viti).

развлекаться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of развлекать ('to divert, entertain', originally 'to draw/pull apart [one's thoughts from care]', calquing French distraire / divertir), built on Old Church Slavonic развлѣщи (from *velkti 'to draw, drag').

развод.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from разводить / развести ('to lead apart, separate; to dissolve a marriage; to breed; in slang, to string someone along / con'), built from раз- ('apart') + водить ('to lead', Proto-Slavic *voditi). Literally 'a leading apart', whence 'divorce' (and in modern colloquial slang, 'a scam, con, hustle').

history.meaning: leading apart, separation → divorce; (slang) scam, con

разводить.etymology: Imperfective of развести ('to lead apart, separate, divorce; to breed, raise; to dilute'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, in various directions') + водить ('to lead, conduct', from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to lead apart, divorce; to breed
to breed, raise; to divorce; (slang) to scam

разволноваться.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- (indicating rising intensity of a state) + волноваться ('to worry, be agitated', originally 'to surge in waves', derived from волна 'wave', from Proto-Slavic *vьlna).

history.meaning: to get worked up, become very nervous

разворовать.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- ('in all directions, completely') + воровать ('to steal, thieve', derived from вор 'thief; in 16th–17th c. Russian rebel, state criminal, impostor').

развязать.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix раз- ('apart, un-') and вязать ('to tie, bind, knot', inherited from Old East Slavic вязати, Proto-Slavic *vęzati). Means literally 'to untie, unbind' and figuratively 'to unleash, start (a war or quarrel): развязать войну'.

history.meaning: to untie, unknot; to unleash (a conflict)

развязывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the secondary imperfectivizing suffix -ывать from развязать ('to untie, unfasten'), built on prefix раз- ('apart, un-') + вязать ('to tie, bind', from Proto-Slavic *vęzati).

разгадать.etymology: Formed with the prefix раз- ('apart, unravelling') + гадать ('to guess, divine, ponder'), inherited from Old East Slavic гадати and Proto-Slavic *gadati ('to suppose, divine, speak').

history.meaning: to solve, figure out (a riddle, mystery, or code)

разгар.etymology: Deverbal noun from разгореться / разгораться ('to flare up, burn brightly'), formed from prefix раз- + гар- (ablaut grade of гореть 'to burn', from Proto-Slavic *gorěti / *garъ 'burning, heat').

разгибаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of разогнуться ('to unbend, straighten one's back'), formed from prefix раз- ('un-, apart') + гибать (iterative of гнуть 'to bend', from Proto-Slavic *gъbnǫti / *gybati) + -ся.

разгладиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form in -ся of разгладить ('to smooth out, iron flat'), formed with prefix раз- ('out flat') + гладить ('to smooth, stroke, iron', from гладкий 'smooth', Proto-Slavic *gladъkъ).

history.meaning: to smooth out → to smooth out, unpucker (of a wrinkled brow or cloth)

разговаривать.etymology: Formed in Russian as the imperfective of an older perfective разговорить, from раз- ('back and forth, in various directions') + говаривать (iterative of говорить 'to speak, talk', from говор 'talk, speech', Proto-Slavic *govorъ): 'to converse, talk with someone'.

history.meaning: to speak -> to converse, talk back and forth

разговор.etymology: Formed as a prefixal-stem noun from разговаривать ('to talk, converse', from раз- 'back and forth' + говор 'speech, talk', Proto-Slavic *govorъ): 'an exchange of speech, conversation, talk'.

разговорить.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- (indicating getting an action going thoroughly) + говорить ('to speak, talk', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

history.meaning: to get someone talking, draw into conversation

разговорчик.etymology: Diminutive of разговор ('conversation, talk', deverbal from разговориться / разговаривать 'to converse', from раз- + говорить 'to speak', Proto-Slavic *govoriti) + suffix -чик.

history.meaning: little chat; (in plural разговорчики!) backtalk, chatter

разгребать.etymology: Imperfective of разгрести ('to rake apart, shovel away, clear up'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, away') + гребать (iterative of грести 'to rake, row, scrape', from Proto-Slavic *grebti).

history.meaning: to rake aside; (figurative) to clear up a mess

разгром.etymology: Deverbal noun from разгромить ('to smash, rout, devastate'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, completely') + громить ('to smash, destroy, thunder against', from гром 'thunder', Proto-Slavic *gromъ).

разгромный.etymology: Adjective formed with -ный from разгром ('utter rout, devastation'), deverbal noun from разгромить ('to smash, rout'), from раз- + громить ('to smash, thunder against'), derived from гром ('thunder', Proto-Slavic *gromъ).

разгружать.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of разгрузить ('to unload'), from раз- ('apart, off, un-') + грузить ('to load', from груз 'load, cargo, heavy weight', Proto-Slavic *grǫzъ 'sinking weight, ballast', with з -> ж in the imperfective).

history.meaning: to unload (a truck, ship, or boxes)

разгрузить.etymology: Formed from reversative prefix раз- ('un-') + грузить ('to load; originally to sink, submerge under weight', derived from груз 'load, cargo', from Proto-Slavic *grǫziti 'to sink, load').

разгрузка.etymology: Action noun derived from разгрузить / разгружать ('to unload', from prefix раз- 'un-' + грузить 'to load', from груз 'cargo, load', Proto-Slavic *grǫziti) + suffix -ка.

раздать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic роздати / раздати (Proto-Slavic *orzdati), formed from раз- ('out in different directions, to several recipients') + дать ('to give', Proto-Slavic *dati): 'to hand out, distribute'.
раздать.notes: Conjugates like дать: я раздам, ты раздашь, он раздаст, они раздадут.

раздевать.etymology: Imperfective of раздеть ('to undress'), formed from reversative prefix раз- ('un-') + девать (iterative of деть 'to put, place; in clothing compounds to put on', from Proto-Slavic *děvati / *děti).

раздеваться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of раздевать ('to undress'), imperfective of раздеть, formed with prefix раз- ('un-, apart', by antonymic analogy with одеть 'to dress') from деть ('to put', Proto-Slavic *děti).

history.meaning: to take off one's coat; to undress

раздел.etymology: Deverbal noun from разделить ('to divide, partition, share'), inherited from Old East Slavic роздѣлъ / Old Church Slavonic раздѣлъ, from раз- ('apart') + делить ('to divide', from Proto-Slavic *děliti).

разделать.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- + делать ('to do, make, work, dress [skins, timber, meat]', from дело 'work, deed', from Proto-Slavic *dělati).

history.meaning: to dress, butcher, fillet (meat or fish)

разделение.etymology: Verbal noun from разделить ('to divide, separate'), inherited from Old Church Slavonic раздѣление, from раз- ('apart') + дѣлити ('to divide, share', Proto-Slavic *děliti).

разделить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic раздѣлити ('to divide, part, distribute'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart, into parts') + делить ('to divide, share', from Proto-Slavic *děliti, related to *dělъ 'part, share').

разделка.etymology: Action noun derived from разделать / разделывать ('to dress, butcher, fillet meat or fish', from prefix раз- + делать 'to work, dress', from Proto-Slavic *dělati) + suffix -ка.

разделывать.etymology: Imperfective of разделать ('to dress/butcher a carcass, finish off, prepare'), formed with prefix раз- ('apart') from делать ('to do, make, work on'), from Proto-Slavic *dělati.

раздельно.etymology: Adverb formed from раздельный ('separate, distinct'), derived from разделить ('to divide apart'), from раз- + делить ('to divide', Proto-Slavic *děliti).

разделять.etymology: Imperfective of разделить ('to divide, separate; to share'), borrowed from or influenced by Old Church Slavonic раздѣляти, from раз- ('apart') + делить ('to divide, share', from Proto-Slavic *děliti).

history.meaning: to divide; to share (views or feelings)

раздеть.etymology: Formed from reversative prefix раз- ('un-') + деть ('to put, place; in одеть/надеть to dress', inherited from Old East Slavic дѣти, from Proto-Slavic *děti 'to put, do').

раздеться.etymology: Reflexive of раздеть ('to undress', formed from reversative prefix раз- 'un-' + деть 'to put, dress', from Proto-Slavic *děti) + -ся ('to undress oneself').

раздражать.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic раздражати ('to provoke, incite, irritate'), imperfective of раздражити, formed from раз- + дражити ('to tease, provoke, irritate', cognate with Russian дразнить, from Proto-Slavic *dražiti).

раздражённый.etymology: Past passive participle of раздражить ('to irritate, provoke, anger', from Old Church Slavonic раздражити, from раз- + дражити 'to tease, provoke', Proto-Slavic *dražiti).

раздумывать.etymology: Imperfective of раздумать ('to ponder, deliberate; to change one's mind'), formed with prefix раз- from думать ('to think'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *dumati.

раздумье.etymology: Derived from раздумать / раздумывать ('to ponder, muse, deliberate', from prefix раз- + думать 'to think, meditate', from дума 'thought, council', Proto-Slavic *duma) + neuter abstract suffix -ье.

разливать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from разлить ('to pour out into vessels; to spill'), built on prefix раз- ('out, into several containers') + ливать (iterative of лить 'to pour', from Proto-Slavic *liti).

history.meaning: to pour out (tea, soup into cups/bowls); to spill

разливаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive of разлиться ('to overflow, spill out, spread'), formed from prefix раз- ('out, in all directions') + ливаться (iterative of лить 'to pour', from Proto-Slavic *liti) + -ся.

разлить.etymology: Formed with prefix раз- ('out, apart, into vessels') from лить ('to pour'), inherited from Old East Slavic лити (лию), from Proto-Slavic *liti ('to pour').

различать.etymology: Imperfective of различить ('to distinguish, tell apart'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic различати / различити ('to differentiate, distinguish', derived from ликъ / лице 'face, form, appearance', Proto-Slavic *likъ, *lice).

разложить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic розложити / Old Church Slavonic разложити ('to lay out, spread out, distribute'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, out') + ложить ('to lay, place', from Proto-Slavic *ložiti).

history.meaning: to lay out, spread out; to decompose

разлучить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разлучити ('to separate, part, sever', corresponding to Old East Slavic розлучити), formed from раз- ('apart') + лучити ('to join, destin, separate', from Proto-Slavic *lǫčiti).

размазать.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- ('out, over a surface') + мазать ('to smear, daub, anoint', inherited from Old East Slavic мазати, from Proto-Slavic *mazati).

размах.etymology: Deverbal noun from размахнуть / размахивать ('to swing wide, brandish'), formed from prefix раз- ('wide, apart') + мах ('swing, stroke', from махать 'to wave, swing', from Proto-Slavic *maxati).

разменять.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- ('into smaller parts, apart') + менять ('to change, exchange', from мена 'exchange', from Proto-Slavic *měniti / *měna).

history.meaning: to change (money), break a larger note

размер.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from размерить ('to measure out, proportion'), built from prefix раз- ('out, apart') + мерить / мера ('to measure / measure', from Proto-Slavic *měra, from PIE *meh₁- 'to measure').

history.meaning: to measure out → size, dimension, meter

разместить.etymology: Formed from prefix раз- ('around, in respective places') + местить ('to place, locate', derived from место 'place, space, site', from Proto-Slavic *město).

разминаться.etymology: Reflexive imperfective of размяться ('to stretch one's limbs, warm up'), formed with prefix раз- from мять (мну, iterative -минать, 'to knead, rub, limber up'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *męti ('to knead, press').

history.meaning: to knead, press, work until supple
to warm up, to limber up

разморозить.etymology: Formed from reversative prefix раз- ('un-, de-') + морозить ('to freeze', derived from мороз 'frost, freezing cold', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *morzъ).

разморозиться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive of разморозить ('to defrost, thaw', formed from reversative prefix раз- 'un-' + морозить 'to freeze', from мороз 'frost', Proto-Slavic *morzъ) + -ся.

размытый.etymology: Past passive participle of размыть ('to wash out, blur with water'), formed from prefix раз- + мыть ('to wash', from Proto-Slavic *myti).

history.meaning: to wash out → blurred, washed-out, smudged

размыть.etymology: Formed with the prefix раз- ('apart, dissolving') + мыть ('to wash', inherited from Old East Slavic мыти and Proto-Slavic *myti): 'to wash away, erode with water, blur ink or paint'.

history.meaning: to wash out, blur (with water or moisture)

размышлять.etymology: Imperfective of размыслить ('to ponder, reflect, deliberate'), borrowed from or influenced by Old Church Slavonic размышляти (with Church Slavonic -шл- from *slj), from раз- + мыслити ('to think', from мысль 'thought', Proto-Slavic *myslь).

разнервничаться.etymology: Inceptive/intensive reflexive formed with circumfix раз-...-ся from нервничать ('to be nervous, fret'), derived from нервный / нерв ('nerve', borrowed via German Nerv / French nerf from Latin nervus 'sinew, nerve').

history.meaning: to get worked up, to get all nervous

разнести.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic рознести / Old Church Slavonic разнести ('to carry in different directions, scatter'), formed from prefix раз- ('apart, around') + нести ('to carry', from Proto-Slavic *nesti).

history.meaning: to deliver around; to smash to pieces

разница.etymology: Derived with the feminine noun suffix -ица from разный ('different, various'), which goes back via Old Church Slavonic разьнъ ('apart, different') to Proto-Slavic *orzьnъ, built on the prefix/preposition *orz- (Russian раз- 'apart, asunder').
разница.notes: Used constantly in какая разница? ('what's the difference? / what does it matter?').

разногласие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic разногласиѥ ('discord, dissonance, disagreement', calquing Ancient Greek διαφωνία), compound of разный ('different, diverse', from *orznъ) + -о- + гласъ ('voice, sound', Church Slavonic reflex of *golsъ) + -ие.

разнообразный.etymology: Compound adjective (modeled on Old Church Slavonic разнообразьнъ, calquing Ancient Greek ποικιλόμορφος / πολυειδής) formed from разный ('different, various', from *orznъ) + -о- + образ ('form, shape, image', from Proto-Slavic *oborzъ) + -ный.

разносить.etymology: Imperfective of разнести ('to carry around, deliver; to scatter, smash'), formed from prefix раз- ('around, apart') + носить ('to carry', iterative of нести, from Proto-Slavic *nositi).

history.meaning: to deliver around, hand round; to wear in (shoes)

разносторонний.etymology: Compound adjective formed from разный ('different, various', from Church Slavonic разнъ, Proto-Slavic *orznъ) + -о- + сторонний (from сторона 'side, direction', East Slavic pleophonic form of Proto-Slavic *storna).

разный.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic prefix vocalism раз- (alongside older native розный) from Old Church Slavonic разьнъ ('divided, separate, different'), built on the prefix/preposition *orz- ('apart, asunder', related to резать 'to cut') + adjectival suffix -ный.

разобрать.etymology: Formed with prefix разо- ('apart') from брать ('to take'), inherited from Old East Slavic бърати, from Proto-Slavic *bьrati ('to take, gather').

history.meaning: to take apart, to dismantle; to sort out

разобраться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from разобрать ('to take apart, sort out, dismantle'), built from раз- / разо- ('apart') + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati). From the concrete sense of 'sorting items out one by one', it developed the figurative sense 'to figure out, understand thoroughly, settle a matter'.

history.meaning: to sort out → to figure out, get to the bottom of

разогревать.etymology: Imperfective of разогреть ('to warm up, reheat'), formed with prefix разо- ('thoroughly, up') from греть ('to warm, heat'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *grěti.

разозлить.etymology: Perfective formed with intensive prefix разо- from злить ('to anger, make mad'), derived from злой ('angry, wicked, evil'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *zъlъ.

разойтись.etymology: Formed from prefix разо- ('apart, in different directions') + идти ('to go, walk', from Proto-Slavic *jьti) + reflexive suffix -сь ('to walk apart, disperse, part ways, divorce').

history.meaning: to disperse, part ways, break up

разок-другой.etymology: Colloquial compound adverbial phrase formed from разок (diminutive in -ок of раз 'time, occasion', from Proto-Slavic *razъ 'stroke, time') + другой ('another, a second', from Proto-Slavic *drugъ).

разорвать.etymology: Formed with the prefix разо- ('apart, in pieces') + рвать ('to tear, rip, rend'), inherited from Old East Slavic ръвати and Proto-Slavic *rъvati ('to tear, pluck').

history.meaning: to tear in two, tear up

разорить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic разорити ('to destroy, demolish, lay waste'), formed from раз- ('apart') + орити ('to tear down, overthrow, destroy', Proto-Slavic *oriti).

history.meaning: to ruin, to bankrupt, lay waste

разослать.etymology: Formed from prefix разо- ('out in various directions') + слать ('to send', inherited from Old East Slavic сълати, from Proto-Slavic *sъlati).

history.meaning: to send out in various directions

разочарование.etymology: Verbal noun from разочаровать ('to disenchant, disappoint'), formed as a calque on French désenchantement / German Enttäuschung from раз- ('un-') + очарование ('enchantment, charm', from чары 'magic, sorcery').
