собранный.etymology: Past passive participle of собрать ('to gather, assemble, collect', from Proto-Slavic *sъbьrati); as an adjective of personality, 'collected, focused, self-disciplined'.

собрать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic събрати and Proto-Slavic *sъbьrati ('to gather together, collect'), formed from со- (from *sъ- 'together') + брать ('to take', Proto-Slavic *bьrati, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- 'to carry, bear').

history.meaning: to gather, collect, pack (a bag), assemble

собрать.notes: Future tense inserts the fleeting vowel -е- in the root: я соберу, ты соберёшь, они соберут.

собраться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from собрать ('to gather, collect, assemble'), inherited from Old East Slavic събьратися, from Proto-Slavic *sъbьrati sę, built from *sъ- ('together') + *bьrati ('to take', Russian брать). From 'gathering oneself or one's belongings together for a journey', it developed the everyday meaning 'to get ready, intend, plan to do something'.

history.meaning: to gather, meet up; to get ready, plan to

rootFamily.gloss: to be going to, get ready (impf.)

собственно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb and parenthetical discourse marker formed with -о from собственный ('one's own, proper'), derived from Church Slavonic собьство ('individuality, property, essence', from собь / себе 'oneself', Proto-Slavic *sebě / *sobě).

history.meaning: strictly speaking, actually, as a matter of fact

собственный.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic собьствьныи ('peculiar to oneself, one's own'), derived from собьство ('individuality, property') and собь ('one's own self, possession'), built on the reflexive pronoun stem *sob- / *seb- (compare себя 'oneself').

history.meaning: one's own self → one's own, personal

событие.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic събытиѥ ('occurrence, realization, event'), verbal noun from събытися / сбыться ('to come to pass, happen'), formed from съ- + быти ('to be').

совать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic совати (1 sg. сую, 'to thrust, shove, poke, hurl'), from Proto-Slavic *sovati ('to thrust, push, toss'), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷewH- / *skewH- ('to throw, shove', cognate with Lithuanian šauti 'to shoot, shove').

совершенно.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of совершенный ('complete, utter, perfect'), which comes via Old Church Slavonic съврьшенъ ('brought to the top, completed, perfected') from съврьшити ('to bring to the summit/completion', built on верх 'top, summit', Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ).

совершить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвръшити ('to bring to the top, crown, complete, accomplish'), formed from съ- + връшити / вершить ('to top off, complete'), derived from връхъ / верх ('top, summit, peak', from Proto-Slavic *vьrxъ). Literally, 'to bring to the summit or completion', whence 'to accomplish, perform, commit (a deed, crime, or feat)'.

history.meaning: top, peak → to crown, bring to completion

совесть.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съвѣсть ('conscience, shared/inner knowledge'), formed in the 9th century by Cyril and Methodius's circle as a structural calque of Ancient Greek συνείδησις (syneídēsis, 'shared knowledge, inward moral awareness, conscience', which likewise calqued into Latin cōnscientia and English conscience), from съ- ('with, together') + вѣсть ('knowledge', from вѣдѣти 'to know', PIE *weyd-).

совет.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic съвѣтъ ('counsel, deliberation, council', translating Ancient Greek συμβούλιον and βουλή), formed from съ- ('together') + вѣтъ ('speech, counsel, pact', from Proto-Slavic *větъ, preserved in ответ 'answer', привет 'greeting', and обет 'vow'). In 1905 and 1917, Совет (literally 'council') also became the title of workers' and deputies' councils, whence советский ('Soviet').

советник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic съвѣтьникъ ('counselor, adviser'), formed from совет ('council, advice') + the personal agent suffix -ник.

советовать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съвѣтовати ('to take counsel, advise'), formed with -овать from съвѣтъ (modern Russian совет, 'counsel, advice, council', calquing Greek συμβούλιον from *sъ- 'with' + *větъ 'speech, counsel').

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

советчик.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -чик from советовать / совет ('to advise / advice'), denoting one who gives advice or counsel.

совладелец.etymology: Prefixal derivative formed with со- ('co-, joint') from владелец ('owner, proprietor'), itself derived from владеть ('to own, rule', Church Slavonic form corresponding to Proto-Slavic *volděti).

совместить.etymology: Perfective verb borrowed from Church Slavonic съвъмѣстити ('to place together in one space, combine'), composed of съ- ('together') + въмѣстити ('to fit into a place', from мѣсто 'place', Proto-Slavic *město).

совместный.etymology: Adjective formed from совместно / совместить ('together in one place, combined'), composed of со- ('together') + в- ('in') + место ('place', Proto-Slavic *město) + adjectival suffix -ный.

совмещать.etymology: Imperfective verb corresponding to совместить ('to combine, hold concurrently'), with the Church Slavonic reflex -щ- (< *-stj-) from съ- + въмѣщати (from мѣсто 'place').

history.meaning: to fit together in one place
to combine, hold two roles at once

совпадать.etymology: Borrowed or modelled on Old Church Slavonic съвпадати / съпадати ('to fall together'), built from prefix со- (в-) ('together') + падать ('to fall', from Proto-Slavic *padati), a semantic calque of Latin coincidere (from co- + incidere 'to fall together, coincide') and Greek συμπίπτειν.

history.meaning: to fall together → to coincide, match up

совпасть.etymology: Formed in Russian with the prefix со- ('together') + впасть ('to fall into', from в- + пасть 'to fall'), as a calque of Latin coincidere ('to fall together in one place or time').

соврать.etymology: Perfective counterpart of врать ('to lie, tell a lie'), formed with the perfectivizing prefix со- and врать (from Old East Slavic вьрати 'to babble, chatter, lie', Proto-Slavic *vьrati).

современно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from современный ('contemporary, modern'), a Church Slavonic-modeled calque of Late Latin contemporāneus (со- 'with, together' + время, stem времен- 'time').

history.meaning: in a modern way, up to date

современность.etymology: Formed from современный ('contemporary, modern', an Old Church Slavonic calque of Greek σύγχρονος from съ- 'with' + время 'time') + the abstract noun suffix -ость.

совсем.etymology: Univerbation of the Old Russian prepositional phrase со всѣмь ('with everything, altogether'), composed of the preposition съ / со ('with') + всѣмь, the instrumental singular of весь ('all, everything').

history.meaning: completely, quite; (with не) not at all

согласие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съгласие ('harmony of voices, accord, consent', with South Slavic non-pleophonic гласъ 'voice'), calquing Ancient Greek συμφωνία (symphōnía, from σύν 'with' + φωνή 'voice').

согласиться.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic съгласити сѧ ('to sound together, be in harmony, agree'), formed from со- ('together, with') + глас ('voice', the South Slavic / Church Slavonic counterpart of native East Slavic голос, Proto-Slavic *golsъ) + -ить + -ся: literally 'to join one's voice with another's' (compare Latin concordāre and German übereinstimmen).
согласиться.notes: Takes с + instrumental for the person or opinion agreed with (согласиться с другом) and на + accusative for a proposal (согласиться на предложение).

согласный.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съгласьнъ ('harmonious, of one voice, agreeing'), a calque of Ancient Greek σύμφωνος (sýmphōnos, 'sounding together, agreeing'), formed from съ- ('with, together') + гласъ ('voice', East Slavic голос) + -ный.
согласный.notes: Usually used in the short predicate form when expressing agreement: **Я согласен / согласна** ('I agree').

согласованный.etymology: Past passive participle of согласовать ('to coordinate, bring into agreement, harmonize'), derived from согласие / согласный (from Old Church Slavonic съгласьнъ 'harmonious, in accord', from съ- + гласъ 'voice').

содержание.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ние from содержать ('to contain, maintain, support financially'), from Old Church Slavonic съдьржание ('holding together, maintenance, contents').

содержать.etymology: Inherited via Church Slavonic съдьржати ('to hold together, contain, maintain', often calquing Latin continēre or Ancient Greek συνέχειν), composed of со- ('together') + держать ('to hold', Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

history.meaning: to contain; to maintain, support financially

содержаться.etymology: Reflexive passive/middle verb formed with -ся from содержать ('to contain, keep, maintain'), from со- + держать (Proto-Slavic *dьržati).

соединить.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic съѥдинити ('to unite, join into one', with initial ѥ- rather than East Slavic о- in один), composed of съ- ('together') + ѥдинити ('to make one', from ѥдинъ 'one', Proto-Slavic *jedinъ).

history.meaning: to connect, join, put through (by phone)

сожитель.etymology: Compound agent noun formed from со- ('together, co-') + житель ('dweller, inhabitant', from жить 'to live', Proto-Slavic *žiti), originally meaning 'fellow resident, housemate' and later also 'unmarried live-in partner'.

созреть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the resultative prefix со- from зреть ('to ripen, mature'), inherited from Old East Slavic зрѣти, from Proto-Slavic *zьrěti ('to ripen, grow mature', related to зерно 'grain').

history.meaning: to ripen completely; to mature (of a plan)

сойти.etymology: Perfective verb formed from the prefix с- / со- ('down from, off') and идти ('to go, walk'), continuing Old East Slavic съити and Proto-Slavic *sъniti ('to come down, descend; to come together').

history.meaning: to get off, descend; (с ума) to go mad

rootFamily.gloss: to go down; to go and return

сойтись.etymology: Formed from сойти ('to come together, go down', from prefix с-/со- + идти 'to go') + the reflexive particle -сь, expressing mutual convergence ('to come together, meet, agree').

сок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сокъ ('sap, plant juice, broth'), from Proto-Slavic *sokъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *sokʷós ('sap, resin, juice'), directly cognate with Lithuanian sãkai ('tree resin'), Ancient Greek ὀπός ('fig sap, plant juice'), and English sap.

соковыжималка.etymology: Compound instrument noun formed from сок ('juice, sap', Proto-Slavic *sokъ) + connecting vowel -о- + выжималка ('squeezer, wringer', formed with -лка from выжимать 'to squeeze out', from вы- + жать, Proto-Slavic *žęti).

сократить.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкратити ('to shorten, abridge', with South Slavic non-pleophonic -ра- corresponding to native Russian коротить / короткий), from Proto-Slavic *sъkortiti, from *kortъkъ ('short').

сокращать.etymology: Imperfective verb borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съкращати ('to shorten, abridge', with South Slavic -ра- and -щ- < *-tj-), corresponding to сократить, from Proto-Slavic *kortъkъ ('short').

сокращение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from сократить / сокращать ('to shorten, reduce, lay off'), from Old Church Slavonic съкращение ('shortening, abridgment').

сокровище.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic съкровище ('treasure, treasure-chamber'), formed from съкрыти / сокрыть ('to hide away, cover', built on крыть 'to cover') + the suffix -ище.

солдат.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century via German Soldat from Italian soldato ('mercenary, soldier who receives pay'), past participle of soldare ('to pay military wages'), from soldo ('coin, pay'), from Late Latin solidus ('gold coin').

солидарность.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century (adapted with the abstract noun suffix -ность) from French solidarité ('mutual responsibility, fellowship'), from solidaire ('jointly liable'), from Latin solidus ('whole, solid, undivided').

солидность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from солидный ('solid, substantial, respectable').

солидный.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French solide or German solid / solide (adapted with -ный) from Latin solidus ('firm, dense, substantial, sound').

солить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *soliti ('to season or preserve with salt'), denominal verb derived from *solь (Russian соль 'salt', from PIE *seh₂l- 'salt').

солнечный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сълньчьныи (Proto-Slavic *sъlnьčьnъ), the relational adjective derived from солнце ('sun', with ц -> ч before -ный) + the suffix -ный.

morphemes.meaning: sun (солнце, with fleeting е and ц -> ч)

солнечный.notes: Unlike солнце (where -л- is silent), the -л- in солнечный IS pronounced in standard Russian!

солнце.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сълньце and Proto-Slavic *sъlnьce ('sun'), originally a diminutive in *-ьce of Proto-Slavic *sъlnь, from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥ ('sun'), cognate with Latin sōl, Lithuanian saulė, and English sun.

morphemes.meaning: neuter diminutive suffix (now part of the base word)

солнце.notes: The consonant -л- is silent in standard pronunciation (pronounced [со́нце], spelled солнце), though it reappears clearly in солнышко and солнечный.

солоно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic солоно, the short neuter and adverbial form of солёный / солоный ('salty'), showing native East Slavic pleophony (-оло-) from Proto-Slavic *solnъ ('salted, salty', compare Old Church Slavonic сланъ and Polish słony), derived from соль ('salt').

соль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic соль and Proto-Slavic *solь ('salt'), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ls ('salt'), one of the most stable words across Indo-European languages, cognate with Latin sāl, English salt, German Salz, and Latvian sāls.
соль.notes: Note that the musical note соль ('G, sol' in do-re-mi-fa-sol) is a homonym borrowed from Italian sol.

солянка.etymology: Derived in Russian either directly from соляной ('salted, pickled', from соль 'salt') for a soup made with pickled cucumbers, olives, and brine, or as an alteration of older селянка ('peasant/village stew', from село 'village') reshaped by association with соль.

history.meaning: spicy village stew or salty-sour soup

соляной.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -яной from соль ('salt'), inherited from Old East Slavic соль, from Proto-Slavic *solь ('salt'), from Proto-Indo-European *sály- ('salt').

солёный.etymology: Participial adjective formed from солить ('to salt'), derived from соль ('salt', from Old East Slavic соль, Proto-Slavic *solь, continuing Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ls 'salt'; directly cognate with English salt, Latin sāl, and French sel).

сом.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сомъ, from Proto-Slavic *somъ ('wels catfish', Silurus glanis), of uncertain further Indo-European connections.

сомелье.etymology: Borrowed from French sommelier ('wine steward in a restaurant'), from Middle French sommelier ('court official in charge of provisions and wine transportation'), from Old French somier ('pack-horse driver, pack animal'), from Vulgar Latin *sagmārius (from Ancient Greek σάγμα 'pack-saddle').

history.meaning: pack-animal driver → officer of provisions and wine

сомнительный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from сомневаться / усомниться ('to doubt'), from Old Church Slavonic съмьнѣние ('doubt, hesitation'), composed of съ- + мьнѣти ('to think, opine', Proto-Slavic *mьněti).

history.meaning: to be of two minds, doubt

сон.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сънъ ('sleep, dream'), from Proto-Slavic *sъnъ (< earlier *sъpnъ), from Proto-Indo-European *sup-no-s (derived from *swep- 'to sleep', cognate with Latin somnus and Greek ὕπνος).

соня.etymology: Formed from the stem сн-/сон- of сон ('sleep') + the expressive common-gender personal suffix -я, designating a person fond of sleeping (and also the dormouse).

соображать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from сообразить ('to figure out, correlate in the mind, grasp'), originally a Church Slavonic-patterned formation съобразити ('to conform to an image/model, correlate', from съ- 'together' + образ 'image, form, manner').

history.meaning: to think, catch on, use one's head

сообщать.etymology: Adopted via Old Church Slavonic съобьщати ('to make common, share, communicate'), formed from съ- ('together') + обьщии (общий 'common, shared'), a calque of Greek κοινωνέω / Latin communicare.

сообщение.etymology: Formed as the verbal noun in -ение from сообщить ('to make common, share information, report, communicate'), which was built in the eighteenth century with the Church Slavonic prefix со- ('together') + общий ('common, shared', Proto-Slavic *obьťь, from *ob 'around'): literally 'making information shared', hence 'a message, report, or transport link'.

сообщить.etymology: Adopted from Church Slavonic съобьщити ('to make common, share, communicate', calquing Latin commūnicāre from commūnis 'common'), composed of съ- + обьщити (from обьщии 'common, shared', Proto-Slavic *obьťь).

соперник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съпьрьникъ ('adversary in a lawsuit, opponent, rival'), formed from съ- ('with, against') + пьря ('dispute, contention, lawsuit', related to переть 'to press, contend') + -ник.

соперница.etymology: Feminine noun formed with the suffix -ница from соперник ('rival, adversary'), inherited from Old East Slavic съпьрьникъ, from съпьря ('dispute, litigation, contest', from съ- 'with/against' + пьрѣти 'to contend, press, argue', Proto-Slavic *pьrěti).

соперничать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ничать from соперник ('rival, competitor', from Old East Slavic съпьрьникъ 'opponent in a dispute').

сопли.etymology: Plural of сопля ('nasal mucus, snot'), inherited from Old East Slavic сопля, from Proto-Slavic *sopľa ('nasal mucus'), derived from *sopti / *sopěti ('to wheeze, snuffle, breathe noisily through the nose').

сопротивляться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from сопротивиться ('to resist, oppose'), from Old Church Slavonic съпротивити сѧ, composed of съ- + противити сѧ (from противъ 'against', Proto-Slavic *protivъ).

сорбет.etymology: Borrowed via French sorbet (and Italian sorbetto) from Ottoman Turkish شربت (şerbet, 'sweet fruit drink'), from Arabic شَرْبَة (šarba, 'a drink'), from the verb šariba ('to drink'; doublet of шербет and сироп).

сорвать.etymology: Formed with the ablative prefix с-/со- ('off, away') + рвать ('to tear, pluck'), from Proto-Slavic *rъvati ('to tear, pull up').

history.meaning: to tear off; to disrupt, ruin

сорваться.etymology: Reflexive/intransitive form of сорвать ('to tear off') + -ся, literally 'to tear oneself loose, slip off from a hold', hence figuratively 'to fall through' or 'to lose one's temper'.

history.meaning: to break loose, slip off, snap

соревнование.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ние from соревновать ('to emulate, compete'), derived from Old Church Slavonic съревновати ('to be zealous together, emulate', calquing Ancient Greek ζηλόω), from съ- + ревновать (from ревьность 'zeal, ardor').

соринка.etymology: Singulative and diminutive noun formed with the suffix -инка from сор ('rubbish, sweepings, dust'), an East Slavic deverbal noun from the root of срать (*sъr- 'droppings, dirt, sweepings').

сорок.etymology: Unique East Slavic numeral (replacing older четыре десяте 'four tens', which survives in all other Slavic languages and in Russian сороковой / четыре). In Old East Slavic сорокъ denoted a bundle of forty sable or marten pelts — the exact number needed to sew a full fur coat; Vasmer compares Old Norse serkr ('shirt, coat, bundle of skins') or Byzantine Greek τεσσαράκοντα ('forty'). From fur-trade accounting, 'a bundle of forty' became the ordinary number 'forty'.

history.meaning: bundle of forty sable pelts; forty

сорок.notes: Unlike двадцать, тридцать, and пятьдесят, **сорок** has only two case forms: nominative/accusative **сорок** and oblique **сорока**.

сосед.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сусѣдъ (reshaped in standard Russian with the prefix со- after Old Church Slavonic съсѣдъ) and Proto-Slavic *sǫsědъ ('neighbour'), an ancient nominal compound of *sǫ- ('together, alongside') + *sěděti / *sěsti ('to sit, settle, dwell'): literally 'one who sits or dwells alongside you'.
сосед.notes: Has a soft plural stem despite its hard singular: nominative plural сосе́ди, genitive plural сосе́дей, instrumental сосе́дями.

сосед-скрипач.etymology: A hyphenated Russian appositional compound combining сосед ('neighbour', from Proto-Slavic *sǫsědъ 'one who dwells alongside') and скрипач ('violinist', formed with the agent suffix -ач from скрипка 'violin', built on the onomatopoeic root скрип- 'to squeak, creak,bow').
сосед-скрипач.notes: Both parts decline when used in a sentence: у соседа-скрипача ('at the violinist neighbour's').

соседка.etymology: Formed from сосед ('neighbour') with the feminine person suffix -ка.

соседний.etymology: Derived in Russian from сосед ('neighbour') with the soft positional adjectival suffix -ний: 'neighbouring, next-door, adjacent'.

соскользнуть.etymology: Formed in Russian from со- ('off from a surface') + скользнуть ('to slip, slide once', semelfactive of скользить 'to slide, slip', Proto-Slavic *skъlziti).

соскучиться.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix со- + скучиться / скучать ('to be bored, pine, miss someone'), derived from скука ('boredom, longing, weariness'), which Vasmer connects with an expressive Slavic root *skuk- / *skuč- originally meaning 'to whine, pine, fret'.

history.meaning: to come to miss someone or something (по кому/чему)

сосна.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сосна, from Proto-Slavic *sosna ('pine tree'). Vasmer connects it with a color or resin root (often compared with Old Prussian sasnis or Sanskrit śaśá 'grayish').

сосредоточиться.etymology: Reflexive form of сосредоточить ('to concentrate, center'), coined in eighteenth-century Russian with prefix со- ('together') + средоточие ('center, midpoint', Church Slavonic calque of Latin centrum from среда 'middle').

составить.etymology: Formed with the prefix со- ('together') + ставить ('to put, place, set standing'), from Proto-Slavic *sъstaviti ('to put together, compose').

составлять.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from составить ('to put together, compose, constitute'), from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic съставити, composed of съ- ('together') + ставити ('to place, set, stand', Proto-Slavic *staviti).

history.meaning: to make up, draw up, constitute

состариться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with the prefix со- and -ся from старить / стареть ('to age, grow old'), derived from старый ('old', from Proto-Slavic *starъ).

состояние.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic състояние ('standing together, firmness, state, condition'), formed from со- + стоять ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati) + -ние, and used in the eighteenth century to calque Latin status and French état ('state, condition; fortune/estate').

состоятельный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from состоять / состояние ('state, fortune, wealth, property'), meaning 'possessing means/substance, affluent' as well as 'well-founded, valid'.

состоять.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic състояти ('to stand together, consist of, subsist', calquing Latin cōnsistere and Ancient Greek συνίστημι), composed of съ- ('together') + стояти ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati).

history.meaning: to consist (of); to belong to, be a member of

сострадание.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic състраданиѥ ('compassion, fellow-suffering'), a morphological calque of Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sympatheia) and Latin compassio: съ- ('together with') + страдание ('suffering').

состряпать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix со- from стряпать ('to cook, prepare food; to concoct'), inherited from Old East Slavic стряпати ('to work, manage affairs, prepare food'), from Proto-Slavic *strępati.

history.meaning: to whip up (food); to concoct hastily

сосулька.etymology: Derived in Russian from сосать ('to suck', from Proto-Slavic *sъsati) + suffixes -уля and diminutive -ка; originally referring to something sucked on (a candy stick, nipple, or hanging icicle sucked by children).

сосчитать.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix со- ('together, to the end') + считать ('to count'), from Proto-Slavic *čitati: 'to count up completely'.

сотейник.etymology: Formed in Russian culinary terminology with the instrument suffix -ник from соте ('sautéed dish'), borrowed from French sauté ('jumped, tossed in a pan'), past participle of sauter ('to jump', from Latin saltāre).

history.meaning: to jump/toss in a pan → sautéed dish

сотка.etymology: Colloquial noun formed with the suffix -ка from сотый / сто ('hundredth / hundred', from Proto-Slavic *sъto, PIE *ḱm̥tóm), denoting either a hundred-unit note/number or one hundredth of a hectare (100 square meters of land).

history.meaning: 100 sq. m plot (one hundredth of a hectare); a hundred

сотрудник.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сътроудьникъ ('fellow laborer, co-worker', a calque of Ancient Greek συνεργός synergós), formed from съ- ('together, with') + троудъ / труд ('labor, work', Proto-Slavic *trudъ) + agent suffix -ник.

сотрудница.etymology: Feminine noun formed with the suffix -ница from сотрудник ('co-worker, collaborator, employee'), from Old Church Slavonic сътрудьникъ (calquing Ancient Greek συνεργός, from съ- 'with' + трудъ 'labor, work').

сотрудничать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ничать from сотрудник ('collaborator, co-worker', from со- 'together' + труд 'work, labor', Proto-Slavic *trǫdъ).

сотрудничество.etymology: Derived from сотрудник ('collaborator, co-worker', from Old Church Slavonic сътрудьникъ: съ- 'with' + трудъ 'labor, work' + -ник) + the abstract suffix -ество.

соус.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French sauce ('sauce, dressing'), from Old French salse, which goes back to Late Latin salsa ('salted seasoning, brine'), the substantivized feminine of Latin salsus ('salted', from sāl 'salt').

соучастница.etymology: Feminine noun formed with the suffix -ница from соучастник ('accomplice, co-participant'), composed of со- ('co-, together') + участник ('participant', from участие 'participation', from часть 'part').

сохнуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съхнути and Proto-Slavic *sъxnǫti ('to dry, become dry, wither'), an inchoative verb in *-nǫti built on the zero-grade of the root of сухой ('dry', Proto-Slavic *suxъ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂sews- 'to dry', cognate with Ancient Greek aûos and English sere).
сохнуть.notes: Past tense drops the -ну- suffix: бельё сохло ('the laundry was drying').

сохраниться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from сохранить ('to preserve, keep safe, save'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съхранити (with South Slavic non-pleophonic -ра- corresponding to native хоронить, from Proto-Slavic *xorniti 'to guard, keep').

history.meaning: to be preserved, survive; to save one's game

сохранять.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of сохранить ('to keep safe, preserve, save'), adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic root vocalism -хран- (compare native East Slavic хоронить) from Proto-Slavic *sъxorniti ('to guard, keep safe').

социальный.etymology: Borrowed via French social or German sozial from Latin socialis ('of companionship, allied, social'), derived from socius ('companion, ally, partner').

сочинять.etymology: Formed as the imperfective counterpart of сочинить ('to compose music or verse, write, make up'), originally meaning in Middle Russian 'to arrange in proper order, put together' from со- ('together') + чинить ('to arrange, order', built on чин 'order, rank', Proto-Slavic *činъ).

history.meaning: to compose (music, poetry); to make up

сочинять.notes: Notice how сочинять ('to compose') and починить ('to repair') share the same Slavic root чин ('order'): composing is 'putting words or notes together in order', while repairing is 'putting a broken object back in order'.

спагетти.etymology: Borrowed from Italian spaghetti, plural of spaghetto ('thin string, twine'), diminutive of spago ('string, cord'), from Late Latin spacus ('twine, cord').

спалить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from палить ('to burn, scorch, singe'), inherited from Old East Slavic палити, from Proto-Slavic *paliti (causative of *polěti 'to blaze, burn'); in slang, 'to catch red-handed, expose'.

history.meaning: to burn down; (slang) to bust, catch out

спалиться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with -ся from спалить ('to burn down; in slang, to expose, catch out'), literally 'to burn oneself' and in modern slang 'to blow one's cover, get caught'.

history.meaning: to get caught, give oneself away (slang)

спальня.etymology: Room noun formed with the locative suffix -ня from спальный ('for sleeping'), derived from спать ('to sleep', inherited from Old East Slavic съпати, from Proto-Slavic *sъpati, PIE *swep-).

спаржа.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century (probably via Polish szparag or Italian sparagio / Dialectal German Sparge) from Latin asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος ('asparagus shoot').

спарринг.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English sparring (verbal noun of to spar, 'to practice boxing, make feints'), from Middle English sparren ('to strike out, dart, contend with spurs like fighting cocks').

спарринговать.etymology: Denominal verb formed with the suffix -овать from спарринг ('sparring', borrowed from English sparring).

спартаковский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from Спартак (the Moscow sports club founded in 1935 and named after Spartacus, Latin Spartacus, Ancient Greek Σπάρτακος, the Thracian gladiator who led a slave uprising against Rome).

спасательный.etymology: Derived in Russian from спасать ('to save, rescue', imperfective of спасти < Old East Slavic съпасти, from съ- + пасти 'to herd, guard, protect') + the adjectival suffix -тельный.

спасать.etymology: Imperfective partner of спасти ('to save, rescue'), from Old East Slavic съпасати / съпасти, formed from the prefix съ- + пасти ('to herd, guard, watch over a flock', from Proto-Slavic *pasti, from PIE *peh₂- 'to protect, shepherd'; cognate with Latin pāscō and pāstor). Also the source of спасибо (< съпаси богъ).

спасение.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic съпасение ('salvation, rescue, deliverance'), verbal noun of съпасти (modern Russian спасти, 'to save, rescue', from *sъ- + *pasti 'to pasture, guard, protect').

спасибо.etymology: Спасибо developed from the wish “may God save you”, historically съпаси богъ. A blessing became an everyday expression of thanks. Vasmer also records its use as a noun meaning gratitude.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: спасибо

спасибо.notes: Use *Большое спасибо* for 'thank you very much'. Reply with *Пожалуйста*.

спаситель.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic съпаситель ('savior, deliverer', originally translating Ancient Greek σωτήρ), formed with the agent suffix -тель from съпасти / спасать ('to save').

спасти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съпасти ('to save, protect, rescue'), from Proto-Slavic *sъpasti, formed from prefix *sъ- + *pasti ('to guard, pasture, watch over a flock', from PIE *peh₂- 'to protect'). The imperative phrase съпаси богъ ('may God save you') contracted into спасибо ('thank you').

спасённый.etymology: Originally the past passive participle of спасти ('to save, rescue', Old East Slavic съпасти, from съ- + пасти 'to herd, watch over, protect', Proto-Slavic *pasti), used as an adjective meaning 'saved, rescued'.

rootFamily.gloss: thank you (from съпаси богъ 'may God save you')

спать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съпати, from Proto-Slavic *sъpati, from Proto-Indo-European *swep- ('to sleep'), cognate with Latin somnus and sopor (whence English somnolent) and Sanskrit svápiti.

спаться.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the impersonal-middle postfix -ся to спать ('to sleep', Old East Slavic съпати, Proto-Slavic *sъpati, from Proto-Indo-European *swep- 'to sleep', cognate with сон 'sleep, dream' and Latin sopor): used impersonally with a dative subject to describe how well or poorly one is able to sleep.

history.meaning: to sleep -> to feel like sleeping / sleep (impersonally)

спаться.notes: Used only in impersonal third-person singular/neuter forms with a dative experiencer: Мне не спится ('I can't get to sleep'), Как спалось? ('How did you sleep?').

спелый.etymology: Originally the past active l-participle of спеть ('to ripen, mature; to succeed in time'), inherited from Old East Slavic спѣлыи and Proto-Slavic *spělъ (from *spěti 'to prosper, ripen, be on time', cognate with English speed).

cognates.meaning: success, swiftness (from the same Indo-European root *speh₁-)

сперва.etymology: Adverb formed from the fusion of the preposition с ('from') with the genitive singular short form перва of первый ('first', from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ, PIE *pŕ̥h₂wos 'foremost, first').

спереди.etymology: Formed in East Slavic by fusing the preposition с ('from, at') with the old locative/genitive переди of перед ('front', showing native East Slavic pleophony -ере- from Proto-Slavic *perdъ).

history.meaning: at the front, from the front

спереть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from переть ('to press, push, haul with effort', from Proto-Slavic *perti); in colloquial slang shifted from 'to push/lug away' to 'to swipe, steal, filch'.

спеть.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix с- to петь ('to sing', Old East Slavic пѣти, Proto-Slavic *pěti).
спеть.notes: Future tense uses the o-grade stem поj-: я спою, ты споёшь, они споют.

спех.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic спѣхъ ('striving, success, haste'), from Proto-Slavic *spěxъ, deverbal noun from *spěti ('to succeed, ripen, hurry', modern спеть / спешить, from PIE *speh₁- 'to prosper, succeed, move forward').

history.meaning: hurry, haste (in idioms like не к спеху 'no rush')

специалист.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French spécialiste (or German Spezialist), derived from spécial ('special, particular'), from Latin speciālis ('individual, particular, of a specific kind'), from speciēs ('appearance, kind, species').

history.meaning: of a particular kind → expert in a specific field

специально.etymology: Formed as the adverbial derivative in -о of специальный ('special, particular'), borrowed via Polish specjalny or German speziell from Latin speciālis ('particular, individual, of a specific kind', from speciēs 'appearance, kind, sort').
специально.notes: Means both 'specifically for a purpose' (купить специально для гостей 'to buy specially for guests') and 'deliberately, on purpose' (я не специально 'I didn't do it on purpose').

спецобслуживание.etymology: Twentieth-century compound formed from the clipped stump спец- (from специальный 'special', via French spécial from Latin speciālis) + обслуживание ('service, catering', verbal noun of обслуживать, from служить 'to serve').

history.meaning: special service, private VIP event catering

спешить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic спѣшити and Proto-Slavic *spěšiti ('to hurry, make haste'), derived from *spěxъ (Russian спех 'haste', preserved in не к спеху 'no rush') and *spěti ('to succeed, ripen, be in time', as in успеть 'to be in time', cognate with English speed and German sputen).

history.meaning: to advance, succeed -> haste -> to hurry
to hurry, rush, be in a hurry

спешить.notes: Also used of clocks and watches that run fast: часы спешат на пять минут ('the clock is five minutes fast').

спина.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic спина ('back, spine', attested in Old Russian and shared with Polish spina 'arch, spine' and Ukrainian спина). Most scholars (including Vasmer) consider it an early learned or mediated borrowing via West Slavic from Latin spīna ('thorn, backbone, spine'), though some propose a native Slavic connection to пясть / пнуть ('to stretch, bend').

спирт.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (originally as спиритус, then shortened via English spirit or Dutch/German Spiritus) from Latin spiritus ('breath, spirit; volatile distilled essence in alchemy').

спица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic спица ('sharp wooden peg, splinter, wheel spoke, knitting needle'), from Proto-Slavic *stьpica or early borrowing from Middle Low German spitse / Old High German spizza ('sharp point, spike').

спичечный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from спичка ('matchstick', with regular velar palatalization к > ч and mobile vowel е).

спичка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка from спица ('sharp wooden peg, splinter'); originally denoted a small wooden shoe-peg or splinter, then in the nineteenth century specialized for a sulfur/phosphorus wooden matchstick.

спланировать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from планировать ('to plan, design'), derived from план ('plan', borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Plan and French plan from Latin plānus 'flat, level').

сплетничать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the behavioral suffix -ничать from сплетня ('gossip, rumor').

сплетня.etymology: Noun formed from сплетать / сплести ('to weave together, plait, fabricate a story'), composed of the prefix с- ('together') + плести ('to braid, weave; figuratively to spin tales', from Proto-Slavic *plesti, PIE *pleḱ-).

history.meaning: to weave together; to fabricate stories

споить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the resultative prefix с- from поить ('to give to drink, ply with drink'), inherited from Old East Slavic поити, from Proto-Slavic *pojiti (causative of *piti 'to drink', PIE *peh₃(y)-).

history.meaning: to give to drink, ply with alcohol
to get someone drunk, drive to alcoholism

спокойно.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of спокойный ('calm, peaceful, quiet'), built on покой ('rest, peace, quiet', from Proto-Slavic *pokojь).

спокойный.etymology: Formed from покой / спокоить ('rest, peace, calm', from Old East Slavic покои, Proto-Slavic *pokojь, an o-grade noun from *počiti 'to rest', cognate with Latin quiēs 'rest, quiet') with prefix с- and adjectival suffix -ный.

сполна.etymology: Adverbialized prepositional phrase formed from the preposition с ('from, of') + the genitive singular short-form adjective полна (from полный 'full', Proto-Slavic *pьlnъ).

спонсор.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English sponsor, from Latin sponsor ('surety, guarantor, bondsman'), derived from spondere ('to pledge solemnly, promise').

спор.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic споръ and Proto-Slavic *sъporъ ('dispute, contention, argument'), a prefixal noun built on *sъ- ('against one another, together') + the o-grade of *perti (Russian переть 'to press, push against', cognate with соперник 'rival'): literally 'a pushing or pressing against one another'.

спорить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic спорити and Proto-Slavic *sъporiti ('to contend, argue, dispute'), a denominal verb built on спор ('dispute, argument', Proto-Slavic *sъporъ).

спорт.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English sport, aphetic shortening of Middle English disport ('pastime, recreation'), from Old French desport (from desporter 'to divert, amuse oneself').

спортбар.etymology: Late twentieth-century compound formed from спорт ('sport', borrowed from English sport) and бар ('bar, pub', borrowed from English bar), modeled on English sports bar.

спортзал.etymology: Twentieth-century syllabic compound shortening спортивный зал ('sports hall, gymnasium'), combining спорт ('sport', from English sport) and зал ('hall', from German Saal / French salle).

спортивный.etymology: Formed in Russian from спорт ('sport') + the relational adjective suffix -ивный (modeled on French sportif).

спортсмен.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English sportsman, compound of sport's + man.

споткнуться.etymology: Formed in East Slavic with prefixes с- + по- + ткнуться ('to strike against, poke into', reflexive of ткнуть 'to poke, thrust', from Proto-Slavic *tъknǫti): literally 'to strike one's foot against an obstacle and stumble'.

справа.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase с права ('from/on the right side'), combining the preposition с ('from, on') with the old short genitive singular (-а) of правый ('right, straight', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.meaning: on the right, from the right

справедливо.etymology: Deadjectival adverb and predicative formed with -о from справедливый ('just, fair'), borrowed in the sixteenth–seventeenth century via Polish sprawiedliwy (and Old Czech spravedlivý), derived from правда ('truth, justice', Proto-Slavic *pravьda).

справедливость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with -ость from справедливый ('just, fair', via Polish sprawiedliwy) or directly adapted from Polish sprawiedliwość ('justice, fairness'), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pravъ ('straight, right, just').

справедливый.etymology: Borrowed via Old Ruthenian/Ukrainian and Polish sprawiedliwy ('just, righteous, fair'), derived from Czech spravedlivý (built on spravedlný, from с- + правда 'truth, justice').

справиться.etymology: Perfective reflexive verb formed from справить ('to set right, manage, celebrate'), built from с- + править ('to direct, steer, make straight', from правый 'right, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravъ). Literally, 'to set oneself straight with a task, to manage or cope with it'.

history.meaning: straight, right → to direct, set right

справка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from справить / справлять ('to set right, verify, inquire', cf. справиться 'to inquire about'), ultimately from правый ('right, correct', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

справляться.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of справиться ('to manage, cope with'), formed with the suffix -я- and reflexive -ся from справить ('to set right, direct, manage'), built on правый ('straight, right', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

history.meaning: to cope with, manage (imperfective); to inquire

спрашивать.etymology: Formed in Russian as the imperfective counterpart of спросить ('to ask a question'), built from с- + прашивать (lengthened iterative stem of просить 'to ask, request', Proto-Slavic *prositi, with о -> а and с -> ш).

morphemes.meaning: ask (lengthened grade of просить, о -> а, с -> ш)

спрашивать.notes: Usage rule: спрашивать / спросить means 'to ask a question (for information)', whereas просить / попросить means 'to ask for a favour or object (request)'.

спровоцировать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from провоцировать ('to provoke, instigate'), borrowed via German provozieren from Latin prōvocāre ('to call forth, challenge, provoke', from prō- 'forth' + vocāre 'to call').

спрос.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from спросить ('to ask, demand accountability', from с- + просить 'to ask, request', Proto-Slavic *prositi).

спросить.etymology: Formed in Russian by prefixing с- to просить ('to ask, request', from Old East Slavic просити, Proto-Slavic *prositi, PIE *preḱ- 'to ask'). While просить / попросить kept the sense 'to request a favour or object', спросить specialized in 'to ask a question for information'.

спрятать.etymology: Formed in Russian by adding the perfectivizing prefix с- to прятать ('to hide, put away', Old East Slavic прятати, Proto-Slavic *prętati).
спрятать.notes: Future tense shows т -> ч palatalization: я спрячу, ты спрячешь.

спускать.etymology: Formed with the downward/ablative prefix с- ('down from') + пускать ('to let go, release', iterative of пустить, from Proto-Slavic *pustiti).

спустя.etymology: Originally the verbal adverb (gerund) of спустить ('to let down, let pass, release', from с- + пустить 'to let go'), lexicalized as a preposition meaning 'after the lapse of, later' (literally 'having let [a period of time] pass').
спустя.notes: Can stand either before or after its accusative time expression: спустя неделю or неделю спустя ('a week later').

спутник.etymology: Compound noun formed from с- ('with, together') + путь ('way, road, journey', Proto-Slavic *pǫtь) + agent suffix -ник ('fellow traveler, companion', calquing Latin comes or German Weggefährte); applied in eighteenth-century astronomy to a planetary moon (calquing Latin satelles) and in 1957 to the first artificial Earth satellite.

спящий.etymology: Adjectival present active participle of спать ('to sleep'), inherited from Old East Slavic съпячии / Old Church Slavonic съпѧщии (with the Church Slavonic participial suffix -щ- < *-tj-), from Proto-Slavic *sъpati (PIE *swep-).

сработаться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('together') and -ся from работать ('to work', from работа 'work', Proto-Slavic *orbota), meaning 'to learn to work smoothly together as a team'.

history.meaning: to work well together, harmonize at work

сравнивать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from сравнить ('to compare, liken'), derived from the Church Slavonic-rooted stem равный ('equal, even', Old Church Slavonic равьнъ, corresponding to native ровный, from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ).

сравнить.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic vocalism равн- (compare native East Slavic ровный 'even, equal', from Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ), formed from prefix с- ('together') + равнить ('to make equal, place side by side on the same level'): 'to compare'.

history.meaning: to place on a par together → to compare

сражение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic съражение ('collision, clash, battle', with South Slavic non-pleophonic -ра- corresponding to native сразить), verbal noun of съразити ('to strike together, smite down', from съ- + разити 'to strike, cut', Proto-Slavic *raziti).

сразу.etymology: Formed in Russian by fusing the preposition с ('from') with the partitive/locative genitive singular разу of раз ('stroke, blow, one time', Proto-Slavic *razъ): literally 'from a single stroke, at one go', hence 'at once, right away, immediately'.

history.meaning: at one stroke, at one go

среда.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic non-pleophonic form среда (compare native East Slavic середа, preserved in середина 'middle') from Old Church Slavonic срѣда ('middle; Wednesday'), from Proto-Slavic *serda ('middle, heart'). Wednesday is literally the 'middle day' of the week (compare German Mittwoch).
среда.notes: In the sense 'Wednesday', accusative singular shifts stress to the first syllable: в сре́ду ('on Wednesday').

средний.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic stem сред- (compare native East Slavic середний) from Old Church Slavonic срѣдьнь ('situated in the middle'), from Proto-Slavic *serdьnьjь, built on *serda ('middle').

срезать.etymology: Perfective (срéзать) and imperfective (срезáть) verb formed with the prefix с- ('off, away') from резать ('to cut, slice'), inherited from Old East Slavic рѣзати, from Proto-Slavic *rězati ('to cut, carve').

history.meaning: to cut off, trim; to dock (pay)

срок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сърокъ (and Old Church Slavonic сърокъ 'agreement, appointed time, stipulation'), from Proto-Slavic *sъrokъ, formed with the prefix *sъ- ('together') and o-grade ablaut *rok- from *rekti ('to speak, say, declare', Old East Slavic речи, preserved in речь 'speech'; compare Polish rok 'year', originally 'appointed time'). Literally, срок meant 'that which has been agreed upon by word: a fixed date, deadline, or term (including a prison term)'.

history.meaning: verbal agreement → appointed date, fixed term

срочный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from срок ('appointed time, deadline, term'), inherited from Old East Slavic сърокъ ('agreement, appointed date') and Proto-Slavic *sъrokъ (built on *sъ- 'together' + *rekti 'to speak, stipulate').

срывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('off, down') and iterative stem -рывать (corresponding to perfective сорвать 'to tear off, pluck, foil'), from Proto-Slavic *rъvati ('to tear, pluck').

history.meaning: to tear off; to ruin, derail (a plan)

ссора.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic ссора (< *съсора, 'quarrel, discord'), deverbal noun from *съсорити ('to scatter, embroil, set at odds', related to сорить 'to scatter litter' or dialectal свара 'quarrel').

стабильно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from стабильный ('stable, steady'), borrowed via German stabil from Latin stabilis ('firm, steadfast, stable', from stāre 'to stand').

ставень.etymology: Derived from ставить 'to set, put upright' with the suffix -ень: originally a wooden board or hinged panel set into place to close a window opening.
ставень.notes: Usually used in the plural ставни ('window shutters'); singular forms both masculine ставень and feminine ставня occur in speech.

ставка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from ставить ('to put, place, set; to stake money on a game'), from Old East Slavic ставити and Proto-Slavic *staviti (causative of *stati 'to stand'). Denotes a bet or stake placed on a table, a wage/interest rate, or a commander's pitched tent/headquarters.

history.meaning: to set up, place → tent/camp; stake placed in a game
bet, stake; rate/salary; high command headquarters

стадион.etymology: Borrowed via German Stadion or French stade from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion, 'a racecourse of 600 Greek feet, stadium'), related to ἵστημι ('to stand, fix').

history.meaning: measure of length (600 feet); footrace arena

стакан.etymology: Shortened in Middle Russian from Old East Slavic достоканъ (attested in fourteenth-century charters), borrowed from Turkic dostaqan ('wooden drinking cup'), itself from Persian dustkan ('large drinking cup shared with friends').

стальной.etymology: Derived in Russian from сталь ('steel') with the adjectival suffix -ной. Russian сталь was borrowed in the early eighteenth century via German Stahl (or Dutch staal) from Proto-Germanic *stahliją ('steel', literally 'that which stands firm', cognate with English steel).

стандарт.etymology: Borrowed from English standard ('flag, benchmark, norm'), from Old French estandard ('rallying banner, standard measure').

стандартный.etymology: Relational and qualitative adjective formed with the suffix -ный from стандарт ('standard'), borrowed from English standard, from Old French estandart ('rallying banner, official standard of measure').

станок.etymology: Formed with the diminutive/instrument suffix -ок from стан ('frame, stand, loom, camp'), inherited from Old East Slavic станъ, from Proto-Slavic *stanъ ('standing place, frame, camp', from *stati 'to stand', PIE *steh₂-).

станцевать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- + танцевать ('to dance'), borrowed via Polish tańcować from Middle High German tanzen ('to dance').

станция.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era (via Polish stacja or directly) from Latin statio (stem station-, 'standing place, post, stage, station'), derived from stare ('to stand').

старание.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ние from стараться ('to try hard, endeavor, take pains'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *starati sę ('to take care of, strive', related to *starъ 'old, strong, firm', PIE *ster- 'stiff, firm').

history.meaning: to try hard, make an effort

старательно.etymology: Adverb formed from старательный ('diligent, assiduous'), derived from стараться ('to try hard, endeavor', from Proto-Slavic *starati sę 'to take pains, care for').

старательный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from стараться ('to try hard, apply oneself', from Proto-Slavic *starati sę).

стараться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic старатися and Proto-Slavic *starati sę ('to exert oneself, strive, take pains, care for'), built on the same Indo-European root *ster- ('stiff, firm, enduring, strong') that gave старый ('old, seasoned') and German starr ('rigid, fixed').

history.meaning: to try, make an effort, do one's best

старенький.etymology: Affectionate/attenuative adjective formed with the suffix -енький from старый ('old'), inherited from Old East Slavic старыи, from Proto-Slavic *starъ ('old').

стареть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть from старый ('old'), inherited from Old East Slavic старѣти, from Proto-Slavic *starěti ('to grow old', from *starъ 'old').

старец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic старьць / Old Church Slavonic старьць ('old man, elder, senior monk'), formed with the noun suffix *-ьcь from Proto-Slavic *starъ ('old').

history.stage: Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic

старинный.etymology: Derived in Russian from старина ('antiquity, the olden days', formed from старый 'old' + -ина) with the adjectival suffix -ный: 'dating from olden times, historic, antique, time-honoured'.
старинный.notes: Whereas старый simply means 'old' (including worn-out), старинный has a positive connotation of age and heritage ('historic, antique, vintage').

старичок.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed from старик ('old man', from старый 'old', Proto-Slavic *starъ) + the diminutive suffix -ок (with velar palatalization к > ч).

староватый.etymology: Attenuative adjective formed with the suffix -оватый ('somewhat, a bit too') from старый ('old', from Proto-Slavic *starъ).

старт.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century from English start ('beginning of a race, takeoff'), from Middle English sterten ('to leap, bound, start'), from Old English styrtan (Proto-Germanic *sturtijaną).

history.meaning: beginning of a race or venture

стартовать.etymology: Denominal verb formed with the suffix -овать from старт ('start', borrowed from English start).

старуха.etymology: Formed from старый ('old', from Proto-Slavic *starъ) + the expressive feminine personal suffix -уха.

старушка.etymology: Diminutive formed from старуха ('old woman', from старый 'old') + the diminutive suffix -ка (with х > ш palatalization).

старше.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic старьше, the comparative of старый ('old', Proto-Slavic *starъ, cognate with Lithuanian storas 'thick, sturdy'): 'older (in age or seniority)'.
старше.notes: Used as a predicate when comparing people's ages: сестра старше меня на два года ('my sister is two years older than me').

старший.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic старьшии (Proto-Slavic *starjьšьjь), theattributive comparative and superlative adjective of старый ('old'): 'older, elder (brother/sister), or senior (in rank)'.

старый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic старъ, from Proto-Slavic *starъ ('old, long-standing'), connected with стать/стоять and PIE *steh₂- ('to stand'; compare Lithuanian stóras 'thick, sturdy' and Old Norse stórr 'big, great').

статус.etymology: Borrowed from Latin status ('standing, posture, condition, legal or social position'), action noun from stāre ('to stand', from PIE *steh₂-).

статусный.etymology: Formed in Russian from статус ('status, standing', borrowed from Latin status 'standing, position, condition', from stare 'to stand') + the adjectival suffix -ный.

стать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стати and Proto-Slavic *stati ('to take a stand, step into position, come to a stop; to begin; to become'), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- ('to stand up'), cognate with стоять ('to be standing'), Latin stāre, and English stand.

history.meaning: to stand up, stop; to become
to become (+ instrumental); to begin (+ imperfective infinitive)

morphemes.meaning: stand, become (alternating with стан- in future tense)

стать.notes: Future tense uses the nasal-suffixed stem стан-: я стану, ты станешь, они станут; past tense стал, стала.

стащить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('off, away') from тащить ('to drag, pull, haul', related to Old East Slavic тъщати 'to hasten, strive', Proto-Slavic *tъščiti); colloquially 'to swipe, pilfer'.

history.meaning: to drag off; (colloquial) to swipe, pinch

ствол.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стълъ / ствол (from Proto-Slavic *stъvolъ 'plant stalk, hollow stem, tree trunk'), built on the Indo-European root *stew- / *stā- ('to stand stiffly upright', cognate with Ancient Greek στῦλος 'pillar'). Extended later to a gun 'barrel' or mine 'shaft'.

стекло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стькло and Proto-Slavic *stьklo ('glass'), an early pan-Slavic borrowing from Gothic stikls ('drinking horn, goblet, chalice', originally 'pointed horn' from the Germanic root of stick / stitch). When Slavic speakers encountered imported Roman and Germanic glass drinking vessels, they transferred the name of the goblet to the material 'glass' itself.
стекло.notes: Nominative plural vocalizes е -> ё: стёкла ('windowpanes, lenses').

стеклянный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стькляныи (Proto-Slavic *stьklěnъ), the material adjective derived from стекло ('glass') with the suffix -янный.
стеклянный.notes: One of the three famous Russian school-rule exceptions in -янный spelled with double -нн-: стеклянный ('glass'), оловянный ('tin'), деревянный ('wooden').

стена.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стѣна ('wall, cliff face'), from Proto-Slavic *stěna, which Vasmer connects with Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- ('to stiffen, stone'; compare Gothic stains, German Stein, and English stone).

стенка.etymology: Formed as the diminutive and specialized derivative of стена ('wall', Old East Slavic стѣна, Proto-Slavic *stěna, cognate with Gothic stains and English stone): 'a small wall, partition wall, side wall of a box or cabinet, or a wall-unit bookcase'.

history.meaning: wall -> partition wall, side of a vessel, wall unit

стерва.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стьрва / стерво ('carrion, corpse of a dead animal'), from Proto-Slavic *stьrva ('carrion, dead flesh', cognate with Polish ścierwo and German sterben 'to die', from PIE *sterbh- 'to grow stiff, die'); later transferred as a strong invective to a spiteful or ruthless person.

стереотип.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French stéréotype (originally a printing term for a solid metal plate cast from a papier-mâché mold, coined by French printer Firmin Didot in 1796 from Ancient Greek στερεός 'solid, firm' + τύπος 'impression, type').

history.meaning: solid printing plate; fixed mental cliché

стереть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сътьрѣти ('to rub off, grind down, wipe away'), from Proto-Slavic *sъtьrti, composed of *sъ- ('off, away') + *tьrti ('to rub, wipe', modern Russian тереть, PIE *terh₁-).

стерпеть.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from терпеть ('to endure, suffer, tolerate'), inherited from Old East Slavic търпѣти, from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti ('to grow numb, endure patiently').

стеснительный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from стесняться ('to feel constrained, be shy or embarrassed'), derived from стеснить ('to crowd, cramp, constrain', from с- + тесный 'narrow, tight, cramped', Proto-Slavic *těsnъ).

стиль.etymology: Borrowed via French style (or German Stil) from Latin stilus ('pointed metal or bone rod used by the Romans for writing on wax tablets; hence a writer's manner of expression, literary or artistic style').
стиль.notes: In nineteenth-century Russia, старый стиль and новый стиль also referred to the Julian and Gregorian calendars (from Medieval Latin stilus 'calendar reckoning').

стимулятор.etymology: Borrowed from Scientific/New Latin stimulātor ('one who goads or stimulates'), agent noun from Latin stimulāre ('to prick with a goad, urge on, stimulate'), from stimulus ('pointed goad').

стиралка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the instrument suffix -ка from стиральная машина ('washing machine'), ultimately from стирать ('to wash laundry, rub clean', from с- + тирать / тереть 'to rub').

стиральный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from стирать ('to wash clothes by rubbing; to wipe off'), iterative of стереть (from с- + тереть 'to rub', Proto-Slavic *tьrti).

стирка.etymology: Action noun formed from стирать ('to wash laundry, rub off', originally 'to rub away dirt', from с- + тирать, iterative of тереть 'to rub', Proto-Slavic *terti) + suffix -ка.

стих.etymology: Borrowed early into Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic стихъ from Byzantine and Ancient Greek στίχος ('row, line of soldiers; line of verse, poetic verse'), from στείχω ('to walk in a line, step').

history.meaning: verse, line of poetry (plural стихи 'poetry, poem')

стихотворение.etymology: Compound calque of Ancient Greek στιхоποιία (stikhopoiía 'verse-making'): formed from стих ('verse, line of poetry', from Greek στίχος 'row, line, verse') + linking -о- + творение ('creation, making', from творить 'to create, make').

стоимость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from стоимый, present passive participle of стоить ('to cost, be worth', from Proto-Slavic *stojati / *stojiti 'to stand, be worth').

стойка.etymology: Formed in Russian from стоять ('to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati) + the noun suffix -ка: originally an upright support post or standing posture, then a counter or reception desk where staff and guests stand (стойка администратора 'reception desk', барная стойка 'bar counter').

history.meaning: upright post; standing counter, reception desk

стокгольмский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from Стокгольм ('Stockholm', capital of Sweden, from Old Swedish Stokholmber, compounded of stokker 'log, post' + holmber 'islet'); used in стокгольмский синдром ('Stockholm syndrome', coined in 1973 after the Norrmalmstorg bank robbery).

стол.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic столъ ('table, seat, prince's throne' — whence столица 'capital city'), from Proto-Slavic *stolъ, related to стлать ('to spread') and PIE *stel- ('to set up, stand'; compare Lithuanian stalas 'table' and German Stuhl 'chair').

столб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стълбъ (alongside стълпъ) 'post, pillar, column, tower', from Proto-Slavic *stъlbъ / *stъlpъ ('standing post, pillar'), related to Lithuanian stulpas ('post, pillar') and the Indo-European root *stelp- ('to stand stiffly, post').

столик.etymology: Formed in Russian from стол ('table', Old East Slavic столъ, Proto-Slavic *stolъ) with the masculine diminutive suffix -ик: 'a small table, coffee table, or restaurant/café table'.

столица.etymology: Formed with the feminine noun suffix -ица from столъ in its Old East Slavic princely sense 'throne, reigning seat' (compare стольный град 'throne city, capital'), from Proto-Slavic *stolъ ('seat, throne, table', from *stьlati / *stati).

столовая.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective from столовый ('relating to a table or meals', as in столовая комната 'dining room' or столовая изба), derived from стол ('table, meal', from Proto-Slavic *stolъ).

столпиться.etymology: Reflexive perfective verb formed with the prefix с- ('together') and -ся from толпиться ('to crowd, throng'), derived from толпа ('crowd, throng', from Proto-Slavic *tъlpa).

history.meaning: to crowd together, gather in a throng

столько.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic столько, formed by prefixing с- (from the demonstrative stem *sь 'this') to только ('so much, only', originally from толико 'that much', built on *to + *-liko): 'this much, so much, so many'.
столько.notes: Takes the genitive singular of uncountable nouns and genitive plural of countable nouns: столько работы ('so much work'), столько друзей ('so many friends').

столяр.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth century via Polish stolarz ('joiner, cabinetmaker', itself calqued on German Tischler 'table-maker, joiner', from Tisch 'table') and adapted to Russian стол ('table') + agent suffix -яр: literally 'a maker of tables and fine wooden furniture'.
столяр.notes: In traditional Russian crafts, a плотник ('carpenter') builds rough timber structures (houses, roofs, bridges), whereas a столяр ('cabinetmaker, joiner') makes fine indoor furniture, doors, and window frames. Stress falls on the ending throughout: столя́р, genitive столяра́.

столярный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from столяр ('carpenter, cabinetmaker, joiner'), borrowed via Polish stolarz (calquing German Tischler 'table-maker, joiner', from Tisch 'table') and built on Slavic стол ('table', from Proto-Slavic *stolъ).

стонать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стонати ('to groan, moan'), from Proto-Slavic *stonati (iterative/durative of *stenati, with o-grade vocalism as in стон 'groan'), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ten- ('to groan, thunder, resound', cognate with Ancient Greek στένω and English thunder).

стоп.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century (first as a maritime engine-room telegraph command on steamships, then generalized to traffic and everyday speech) directly from English stop!

стоп-лист.etymology: Compound borrowed in the late twentieth century from English stop list (composed of stop + list); in Russian restaurant jargon, the kitchen's daily list of dishes temporarily unavailable due to missing ingredients.

history.meaning: list of blocked or unavailable items

сторожить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сторожити ('to guard, watch over, lie in wait'), denominal verb with East Slavic pleophony (-оро-) from сторожь ('guard, watchman'), from Proto-Slavic *storžь (from *stergti 'to guard, watch').

сторона.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сторона ('side, region, country', showing East Slavic pleophony -оро-; compare Old Church Slavonic страна 'country, land'), from Proto-Slavic *storna, derived from *sterti ('to spread out, extend', from PIE *sterh₃- 'to spread').

сторониться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from сторонить ('to move aside'), derived from сторона ('side', with East Slavic pleophony -оро- from Proto-Slavic *storna 'side, region').

history.meaning: to step aside; to avoid, shun

стоя.etymology: Originally the present verbal adverb (gerund) of стоять ('to stand', Proto-Slavic *stojati), fully lexicalized as an adverb of posture meaning 'standing up, in a standing position'.
стоя.notes: Note the stress contrast: сто́я ('standing up', adverb) vs. стоя́ть ('to stand', verb).

стоять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стояти ('to stand'), from Proto-Slavic *stojati, a stative verb built on the Proto-Indo-European root *steh₂- ('to stand'), cognate with English stand, German stehen, Latin stō / stāre, and Sanskrit tiṣṭhati.

страница.etymology: Adopted with the South Slavic / Church Slavonic non-pleophonic stem стран- (compare native East Slavic сторона 'side') from Old Church Slavonic страница ('side of a parchment leaf, page'), a diminutive of страна ('side, region', Proto-Slavic *storna): a page is literally 'one side of a leaf in a book'.

страничка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ка (with velar/affricate alternation ц > ч) from страница ('page'), which was borrowed from Old Church Slavonic страница ('side, page of a manuscript', with South Slavic -ра- corresponding to native сторона, from Proto-Slavic *storna 'side').

странность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from странный ('strange, odd, peculiar'), originally a Church Slavonicism страньнъ ('foreign, alien, wandering', from страна 'foreign land, side', Proto-Slavic *storna).

страстный.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic страстьныи ('suffering; passionate'), formed with the suffix -ный from страсть ('suffering, passion', from Proto-Slavic *strastь < *strād-ti-s, from *stradati 'to suffer, toil').

стратег.etymology: Borrowed via French stratège or German Stratege from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós, 'army commander, general'), compound of στρατός (stratós, 'army, host') and ἄγω (ágō, 'to lead').

стратегия.etymology: Borrowed via French stratégie / German Strategie from Ancient Greek στρατηγία (stratēgía, 'office or art of a general, generalship'), derived from στρατηγός ('general', from στρατός 'army' + ἄγω 'to lead').

страховать.etymology: Derived in Russian from страх ('fear, risk, peril', as in на свой страх и риск 'at one's own peril', from Proto-Slavic *straxъ) + verbal suffix -овать, calquing German versichern / French assurer ('to insure against risk, safeguard').

history.meaning: to insure against risk; to spot/belay

страховка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from страховать ('to insure; to spot/belay against risk'), built on страх ('fear, dread; risk, peril', inherited from Old East Slavic страхъ, Proto-Slavic *straxъ). In 18th-century Russian commercial law, на свой страх ('at one's own peril/risk', calquing German Gefahr / French risque) gave rise to страховать ('to indemnify against peril/risk') and страховка ('insurance; safety belay').

history.meaning: indemnity against risk → insurance, safety backup

страховой.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овой from страх ('fear, risk, peril'; in nineteenth-century commercial usage на свой страх 'at one's own risk', whence страховать 'to insure against risk', calquing German Gefahr / Versicherung).

страшно.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic страшьно, the short neuter and adverbial form of страшный ('frightening, terrible, scary'), derived from страх ('fear, terror', Proto-Slavic *straxъ, with х -> ш before -н-).
страшно.notes: With a dative pronoun (Мне страшно) it means 'I am scared'; in Ничего страшного! ('No problem! / Never mind!') it literally means 'Nothing terrible!'.

стрелка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of стрела ('arrow, shaft', Old East Slavic стрѣла, Proto-Slavic *strěla 'arrow', cognate with Old High German strāla 'arrow, flash of lightning' and Lithuanian strėlė): from a small arrow, it came to denote a pointer, clock hand (стрелка часов), compass needle, or railway switch.

history.meaning: arrow -> small arrow, pointer, clock hand

стреляться.etymology: Reflexive and reciprocal verb formed with -ся from стрелять ('to shoot'), inherited from Old East Slavic стрѣляти, from Proto-Slavic *strěľati (derived from *strěla 'arrow, shaft').

history.meaning: to shoot oneself; to fight a pistol duel

строгий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic строгыи and Proto-Slavic *strogъ ('strict, severe, stern, vigilant'), related by ablaut to стеречь / сторож ('to guard, keep watch', Proto-Slavic *stergti / *storžь).

строго.etymology: Adverb formed from строгий ('strict, stern, severe'), inherited from Old East Slavic строгыи, from Proto-Slavic *strogъ ('sharp, stern, vigilant'), related by ablaut to стеречь ('to guard, watch over', Proto-Slavic *stergti, compare Lithuanian sárgas 'watchman').

строительный.etymology: Derived in Russian from строить ('to build, construct', Proto-Slavic *strojiti, from *strojь 'order, array, structure') with the agent/instrument adjectival suffix -тельный: 'relating to building or construction'.

строиться.etymology: Reflexive and passive verb formed with -ся from строить ('to build, construct; to draw up in formation'), inherited from Old East Slavic строити ('to arrange, order, build'), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti (from *strojь 'order, arrangement, formation').

history.meaning: to arrange, put in order, build
to be built; to line up in formation

стройный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from строй ('order, harmonious arrangement, proportion, formation'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *strojь; evolved from 'well-ordered, harmonious' to 'well-proportioned, slender, shapely'.

строка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic строка ('row, line of writing, seam of stitching, gadfly prick'), from Proto-Slavic *stroka, related by o-grade ablaut to стрекать ('to prick, sting, stitch'): originally a row of needle-pricks in embroidery or ruled parchment, then a line of text.

rootFamily.gloss: line of text; seam of stitching

строчка.etymology: Formed as the diminutive (now everyday synonym) of строка ('line of writing; row of stitching'), inherited from Old East Slavic строка ('row of dots or stitches, written line; gadfly') and Proto-Slavic *stroka, related to *strekati ('to prick, stitch, dot'). Just as Latin versus meant a 'ploughed furrow' and then a 'line of text', Slavic строка / строчка moved from a 'pricked seam of stitches' to a 'line of handwriting or print'.

history.meaning: line of text; line of stitching

струбцина.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth or nineteenth century from German Schraubzwinge ('screw clamp'), a compound of Schraube ('screw') + Zwinge ('clamp, vise, ferrule').

стружка.etymology: Formed with the suffix -ка from стругать / строгать ('to plane wood, shave off thin curls', with г → ж before -к-), from Proto-Slavic *strugati ('to scrape, shave, plane').

history.meaning: to plane, shave → wood shaving, curl (of wood, chocolate, or citrus zest)

струна.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic струна and Proto-Slavic *struna ('musical string, bowstring, taut cord, sinew'), from Proto-Indo-European *strew- ('stretched cord, sinew, streak'), cognate with Old High German strīmo ('streak, stripe').

history.meaning: string of a gusli or bow
string (of a violin, guitar, or piano)

струсить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from трусить ('to be afraid, act like a coward'), derived from трус ('coward', originally 'trembling, shaking', from Old East Slavic трусъ 'shaking, earthquake, fear', Proto-Slavic *trǫsъ, related to трясти 'to shake').

history.meaning: to chicken out, lose one's nerve

стряпня.etymology: Collective/action noun formed with the suffix -ня from стряпать ('to cook, prepare food'), inherited from Old East Slavic стряпати ('to work, manage household affairs, cook'), from Proto-Slavic *strępati.

стрястись.etymology: Formed from стрясти ('to shake off, shake down', from prefix с- + трясти 'to shake', Proto-Slavic *tręsti) + the reflexive particle -сь; literally 'to shake loose and fall down upon someone (of a misfortune)'.

студенческий.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -еский (with consonant alternation т > ч) from студент ('university student'), borrowed via Polish student or German Student from Latin studēns (present participle of studēre 'to be eager, study').

студия.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from Italian studio ('artist's or sculptor's workshop; study'), from Latin studium ('zeal, eager pursuit, study, place of study').

стукач.etymology: Twentieth-century slang agent noun formed with the suffix -ач from стучать ('to knock, tap; in prison/underworld argot, to inform on someone, snitch', originally from knocking on the cell door to summon a guard).

стукнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed with the suffix -нуть from стукать / стучать ('to knock, strike, rap'), derived from the onomatopoeic Proto-Slavic root *stuk- ('knock, thud').

стукнуться.etymology: Reflexive semelfactive verb formed with -ся from стукнуть ('to knock, hit once'), from the onomatopoeic Slavic root *stuk- ('knock, bump').

history.meaning: to bump into, hit oneself against

стул.etymology: Recorded in East Slavic from the 16th century, borrowed from Middle Low German stōl or Old Norse stóll / German Stuhl ('chair, seat'), from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz ('seat, stand'), which itself comes from the same Proto-Indo-European root *steh₂- / *stel- as native Russian стол ('table') and стоять ('to stand').
стул.notes: False friend for English speakers: a Russian **стул** is a chair with a backrest, whereas a backless stool is **табуретка**.

ступать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ступати ('to step, tread, walk'), imperfective counterpart of ступить, from Proto-Slavic *stǫpati / *stǫpiti ('to step, tread').

ступень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ступень ('step, stair, rung, degree'), from Proto-Slavic *stǫpenь, derived from *stǫpati / *stǫpiti ('to step, tread').

ступенька.etymology: Formed in Russian as the everyday diminutive (with suffix -ка) of ступень ('step, stair, stage'), inherited from Old East Slavic ступень, from Proto-Slavic *stǫpenь, derived from *stǫpati / *stǫpiti ('to step, tread', modern Russian ступать / ступить).

стучаться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from стучать ('to knock, rap', seeking admittance at a door), from Proto-Slavic *stučati (from the onomatopoeic root *stuk- 'knock').

history.meaning: to knock (on a door asking to be let in)

стыд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic стыдъ ('shame, disgrace; cold'), from Proto-Slavic *stydъ, originally 'chilling, freezing, shrinking back in cold or revulsion' (related to стыть / студить 'to grow cold, chill', from PIE *(s)tewd-).

стыдно.etymology: Impersonal predicate and adverb formed from стыдный ('shameful'), derived from стыд ('shame'), inherited from Old East Slavic стыдъ and Proto-Slavic *stydъ ('cold, chill; shame'), from the same root as стыть / остыть ('to grow cold, freeze'). Shame was conceptualized from the physical sensation of a sudden chill or freezing in embarrassment.

стык.etymology: Formed in Russian as a prefixal-stem noun from стыкать / соknуться ('to bring together point-to-point, butt together'), built on с- ('together') + тыкать ('to poke, thrust, touch ends', Proto-Slavic *tykati, related to точка 'point, dot'): 'the seam or joint where two boards, rails, or panels meet end to end'.

history.meaning: to join ends -> joint, butt seam, junction

стюардесса.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English stewardess ('female ship's or flight attendant'), formed from steward (from Old English stīweard 'hall-warden, housekeeper') + feminine suffix -ess.

су-шеф.etymology: Borrowed in modern culinary Russian from French sous-chef (short for sous-chef de cuisine, 'under-chef, second in command in a professional kitchen'), formed from French sous ('under', from Latin subtus) + chef ('head, chief', from Latin caput).

суббота.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic субота and Old Church Slavonic сѫбота (with nasal *ǫ -> у) from popular Byzantine/Balkan Greek *sámbaton (standard Ancient Greek sábbaton), ultimately from Hebrew šabbāṯ ('Sabbath, day of rest', from šāḇaṯ 'to cease from work, rest').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

cognates.meaning: Saturday (from the same Vulgar Latin/Greek *sambatum variant)

суббота.notes: Spelled with double -бб- after Church Slavonic and Greek orthography, though pronounced with a single [б].

субботний.etymology: Derived from суббота ('Saturday') with the soft relational adjectival suffix -ний.

субординация.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via German Subordination or Polish subordynacja from Medieval Latin subōrdinātiō ('placing in a lower rank, hierarchy'), from Latin sub- ('under') + ōrdināre ('to arrange in order, rank').

history.meaning: placing in a lower order, subordination

сувенир.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French souvenir ('remembrance, keepsake, token'), substantivized infinitive of souvenir ('to remember, come to mind'), from Latin subvenire ('to come up to mind, occur').
