сугроб.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic nominal prefix су- ('together') + the o-grade root *grob- of грести / гребу ('to rake, sweep, heap up', Proto-Slavic *grebti), literally 'a raked-up or drifted heap (of snow)'.

суд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic судъ (and Old Church Slavonic сѫдъ 'judgment, court, trial'), from Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ, originally a compound of *sǫ- ('together', cognate with Sanskrit sam-) and *dhe- ('to put, set', as in деть / дело), literally 'a putting together, settlement, assembly'.

сударыня.etymology: Formed with the feminine suffix -ыня from сударь ('sir, master'), itself a rapid-speech allegro shortening of государь ('lord, sovereign', from Old East Slavic господарь).
сударыня.notes: A traditional polite or old-fashioned form of address to a woman ('madam').

судейство.etymology: Formed from судья ('judge, referee', from Old East Slavic судья, derived from судъ 'judgment, court') + the abstract noun suffix -ство.

судить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic судити ('to judge, try at law, govern'), from Proto-Slavic *sǫditi, denominal verb from *sǫdъ ('judgment, court', modern Russian суд, composed of *sǫ- 'together' + *-dъ from *děti 'to put, set').

судьба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic судьба ('judgment, decree, God's judgment, fate'), formed with the abstract noun suffix -ьба from судить ('to judge') / суд ('judgment, court', Proto-Slavic *sǫdьba from *sǫdъ). Fate was originally conceived as a higher judicial decree or allotment.

судьбоносный.etymology: Compound adjective formed in twentieth-century Russian from судьба ('fate, destiny', from суд 'judgment') + linking -о- + -носный (from носить 'to carry, bring'), literally 'fate-bringing, fateful'.

судья.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic судии / судья and Old Church Slavonic сѫдии ('judge'), formed with the agent suffix *-ьji from судъ ('judgment, court, trial', from Proto-Slavic *sǫdъ, originally a compound *sǫ-dъ 'putting together, joint decision').
судья.notes: Grammatically masculine when referring to a judge or referee, while declining like a feminine -я noun.

судя.etymology: Adverbial participle (gerund) of судить ('to judge', from Proto-Slavic *sǫditi), lexicalized in the prepositional phrase судя по ('judging by').

суеверие.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic суѥвѣрие ('vain/empty belief, superstition', calquing Ancient Greek κενοδοξία or δεισιδαιμονία), compound of суи ('vain, empty, hollow', Proto-Slavic *sujь, cf. всуе 'in vain') + вѣра ('faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra).

суеверный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from суеверие ('superstition', from Old Church Slavonic суѥвѣрьнъ 'holding vain beliefs, superstitious', from суи 'empty, vain' + вѣра 'belief').

сужать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from сузить ('to make narrower, constrict'), composed of the prefix с- + узить ('to narrow', from узкий 'narrow', Proto-Slavic *ǫzъkъ, PIE *h₂emǵʰ-).

суженый.etymology: Substantivized passive participle of судить ('to judge, ordain by fate', Old East Slavic судити, Proto-Slavic *sǫditi); in traditional Russian folklore, the 'fated one' or 'betrothed' destined by God or fate to be one's spouse.

суметь.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from уметь ('to know how, be able'), inherited from Old East Slavic умѣти, from Proto-Slavic *uměti (derived from *umъ 'mind, intellect', modern Russian ум).

сумка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from сума ('scrip, pouch, saddlebag'), attested in Old East Slavic сума and borrowed via Polish/West Slavic suma and Middle High German soum from Vulgar Latin sauma / sagma ('pack-saddle, pack-bag', from Ancient Greek σάγμα).

сумочка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from сумка ('bag, pouch, purse'), itself a diminutive of сума ('scrip, saddlebag, pouch', borrowed in Old East Slavic via Old High German soum or Polish suma from Medieval Latin sauma / Late Latin sagma 'pack-saddle, pack').

сундук.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic (attested from 1489 as сундукъ) from Kipchak Turkic sunduq / sanduq ('chest, coffer'), from Arabic ṣundūq ('box, trunk'), which in turn goes back to Byzantine Greek σενδούκιον (from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις or σάνδυξ).

суп.etymology: A borrowing from French soupe. Vasmer connects the same French source with English soup, Dutch soep and German Suppe. He traces the earlier Gallo-Romance form to a Germanic source.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: суп

суп.notes: Say *есть суп* 'to eat soup' (not 'drink'). *Первое* is the menu term for the soup course.

суп-пюре.etymology: Culinary compound modeled on French soupe purée, combining суп ('soup', from French soupe) + пюре ('purée', from French purée, originally 'strained or purified mash').

супер-шеф.etymology: Modern compound combining the international prefix супер- (from Latin super 'above, beyond') + шеф ('boss, head chef', from French chef).

суперзвезда.etymology: Late twentieth-century semi-calque of English superstar, combining the borrowed prefix супер- (from Latin super 'above, beyond') with native звезда ('star', from Proto-Slavic *gvězda).

супруга.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic съпрѫга ('wife, yoke-fellow'), feminine of съпрѫгъ ('husband, one yoked together in a pair'), from prefix съ- ('together') + the nasal root of прячь / упряжь ('to harness, yoke', Proto-Slavic *sǫprǫgъ), calquing Greek σύζυγος and Latin coniux.

супружеский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -еский (with velar alternation г > ж) from супруг ('spouse'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic сѫпрѫгъ ('yoke-fellow, spouse', literally 'one yoked together', from *sǫ- 'together' + *pręgti 'to harness, yoke').

супчик.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed from суп ('soup', borrowed from French soupe) + the masculine diminutive suffix -чик.

сургучный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from сургуч ('sealing wax'), borrowed in the seventeenth century from Turkic surguc / surğuç ('sealing wax, bitumen, crest', related to Turkic surqa- 'to drip, smear').

сурово.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from суровый ('stern, harsh, severe').

суровый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic суровыи ('raw, unbleached, coarse; fierce, stern'), from Proto-Slavic *surovъ ('raw, green, unworked, harsh'), closely related to *syrъ ('raw, damp', modern сырой, from PIE *suH-ro- 'sour, raw, bitter').

сухарик.etymology: Diminutive formed from сухарь ('rusk, dried bread crust', derived from сухой 'dry', Proto-Slavic *suxъ) + the diminutive suffix -ик.

сухой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сухъ / сухыи ('dry, withered'), from Proto-Slavic *suxъ, continuing Proto-Indo-European *sausós ('dry, parched', from *h₂sews- 'to dry out'), directly cognate with Lithuanian saũsas ('dry'), Ancient Greek αὖος, Sanskrit śúṣka, and English sear.

суши.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century (via English sushi) from Japanese 寿司 / すし (sushi, originally 'sour-tasting', referring to vinegared rice paired with fish).

сушить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сушити ('to dry'), from Proto-Slavic *sušiti, causative verb formed from *suxъ ('dry', modern Russian сухой, from PIE *h₂sews- 'to become dry').

существо.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic сѫщьство ('being, essence, nature, creature'), formed from сѫщии (present active participle of быти 'to be', equivalent to Latin ens / Greek ὄν) + abstract suffix -ьство, originally calquing Greek οὐσία ('essence, being').

существовать.etymology: Derived in Russian from существо ('being, existence', from Old Church Slavonic сѫщьство) + the verbal suffix -овать, translating Latin exsistere / French exister.

сфотографировать.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix с- from фотографировать ('to photograph'), derived from фотография ('photography', coined from Ancient Greek φῶς, stem φωτ- 'light' + γράφω 'to write, draw').

схватить.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix с- ('together, seizing quickly') + хватить ('to grab, snatch'), from Proto-Slavic *xvatiti ('to seize, catch hold of').

схватка.etymology: Deverbal noun formed with the suffix -ка from схватить / схватывать ('to seize, grapple, clash'), composed of с- ('together') + хватить ('to grab, snatch', Proto-Slavic *xvatiti).

схваченный.etymology: Past passive participle of схватить ('to grab, seize, catch'), from с- + хватить (Proto-Slavic *xvatiti); in colloquial idioms (всё схвачено), 'all tied up, under control, taken care of'.

схема.etymology: Borrowed via Latin schema or directly from Ancient Greek σχῆμα (skhêma 'form, shape, figure, outline'), derived from ἔχειν (ékhein 'to hold, have, be in a state').

сходить.etymology: Formed from the prefix с- and ходить ('to walk, go', the multidirectional counterpart of идти, from Proto-Slavic *xoditi). Has two distinct aspectual uses in Russian: as a perfective verb ('to go somewhere and come back', e.g., сходить в магазин) and as an imperfective counterpart of сойти ('to go down, descend, get off').

history.meaning: to walk down; to go and return
to go somewhere and return (pf.); to descend (impf.)

сходиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of сходить ('to come together'), formed from prefix с- ('together') + ходить ('to walk, go', from Proto-Slavic *xoditi). When two paths, lines, or accounts 'come together', they 'converge, meet, tally, match up'.

history.meaning: to meet, converge; to match up, tally

сценарий.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via Italian scenario (and French scénario) from Late Latin scaenārium ('place for stage sets, theatrical outline'), derived from Latin scaena ('stage, scene'), from Ancient Greek σκηνή ('tent, stage booth').

счастливо.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of счастливый ('happy, fortunate'), derived from счастье ('good fortune, happiness', historically съчастие: съ- 'good, with' + часть 'part, lot, share'). Used idiomatically on parting to mean 'all the best!, bye!'.
счастливо.notes: In the farewell *Счастливо!* ('All the best!'), stress commonly falls on the third syllable (счастли́во).

счастливчик.etymology: Colloquial person noun formed with the diminutive/expressive suffix -чик from счастливый ('happy, lucky'), derived from счастье ('good fortune, happiness', from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje, literally 'good share/portion', from *sъ- 'good' + *čęstь 'part, share').

счастливый.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ливый from счастье ('happiness, good fortune'), historically съчастие ('a good share or lot', from съ- 'good, with' + часть 'part, share, fate').
счастливый.notes: The consonant cluster -стл- simplifies in pronunciation to [-сл-] (pronounced [щасли́вый]).

счастье.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съчастие, from Proto-Slavic *sъčęstьje ('good fortune, good share'), a compound of the archaic prefix *sъ- ('good, well; together with', cognate with Sanskrit su- 'good') and *čęstь ('part, share, portion, lot', modern Russian часть). Literally, счастье meant 'a good share, a fortunate allotment in life'.

history.meaning: good share / joint portion → good fortune

счастье.notes: Pronounced **[ща́стье]**: the cluster **сч** merges into a long soft **[щ:]**.

считать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съчитати ('to count up, read together, reckon'), formed from съ- ('together') + читати ('to read, reckon, honour'), from Proto-Slavic *čitati.

считаться.etymology: Reflexive and passive verb formed with -ся from считать ('to count, reckon, consider'), inherited from Old East Slavic съчитати, from Proto-Slavic *sъčitati (iterative of *sъčьsti 'to count, read').

history.meaning: to be considered; to count; to take into account

счёт.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съчьтъ ('count, reckoning'), a deverbal noun from съчести ('to count up'), built on съ- ('together') + Proto-Slavic *čьt- ('to count, reckon, read').
счёт.notes: In a restaurant, *Счёт, пожалуйста!* means 'The bill, please!'.

счётчик.etymology: Instrument and agent noun formed with the suffix -чик from счёт ('count, reckoning, bill', from считать 'to count', Proto-Slavic *sъčьtъ).

сшить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съшити ('to sew together, stitch'), from Proto-Slavic *sъšiti, composed of the prefix *sъ- ('together') + *šiti ('to sew', modern Russian шить, PIE *syuH-).

съедать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix съ- ('up, completely') and iterative stem -едать (corresponding to perfective съесть 'to eat up'), from Proto-Slavic *sъjědati (from *jěsti 'to eat', PIE *h₁ed-).

съедобный.etymology: Derived from съедомый / съедать ('to eat up', from с- + еда / есть 'to eat', Proto-Slavic *ěsti) with the adjectival suffix -обный (by analogy with подобный, удобный).

съезд.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съѣздъ ('coming together on horseback or by vehicle, assembly, congress; downward ramp'), deverbal noun from съѣхати / съехать ('to ride down; to ride together').

съездить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix съ- (denoting a completed round trip: going somewhere by vehicle and returning) from ездить ('to go by vehicle, ride', from Proto-Slavic *jězditi).

history.meaning: to make a round trip (go and come back)

съесть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic съѣсти, formed with the perfective prefix съ- (modern с-, spelled съ- before е) + ѣсти (modern есть 'to eat'), from Proto-Slavic *sъjěsti.

morphemes.meaning: perfective / completely (with hard sign before е)

съёмка.etymology: Action noun formed with the suffix -ка from съём / снимать ('taking off, surveying, photographing, filming'), derived from снять (Old East Slavic съняти 'to take off, capture', from *sъn- + *jęti 'to take').

history.meaning: to take (a plan, photograph, or film)

съёмный.etymology: Formed from съём ('taking off, renting, leasing', deverbal noun from снять / снимать 'to take off, rent', from Proto-Slavic *sъnęti) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

сыворотка.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic (with metathesis of *r and *v from Proto-Slavic *syrovatъka, compare Polish serwatka, Ukrainian сироватка), derived from *syrъ ('cheese, curd; raw', modern Russian сыр / сырой, from PIE *suH-ro- 'sour, salty, curdled').

сыграть.etymology: Formed in Russian with the perfective prefix с- + играть ('to play'), from Old East Slavic играти (Proto-Slavic *jьgrati). After the hard consonant prefix с-, initial и- shifts in spelling and pronunciation to ы.

history.meaning: to play (a piece or game) to completion

morphemes.meaning: play (играть, with и → ы after с-)

сын.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сынъ (and Old Church Slavonic сꙑнъ), from Proto-Slavic *synъ ('son'), from Proto-Indo-European *suHnús ('son', literally 'one who is born', from *sewH- 'to give birth'; compare English son, German Sohn, Lithuanian sūnùs, and Sanskrit sūnú-).

сынок.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of сын ('son', Old East Slavic сынъ, Proto-Slavic *synъ), formed with the masculine diminutive suffix -ок (genitive сынка, with fleeting о).

сыночек.etymology: Double affectionate diminutive formed from сынок ('little son', from сын 'son', Proto-Slavic *synъ) + the diminutive suffix -ек.

сыпь.etymology: Deverbal zero-suffixed feminine noun (-i- stem) formed from сыпать ('to pour, strew, scatter, break out in spots', from Proto-Slavic *sypati), denoting a skin eruption or rash scattered over the body.

history.meaning: to scatter; to break out in a rash

сырный.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *syrьnъ, relational adjective formed from сыр ('cheese', Old East Slavic сыръ, Proto-Slavic *syrъ) + suffix -ный.

сыроедение.etymology: Compound noun formed from сырой ('raw, uncooked', from Proto-Slavic *syrъ) + connecting vowel -о- + едение ('eating', verbal noun from есть 'to eat', Proto-Slavic *jěsti).

сырой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сыръ ('damp, moist; raw, uncooked'), from Proto-Slavic *syrъ ('moist, raw, unpasteurized'), cognate with Lithuanian sūras ('salty') and English sour (from Proto-Germanic *sūraz). The noun сыр ('cheese', originally raw curds) comes from the same root.

сырость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from сырой ('damp, moist, raw'), from Proto-Slavic *syrъ.

сытый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сытыи (short form сытъ, 'sated, full, well-fed'), from Proto-Slavic *sytъ, an old *-to- participle from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂- ('to satisfy, sate', cognate with Lithuanian sotus, Gothic saþs, Latin satis 'enough').

сюда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic сюда / сюду ('hither, to this place'), reshaped from Proto-Slavic *sǫdu / *sěmo under the influence of the proximal demonstrative stem *sь ('this', seen in сей and сегодня).
сюда.notes: *Сюда* expresses motion toward the speaker ('to here'), whereas *здесь* or *тут* expresses static location ('at here').

сюрприз.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French surprise ('unexpected event, surprise, gift'), originally the feminine past participle of surprendre ('to overtake, catch unawares', from sur- 'over' + prendre 'to take', from Latin prehendere).

сёмга.etymology: Attested in northern Russian charters since the sixteenth century (семга), borrowed from a Finnic language of northwestern Russia (compare Finnish tonko / Karelian and Sami forms, or Finnic *soomukka 'scaly fish', from *soomu 'fish scale').

табличка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of таблица ('table, chart, tablet'), borrowed via Polish tablica from Latin tabula ('board, plank, inscribed tablet, plaque').

табуретка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the everyday suffix -ка from табурет 'stool', borrowed from French tabouret. In Old French tabouret meant 'little drum' (a diminutive of tabour 'drum'), applied to a round, backless seat shaped like a drum.
табуретка.notes: In everyday speech feminine табуретка is warmer and more common at home than masculine табурет.

таджикистан.etymology: Compound country name formed from таджик ('Tajik', from Persian تاجیک tājīk, historically a Middle Persian/Soghdian designation of Arabs and later Iranian-speaking Central Asians) and the Persian topophoric element -стан (-stān, 'land, place of', from Indo-Iranian *stāna- 'place, stand').

таиланд.etymology: Adopted in the twentieth century (after Siam changed its official international name in 1939) from English Thailand, a hybrid compound of Thai ไทย (Thai, 'Thai people; free') and English land.

тайком.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of an obsolete or dialectal noun *тайко / *таек, derived from the root of таить ('to hide, conceal') and тайна ('secret', from Proto-Slavic *tajiti / *tajьnъ).

history.meaning: secretly, by stealth, on the sly

таймер.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English timer (an agent/instrument noun from time + -er).

тайна.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic таина ('secret, mystery'), substantivized feminine of the adjective таиныи ('secret, hidden'), from Proto-Slavic *tajьna / *tajiti ('to hide, conceal').

тайник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic таиникъ ('secret place, underground passage, confidant'), formed with the suffix -ник from тайный ('secret, hidden', from Proto-Slavic *tajьnъ, from *tajiti 'to hide').

тайно.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of тайный ('secret, clandestine'), from Proto-Slavic *tajьno ('secretly'), built on the root of таить ('to hide, conceal').

тайный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic таиныи ('hidden, secret'), from Proto-Slavic *tajьnъ, built with the adjectival suffix *-ьnъ on the root of *tajiti ('to hide, keep secret').

тайфун.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via English typhoon, a convergence of Arabic/Persian طوفان (ṭūfān, 'great storm, deluge', likely influenced by Ancient Greek Τυφῶν Typhōn, father of whirlwind monsters) and Cantonese 大風 (daai6 fung1 / Mandarin dàfēng, 'big wind').

history.meaning: tropical cyclone of the western Pacific

так.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тако ('thus, so, in that way'), from Proto-Slavic *tako, a manner adverb built on the demonstrative pronoun stem *to- ('that', from PIE *tó-), correlative with как ('how').

так-то.etymology: Colloquial emphatic particle formed from так ('so, thus', from Proto-Slavic *tako) + the enclitic demonstrative/emphatic particle -то (from Proto-Slavic *to 'that').

также.etymology: Compound adverb and conjunction formed by fusing the adverb так ('thus, so', from Proto-Slavic *tako) with the emphasizing enclitic particle же (from Proto-Slavic *že).

таков.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic таковъ ('of such a kind, such'), from Proto-Slavic *takovъ, a pronominal adjective formed from *takъ ('such', modern такой) + suffix *-ovъ. In modern Russian it survives mainly as a short predicate adjective.

такой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic такыи / такои ('such, of that kind'), from Proto-Slavic *takъ, an adjectival derivative of the demonstrative stem *to- / *ta- ('that', from PIE *tó-; compare Latin tālis 'such' and correlative какой 'of what kind').

такт.etymology: Borrowed via German Takt ('musical beat, measure, bar; social tact') from Latin tāctus ('touch, sense of touch, beat'), a noun formed from tangere ('to touch').

тактика.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French tactique or German Taktik from New Latin tactica, from Ancient Greek τακτική (τέχνη) (taktikḗ tékhnē, 'art of arranging troops for battle'), from τακτός ('ordered, arranged'), verbal adjective of τάσσω ('to arrange, draw up in order').

талантливо.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from талантливый ('talented, gifted'), derived from талант ('talent', via Church Slavonic талантъ / French talent from Ancient Greek τάλαντον 'balance, weight of silver/gold', with the sense 'natural gift' arising from the biblical Parable of the Talents).

талисман.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via French talisman from Arabic طِلَسْم (ṭilasm, plural ṭilasmān), from Byzantine Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, 'consecrated religious rite,apotropaic object'), from Ancient Greek τελέω ('to complete, consecrate, perform a rite').

талон.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French talon ('heel; stub or detachable counterfoil of a voucher or check'), from Old French talon ('heel'), from Vulgar Latin *tālōnem (from Classical Latin tālus 'anklebone, heel').

там.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тамо ('there'), from Proto-Slavic *tamo, a locative adverb built with the suffix *-mo on the demonstrative pronoun stem *to- / *ta- ('that', from PIE *tó-).

таможенник.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -ник from таможня ('customs house', derived from adjective таможный, from тамга 'customs seal, duty', borrowed in Old East Slavic from Turkic/Mongolic *tamga 'brand, seal, tribute').

танго.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century via French/international usage from Rioplatense Spanish tango ('Argentine partner dance and music'), originally used in nineteenth-century Buenos Aires and Montevideo for Afro-Argentine drum gatherings and dances (likely of Niger-Congo/Bantu or Spanish onomatopoeic origin).

танк.etymology: Borrowed during World War I (1916) from English tank. British developers of the first tracked armored fighting vehicles in 1915 used the cover name 'water tank' (cistern, reservoir) for counter-intelligence secrecy, and the code word became the permanent name of the vehicle worldwide.

танцевать.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century via Polish tańcować (from taniec 'dance') from Middle High German / German tanzen ('to dance'), which came from Old French danser.

танцпол.etymology: Late twentieth-century semi-calque of English dance floor, combining the stem танц- (from танец / танцевать 'dance / to dance', via Polish taniec from Middle High German tanz) and пол ('floor', from Proto-Slavic *polъ).

тапка.etymology: Back-formed singular from тапки / тапочки ('slippers'), twentieth-century colloquial word of expressive/onomatopoeic origin (compare тяпать / топать 'to patter, shuffle softly with the feet' and dialectal тапать 'to walk slapping the soles').

таракан.etymology: Attested in Russian since the seventeenth century (originally таракан, торокан); generally considered a borrowing from Turkic (compare Chuvash таракан or Kipchak/Tatar forms connected by Vasmer and Räsänen with Turkic tarqan 'dignitary' used humorously/tabooistically, or with Turkic *taryq- 'to disperse, run about').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: таракан

тарелка.etymology: Adapted by dissimilation of r...r to r...l from earlier Russian тарерка / тарель (attested from the sixteenth century), borrowed via Polish talerz and Middle High German talier from Italian tagliere ('wooden chopping board or trencher for slicing meat', from tagliare 'to cut').

тариф.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via French tarif or German Tarif from Italian tariffa ('schedule of customs duties or rates'), from Arabic تَعْرِيفَة (taʿrīfa, 'notification, schedule of fees'), verbal noun of ʿarrafa ('to make known, notify').

тартар.etymology: Borrowed from French (steak) tartare ('finely chopped raw beef or fish seasoned with capers and onion'), shortened from nineteenth-century French culinary à la tartare ('served cold with tartar sauce'), named after the Tatars (French Tartares).

history.meaning: seasoned raw minced meat or fish dish

таскать.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic, iterative verb related to тащить ('to drag, pull'), connected by Vasmer with Proto-Slavic *taskati / *tęskati or expressive root *tъsk- ('to press, squeeze, pull').

таскаться.etymology: Reflexive iterative verb formed with -ся from таскать ('to drag, pull repeatedly', multidirectional counterpart of тащить), meaning 'to drag oneself around, trail after someone, hang about'.

history.meaning: to trail around, tag along, gad about

татарский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from татарин / татары ('Tatar / Tatars'), inherited from Old East Slavic татаринъ, from Old Turkic 𐱃𐱃𐰺 (Tatar).

тату.etymology: Late twentieth-century borrowing from English tattoo (alongside the older nineteenth-century adaptation татуировка via French tatouer), ultimately from Polynesian (Tahitian/Samoan) tatau ('to strike, tap, mark skin with pigment').

history.meaning: to tap, mark skin with tattoo

татуировка.etymology: Action and result noun formed from татуировать ('to tattoo') + suffix -ка; borrowed via French tatouer / German tätowieren and English tattoo from Polynesian (Tahitian/Samoan) tatau ('mark made on the skin').

тачка.etymology: Derived in Russian from тачать ('to roll, wheel' in dialects, related to качать / точить 'to make roll, turn') + instrumental suffix -ка, originally 'wheelbarrow'; in twentieth-century colloquial slang extended to 'car, ride' (initially via 'handcart/taxi').

таять.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic таяти ('to melt, thaw, waste away'), from Proto-Slavic *tajati ('to melt, thaw'), from Proto-Indo-European *teh₂- ('to melt, dissolve', cognate with Ancient Greek τήκω, Latin tābēs, and English thaw).

тверской.etymology: Relational adjective formed from the city name Тверь (Old East Slavic Твѣрь / Тьхвѣрь, attested from the twelfth century, derived from the river name Тверца or related to твердь 'fortress, stronghold') + the adjectival suffix -ской.

творец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic творьць / Old Church Slavonic творьць ('maker, creator, author'), formed with the agent suffix *-ьcь from Proto-Slavic *tvoriti ('to make, fashion, create', modern творить).

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

твориться.etymology: Reflexive/passive form of творить ('to do, make, create', from Proto-Slavic *tvoriti) + -ся, meaning 'to be done, go on, happen'.

творчески.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with the suffix -и from творческий ('creative'), derived from творец ('creator', with velar/affricate alternation ц > ч before -еский), from творить ('to create', Proto-Slavic *tvoriti).

творческий.etymology: Derived from творец ('creator, maker', from творить 'to create', Proto-Slavic *tvorьcь) + the adjectival suffix -ский (with ц > ч alternation).

творчество.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ество from творец ('creator', with ц > ч), from творить ('to make, create', Proto-Slavic *tvoriti).

твёрдо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic твьрдо ('firmly, steadfastly'), adverbial form of твёрдый ('hard, firm, solid'), from Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ ('hard, firm, fortified').

твёрдый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic твьрдыи ('firm, solid, steadfast, fortified'), from Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ ('hard, firm'), cognate with Lithuanian tvirtas ('strong, firm, durable').

текила.etymology: Borrowed via Spanish tequila ('distilled blue agave spirit'), named after the town of Tequila in Jalisco, Mexico (from Nahuatl Tecuila / Tekwilan, 'place of tribute' or 'place where work/cutting is done').

history.meaning: town of Tequila, Jalisco → blue agave liquor

текст.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century via German Text from Latin textus ('tissue, structure, connected wording of a written work'), passive participle noun from texere ('to weave').

текучка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from текучесть кадров ('staff turnover') or текущие дела ('day-to-day routine'), derived from текучий ('fluid, flowing, fluctuating', from течь 'to flow', Proto-Slavic *tekti).

телевизионный.etymology: Formed from телевизия (older borrowing from French télévision, compounded from Greek τῆλε 'far' + Latin visio 'sight, vision') + the adjectival suffix -онный.

телевизор.etymology: Borrowed in the 1930s via German Televisor / English televisor (coined from Ancient Greek τῆλε tēle 'far off' + Latin vīsor 'viewer', from vidēre 'to see'). In Russian, телевидение denotes the medium ('television'), while телевизор denotes the physical receiver ('television set, TV').

тележка.etymology: Diminutive in -ка of телега ('four-wheeled wooden cart or wagon', with г → ж before -к-), attested in Old East Slavic as телѣга (an early eastern borrowing often compared by Vasmer with Turkic and Mongolic words for a transport cart).

телефон.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from French téléphone (or German Telephon), a neo-classical compound coined from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, 'far off, at a distance') + φωνή (phōnḗ, 'voice, sound').

телефонный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from телефон ('telephone'), borrowed from French téléphone / English telephone (coined from Ancient Greek τῆλε 'far off' + φωνή 'voice, sound').

телефончик.etymology: Affectionate diminutive formed with the suffix -чик from телефон ('telephone; phone number').

телоломатель.etymology: Jocular Russian compound modeled as an ironic pun on телохранитель ('bodyguard'), combining тело ('body', Proto-Slavic *tělo) + linking -о- + ломатель ('breaker', from ломать 'to break' + agent suffix -тель).

телохранитель.etymology: Compound noun modeled on Ancient Greek σωματοφύλαξ / German Leibwächter: formed from тело ('body', Proto-Slavic *tělo) + linking -о- + хранитель ('guardian, keeper', from хранить 'to guard, keep').

телячий.etymology: Relational/possessive adjective formed from теля (oblique stem телят-, Old East Slavic теля 'calf', modern телёнок), inherited from Proto-Slavic *telę (gen. *telęte, 'calf'), with regular palatalization т > ч before *-jь.

тема.etymology: Borrowed via Polish temat / German Thema and Latin thema from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma, 'something set down, proposition, topic for discussion'), derived from τίθημι (títhēmi, 'to put, place, set down', from PIE *dʰeh₁-).

темнеть.etymology: Inchoative verb formed with the suffix -еть from тёмный ('dark'), inherited from Old East Slavic тьмьныи, derived from тьма ('darkness', from Proto-Slavic *tьma, PIE *témHes- 'darkness').

темно.etymology: Adverbial and impersonal predicate form in -о of тёмный ('dark'), from Old East Slavic тьмьно and Proto-Slavic *tьmьno, built on тьма ('darkness').

темп.etymology: Borrowed from Italian tempo ('time, musical pace, rate of movement'), from Latin tempus ('time, season').

тень.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣнь ('shadow, shade'), from Proto-Slavic *těnь, which developed alongside *stěnь / *scěnь from a Proto-Indo-European root connected with Ancient Greek σκιά ('shadow') and Sanskrit chāyā́ ('shade, reflection').
тень.notes: Feminine noun ending in a soft sign: в тени́ ('in the shade').

теоретически.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with the suffix -и from теоретический ('theoretical'), derived from теория / теоретик (from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός 'contemplative, speculative, theoretical').

теория.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via Polish teoria or German Theorie from Late Latin theōria, from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría, 'viewing, contemplation, speculation'), from θεωρός ('spectator, observer').

теперь.etymology: Reduced from Old East Slavic топерво / теперво ('first of all, just now, now'), a univerbation of the demonstrative particle то ('that, then') + пьрво ('first', neuter short form of первый, from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ).

history.meaning: just now, for the first time, now

теперь.notes: Contrasts the present situation with an earlier one ('now, as opposed to before'), whereas **сейчас** simply means 'right now, at this moment'.

теплее.etymology: Comparative degree formed with the suffix -ее from тёплый ('warm'), from Proto-Slavic *teplъ ('warm, hot').

теплеть.etymology: Inchoative verb in -еть ('to become...') formed from тёплый ('warm'), from Proto-Slavic *teplъ.

тепло.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тепло ('warmth; warmly'), the short neuter singular of тёплый ('warm', from Proto-Slavic *teplъ, from PIE *tep- 'to be warm'). Functions both as an impersonal predicate/adverb ('it is warm, warmly') and as a neuter noun ('warmth').

тереть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic терети / тьрти (1 sg. търу, 'to rub, grind, wipe'), from Proto-Slavic *tьrti, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- ('to rub, turn, bore', cognate with Latin terere 'to rub, thresh' and Ancient Greek τείρω).

терзать.etymology: Inherited via Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic тързати ('to tear to pieces, rend, pluck, torment'), from Proto-Slavic *tьrzati (iterative of *tьrgnǫti, modern расторгнуть / дергать, from PIE *dregʰ- / *tergʰ- 'to tear, pull').

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

history.meaning: to tear at; to torment, anguish

термин.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via Polish termin or German Termin from Medieval and Classical Latin terminus ('boundary marker, limit; in medieval logic, a word or expression having a defined meaning').

history.meaning: boundary stone, limit; defined logical term

тернистый.etymology: Derived from Church Slavonic терние / тръние ('thorns, brambles', collective of трънъ / тёрн 'thorn, blackthorn', Proto-Slavic *tьrnъ) + the adjectival suffix -истый.

терпеливо.etymology: Adverbial form in -о of терпеливый ('patient'), derived from терпеть ('to endure, bear patiently', from Old East Slavic трьпѣти and Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti).

терпеть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic търпѣти (and Old Church Slavonic тръпѣти 'to suffer, endure, bear patiently'), from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti ('to grow numb, stiffen; to endure, bear'), cognate with Lithuanian tir̃pti ('to grow numb, stiffen') and Latin torpēre ('to be numb or stiff', whence English torpid). Endurance was originally expressed as stiffening oneself or becoming numb to pain.

history.meaning: to stiffen, grow numb → to endure, bear
to bear, tolerate, put up with; to hold on

rootFamily.gloss: to be patient for a while

терпеться.etymology: Impersonal reflexive verb formed from терпеть ('to endure, have patience', from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti) + -ся, used predominantly with negation (не терпится 'one cannot wait').

терпкий.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic терпкий ('tart, astringent, puckering to the taste'), from Proto-Slavic *tьrpъkъ, derived from *tьrpěti / *tьrpnǫti ('to grow numb, stiffen', modern терпеть / терпнуть), because astringent fruit makes the mouth feel numb or constricted.

террорист.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French terroriste (originally referring to agents of the Jacobin Reign of Terror during the French Revolution), derived from terreur ('terror', from Latin terror 'great fear, dread').

тесно.etymology: Short neuter predicate form and adverb from тесный ('tight, narrow, cramped'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *těsnъ (from *těsknъ, related to тискать 'to squeeze, press').

теснота.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣснота ('narrowness, cramped space, distress'), formed with the abstract noun suffix -ота from тѣсныи (modern Russian тесный, 'tight, narrow, cramped', from Proto-Slavic *těsnъ).

тесный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тѣсьныи ('narrow, cramped, tight, closely pressed'), from Proto-Slavic *těsnъ, related to тискать / теснить ('to squeeze, press tightly').

history.meaning: tight, cramped, small (мир тесен: it's a small world)

тест.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English test ('trial, examination, diagnostic check'), from Middle English test ('small cupel used to assay precious metals'), from Old French test, from Latin testum ('earthenware pot').

тетрадь.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic тетрадь / тетрать from Byzantine Greek τετράδιον (tetrádion, 'a quire of four folded sheets of parchment'), derived from Ancient Greek τετράς (tetrás, 'a group of four', from τέτταρες 'four', cognate with Russian четыре). Originally a four-sheet manuscript gathering, it came to mean any school or desk notebook.

history.meaning: quire of four folded parchment sheets

техника.etymology: Borrowed via German Technik or French technique from Ancient Greek τεχνική (tekhnikḗ '[art/science] of craft'), feminine of τεχνικός ('skilled, artistic'), from τέχνη ('art, craft, skill').

технически.etymology: Adverb formed from технический ('technical') by dropping the final -й, from Ancient Greek τεχνικός ('relating to skill or craft').

технический.etymology: Derived from техника ('technique, technology') + adjectival suffix -еский, patterned on German technisch / French technique, from Ancient Greek τεχνικός ('skilled, relating to craft').

течь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic течи ('to flow, run'), from Proto-Slavic *tekti ('to flow, run'), from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- ('to run, flow').

тигр.etymology: Borrowed via French tigre or German Tiger (replacing older East Slavic тигръ via Greek) from Latin tigris, from Ancient Greek τίγρις (tígris, 'tiger'), ultimately from an Old Iranian source (compare Avestan tiγri- 'arrow', Old Persian tigra- 'sharp-pointed').

тик.etymology: Borrowed from French tic ('involuntary muscular twitch'), of expressive/onomatopoeic origin imitating a quick sharp movement or ticking sound.

тимьян.etymology: Borrowed via German Thymian (or Polish tymian) from Medieval Latin thymiāma / Latin thymum, from Ancient Greek θύμον (thýmon) and θυμίαμα (thymíama, 'aromatic herb burned as incense'), from θύω ('to burn sacrifice, smoke').

тинейджер.etymology: Borrowed in the late twentieth century from English teenager ('person aged thirteen to nineteen'), derived from teen (the suffix -teen of numerals thirteen to nineteen, from Old English -tēne) + age + -er.

тип.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth–nineteenth century via French type or German Typ from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (týpos, 'blow, impression of a seal, cast, model, general form or character'), from τύπτω ('to strike').

типичный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from типический / тип ('typical / type'), via German typisch or French typique from Late Latin typicus, from Ancient Greek τυπικός (typikós, 'characteristic of a type, figurative').

тиран.etymology: Borrowed via French tyran, German Tyrann, or Polish tyran from Latin tyrannus, from Ancient Greek τύραννος (týrannos, 'absolute ruler who seized power unconstitutionally, despot'), a pre-Greek Mediterranean or Anatolian loanword (compare Hieroglyphic Luwian tarwanis 'ruler, judge').

тиснение.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from тиснить ('to stamp, impress, emboss under pressure'), derived from тискать / тиснуть ('to press, squeeze, print'), from Proto-Slavic *tiskati ('to press, squeeze'; related to тесный 'tight').

history.meaning: to stamp, press into leather or paper → embossing, stamped lettering

титул.etymology: Borrowed in the sixteenth–seventeenth century via Polish tytuł and German Titel from Latin titulus ('inscription, label, title of honor').

тихий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тихъ / тихии ('quiet, calm, gentle, slow'), from Proto-Slavic *tixъ, continuing Balto-Slavic *teišas (cognate with Lithuanian teisùs 'straight, calm, just', where the Slavic branch specialized the sense 'peaceful, quiet').

тихо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тихо ('quietly, calmly, softly'), the short neuter singular and adverb of тихий ('quiet, still', from Proto-Slavic *tixъ).

тихонечко.etymology: Affectionate double-diminutive adverb formed from тихонько ('quietly, gently'), from тихий ('quiet, still, slow', Proto-Slavic *tixъ) + diminutive suffixes -оньк- / -онечк- + -о.

тише.etymology: Comparative degree of тихий ('quiet, still') and тихо ('quietly'), formed with the palatalizing comparative suffix -е (with regular consonant mutation х → ш), from Proto-Slavic *tixъ ('quiet, calm').

тканевый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -евый from ткань ('woven cloth, fabric', derived from ткать 'to weave', Proto-Slavic *tъkati).

ткань.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -нь from ткать ('to weave'), inherited from Old East Slavic тъкати and Proto-Slavic *tъkati ('to weave, thrust in the shuttle'). Literally 'that which is woven'.

history.meaning: to weave → woven cloth, fabric; biological tissue

то.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic то, neuter singular of the demonstrative pronoun тъ ('that', from Proto-Slavic *tъ, Proto-Indo-European *tód, cognate with English that). Used as a correlative conjunction ('then', after если) and in the phrase а то ('otherwise, or else').

товар.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic товаръ (attested since the 11th century in the senses 'camp, baggage train, livestock, property, trade goods'), borrowed early from Turkic tavar ('livestock, cattle, movable property, wealth, merchandise'; compare Old Turkic tavar and Turkish davar 'livestock, sheep and goats'). Parallels the semantic shift of Latin pecūnia ('cattle → money') and English cattle / chattel / capital.

товарищ.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic товарищь ('business partner, travelling companion, comrade-in-arms'), formed with the Slavic companion suffix -ищь from товар ('goods, merchant caravan, camp', borrowed early from Turkic tavar 'livestock, property, merchandise'). Originally a fellow merchant sharing a caravan or trade venture.

history.meaning: trade goods, camp → trade partner, companion

ток.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic токъ ('flow, current, stream'), o-grade action noun from течь / *tekti ('to flow'); in the nineteenth century specialized in physics as a calque of French courant (électrique) for 'electric current'.

токсикоз.etymology: Medical term formed in New Latin / international scientific vocabulary from Ancient Greek τοξικός (toxikós 'relating to poison, originally arrow-poison', from τόξον 'bow') + the pathological condition suffix -osis (-оз).

толк.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тълкъ ('interpretation, explanation, meaning, sense'), from Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ ('explanation, interpreter, sense', whence also Old Norse tulkr 'interpreter' and Lithuanian tulkas).

толкнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb formed with the suffix -нуть from толкать ('to push, shove'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *tъlkati / *tъlknǫti, iterative/intensive related to *tьlkti ('to pound, strike', modern толочь).

толком.etymology: Adverbialized instrumental singular of толк ('sense, meaning, clear order', from Old East Slavic тълкъ, Proto-Slavic *tъlkъ), literally 'with sense, coherently, properly'.

history.meaning: with sense, in an orderly way

толпа.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тълпа ('crowd, throng, multitude'), from Proto-Slavic *tъlpa ('crowd, mass of people', cognate with Lithuanian talpa 'capacity, room to fit' and telpù, tilpti 'to fit in').

толстый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тълстыи ('thick, stout, fat'), from Proto-Slavic *tъlstъ ('thick, swelling'), cognate with Lithuanian tulžti ('to swell, soften in water').

толстяк.etymology: Person noun formed with the colloquial suffix -як from толстый ('thick, fat, stout'), inherited from Old East Slavic тълстыи, from Proto-Slavic *tъlstъ ('thick, fat').

толщина.etymology: Abstract/dimensional noun formed with the suffix -ина (with consonant mutation ст > щ) from толстый ('thick'), inherited from Old East Slavic тълщина, from Proto-Slavic *tъlščina (from *tъlstъ 'thick').

только.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic только / толико ('so much, only that much'), from Proto-Slavic *toliko, formed from the demonstrative stem *to- ('that') + the quantitative suffix *-liko (compare сколько 'how much'). The meaning narrowed from 'that much and no more' to 'only, just'.

томатный.etymology: Relational adjective in -ный formed from томат ('tomato'), borrowed via French tomate and Spanish tomate from Classical Nahuatl tomatl.

томить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic томити ('to weary, exhaust, torment'), from Proto-Slavic *tomiti, causative of a lost verb from Proto-Indo-European *temH- ('to faint, grow dark/exhausted, suffocate', cognate with Sanskrit tamyati 'is exhausted, gasps for breath' and Latin tēmētum); in cooking, 'to braise or slow-cook gently in a sealed pot'.

history.meaning: to torment, keep in suspense; (culinary) to slow-braise

томография.etymology: Twentieth-century international medical compound coined from Ancient Greek τόμος (tómos, 'slice, section', from τέμνω 'to cut') + -γραφία (-graphía, 'writing, recording', from γράφω).

тон.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth–eighteenth century via Polish ton, German Ton, and French ton from Latin tonus ('stretching, pitch, tone of voice'), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, 'taut cord, tension, musical pitch'), from τείνω ('to stretch').

history.meaning: musical pitch, tone of voice, manner

тоненький.etymology: Diminutive/affectionate adjective formed from тонкий ('thin, slender', from Proto-Slavic *tьnъkъ, PIE *ténh₂us 'thin, stretched') + the diminutive suffix -енький.

тонкий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тънъкыи ('thin, slender, fine'), from Proto-Slavic *tьnъkъ, extended with *-ъkъ from the ancient Proto-Indo-European adjective *ténh₂us ('thin, stretched out'), cognate with Latin tenuis and English thin.

тонко.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тънъко, deadjectival adverb from тонкий ('thin, fine, delicate, subtle'), from Proto-Slavic *tьnъkъ ('thin', from PIE *ténh₂us 'thin, stretched').

тонкость.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from тонкий ('thin, fine, delicate, subtle', from Proto-Slavic *tьnъkъ).

тонна.etymology: Borrowed via German Tonne or French tonne ('large cask, metric ton'), from Medieval Latin tunna ('barrel, cask', probably of Celtic origin).

топ-модель.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English top model, a compound of top ('highest in rank') and model (from French modèle and Italian modello, diminutive of Latin modulus 'measure, standard').

топливо.etymology: Formed with the substance/material suffix -ливо (by analogy with молозиво, варево) from топить ('to heat a stove, burn fuel'), inherited from Old East Slavic топити, from Proto-Slavic *topiti (causative of the PIE root *tep- 'to be warm', as in тёплый).

торговать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic търговати ('to trade, barter, do business at market'), denominal verb formed from търгъ ('marketplace, trade', modern Russian торг, from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ).

торговаться.etymology: Reflexive and reciprocal verb formed with -ся from торговать ('to trade', from торг 'market, bargain', Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ), meaning 'to haggle, bargain over a price'.

торговый.etymology: Relational adjective inherited from Old East Slavic търговыи, formed with the suffix -овый from търгъ / торг ('marketplace, trade, bargaining'), from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ ('market, trade'; compare Polish targ, Swedish torg borrowed from Slavic, and Lithuanian tur̃gus).

history.meaning: pertaining to trade or the market
trade, commercial, shopping (e.g. торговый центр 'shopping mall')

торжественно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from торжественный ('solemn, festive, ceremonial'), derived from торжество ('celebration, triumph').

торжество.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic тържьство ('public festival, market gathering, celebration, triumph', originally translating Greek πανήγυρις 'public assembly/festival'), derived from търгъ ('marketplace, public square', Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ).

тормозить.etymology: Denominal verb derived in Russian from тормоз ('brake, drag-shoe on a sledge or wagon', likely borrowed from Turkic turmuz or Greek τόρμος 'socket, peg holding a wheel') + verbal suffix -ить.

тормознуть.etymology: Colloquial semelfactive perfective verb formed with the suffix -нуть from тормозить ('to brake, slow down'), derived from тормоз ('brake, iron sleigh-runner drag', borrowed in the eighteenth century, likely from Turkic turmaz or Greek τόρμος 'socket, peg keeping a wheel from turning').

history.meaning: to brake, stop, hail (a cab); to be slow on the uptake

торопить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic торопити ('to hurry, urge on, startle'), derived from Proto-Slavic *torpъ ('sudden fright, haste, confusion', preserved in оторопь 'stupor, bewilderment').

торпеда.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century from English torpedo (or French torpille / German Torpedo), from Latin torpēdō ('numbness, sluggishness; electric ray fish that stuns its prey'), derived from torpēre ('to be numb or stiff').

торт.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century via German Torte or directly from Italian torta ('round pastry, tart, layered cake'), from Late Latin tōrta ('round loaf of bread or pastry', originally past participle of torquēre 'to twist, turn').

торчать.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic торчать ('to stick out, protrude, jut'), from Proto-Slavic *tъrčati, stative verb related to *tъrknǫti / *tъrkati ('to poke, thrust, stick in', compare Old Church Slavonic тръкнути).

history.meaning: to stick out, jut; (colloq.) to hang around, be stuck somewhere

тоска.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тъска ('oppression, anguish, grief, longing'), from Proto-Slavic *tъska ('tightness of chest, anxiety, yearning'; related to тщетный and тощий 'empty, hollow').

тоскана.etymology: Borrowed from Italian Toscana ('Tuscany', region of central Italy), from Late Latin Tuscāna, derived from Classical Latin Tuscī (earlier *Turscī, 'the Etruscans, inhabitants of Etruria').

тоскливо.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from тоскливый ('dreary, melancholy, yearning'), derived from тоска ('anguish, yearning, melancholy', Old East Slavic тъска, Proto-Slavic *tъska).

тост.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from English toast (both 'sliced bread browned by heat' and 'call to drink to someone's health', the latter from the seventeenth-century English custom of flavoring a spiced cup of wine with a piece of toasted bread), from Old French toster ('to roast, grill'), from Latin tostus (past participle of torrēre 'to parch, roast').

history.meaning: toasted bread; drink to someone's health
toast (drink in honor of someone; toasted bread)

тот.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тътъ ('that'), a reduplicated emphatic form (*tъ-tъ) of the simple Proto-Slavic demonstrative pronoun *tъ (feminine *ta > та, neuter *to > то, plural *ti > те), continuing Proto-Indo-European *só / *tód ('that, the'; cognate with English that and the, Ancient Greek τό, and Sanskrit tád).

history.form: тътъ → тот (f. та, n. то, pl. те)

точилка.etymology: Instrumental noun formed in Russian from точить ('to sharpen, whet, grind', from Proto-Slavic *točiti, causative of *tekti 'to run, make turn') + the tool suffix -лка.

точка.etymology: Formed with the diminutive/noun suffix -ка from Old East Slavic тъчь ('point, dot, instant'), derived from Proto-Slavic *tъknǫti ('to poke, prick, touch with a sharp point', modern ткнуть; thus literally 'a prick mark' like Latin pūnctum from pungere).

history.meaning: to prick, poke → small prick mark, dot

точно.etymology: Adverb formed from the short neuter of точный ('exact, precise, punctual'), derived from точка ('point, dot', from Proto-Slavic *tъčьka, built on *tъknǫti 'to poke, prick, touch a point'): literally 'down to the exact point'.

точность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from точный ('exact, precise'), itself derived from точка ('point, dot', historically linked to ткнуть 'to prick, touch a single point').

точный.etymology: Derived with the adjectival suffix -ный from точка ('dot, point') / точь ('exact point', from Proto-Slavic *tъčьka, connected with *tъknǫti 'to touch a single point, prick'). Literally 'hitting the exact point, precise'.

точь-в-точь.etymology: Reduplicated adverbial phrase built from dialectal and older Russian точь ('dot, point, speck', the older base behind diminutive точка), literally 'point into point, dot for dot'.

history.meaning: exact to the dot, just like

тошнота.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ота from тошный ('nauseating, wearisome, dreary'), from Old East Slavic тъшно ('anxiously, oppressed'), related to тоска ('anguish, oppression') and тощий ('empty-bellied, gaunt', Proto-Slavic *tъščь).

тощий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тъщии / Old Church Slavonic тъщь ('empty, hollow, fasting, gaunt', compare натощак 'on an empty stomach'), from Proto-Slavic *tъščь (< *tъsk-jь), from Proto-Indo-European *tus-k-yós ('empty, devoid', cognate with Sanskrit tucchyá- 'empty, vain' and Lithuanian tuščias 'empty').

травить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic травити ('to graze cattle, consume grass, waste, bait with hounds, poison'), from Proto-Slavic *traviti ('to consume, graze down'), causative of *truti ('to consume, poison') and closely associated with *trava ('grass, herb, potion', modern трава).

травма.etymology: Borrowed in medical usage via German Trauma from Ancient Greek τραῦμα (traûma, 'wound, hurt, damage'), related to τιτρώσκω ('to wound, pierce', from PIE *terh₁- 'to rub, pierce').

травмпункт.etymology: Twentieth-century Soviet syllabic compound shortening травматологический пункт ('trauma care station'), combining травма ('injury, trauma', from Ancient Greek τραῦμα) and пункт ('point, station', via German Punkt from Latin pūnctum).

трагедия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish tragedia and Latin tragoedia from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía 'tragedy'), literally 'goat-song' (from τράγος 'he-goat' + ᾠδή 'song').

трагически.etymology: Adverb formed from трагический ('tragic', from Ancient Greek τραγικός via Latin tragicus) by dropping the final -й.

традиционный.etymology: Relational and qualitative adjective formed with the suffix -онный from традиция ('tradition', from Latin trāditiō).

традиция.etymology: Borrowed in the early eighteenth century via Polish tradycja or German Tradition from Latin trāditiō ('a handing over, delivery, teaching handed down across generations'), derived from trādere ('to hand over, transmit', from trāns- 'across' + dare 'to give').

транс.etymology: Borrowed via French transe and English trance from Old French transe ('fear of coming evil; passage from life to death, swoon'), derived from transir ('to pass away, be numbed'), from Latin trānsīre ('to go across, pass over').

трансформатор.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth century via German Transformator or French transformateur, formed as a Neo-Latin agent/instrument noun from Latin trānsformāre ('to change in shape, transform', from trāns- 'across' + fōrma 'shape, form').

тратить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тратити ('to spend, consume, waste'), from Proto-Slavic *tratiti ('to wear down, spend'), related to тереть ('to rub, grind away').

требование.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ние from требовать ('to demand, require, need'), inherited from Old East Slavic трѣбовати / Old Church Slavonic трѣбовати, derived from Proto-Slavic *trěba ('need, necessity; pagan sacrifice').

тревога.etymology: Attested in Russian and Ukrainian/Polish (trwoga) from the sixteenth century; etymology debated — connected by Vasmer and others either with отвага / German Wage ('peril, risk'), with Proto-Slavic *tьrvoga (from *tьrvati / trwać 'to endure, last'), or by folk-etymological association with три ('three', as a triple alarm signal).

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: тревога

тревожить.etymology: Denominal verb formed with the suffix -ить (with velar palatalization г > ж) from тревога ('alarm, anxiety, unrest', attested in East Slavic and Polish trwoga, likely from Proto-Slavic *trъvoga, related to *truti / *tryvati 'to wear down, consume').

трезвый.etymology: Borrowed in this vocalism from Old Church Slavonic трѣзвъ ('sober, abstinent'; native East Slavic had терезвый), from Proto-Slavic *tverzъ / *trězvъ, of uncertain further Indo-European etymology.

трейлер.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English trailer (both 'towed vehicle/mobile home' and 'promotional film preview', the latter because early previews were screened trailing after the main feature film), agent noun from to trail.

тренер.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century from English trainer ('sports coach, horse trainer'), agent noun from to train (from Old French trainer 'to draw, drag, educate', from Vulgar Latin *trahīnāre).

тренироваться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from тренировать ('to train, coach'), derived from тренер / тренинг (from English train / trainer).

трепло.etymology: Colloquial pejorative noun formed with the neuter agent/instrument suffix -ло from трепать ('to tousle, fray, shake; in colloquial speech трепать языком, to wag one's tongue, babble', from Proto-Slavic *trepati).

третий.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic третии (f. третия, n. третие), from Proto-Slavic *tretьjь ('third'), continuing Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tíos ('third', built on *tréyes 'three'), directly cognate with English third, Latin tertius, and Lithuanian trẽčias.

треугольник.etymology: Compound noun calquing Latin triangulum / Ancient Greek τρίγωνον, formed from три (combining stem тре-, 'three', Proto-Slavic *trьje) + угол ('angle, corner', Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ) + suffix -ник.

три.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic три (masculine трие), from Proto-Slavic *trьje / *tri, continuing Proto-Indo-European *tréyes / *tríh₂ ('three'), directly cognate with English three, Latin trēs, Ancient Greek τρεῖς, and Sanskrit tráyas.

три-дэ.etymology: Late twentieth-century hybrid borrowing from English 3D (short for three-dimensional), combining Russian три ('three') + the phonetic transcription дэ of the English letter D (for dimensional).

тридцатилетний.etymology: Compound adjective formed from тридцати (genitive form of тридцать 'thirty') + -летний ('-year-old, lasting ... years', from лето 'summer, year', Proto-Slavic *lěto).

тридцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral formed from тридцать ('thirty'), which contracted in East Slavic from Old East Slavic три десяте ('three tens', from Proto-Slavic *trьje desęte).

тридцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic numeral phrase трие десяте / три десяти ('three tens', with три 'three' + nominative plural of десять 'ten'). In rapid speech the unstressed second element reduced to -дцать.

трижды.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic тришьды / Old East Slavic трижды ('three times'), formed from три ('three') + multiplicative suffix *-šьdy (originally from *šьd- 'going, stride', i.e. 'in three goings').

тринадцатый.etymology: Ordinal numeral formed from тринадцать ('thirteen'), inherited from Old East Slavic трие на десяте ('three upon ten').

тринадцать.etymology: Contracted from the Old East Slavic numeral phrase трие на десяте ('three on ten'), from Proto-Slavic *trьje na desęte (composed of *trьje 'three' + *na 'on' + locative singular *desęte 'ten').

триумф.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Polish triumf and German Triumph from Latin triumphus ('solemn victorious procession of a Roman general'), via Etruscan from Ancient Greek θρίαμβος (thríambos, 'hymn and procession in honor of Dionysus').

трогательно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of трогательный ('touching, moving'), derived from трогать ('to touch; to move emotionally', calquing French touchant 'touching' in the eighteenth century).

history.meaning: to touch, move emotionally → touching → touchingly; how touching!

трогать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed in East Slavic (alongside semelfactive тронуть) from an expressive root *torg- / *trog- ('to pull, twitch, touch lightly'); Vasmer compares Old East Slavic тръгати ('to tug, pluck').

трое.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic троѥ, from Proto-Slavic *troje ('group of three'), collective numeral derived from *trьje ('three'), from Proto-Indo-European *treyes.

тройка.etymology: Noun formed with the suffix -ка from трое ('group of three', collective numeral from три 'three', Proto-Slavic *trojь); denotes the figure 3, a three-horse team, a three-piece suit, or three of a kind in cards.

history.meaning: three-horse team; group of three; three of a kind

тронуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть corresponding to трогать ('to touch'), formed on the expressive East Slavic stem трог- / трон- (with simplification of *gn → н) meaning 'to touch once, stir; to move emotionally'.

history.meaning: to touch → to touch once; to move emotionally

тростниковый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from тростник ('reed, cane, sugar cane'), derived from трость ('reed, walking stick', from Old East Slavic тръсть and Proto-Slavic *trъstь 'reed', cognate with Lithuanian trušis 'reed').

history.meaning: reed, cane → cane, reed (тростниковый сахар 'cane sugar')

тротуар.etymology: Borrowed in the early nineteenth century from French trottoir ('pavement, sidewalk, footpath'), derived from trotter ('to trot, walk briskly') + the place suffix -oir.

труба.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic труба ('trumpet, horn, pipe, tube'), from Proto-Slavic *trǫba. Vasmer regards it as an early borrowing into Slavic from Germanic *trumbō or Romance *trumba ('trumpet, tube'; compare Old High German trumba and Italian tromba).

трубадур.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French troubadour ('medieval lyric poet-musician of southern France'), from Old Occitan trobador (oblique case of trobaire, 'composer, finder of verses'), from trobar ('to find, compose verse', from Vulgar Latin *tropāre, from Late Latin tropus 'melody, rhetorical trope').

трубка.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of труба ('pipe, tube, horn') with suffix -ка: first meaning 'a small tube, rolled scroll, or smoking pipe', and from the late 19th century applied to a telephone receiver/handset (originally an acoustic ear-tube; снять / положить трубку 'pick up / hang up the phone').

трубочка.etymology: Double diminutive formed from трубка ('small tube, pipe, telephone receiver', diminutive of труба 'pipe, tube, trumpet', Proto-Slavic *trǫba) + suffix -ка.

history.meaning: little tube, drinking straw; phone receiver

трудиться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic трудитися ('to toil, labor, take pains'), reflexive of трудити ('to burden, weary, work'), from Proto-Slavic *trǫditi (derived from *trǫdъ 'toil, hardship, labor', modern труд).

трудновато.etymology: Deadjectival adverb and impersonal predicative formed with -о from трудноватый ('somewhat difficult'), attenuative derivative (-оватый) of трудный ('difficult, hard', from труд 'labor, effort', Proto-Slavic *trǫdъ).

трудный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic трудьныи ('toilsome, arduous, grievous'), derived from трудъ / труд ('toil, labor, hardship'), from Proto-Slavic *trudъ ('oppression, toil, effort', cognate with Latin trūdō 'to push, thrust, press' and Gothic us-þriutan 'to trouble, weary').

трудовая.etymology: Substantivized feminine adjective clipped in Soviet and modern Russian from трудовая книжка ('employment record book'), derived from труд ('labor, work', Proto-Slavic *trudъ).

труп.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic трупъ ('corpse, dead body; tree trunk, stump'), from Proto-Slavic *trupъ ('log, trunk, body, corpse'), cognate with Lithuanian trupėti ('to crumble, break into pieces').

трус.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic трусъ ('shaking, trembling, earthquake; coward'), a deverbal noun from трясти / трусить ('to shake, tremble', Old Church Slavonic трѧсти / троусъ, from Proto-Slavic *trǫsъ, o-grade ablaut of *tręsti 'to shake, tremble'). Originally referring to physical trembling (as in землетрясение) and then to 'one who trembles with fear'.

трусики.etymology: Diminutive plural formed with the suffix -ики from трусы ('shorts, underpants, briefs').

трусливый.etymology: Formed with the adjectival suffix -ливый from трус ('coward') and трусить ('to be afraid, tremble'), from Old East Slavic трусъ ('shaking, tremor, earthquake') and Proto-Slavic *trǫsъ ('trembling', nasal-vowel ablaut relative of трясти 'to shake').

morphemes.meaning: inclined to, having the quality of

трусы.etymology: Early twentieth-century shortening of трусики (originally borrowed into Russian sports terminology for short athletic/swimming trunks), adapted from English trousers (which in turn came from Irish/Scottish Gaelic triubhas 'close-fitting trews/breeches').

трюк.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century from French truc ('deft trick, stage contrivance, stunt, knack'), from Occitan truc ('blow, stroke, impact, clever move'), of onomatopoeic/Romance origin (*truccare 'to strike, knock').

трюфель.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from German Trüffel (earlier Tartuffel) or French truffe, from Old Occitan trufa, which goes back to Vulgar Latin *tūfera, a dialectal variant of Classical Latin tūber ('lump, swelling, truffle').

тряпка.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ка from the Slavic expressive stem *tręp- ('to shake, flap, fray'; compare dialectal тряпица 'rag, scrap of cloth' and Polish strzęp 'tatter, shred').

трясти.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic трясти ('to shake, jolt, cause to tremble'), from Proto-Slavic *tręsti ('to shake', < *trem-s-ti, with nasal vowel from PIE *trem- / *tres- 'to tremble, shake', cognate with Latin tremere and Ancient Greek τρέω).

трястись.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -сь from трясти ('to shake'), inherited from Old East Slavic трястися, from Proto-Slavic *tręsti sę ('to tremble, quake, shiver').

туалет.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French toilette ('dressing cloth, dressing table, attire; later washroom, lavatory'), a diminutive of toile ('cloth, linen'), from Latin tēla ('web, woven cloth'). Originally referring in Russian to a lady's dressing table and evening dress (вечерний туалет), in the 20th century it also adopted the modern French euphemistic sense of 'lavatory, restroom'.

history.meaning: small cloth → dressing table, grooming → washroom

туго.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic туго, adverbial and predicative form of тугой ('tight, taut, stiff, hard to bend'), from Proto-Slavic *tǫgъ ('tight, taut, firm; oppressive', related to тяга 'pull, tension', from PIE *tengh- 'to pull, stretch').

туда.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic туды / туда ('thither, to that place'), from Proto-Slavic *tǫda / *tuda, a directional adverb built on the demonstrative stem *t- ('that') with the spatial suffix *-da (correlative with куда 'where to' and сюда 'here, to this place').

туда-сюда.etymology: Reduplicative directional compound combining туда ('there, to that place', from Proto-Slavic *tǫdu / *tuda) + сюда ('here, to this place'): literally 'thither and hither, back and forth'.

history.meaning: that way + this way → back and forth, to and fro

тук.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection imitating a sharp tap, knock on a door, or heartbeat, inherited from the Proto-Slavic sound-symbolic root *tuk- (compare стук 'knock' and Polish tukać).

тумблер.etymology: Borrowed in the twentieth century from English tumbler (specifically in electrical engineering, tumbler switch 'a spring-loaded lever switch that tumbles/flips between positions'), from to tumble.

тумбочка.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -очка from тумба ('low pillar, bollard, pedestal cabinet'), borrowed via Polish tumba or Italian tomba from Late Latin tumba ('tombstone, pedestal'), from Ancient Greek τύμβος ('burial mound, cairn').

тунец.etymology: Borrowed (adapted with the masculine suffix -ец) via Polish tuńczyk / German Thunfisch from Medieval Latin thunnus / Latin thunnus, from Ancient Greek θύννος (thýnnos, 'tuna fish', literally 'the darter/rusher', from θύνω 'to rush, dart along').

тунеядство.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ство from тунеядец ('parasite, idler, freeloader'), a Church Slavonic-patterned compound of туне ('in vain, gratis, for nothing', Old Church Slavonic тунѥ, from Proto-Slavic *tuňe) + ядец (from ясти / есть 'to eat', Proto-Slavic *jěsti: literally 'one who eats for nothing').

туника.etymology: Borrowed from Latin tunica ('loose sleeveless or short-sleeved undergarment worn in ancient Rome'), an ancient Mediterranean loanword (compare Ancient Greek χιτών and Semitic *kittān 'linen garment', Hebrew kuttōneṯ).

тупик.etymology: Formed in Russian from тупой ('blunt, blind, having no outlet', from Proto-Slavic *tǫpъ) + the noun suffix -ик, originally designating a blind alley, cul-de-sac, or railway siding closed at one end.

тупить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *tǫpiti ('to make blunt, dull'), denominal verb from *tǫpъ (Russian тупой 'blunt, dull, slow-witted'); in modern colloquial slang used intransitively for 'to be slow on the uptake, act dumb'.

history.meaning: to blunt; (slang) to act dumb, be slow-witted

тупой.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тупыи ('blunt, dull, slow-witted'), from Proto-Slavic *tǫpъ ('blunt, not sharp', nasally infixed root related to *tepti 'to beat, strike down the edge', from PIE *(s)tewp- 'to strike, push, blunt').

тур.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth–nineteenth century from French tour ('turn, circuit, round, journey'), deverbal noun from tourner ('to turn'), from Latin tornāre ('to turn on a lathe'), from Ancient Greek τόρνος ('lathe, compass').

турецкий.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from турок ('Turk', with stem турк- + -ский > турецкий), inherited from Old East Slavic туръкъ, from Turkic Türk.

турист.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via French touriste from English tourist ('one who travels for pleasure'), formed from tour (from Old French tour 'circuit, journey') + -ist.

турникет.etymology: Borrowed from French tourniquet ('revolving turnstile barrier; surgical tourniquet'), diminutive derived from tourner ('to turn, revolve', from Latin tornāre).

турнир.etymology: Borrowed via German Turnier ('chivalric tournament, sporting competition') from Old French tornier / tornei ('joust, tournament', from torner 'to turn, wheel horses about').

history.meaning: to wheel about in a joust

турция.etymology: Borrowed in the seventeenth–eighteenth century via Polish Turcja from Medieval Latin Turcia ('land of the Turks'), derived from Turcus ('Turk', from Ottoman Turkish ترك Türk).

тусовка.etymology: Late Soviet youth slang (popularized in the 1970s–1980s) formed with the suffix -ка from тусоваться ('to mingle, hang out') / тасовать ('to shuffle a deck of cards', with pretonic vowel assimilation а > у), which was borrowed in the eighteenth century from French tasser ('to heap, pack together') or Polish tasować.

history.meaning: to shuffle → to mingle, hang out

тут.etymology: Expanded by consonant reduplication from Old East Slavic ту ('there, then, here'), from Proto-Slavic *tu, an old locative adverb from the demonstrative stem *to- ('that/this place'). In modern Russian тут is the everyday conversational partner of slightly more formal здесь ('here').

туфля.etymology: Borrowed from Middle Low German tuffele (Low German Tuffel 'shoe, slipper'), shortened from older pantuffel, which came via French pantoufle and Italian pantofola.
туфля.notes: Standard Russian stresses the stem throughout (туфля, туфли, genitive plural туфель).

тухлый.etymology: Formed with the past-participle/adjectival suffix -лый from тухнуть ('to go out [of fire]; to spoil, rot, go bad'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *tuxnǫti ('to subside, go out, grow stale and foul-smelling', related to *duxъ 'breath, smell').

туча.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic туча ('raincloud, storm cloud, downpour'), from Proto-Slavic *tǫča ('heavy raincloud, hailstorm', < *tonk-jā), related to *tǫkъ ('fat, richness') and Lithuanian tùkti ('to grow fat, swell'), referring to a dark, swollen cloud.

туша.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic туша ('dressed animal carcass; bulky body'), related to Proto-Slavic *tux- / *tukъ ('fat, fleshiness') or borrowed from a Turkic source (compare Tatar/Bashkir түшкә 'animal breast/carcass', Turkic *töš 'chest, breast of a slaughtered animal').

тушить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тушити ('to extinguish, quench'), from Proto-Slavic *tušiti, causative of *tuxnǫti ('to go out, subside', modern тухнуть); the culinary sense 'to stew, braise slowly in a covered pot' developed from 'to smother/simmer over a low, damped fire' (compare French étouffer / étuvée).

history.meaning: to put out a fire, calm
to extinguish (a fire); to stew, braise

тушь.etymology: Borrowed via German Tusche ('India ink, black drawing ink') from French toucher ('to touch, lay on ink or wash in drawing'). (A homonym тушь ' celebratory fanfare' comes from German Tusch.)

тушёнка.etymology: Colloquial univerbation formed with the suffix -ка from тушёное мясо ('stewed meat'), passive participle of тушить ('to stew, braise').

ты.etymology: Ты is an inherited second-person singular pronoun, already recorded in Old Russian and Old Church Slavonic. Vasmer connects it with an ancient Indo-European pronoun and compares Latin tu and related forms in Baltic and Germanic languages. Its history is much older than the modern distinction between familiar ты and polite вы.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: ты

тыкать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тыкати ('to poke, thrust, jab'), iterative of ткнуть (< *tъknǫti), from Proto-Slavic *tykati ('to poke, prod, stick in').

history.meaning: to poke, jab, tap; (also from ты) to address as 'thou'

тысяча.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тысяча (Old Church Slavonic тысѧщи), from Proto-Slavic *tysęťa / *tysǫťa ('thousand'), shared with Baltic (Lithuanian tū́kstantis) and Germanic (Gothic þūsundi, English thousand), built on a Proto-Indo-European compound *tūs-ḱm̥tī meaning 'swollen/strong hundred'.

тюлень.etymology: Attested in northern Russian since the sixteenth–seventeenth century, borrowed from a Sami language of the Kola Peninsula (compare Kildin Sami тю̄лльй / Skolt Sami tullj, 'seal; seal hide').

тюрбо.etymology: Borrowed in culinary usage from French turbot ('turbot, large diamond-shaped European flatfish'), from Old French turbot, likely borrowed from Old Swedish törnbut ('thorn-butt, spiny flatfish', from törne 'thorn' + but 'flatfish').

тяжело.etymology: Adverb and impersonal predicate formed from тяжёлый ('heavy, hard, difficult'), derived from Old East Slavic тяжькыи / тяга ('weight, pull, burden'), from Proto-Slavic *tęžьkъ / *tęga (with nasal *ę from PIE *tengh- 'to pull, weigh, stretch'), related to тянуть ('to pull').

тяжесть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тяжесть ('heaviness, weight, burden'), formed with the abstract suffix -есть from тяжькыи (modern тяжкий / тяжёлый, 'heavy', from Proto-Slavic *tęžьkъ, related to *tęga 'weight, pull').

тяжёлый.etymology: Developed in East Slavic from Old East Slavic тяжькыи / тяжелыи ('heavy, burdensome, weighty'), built on тяга / тягать ('pull, weight, traction, burden', from Proto-Slavic *tęg-, related to тянуть 'to pull, draw').

тянуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тянути ('to pull, draw, stretch'), from Proto-Slavic *tęgnǫti (with loss of *g before *n), built on the root *tęg- ('pull, tension', also seen in тяжесть 'weight' and тугой 'tight, taut').

тяп-ляп.etymology: Expressive rhyming reduplication combining the interjections/verbal stems тяп (from тяпать 'to chop, hack, slap hastily') and ляп (from ляпать 'to slap on, daub, bungle'), imitating a slapdash 'hack-and-slap' job.

history.meaning: to chop hastily + to slap/daub clumsily

тёмно-зелёный.etymology: Compound colour adjective formed from тёмно- (combining form of тёмный 'dark', from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnъ) + зелёный ('green', from Proto-Slavic *zelenъ).

тёмно-серый.etymology: Compound colour adjective formed from тёмно- (combining form of тёмный 'dark', from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnъ) + серый ('grey', from Proto-Slavic *sěrъ).

тёмно-синий.etymology: Compound colour adjective formed in Russian from тёмно- (combining stem of тёмный 'dark', from Old East Slavic тьмьныи, built on тьма 'darkness', PIE *temH-) + синий ('dark blue, navy blue', from Proto-Slavic *sinjь).

тёмный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тьмьныи ('dark, obscure'), from Proto-Slavic *tьmьnъ, an adjective formed from *tьma ('darkness', modern тьма), cognate with Lithuanian tamsa ('darkness') and Sanskrit tamas ('gloom, darkness').

тёплый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic теплыи ('warm'), from Proto-Slavic *teplъ, formed with the suffix *-lъ from the Proto-Indo-European heat root *tep- ('to be warm'; directly cognate with Latin tepidus 'lukewarm, tepid' and Sanskrit tápati 'warms, burns').

тёрка.etymology: Instrument noun formed with the suffix -ка from тереть (past stem тёр-, 'to rub, grate', from Proto-Slavic *tьrti).

тёртый.etymology: Past passive participle of тереть ('to rub, grate'), inherited from Old East Slavic терти and Proto-Slavic *tьrti ('to rub, grind, grate', cognate with Latin terere 'to rub, wear away').

history.meaning: to grate → grated (тёртая цедра 'grated zest', тёртый сыр 'grated cheese')

тётя.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic тета / тетя ('aunt'), from Proto-Slavic *teta, an ancient reduplicated nursery kinship word (compare Lithuanian teta 'aunt' and German Tante).

у.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic у ('at, by; away from'), from Proto-Slavic *u, continuing Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew ('off, away, beside'; compare Sanskrit áva and Latin au- in auferō). In East Slavic, the spatial sense 'at, by' (у + genitive) developed into the standard Russian construction for possession (у меня 'by me / I have').

history.meaning: by, near, at the house of
