у.notes: Always governs the genitive case: у окна ('by the window'), у Киры ('Kira has / at Kira's place').

убедительно.etymology: Adverb formed from убедительный ('convincing, persuasive'), derived from убедить ('to convince, persuade').

убедить.etymology: Adopted from Old Church Slavonic убѣдити ('to compel, prevail upon, persuade'), formed from prefix у- + бѣдити ('to compel, force, urge', from бѣда 'necessity, distress', Proto-Slavic *běda < PIE *bʰeydʰ- 'to persuade, compel', cognate with Latin fidere and Greek πείθω 'to persuade').

убедиться.etymology: Reflexive form of убедить ('to convince') + -ся, meaning 'to convince oneself, become convinced, make sure'.

убеждаться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from убедиться ('to become convinced, make sure'), derived from убедить ('to convince, persuade', borrowed with Church Slavonic phonetic reflex -жд- < *-dj- in убеждать from у- + бедить 'to compel, prevail over', from беда 'need, compulsion, trouble', Proto-Slavic *běda).

уберечь.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix у- ('away from harm, completely') from беречь ('to guard, keep safe'), inherited from Old East Slavic уберечи, from Proto-Slavic *ubergti (from *bergti 'to guard, protect').

убиваться.etymology: Reflexive form of убивать ('to kill, beat down', iterative of убить, from у- + бить 'to beat, strike'), literally 'to beat oneself in grief' (reflecting the traditional mourning custom of beating one's breast or head).

history.meaning: to grieve bitterly, wear oneself out

убирать.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of убрать ('to take away, clear off, tidy up'), formed from the prefix у- ('away') and -бирать (the iterative stem of брать 'to take', from Proto-Slavic *bьrati / *birati). From 'taking things away / clearing the table or field', it developed the sense 'to put in order, tidy up, clean a room'.

history.meaning: to clear away, put away; to tidy up, clean

убить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic убити, from Proto-Slavic *ubiti ('to kill, slay'), formed from the perfective/exhaustive prefix у- ('away, completely') and *biti ('to beat, strike', Russian бить).

уборка.etymology: Action noun formed from убрать / убирать ('to take away, tidy up, harvest', from prefix у- + брать 'to take') + the suffix -ка.

history.meaning: to clear away, tidy up, harvest

уборщик.etymology: Agent noun formed with the suffix -щик from уборка ('cleaning, tidying up'), derived from убирать / убрать ('to tidy up, clear away', from у- + брать, Proto-Slavic *bьrati).

уборщица.etymology: Feminine agent noun formed with the suffix -щица (feminine of -щик) from уборка ('cleaning'), from убирать ('to tidy up, clean').

убыть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic убыти ('to diminish, subside, leave'), from Proto-Slavic *ubyti, composed of the prefix *u- ('away') + *byti ('to be', modern Russian быть).

history.meaning: to decrease, subside; (от тебя не убудет) it won't hurt you

уважаемый.etymology: Present passive participle of уважать ('to respect, esteem'), lexicalized in Russian as the standard polite adjective 'respected, esteemed, dear' (especially at the start of formal letters).

уважать.etymology: Borrowed via Polish uważać ('to pay attention, consider, respect') and Ukrainian уважати, built on вага ('weight, importance'), itself an early borrowing from Old High German wāga ('scales, weight'). Literally 'to give weight to, hold in high regard'.

уважение.etymology: Verbal noun formed in Russian from уважить / уважать ('to respect, esteem, give weight to'), borrowed via Polish uważać ('to pay attention, consider, esteem', from uwaga 'attention, weight', ultimately from Old High German wāga 'scales, weight').

уважительный.etymology: Derived from уважить ('to respect, take into account as weighty or valid') + the adjectival suffix -тельный; hence both 'respectful' and (of a reason/excuse) 'valid, worthy of consideration'.

history.meaning: to respect, deem worthy of consideration

уведомление.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from уведомить ('to notify, inform formally'), built on у- + ведать ('to know, be in charge of', from Old East Slavic вѣдати and Proto-Slavic *vědati).

увеличиваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from увеличиться ('to grow larger, increase'), derived from увеличить (from у- + величить 'to make great, magnify', from великий 'great, large', Proto-Slavic *velikъ).

уверенно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from уверенный ('confident, sure, assured').

уверенность.etymology: Abstract noun formed with the suffix -ость from уверенный ('confident, certain'), originally the past passive participle of уверить ('to assure, convince', from у- + верить 'to believe', from вера 'faith, trust', Proto-Slavic *věra).

уверять.etymology: Imperfective of уверить ('to assure, make believe'), formed from prefix у- + верить ('to believe', from вера 'faith, belief', Proto-Slavic *věra).

увлекаться.etymology: Reflexive of увлекать ('to carry away, captivate', Church Slavonic vocalism corresponding to East Slavic уволочь, from у- + влечь 'to draw, drag', Proto-Slavic *velkti), literally 'to be drawn/carried away by enthusiasm'.

history.meaning: to get carried away, be keen on

уводить.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix у- ('away') from водить ('to lead', iterative of вести, from Proto-Slavic *voditi).

history.meaning: to lead away; to steal away

увозить.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix у- ('away') from возить ('to convey by vehicle', iterative of везти, from Proto-Slavic *voziti).

уволенный.etymology: Past passive participle of уволить ('to discharge from service, dismiss, fire'), formed from у- + волить / воля ('will, freedom, release', Proto-Slavic *voľa: originally 'to grant leave, release from service').

history.meaning: to release from service, dismiss, fire

уволить.etymology: Formed with the prefix у- ('away') + волить / воля ('will, freedom, release', from Old East Slavic воля and Proto-Slavic *voľa). Originally 'to grant leave, release from service or obligation', later shifting in modern bureaucratic and workplace usage to 'to discharge, dismiss, fire'.

history.meaning: to release from service, grant leave
to dismiss, fire (or discharge from military service)

уволиться.etymology: Reflexive of уволить ('to release from service, dismiss, grant leave', formed from у- + воля 'will, freedom, liberty', Proto-Slavic *volja) + -ся, literally 'to obtain one's release from service, resign'.

увольнять.etymology: Imperfective counterpart of уволить ('to dismiss, discharge from service, fire; historically to set free, grant leave'), formed from the prefix у- and волить / воля ('will, freedom, liberty', from Proto-Slavic *voľa). Originally уволить от службы meant 'to release or free someone from duty'; in modern employment usage it means 'to fire, dismiss'.

history.meaning: to release from service → to dismiss, fire

увольняться.etymology: Imperfective of уволиться ('to resign, quit'), formed from увольнять ('to discharge, release from employment', derived from воля 'freedom') + reflexive -ся.

увы.etymology: Inherited via Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic увы ('alas!, woe!'), an ancient expressive interjection of grief or lamentation (compare Ancient Greek οὐαί, Latin vae, Gothic wai).

history.stage: Old Church Slavonic / Old East Slavic

угадывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ывать from угадать ('to guess rightly, divine'), composed of the prefix у- + гадать ('to guess, tell fortunes, conjecture', from Proto-Slavic *gadati).

угнать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic угънати ('to drive away [cattle or horses]'), from Proto-Slavic *ugъnati, composed of *u- ('away') + *gъnati ('to drive, chase', modern Russian гнать, PIE *gʷʰen-); in modern Russian extended from rustling horses to stealing motor vehicles or hijacking aircraft.

history.meaning: to drive away; to steal (a vehicle), hijack

уговаривать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from уговорить ('to persuade, talk into'), composed of у- + говорить ('to speak, talk', Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

history.meaning: to persuade, try to talk into (imperfective)

уговор.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by zero suffixation from уговорить / уговариваться ('to agree upon terms, stipulate'), from у- + говорить ('to speak', Proto-Slavic *govoriti).

уговорить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the resultative prefix у- from говорить ('to talk, speak', from Proto-Slavic *govoriti), literally 'to win someone over by talking'.

угодить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic угодити ('to please, oblige; to hit the mark'), from Proto-Slavic *ugoditi, composed of *u- + *goditi ('to fit, suit, be pleasing', derived from *godъ 'fitting time, suitability', cf. годный).

history.meaning: to please, oblige; to land/end up in (a trap or mess)

угол.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic угълъ (Old Church Slavonic ѫгълъ, 'corner, angle'), from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ, continuing a Proto-Indo-European nasalized stem *h₂engulos ('bend, corner, angle'), directly cognate with Latin angulus (whence English angle).
угол.notes: Takes the locative in **-у** when indicating position: **в углу** ('in the corner'), **на углу** ('on the street corner').

уголовник.etymology: Derived from уголовный ('criminal, capital', from Old East Slavic головьщина / уголовие 'murder, crime punishable by loss of one's head', from голова 'head, killed person') + the personal agent suffix -ник.

history.meaning: head; slain person in bloodwite law

уголок.etymology: Diminutive formed with the suffix -ок from угол ('corner, angle'), inherited from Old East Slavic угълъ and Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ ('corner, angle', cognate with Latin angulus).

уголочек.etymology: Double diminutive formed with the suffix -ек from уголок (diminutive of угол 'corner, angle', from Old East Slavic угълъ, Proto-Slavic *ǫgъlъ).

уголь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic угль ('coal, charcoal, glowing ember'), from Proto-Slavic *ǫgľь, an ancient Indo-European word for charcoal and embers cognate with Lithuanian anglis ('coal, charcoal') and Sanskrit áṅgāra ('charcoal').
уголь.notes: Drops the fleeting о in oblique cases: **у́голь** → **угля́** (or **у́гля**).

угон.etymology: Deverbal noun from угнать / угонять ('to drive away cattle or horses, steal by driving off', from prefix у- 'away' + гнать 'to drive, chase', Proto-Slavic *gъnati); in modern law extended to motor vehicles and aircraft.

угонять.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the prefix у- ('away') and iterative stem -гонять (corresponding to perfective угнать 'to drive away, steal a vehicle'), from Proto-Slavic *uganjati (from *gъnati 'to drive').

угораздить.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb (used almost exclusively in impersonal constructions like как тебя угораздило? 'how on earth did you manage to get into this?') formed with у- from archaic/dialectal гораздить ('to contrive skillfully', from горазд 'skillful, clever, capable', Old East Slavic гораздъ, Proto-Slavic *gorazdъ), used with ironic inversion.

history.meaning: (ironic impersonal) to have the misfortune to, get oneself into

угорь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic угьрь ('eel'), from Proto-Slavic *ǫgъrь ('eel'), from Proto-Balto-Slavic *angurīs (cognate with Lithuanian ungurỹs, Old Prussian angurgis, and Latin anguilla 'eel', related to anguis 'snake').

угощать.etymology: Imperfective of угостить ('to entertain as a guest, treat to food and drink'), formed from prefix у- + гостить ('to host/be a guest', derived from гость 'guest', Proto-Slavic *gostь).

history.meaning: to host, treat to food or drink

угощаться.etymology: Reflexive verb formed with -ся from угощать ('to treat to food and drink, entertain hospitably'), iterative of угостить, derived from гость ('guest', Proto-Slavic *gostь, PIE *gʰóstis).

угощение.etymology: Verbal and concrete noun formed with -ение from угостить / угощать ('to entertain a guest, treat to food and drink', from у- + гостить, from гость 'guest', Proto-Slavic *gostь).

угробить.etymology: Colloquial perfective verb formed with the prefix у- and verbal suffix -ить from гроб ('coffin, grave', inherited from Old East Slavic гробъ, from Proto-Slavic *grobъ 'dug pit, grave, coffin'), literally 'to drive into the grave'.

history.meaning: coffin → to ruin, work to death
to ruin, wreck; to do in (colloquial)

угу.etymology: Conversational vocalic interjection formed with nasalized/voiced velar fricative articulation (pronounced [ʊˈɣu] or [m̩ˈɦm̩]), universally used in spoken Russian as an informal affirmative grunt ('uh-huh, yeah').

удаваться.etymology: Imperfective reflexive verb formed from удаться ('to turn out well, succeed'), composed of the prefix у- + даваться / даться ('to be given, yield', from дать 'to give', Proto-Slavic *dati, PIE *deh₃-).

удавить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic удавити ('to strangle, choke, throttle'), from Proto-Slavic *udaviti, composed of the resultative prefix *u- + *daviti ('to press, squeeze, choke', modern давить).

удалять.etymology: Imperfective verb formed from удалить ('to move far away, remove, extract, delete'), derived from у- + даль ('distance, farness', from далёкий 'far', Proto-Slavic *daľь).

history.meaning: distance → to move far off, remove

удар.etymology: Deverbal noun from ударить ('to strike, hit, chime'), inherited from Old East Slavic ударити and Proto-Slavic *udariti (historically connected with *dьrati 'to tear, strike').

ударить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ударити ('to strike, hit'), from Proto-Slavic *udariti. Vasmer connects the root *-dar- (with prefix *u-) to an intensive/causative formation related to драть ('to tear, flay, strike', Proto-Slavic *dьrati) or to Greek δαίρω ('to beat, flay').

удариться.etymology: Reflexive of ударить ('to strike, hit', from Proto-Slavic *udariti, related to *derti 'to tear, strike') + -ся, meaning 'to strike oneself against, bump into'.

удачно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb formed with -о from удачный ('successful, fortunate'), derived from удача ('good luck, success', deverbal noun from удаться 'to succeed, turn out well', from у- + дать 'to give').

удачный.etymology: Derived from удача ('good fortune, success', deverbal noun from удаться 'to turn out well, succeed', from у- + дать 'to give') + the adjectival suffix -ный.

удваивать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ивать from удвоить ('to double'), composed of the prefix у- + двоить ('to divide or multiply by two', from два / двое 'two', Proto-Slavic *dъva / *dъvojь).

удержать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic удьржати ('to hold back, retain, keep'), from Proto-Slavic *udьržati, composed of the prefix *u- + *dьržati ('to hold', modern Russian держать).

history.meaning: to hold on to, retain, hold back

удержаться.etymology: Reflexive of удержать ('to hold back, retain, keep from falling', from prefix у- + держать 'to hold', Proto-Slavic *dьržati) + -ся.

history.meaning: to keep one's footing; to refrain, hold back

удивительно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb and predicative formed with -о from удивительный ('amazing, surprising, wonderful'), derived from удивить ('to astonish, amaze', from у- + дивить, from диво 'wonder, marvel', Proto-Slavic *divo).

удивительный.etymology: Derived from удивить ('to amaze, surprise, cause to marvel', from у- + дивить, from диво 'wonder, marvel', Proto-Slavic *divo) + the adjectival suffix -тельный.

удивиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of удивить ('to surprise, astonish'), formed with prefix у- from дивить ('to marvel, amaze'), built on Old East Slavic диво ('wonder, marvel', from Proto-Slavic *divo).

удивление.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from удивить / удивиться ('to surprise / be surprised'), derived from диво ('marvel, wonder', from Proto-Slavic *divo).

удобно.etymology: Deadjectival adverb and impersonal predicative formed with -о from удобный ('convenient, comfortable'), inherited from Old East Slavic удобьныи / Old Church Slavonic удобьнъ ('easy, fitting, convenient'), from *u- + *doba ('fitting time, season, manner', compare подобный and сдоба).

удобный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic удобьныи ('fitting, timely, easy, convenient'), derived from удобь ('conveniently, easily'), built on prefix у- + доба ('fitting time, proper measure, suitability', from Proto-Slavic *doba, related to добрый 'good').

удобство.etymology: Derived from удобный ('convenient, comfortable') with the abstract noun suffix -ство; удобный stems from Old East Slavic удобь ('easily, suitably'), formed from у- + доба ('fitting time, suitability', from Proto-Slavic *doba).

удовлетворить.etymology: Compound verb adopted via Church Slavonic / Chancery Russian from у- + довлеть / доволь ('enough, sufficiency') + творить ('to make, do'), modeled as a calque of Latin satisfacere ('to make enough, satisfy').

удостоверение.etymology: Verbal and document noun from удостоверить ('to certify, attest as trustworthy'), compounded from у- + достойный / до-сто- ('worthy') + вера ('faith, trust, credence').

уехать.etymology: Formed with the ablative/perfective prefix у- ('away') + ехать ('to go by vehicle, ride'), from Old East Slavic ѣхати and Proto-Slavic *jěxati.

history.meaning: to leave by transport, drive away

уж.etymology: Shortened particle and adverbial variant of уже ('already, really, indeed'), inherited from Old East Slavic уже / ужо and Proto-Slavic *juže (from *ju 'already' + emphatic particle *že).

уже.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic уже (Old Church Slavonic юже / оуже, 'already'), from Proto-Slavic *juže / *uže, formed from the temporal stem *ju / *u ('now, already'; compare Lithuanian jaũ 'already' and Gothic ju) + the emphatic particle *že.

ужин.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ужинъ, from Proto-Slavic *jugъ ('south, midday sun'; compare юг 'south'). In early Slavic, *južina meant the midday meal taken when the sun was in the south; in Russian the word shifted over time to the evening meal ('supper, dinner') once обед became the midday meal.

ужинать.etymology: Derived from ужин ('dinner, supper') with the verbal suffix -ать. Inherited from Old East Slavic ужинъ (originally 'midday meal'), derived from югъ / угъ ('south, midday sun', from Proto-Slavic *jugъ).

ужиться.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix у- + жить ('to live', from Proto-Slavic *žiti) + the reflexive enclitic -ся, developing the sense 'to settle down together, learn to coexist'.

узел.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic узълъ ('knot, tied bundle'), from Proto-Slavic *vǫzъlъ (with loss of initial *v before *ǫ < *on-), formed with the instrument/object suffix *-ъlъ on the nasal-vowel root *vęz- / *vǫz- of вязать ('to tie, bind') and узы ('bonds').
узел.notes: Drops the fleeting е in oblique cases: **у́зел** → **узла́**, **узлы́**.

узнать.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix у- + знать ('to know'), from Old East Slavic знати and Proto-Slavic *znati (cognate with English know and Ancient Greek γιγνώσκω).

history.meaning: to recognize; to find out, learn

узник.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic узникъ / Old Church Slavonic ѫзьникъ ('prisoner'), formed with the agent suffix -ник from уза / узы ('bonds, fetters, chains'), from Proto-Slavic *ǫza ('bond, tie').

уи.etymology: Direct phonetic borrowing of French oui ('yes'), from Old French oïl < Latin hoc ille ('that [is] it / he [did] that').

уйти.etymology: Formed with the prefix у- ('away') + идти / йти ('to go on foot, walk'), from Old East Slavic уити and Proto-Slavic *ujьti.

history.meaning: to leave on foot, walk away

указание.etymology: Verbal noun from указать ('to point out, indicate, order, instruct', from prefix у- + казать 'to show, point', Proto-Slavic *kazati) + suffix -ние.

указать.etymology: Formed from the prefix у- + казать ('to show, point', inherited from Old East Slavic казати, from Proto-Slavic *kazati).

указывать.etymology: Imperfective verb formed with the suffix -ывать from указать ('to point out, indicate'), built on prefix у- + казать ('to show, point', from Proto-Slavic *kazati).

укладка.etymology: Action and result noun formed from укладывать / уложить ('to lay down, pack, arrange in order; to style hair', from prefix у- + класть 'to lay, put', Proto-Slavic *klasti) + suffix -ка.

укол.etymology: Deverbal noun formed by back-formation from уколоть ('to prick, sting, inject'), from the prefix у- + колоть ('to prick, pierce', from Proto-Slavic *kolti).

укор.etymology: Deverbal noun from укорить ('to reproach, blame'), formed with prefix у- from корить ('to reproach, humble'), from Proto-Slavic *koriti ('to humiliate, chastise').

украденный.etymology: Past passive participle of украсть ('to steal'), formed with the perfective prefix у- + красть ('to steal', from Old East Slavic красти, Proto-Slavic *krasti).

украсить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ukrasiti ('to adorn, beautify'), formed from prefix *u- + *krasiti ('to adorn, make beautiful', derived from *krasa 'beauty').

украсть.etymology: Perfective verb inherited from Old East Slavic украсти ('to steal'), formed from the prefix у- ('away') and красть ('to steal', Old East Slavic красти, present краду, from Proto-Slavic *krasti / *kradǫ).

украшать.etymology: Imperfective of украсить ('to decorate, adorn'), inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic украшати (from *ukrašati, with *sj > š palatalization, built on краса 'beauty').

украшение.etymology: Verbal and object noun formed from украсить / украшать ('to adorn, decorate', from краса 'beauty') + the suffix -ение.

укроп.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ukropъ, derived from *ukropiti ('to sprinkle, scald with boiling water'), likely referring either to the plant's scattered umbels or to infusing the aromatic herb in hot water.

уксус.etymology: Borrowed early into Old East Slavic (attested as уксусъ / оцътъ) from Byzantine and Ancient Greek ὄξος ('sour wine, vinegar'), derived from ὀξύς ('sharp, sour, acidic').

уксусный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -ный from уксус ('vinegar'), borrowed into Old East Slavic (уксусъ / оцътъ) from Byzantine Greek ὄξος (óxos, 'sour wine, vinegar'), from Ancient Greek ὀξύς ('sharp, sour').

укус.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from укусить ('to bite', from prefix у- + кусать 'to bite', Proto-Slavic *kǫsati).

укусить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix у- + кусить / кусать ('to bite'), inherited from Proto-Slavic *kǫsiti ('to bite, take a piece'), related to *kǫsъ ('bite, morsel, piece', Russian кусок).

укутать.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix у- + кутать ('to wrap up, muffle'), from Proto-Slavic *kǫtati ('to cover, wrap up, hide'), related to *kǫtъ ('corner, shelter').

history.meaning: to wrap up warmly, bundle up

уладить.etymology: Formed from the perfective prefix у- + ладить ('to put in order, get along'), derived from лад ('harmony, order, peace', from Proto-Slavic *ladъ).

улетать.etymology: Imperfective of улететь ('to fly away'), formed with the ablative prefix у- ('away') + летать ('to fly', iterative of лететь, Proto-Slavic *letěti).

улика.etymology: Deverbal noun associated with уличить ('to convict, expose, prove guilty'), derived from лицо / лик ('face, appearance', from Proto-Slavic *likъ), originally meaning 'bringing face-to-face with the evidence'.

history.meaning: to expose, prove face to face

улитка.etymology: Diminutive of older улит / улита ('snail, hollow shell'), connected by Vasmer with улей ('beehive, hollow') and улица ('hollow passage, street'), from the Proto-Slavic root *ul- ('hollow, cavity').

улица.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic улица, from Proto-Slavic *ulica, originally 'narrow passageway, lane between fences' (derived from *ula 'hollow, passage', from the same family as улей 'hollow-log beehive').

уловить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uloviti, formed from the prefix у- + ловить ('to catch, hunt', from Proto-Slavic *loviti).

уловка.etymology: Derived with the nominal suffix -ка from уловить ('to catch, trap') / улов ('catch'), developing from 'hunting trap or snare' to 'trick, ruse, stratagem'.

уложить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *uložiti, formed from the prefix у- + ложить ('to lay, place', from Proto-Slavic *ložiti).

history.meaning: to put to bed; to lay, pack

улучшиться.etymology: Formed from улучшить ('to improve, make better', from у- + лучший 'better', comparative of хороший) + the reflexive enclitic -ся.

улыбка.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ка from улыбаться ('to smile'), built on у- + the Slavic stem *lyb- / *lub- ('to bare the teeth ligeramente, smile'; Vasmer connects it with лoб 'forehead, skull' via the idea of a smooth or bared expression).

улыбнуться.etymology: Semelfactive perfective verb in -нуть-ся formed from the same stem as улыбаться ('to smile'), denoting a single act of smiling ('to give a smile').

history.meaning: to smile → to smile once, break into a smile

уля-ля.etymology: Borrowed from the French expressive interjection ouh là là / oh là là, used to express playful surprise, admiration, or teasing.

history.form: ouh là là / oh là là

ум.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic умъ (and Old Church Slavonic оумъ), from Proto-Slavic *umъ ('mind, intellect, understanding'), generally traced to Proto-Indo-European *h₁au-mo- ('perception, sense', related to Latin aveō and Sanskrit ávati).
ум.notes: Appears in key idioms: **сойти с ума** ('to go crazy, lose one's mind') and **с ума сойти!** ('unbelievable!').

умелый.etymology: Verbal adjective derived with the suffix -лый from уметь ('to know how, be able', inherited from Proto-Slavic *uměti, from *umъ 'mind, intellect').

умение.etymology: Verbal noun formed from уметь ('to know how, be able', Old East Slavic умѣти, from Proto-Slavic *uměti, derived from *umъ 'mind, intellect') + suffix -ние.

уменьшаться.etymology: Reflexive and intransitive form of уменьшать ('to reduce, diminish'), formed with -ся from у- + меньший ('smaller, lesser', from Proto-Slavic *mьňьjь).

уменьшить.etymology: Formed with the prefix у- and verbal suffix -ить from меньший ('smaller, lesser', inherited from Old East Slavic мьньшии, from Proto-Slavic *mьňьjь).

умеренный.etymology: Lexicalized passive participle of умерить ('to moderate, restrain within bounds', from prefix у- + мерить 'to measure', derived from мера 'measure, limit', Proto-Slavic *měra).

умереть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic умьрѣти (1st sg. умьру), from Proto-Slavic *umerti (1st sg. *umьrǫ), formed with the perfective prefix *u- and *merti ('to die'), from Proto-Indo-European *mer- ('to die, disappear'; compare Latin morī / mors, Sanskrit mriyáte, Persian mordan, and English mortal / murder).

умерший.etymology: Past active participle of умереть ('to die'), inherited from Old East Slavic умьрети / Proto-Slavic *umerti, from *u- + *merti ('to die').

уметь.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic умѣти ('to understand, know how to'), from Proto-Slavic *uměti, a denominative verb formed from *umъ ('mind, intellect', modern ум).

history.meaning: mind, wit → to know how, be skilled
to know how to, be able to

умирать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic умирати ('to die'), imperfective of умереть (Proto-Slavic *umirati / *umerti, from prefix *u- + *merti 'to die', PIE *mer-).

умничать.etymology: Derived from умник ('smart person, wiseacre', from ум 'mind, intellect', Proto-Slavic *umъ) + the verbal suffix -ичать ('to act like, show off as').

умничка.etymology: Affectionate diminutive of умница ('clever person, good boy/girl'), derived from умный ('smart, clever') and ум ('mind', from Proto-Slavic *umъ).

умно.etymology: Adverbial and predicate form in -о of умный ('smart, clever'), derived from ум ('mind, wit', from Proto-Slavic *umъ).

умный.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic умьныи ('intelligent, endowed with reason'), from Proto-Slavic *umьnъ, an adjective formed with *-ьnъ from *umъ ('mind, intellect, reason', modern ум).

умыться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic умытися ('to wash oneself'), reflexive of умыть (from prefix у- + мыть 'to wash', Proto-Slavic *myti).

history.meaning: to wash one's face and hands

универсальный.etymology: Borrowed via Polish uniwersalny or German universal from Latin universalis ('of or belonging to all, universal'), from universus ('whole, entire, turned into one').

университет.etymology: Borrowed via German Universität from Medieval Latin ūniversitās, shortened from ūniversitās magistrōrum et scholārium ('the whole guild or community of masters and scholars'), from Latin ūniversus ('whole, entire').

унижаться.etymology: Reflexive of унижать ('to abase, humiliate, lower'), imperfective of унизить (derived from у- + низкий / низ 'low, bottom', Proto-Slavic *nizъ).

унижение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from унизить ('to humiliate, abase'), from Old Church Slavonic унизити, derived from низъ ('low, bottom', Proto-Slavic *nizъ).

унизить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic / Old Church Slavonic унизити ('to lower, humble'), formed with the prefix у- from низ ('bottom, low place', Proto-Slavic *nizъ).

уникальный.etymology: Borrowed via French unique / German unikal from Latin unicus ('only, sole, single of its kind'), derived from unus ('one').

history.meaning: sole, single, one of a kind

униформа.etymology: Borrowed from French uniforme or German Uniform ('uniform clothing'), from Latin uniformis ('having only one form or shape'), from unus ('one') + forma ('form').

уничтожать.etymology: Imperfective of уничтожить ('to destroy, annihilate', literally 'to reduce to nothing'), formed from у- + ничто ('nothing', from Proto-Slavic *ničьto).

уничтожить.etymology: Formed in Russian and Church Slavonic from prefix у- + ничтоже ('nothing at all', Old Church Slavonic ничьтоже, from ни + чьто + же), modeled as a calque of Latin annihilare ('to reduce to nothing').

history.meaning: to reduce to nothing, destroy, wipe out

унывать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic унывати / Old Church Slavonic унывати ('to grow weary, lose heart'), formed from у- + ныть ('to ache, whine, pine', from Proto-Slavic *nyti 'to grow weary, pine').

уняться.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic унятися, formed from the prefix у- + ять ('to take, seize', from Proto-Slavic *jęti, with epenthetic н-) + reflexive -ся, literally 'to restrain oneself, subside'.

упаковано.etymology: Short neuter past passive participle of упаковать ('to pack, wrap up'), formed with the prefix у- + паковать, borrowed via Polish pakować from German packen ('to pack').

упаковать.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix у- + паковать ('to pack, wrap'), borrowed via German packen and Polish pakować from Middle Low German / Middle Dutch pak ('bundle, bale, pack').

history.meaning: to pack → to pack up, wrap

упаковка.etymology: Action and object noun formed from упаковать ('to pack up', from prefix у- + паковать 'to pack', borrowed via German packen / Polish pakować from Middle Low German pak 'bundle, pack') + suffix -ка.

упасть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic упасти ('to fall down'), formed with the perfective prefix у- + пасти / пасть ('to fall'), from Proto-Slavic *pasti ('to fall').

упитанный.etymology: Past passive participle of упитать ('to nourish well, fatten'), formed from the prefix у- + питать ('to feed, nourish', from Old Church Slavonic питати, Proto-Slavic *pitati).

уползти.etymology: Formed from the directional prefix у- ('away') + ползти ('to crawl, creep', inherited from Old East Slavic пълзти, from Proto-Slavic *pьlzti).

упомянуть.etymology: Formed from the prefix у- + помянуть ('to remember, mention'), from Old East Slavic помянути, derived from Proto-Slavic *pomęnǫti (from the root *mьněti 'to think, remember').

упорно.etymology: Adverb formed from упорный ('persistent, stubborn'), derived from упор ('prop, support, resistance'), from упереть ('to prop against', from у- + переть, Proto-Slavic *perti 'to press, push').

упорство.etymology: Derived with the abstract noun suffix -ство from упорный / упор ('prop, resistance'), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *uperti ('to press or brace against').

управа.etymology: Inherited from East Slavic управа ('justice, administration, management, redress'), deverbal noun from управить ('to direct, govern, set right', from у- + править 'to rule, direct', from правый 'right, straight').

управление.etymology: Verbal noun in -ение from управлять ('to direct, govern, manage'), built on у- + править ('to steer, rule, make straight'), from Proto-Slavic *praviti (from *pravъ 'straight, right').

управлять.etymology: Imperfective verb (paired with управить in older Russian, now used mostly imperfectively) formed from the prefix у- and правлять / править ('to steer, direct, rule, govern'), derived from правый ('straight, right', from Proto-Slavic *pravъ). Literally, 'to steer along a course, direct, manage, govern' (takes the instrumental case: управлять машиной / компанией).

history.meaning: to manage, run, govern, drive/pilot (+ instr.)

управляющая.etymology: Substantivized feminine present active participle of управлять ('to manage, govern, direct'), derived from управить (from у- + править 'to rule, direct', from правый 'right, straight', Proto-Slavic *pravъ).

управляющий.etymology: Substantivized masculine present active participle of управлять ('to manage, govern, direct'), derived from управить (from у- + править 'to direct, rule', from Proto-Slavic *praviti).

упражнение.etymology: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic упражнение ('occupation, practice, exercise'), verbal noun of упражняти ('to occupy, exercise'), related to праздный ('idle, empty') with reversal/occupation of leisure time.

упрекнуть.etymology: Semelfactive perfective of упрекать ('to reproach'), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic упрѣкати, derived from вопреки / преко ('across, against, contrary', from Proto-Slavic *perko).

упрямый.etymology: Formed in East Slavic from у- + прямъ ('straight, rigid, headstrong'; modern прямой), originally describing someone who holds rigidly to one line without yielding ('unbending, stubborn').

упрёк.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from упрекать / упрекнуть ('to reproach, cast in someone's teeth', originally connected with претить / пря 'dispute, contention' and опереть 'to press against').

упускать.etymology: Imperfective of упустить ('to let slip, let go, miss'), formed from ablative prefix у- ('away') + пускать / пустить ('to let go, release', Proto-Slavic *pustiti).

упёртый.etymology: Adjectivized past passive participle of упереть / упереться ('to brace oneself, dig one's heels in', from prefix у- + переть 'to press, push', Proto-Slavic *perti).

history.meaning: to dig one's heels in, resist

ура.etymology: Adopted as a military battle cry and cheer in the Petrine era (compare German hurra! and English hurrah! / hooray!), traced by Vasmer either to Middle High German hurrā (imperative of hurren 'to move swiftly, charge forward') or to Turkic ur- / ura! ('strike!').

ураган.etymology: Borrowed via French ouragan from Spanish huracán ('hurricane'), itself borrowed from Taíno hurakán, an indigenous Caribbean word for a storm god or tropical cyclone.

урезанный.etymology: Past passive participle of урезать ('to cut down, trim, curtail', from prefix у- + резать 'to cut', Proto-Slavic *rězati), used as an adjective meaning 'cut back, reduced, abridged'.

урна.etymology: Borrowed via Polish urna or German Urne from Latin urna ('water jar, cinerary urn, voting vessel').

уровень.etymology: Derived with prefix у- and tool/measure suffix -ень from ровный ('even, level, flat', from Old East Slavic ровьныи and Proto-Slavic *orvьnъ). Originally a builder's plumb-level or spirit-level used to check that a surface is even, then 'level' in general.

history.meaning: even, flat → spirit level; level, standard

уровень.notes: Drops the fleeting е in oblique cases: **у́ровень** → **на у́ровне**.

урод.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *urodъ, formed from the privative/deviant prefix *u- + *rodъ ('birth, kin, nature'), originally denoting someone born outside the norm or deformed (compare Polish uroda 'beauty', where the prefix developed a positive intensive sense).

урожай.etymology: Derived from урожать, imperfective of уродить ('to bear fruit, yield a crop'), formed from the prefix у- + родить ('to give birth, bear', from Proto-Slavic *roditi).

урок.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic урокъ ('agreed term, stipulation, assigned task, tribute'), from Proto-Slavic *urokъ, a deverbal noun from *urekti ('to speak out, stipulate, appoint', built on *u- + *rekti 'to speak'). From 'assigned task' it came to mean a school lesson.

history.meaning: to stipulate, assign → appointed task, rule

урон.etymology: Deverbal noun from уронить ('to drop, let fall, lose'), formed from the prefix у- + ронить ('to drop, shed', causative of *roniti, from Proto-Slavic *ronъ).

уронить.etymology: Perfective verb formed with the prefix у- + ронять / ронить ('to let fall, shed, drop'), from Proto-Slavic *roniti (causative of a root meaning 'to fall, flow', related to ринуться).

ус.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic усъ ('moustache, whisker'), from Proto-Slavic *vǫsъ ('facial hair, whisker, awn').

усатый.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *vǫsatъ, derived from ус ('moustache, whisker', Proto-Slavic *vǫsъ) + the possessive adjective suffix -атый ('having prominent...').

усердно.etymology: Adverb from усердный ('zealous, diligent'), derived from Old Church Slavonic усрьдьнъ / усрьдиѥ ('zeal, earnestness of heart', from prefix у- + срьдьце 'heart', calquing Greek πρόθυμος).

усиление.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from усилить ('to strengthen, reinforce'), derived from у- + сила ('strength, force', from Proto-Slavic *sila).

усиливать.etymology: Imperfective of усилить ('to strengthen, intensify'), formed with the suffix -ивать from у- + сила ('strength, force', from Proto-Slavic *sila).

усилие.etymology: Derived with the abstract neuter suffix -ие from усилить / у- + сила ('strength, force', from Proto-Slavic *sila), literally 'an exertion of strength'.

ускакать.etymology: Formed from the directional prefix у- ('away') + скакать ('to jump, gallop', inherited from Old East Slavic скакати, from Proto-Slavic *skakati).

ускорить.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic ускорити ('to hasten, speed up'), formed from prefix у- + скорый ('fast, quick', Proto-Slavic *skorъ) + verbal suffix -ить.

условный.etymology: Derived from условие ('condition, stipulation, agreement', from prefix у- + слово 'word, promise', Proto-Slavic *slovo) + the adjectival suffix -ный.

усложнять.etymology: Imperfective of усложнить ('to make more complex or difficult'), formed from prefix у- + сложный ('complex, complicated', from сложить 'to put together, fold').

услышать.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix у- + слышать ('to hear'), inherited from Old East Slavic услышати and Proto-Slavic *uslyšati, from the Indo-European auditory root *ḱlew- ('to hear').

history.meaning: to hear → to catch sound of, hear

уснуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic усънути ('to fall asleep'), from Proto-Slavic *usъnǫti (built on *u- + *sъpati / *sъnъ 'sleep', with loss of *p before *n).

успокаивать.etymology: Imperfective of успокоить ('to calm, soothe'), formed from у- + с- + покой ('peace, rest, calm', from Proto-Slavic *pokojь, related to *počiti 'to rest').

успокаиваться.etymology: Reflexive form of успокаивать ('to calm, soothe') with the enclitic -ся, derived from успокоить and покой ('peace, rest', from Proto-Slavic *pokojь).

успокоительный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -тельный from успокоить ('to calm, soothe'), ultimately from покой ('peace, quiet, rest', Proto-Slavic *pokojь).

уставать.etymology: Imperfective of устать ('to get tired'), inherited from Old East Slavic устати, from Proto-Slavic *ustati (from *u- + *stati 'to stand, stop', i.e. 'to come to a halt from exhaustion').

уставиться.etymology: Reflexive of уставить ('to set, fix in place, direct [one's eyes]', from prefix у- + ставить 'to set, place', Proto-Slavic *staviti) + -ся, literally 'to fix one's gaze intently upon'.

history.meaning: to fix one's eyes on, stare

устаканить.etymology: Colloquial Russian verb formed from у- + стакан ('drinking glass') + -ить, originally either referring to settling a dispute over a glass of liquor or to liquid settling smoothly in a glass.

усталость.etymology: Derived with the abstract noun suffix -ость from усталый ('tired, weary'), past verbal adjective of устать ('to get tired', from Proto-Slavic *ustati).

устанавливать.etymology: Imperfective of установить ('to set up, establish, install'), formed with the prefix у- + становить ('to place, stand', causative of стать, from Proto-Slavic *stanoviti).

установить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic установити ('to set upright, establish, ordain'), formed from prefix у- + становить ('to place, set standing', from стан / стоять 'to stand').

установленный.etymology: Past passive participle of установить ('to establish, install, set'), formed from у- + становить (from Proto-Slavic *stanoviti 'to place, set standing').

устать.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic устати, from Proto-Slavic *ustati, formed from the prefix *u- ('away, completely') and *stati ('to stand, come to a standstill', Russian стать). Originally 'to come to a stop from exhaustion, to be unable to go on standing or walking'.

history.meaning: to come to a halt, grow weary

устоять.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ustojati, formed from the prefix у- ('firmly, through to the end') + стоять ('to stand', from Proto-Slavic *stojati).

устраивать.etymology: Imperfective of устроить ('to arrange, organize, build, suit'), derived from prefix у- + строить ('to build, arrange, order', from строй 'order, array', Proto-Slavic *strojь).

устраиваться.etymology: Reflexive form of устраивать ('to arrange, organize, settle'), imperfective of устроить, derived from у- + строить ('to build, arrange, order', from строй, Proto-Slavic *strojь).

history.meaning: to get a job, settle in

устранение.etymology: Verbal noun formed with -ение from устранить ('to remove, eliminate, push aside'), a Church Slavonicism built on у- + страна ('side', corresponding to East Slavic сторона, from Proto-Slavic *storna).

устрица.etymology: Adapted with the Russian suffix -ица from earlier устерс (borrowed under Peter the Great from Dutch oesters, plural of oester), ultimately from Latin ostrea and Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon, 'oyster').

устричный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный (with regular ц → ч palatalization) from устрица ('oyster').

устроить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic устроити ('to put in order, arrange, equip'), formed from у- + строить ('to build, arrange, order'), from Proto-Slavic *strojiti (from *strojь 'order, array, structure').

history.meaning: to order, build → to arrange, establish

устроиться.etymology: Reflexive of устроить ('to arrange, settle, establish', from у- + строить 'to put in order') + -ся, meaning 'to get settled in a place or job, work out'.

history.meaning: to settle in, get a job

устройство.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ство from устроить ('to arrange, construct, organize'), from у- + строить ('to build, order', from Proto-Slavic *strojiti).

уступить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic уступити ('to step back, yield'), formed from the prefix у- ('away') + ступить ('to step, tread', from Proto-Slavic *stǫpiti).

history.meaning: to yield, give in, give way

усы.etymology: Nominative plural of ус ('whisker, moustache'), inherited from Old East Slavic усъ, from Proto-Slavic *vǫsъ ('facial hair, whisker').

усыпить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic усыпити, formed from the prefix у- + causative *sypiti ('to make sleep'), from the root of спать / сон (Proto-Slavic *sъpati / *sъnъ 'sleep').

утвердить.etymology: Inherited from Old Church Slavonic and Old East Slavic утврьдити ('to make firm, strengthen, confirm, ratify'), formed from prefix у- + твердить / твёрдый ('firm, solid, hard', Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ).

утешать.etymology: Imperfective of утешить ('to comfort, console'), inherited from Old East Slavic утѣшати / Old Church Slavonic утѣшати, from у- + тешить ('to amuse, comfort', Proto-Slavic *těšiti, causative of *tichъ 'quiet, calm').

утешить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утѣшити ('to comfort, console'), from Proto-Slavic *utěšiti, formed from *u- + *těšiti ('to soothe, calm', etymologically related to тихий 'quiet').

утка.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утька, diminutive of уты ('duck'), from Proto-Slavic *ǫty (genitive *ǫtъve), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énh₂ts ('duck', cognate with Latin anas, German Ente).

утомить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утомити, formed from the prefix у- + томить ('to weary, torment, languish', from Proto-Slavic *tomiti 'to oppress, exhaust').

утонуть.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утонути ('to sink, drown'), formed from prefix у- + тонуть ('to sink, drown', from Proto-Slavic *tonǫti < *topnǫti, related to топить 'to submerge, sink').

утопить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утопити, formed from the prefix у- + топить ('to sink, submerge, drown', causative of *topnǫti / тонуть, from Proto-Slavic *topiti).

утратить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утратити ('to spend, waste, lose'), formed from prefix у- + тратить ('to spend, consume, lose', from Proto-Slavic *tratiti).

утренний.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утрении / утреннии ('morning, early'), derived from утро ('morning', from Proto-Slavic *jutro / *utro) with the relational time suffix -енний.

утро.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic утро (alongside ютро; compare Polish jutro, where 'morning' shifted to mean 'tomorrow'), from Proto-Slavic *jutro / *utro ('dawn, morning'). Deeper connections outside Slavic remain uncertain.

утром.etymology: Lexicalized instrumental singular of утро ('morning'), used adverbially to express time when ('in the morning'). Inherited from Old East Slavic утро / ютро, from Proto-Slavic *jutro ('morning, dawn').

утюг.etymology: Borrowed from a Turkic language (compare Old Turkic ütüg, Turkish ütü 'flatiron'), derived from the Turkic verb *üt- ('to singe hair, scorch, smooth with heat').

ух.etymology: Primary expressive interjection of onomatopoeic origin, representing a heavy exhalation of breath caused by exertion, relief, surprise, or amazement.

ухаживание.etymology: Verbal noun formed from ухаживать ('to look after, tend; to court, woo', iterative of уходить in its older transitive sense 'to tend thoroughly, look after', from у- + ходить 'to go, walk about').

history.meaning: to tend, care for; to pay court to

ухажёр.etymology: Formed in Russian from ухаживать ('to court, woo, look after') + the playful French-borrowed agent suffix -ёр (modeled on дирижёр, стажёр).

history.meaning: to look after; to court, woo

ухо.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ухо, from Proto-Slavic *uxo ('ear', plural dual *uši), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éws-os ('ear'; compare Lithuanian ausìs, Latin auris, Ancient Greek οὖς, Gothic auso, and English ear). Its irregular plural уши continues the old Slavic dual number for paired body parts.

уход.etymology: Deverbal noun formed from уходить ('to go away, leave; to tend, look after', as in уходить за кем-либо), combining the prefix у- with ход ('going, motion', from Proto-Slavic *xodъ).

history.meaning: to leave; to tend → departure, leaving; care, maintenance

уходить.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic уходити ('to go away, depart'), imperfective counterpart of уйти, formed from prefix у- ('away') + ходить ('to walk, go'), from Proto-Slavic *xoditi.

ухудшать.etymology: Imperfective of ухудшить ('to worsen, make worse'), derived from у- + худший ('worse, worst', comparative/superlative of худой 'bad, meager', from Proto-Slavic *xudъ).

уцелеть.etymology: Formed with the perfective prefix у- + цел- ('whole, unharmed, intact', from целый, Proto-Slavic *cělъ) + inchoative/stative verb suffix -еть: literally 'to remain whole, come through intact'.

history.meaning: whole, intact → to survive intact, be spared

участвовать.etymology: Formed with the verbal suffix -овать from участие ('participation, share'), adopted via Old Church Slavonic оучастиѥ, built on оу- + часть ('part, share, portion', from Proto-Slavic *čęstь): literally 'to have a part or share in something'.

history.meaning: participation → to take part, participate, compete

участковый.etymology: Substantivized relational adjective from участок ('plot, precinct, district', derived from часть 'part, share', Proto-Slavic *čęstь) + suffix -овый, short for участковый инспектор/уполномоченный полиции ('precinct police officer').

участник.etymology: Derived with the agent suffix -ник from участие ('participation, share', from Old Church Slavonic участие, formed from у- + часть 'part, share', Proto-Slavic *čęstь).

участница.etymology: Feminine counterpart of участник ('participant'), formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from участие ('participation', from часть 'part, share').

учебник.etymology: Formed in Russian with the object suffix -ник from учебный ('educational, teaching'), derived from учёба ('study, learning') and учить ('to teach, learn', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

учение.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic учение / Old Church Slavonic учение ('teaching, learning, doctrine'), verbal noun of учить ('to teach, learn', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

ученик.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ученикъ and Old Church Slavonic оученикъ ('disciple, pupil, apprentice'), formed with the agent suffix -ик from ученъ (past passive participle of учить 'to teach', from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

history.meaning: to teach → one who is taught, pupil

учитель.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic and Old Church Slavonic учитель ('teacher, master'), formed from учить ('to teach', Proto-Slavic *učiti, causative related to *vyknǫti 'to learn, get accustomed') + agent suffix -тель.

учительница.etymology: Formed with the feminine agent suffix -ница from учитель ('teacher'), inherited from Old East Slavic учитель and Old Church Slavonic оучитель (from Proto-Slavic *učitelь, built on *učiti 'to teach').

учиться.etymology: Reflexive form in -ся of учить ('to teach, learn'), inherited from Old East Slavic учитися and Proto-Slavic *učiti sę ('to accustom oneself, learn'), from a causative formation on the Proto-Indo-European root *h₁ewk- ('to become accustomed', cognate with Lithuanian jaukinti 'to tame, habituate').

учредитель.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -тель from учредить ('to found, establish, institute'), a Church Slavonicism from у- + чреда ('order, turn, sequence', corresponding to East Slavic череда, Proto-Slavic *čerda).

history.meaning: to arrange in order, institute, entertain

учёба.etymology: Derived with the nominal suffix -ёба from учить ('to teach, study', inherited from Old East Slavic учити, from Proto-Slavic *učiti).

учёный.etymology: Substantivized passive participle of учить ('to teach, school', Proto-Slavic *učiti), literally 'one who has been taught, learned person, scholar', used in Russian as a calque of French savant / German Gelehrter.

ушастый.etymology: Derived from ухо (plural уши, stem уш-, 'ear', from Proto-Slavic *uxo) + the adjective suffix -астый ('having large or prominent...').

ущерб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ущербъ ('notching, waning, loss'), derived from у- + щерба ('notch, chip, gap'), from Proto-Slavic *ščьrbъ ('jagged, notched').

ущербный.etymology: Adjective formed with the suffix -ный from ущерб ('waning, loss, defect', from Proto-Slavic *ščьrbъ 'notched, chipped'), originally referring to a waning moon before developing the sense 'defective, flawed'.

уют.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *ujutъ, formed from the prefix *u- + *jutъ ('shelter, lodging, roof'; compare приют 'shelter' and ютиться 'to huddle, take shelter').

уютненько.etymology: Colloquial diminutive adverb formed from уютненький, diminutive of уютный ('cozy, comfortable'), derived from уют ('coziness, shelter').

уютно.etymology: Adverb from the short neuter of уютный ('cosy, comfortable, sheltered'), derived from уют ('cosy shelter, homey comfort'), formed from prefix у- + an old Slavic root *jut- ('shelter, lodging, roof'; compare приют 'shelter, refuge' and dialectal ютиться 'to nestle, huddle in a shelter').

уютный.etymology: Derived from уют ('coziness, sheltered comfort'), formed from prefix у- + older Russian ют ('shelter, refuge, lodging under a roof', preserved in приют 'shelter, asylum'), from Proto-Slavic *jutъ.

фа.etymology: Borrowed from Italian fa, the fourth solfège syllable introduced by the medieval music theorist Guido of Arezzo from the initial syllable of the Latin half-line 'Famuli tuorum' in the Hymn to St John the Baptist.

history.meaning: opening words of the fourth hymn line

фа.notes: Indeclinable neuter or feminine musical note name in Russian.

факт.etymology: Borrowed via German Fakt or French fait from Latin factum ('deed, act, something done'), substantivized neuter past participle of facere ('to do, make').

фактически.etymology: Adverb formed from фактический ('actual, factual'), derived with -еский from факт ('fact', from Latin factum).

фанат.etymology: Back-formation or clipping from фанатик ('fanatic'), reinforced in the 20th century by English fan ('sports or music enthusiast'), ultimately from Latin fanaticus ('inspired by a deity, frenzied', from fanum 'temple').

history.meaning: inspired by a temple deity, frenzied

фанатик.etymology: Borrowed via German Fanatiker or Polish fanatyk from Latin fanaticus ('belonging to a temple, inspired by a god, frenzied'), from fanum ('sanctuary, temple').

фанера.etymology: Borrowed from German Furnier ('veneer, thin wood sheet'), from French fournir ('to furnish, supply'); in late 20th-century Russian musicians' slang, петь под фанеру ('to lip-sync') arose as a phonetic play on фонограмма ('pre-recorded backing track').

фантазировать.etymology: Borrowed from German phantasieren ('to daydream, improvise, fantasize'), derived from Phantasie ('fantasy, imagination', from Ancient Greek φαντασία).

фантазия.etymology: Borrowed via Polish fantazja or German Phantasie from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía, 'appearance, image, imagination'), from φαίνω (phaínō, 'to bring to light, show').

фантазёрка.etymology: Feminine form of фантазёр ('dreamer, visionary'), formed in Russian with the suffix -ка; фантазёр combines the stem of фантазия with the French-origin agent suffix -ёр.

фантастика.etymology: Derived from фантастический / German Phantastik, ultimately from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós, 'able to present or imagine'), from φαντασία ('imagination').

фантастический.etymology: Borrowed via German fantastisch / French fantastique and Latin phantasticus from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós 'able to imagine, imaginary, visionary'), from φαντάζω ('to make visible, display').

фара.etymology: Borrowed in the early twentieth century from French phare ('lighthouse, beacon; automobile headlight'), from Latin Pharus and Ancient Greek Φάρος (Pháros, the island off Alexandria famed for its ancient lighthouse).

фартук.etymology: Borrowed via Polish fartuch from Middle High German vortuoch (regional German Vortuch), a compound of vor 'in front' and Tuoch 'cloth' — literally a 'fore-cloth' worn over the front of one's clothes.
фартук.notes: The second element -тук (from German Tuch 'cloth') is the same root found in галстук 'necktie' (from Halstuch 'neck-cloth').

фарш.etymology: Borrowed via German Farce or directly from French farce ('stuffing, forcemeat'), from Late Latin farsa, feminine past participle of Latin farcire ('to stuff, cram').

фаршировать.etymology: Derived in Russian from фарш ('forcemeat, stuffing, minced meat', borrowed via German Farce / French farce from Latin farcire 'to stuff, cram') + the verbal suffix -ировать.

фашист.etymology: Borrowed in the 1920s from Italian fascista ('member of the fascist movement'), derived from fascio ('bundle, political league'), from Latin fascis ('bundle of rods carried by lictors as a symbol of authority').

февраль.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic февраль / февруарь (via Old Church Slavonic and Byzantine Greek Φεβρουάριος, with dissimilation of r...r to r...l), from Latin Februarius (mensis) ('month of purification', from februa 'purification rites').

федеральный.etymology: Borrowed via French fédéral or English federal, derived from Latin foedus (stem foeder-, 'league, treaty, covenant, alliance') + Russian adjectival suffix -ный.

фейерверк.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from German Feuerwerk ('fireworks'), a compound of Feuer ('fire') + Werk ('work').

ферзь.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic intermediaries from Persian فرزین (farzīn 'wise man, counselor, vizier; chess queen'), which originally designated the shah's chief counselor on the chessboard.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: ферзь

фестиваль.etymology: Borrowed from French festival ('festival'), from Old French festival ('festive, suitable for a feast'), from Medieval Latin festivalis, from Latin festum ('feast, holiday').

фиаско.etymology: Borrowed via French fiasco from Italian fiasco ('bottle, flask'), from the Italian theatrical idiom far fiasco ('to suffer a complete failure on stage', literally 'to make a bottle').

history.meaning: to make a bottle; to fail utterly

фигня.etymology: Colloquial derivative formed with the collective/pejorative suffix -ня from фиг / фига ('fig; fig sign, nothing'), borrowed via Polish figa or German Feige from Latin ficus ('fig').

фигура.etymology: Borrowed via Polish figura from Latin figura ('form, shape, figure'), from the root of fingere ('to shape, fashion, mold').

физика.etymology: Borrowed via Latin physica (and German Physik / Polish fizyka) from Ancient Greek φυσική (ἐπιστήμη) ('knowledge of nature, natural science'), derived from φύσις ('nature', from φύω 'to grow, bring forth').

физический.etymology: Derived with the adjective suffix -еский from физика ('physics') or borrowed via German physisch from Latin physicus and Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós, 'natural, physical'), from φύσις (phúsis, 'nature').

физкультура.etymology: Early twentieth-century syllabic abbreviation of физическая культура ('physical culture, physical education'), combining физический (from Greek φυσικός 'natural, physical') + культура (from Latin cultura 'cultivation').

фиксировать.etymology: Borrowed from German fixieren ('to fix, fasten, record'), from French fixer, derived from Latin fixus ('fixed, fast'), past participle of figere ('to fasten, fix').

фиксироваться.etymology: Reflexive and passive form of фиксировать ('to fix, record, register') formed with the enclitic -ся.

филейный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with -ный from филей / филе ('fillet, tenderloin, sirloin'), borrowed from French filet ('thin strip of meat, tenderloin'), diminutive of fil ('thread', from Latin filum).

фильм.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century (initially feminine фильма, later masculine фильм via German Film) from English film ('thin membrane, photographic celluloid strip, motion picture'), from Old English filmen ('membrane, skin', related to fell / pelt).

history.meaning: thin layer → celluloid roll → motion picture

финал.etymology: Borrowed via German Finale or French finale from Italian finale ('ending, conclusion'), from Latin finalis ('relating to the end'), from finis ('boundary, end').

финалистка.etymology: Feminine form of финалист ('finalist'), formed with the suffix -ка; финалист derives from финал ('final') + agent suffix -ист.

финальный.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ный from финал ('final, finale', ultimately from Latin finalis).

финансировать.etymology: Borrowed from German finanzieren or French financer ('to finance, fund'), derived from Middle French finance ('payment, settlement, pecuniary resources', from finer 'to end, settle a debt').

финансово.etymology: Adverb formed with -о from финансовый ('financial'), derived from финансы ('finances', from French finances).

финансовый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from финансы ('finances'), borrowed via German Finanzen from French finances ('pecuniary resources, public revenue').

финиш.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th or early 20th century from English finish ('end of a race, finishing line'), via Anglo-Norman from Old French fenir, from Latin finire ('to bound, limit, end').

финский.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -ский from финн ('Finn'), borrowed via German Finne / Swedish finne from Old Norse finnr.

фирма.etymology: Borrowed in the nineteenth century via German Firma from Italian firma ('authenticated signature, commercial house operating under a registered name'), from Latin firmare ('to make firm, ratify, confirm by signature', from firmus 'firm').

фирменный.etymology: Adjective formed with -енный from фирма ('commercial firm, company, house brand'), borrowed via German Firma from Italian firma ('confirmed signature, business trade name', from Latin firmare 'to make firm, validate by signature'). In culinary and retail Russian, фирменный means 'house-special, signature, trademark'.
фирменный.notes: *Фирменное блюдо* means a restaurant's 'signature dish' or 'house speciality'.

фитнес.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English fitness ('physical fitness, exercise'), derived from fit ('healthy, well-suited') + -ness.

фишка.etymology: Adapted with the Russian suffix -ка from French fiche ('gaming counter, peg, token', originally a pointed peg used in games), from ficher ('to fix, drive in', from Vulgar Latin *figicare).

флакон.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French flacon ('small stoppered bottle, perfume vial'), from Old French flascon, from Late Latin flasco ('bottle, flask').

фламбе.etymology: Borrowed from French flambé ('flamed, singed'), past participle of flamber ('to flame, blaze'), from flambe / flamme ('flame', from Latin flamma).

флеш.etymology: Borrowed from English flush (in card games, a hand of cards all of the same suit), related to flush ('full, even, abundant').

history.meaning: hand of cards of one suit

флешка.etymology: Colloquial Russian formation with the suffix -ка from флеш-память / флеш-накопитель, borrowed from English flash drive / flash memory (named because memory blocks are erased in a 'flash').

фломастер.etymology: Genericized in Russian in the second half of the twentieth century from the American brand name Flo-Master (a refillable felt-tip marker produced by Cushman & Denison from 1945, formed from flow + master).

флот.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era from Dutch vloot or French flotte ('fleet of ships, navy'), of Germanic origin (related to Old English flota / float 'to float, sail').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: флот

фмс.etymology: Initialism of Федеральная миграционная служба ('Federal Migration Service'), the Russian government agency overseeing migration from 1992 to 2016.

фокусник.etymology: Formed with the agent suffix -ник from фокус ('magic trick, sleight of hand'), shortened from German Hokuspokus ('hocus-pocus, conjurer's formula').

фон.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from French fond ('bottom, depth, background of a painting or fabric'), from Latin fundus ('bottom, base, foundation').

фонарик.etymology: Formed in Russian as the diminutive of фонарь ('street lamp, lantern') with suffix -ик; фонарь itself comes from Byzantine Greek φανάριον ('lantern'). Today фонарик means both a small decorative lantern and a handheld pocket flashlight.

фонарь.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic (фонарь) from Byzantine Greek φανάριον (phanárion), diminutive of Ancient Greek φανός ('torch, lantern'), from φαίνω ('to shine, bring to light', related to English phantom and phenomenon).

фондан.etymology: Borrowed from French fondant ('melting', short for chocolat fondant or gâteau au chocolat fondant), present participle of fondre ('to melt', from Latin fundere 'to pour, melt').

фонтан.etymology: Borrowed in the Petrine era via Italian fontana (or Polish fontanna) from Late Latin fontāna ('spring, fountain'), substantivized feminine of fontānus ('of a spring'), from Latin fōns, fontis ('spring, source of water').

фора.etymology: Borrowed via German Vorgabe or directly from Italian fora / fuori ('outside, ahead', in billiards and games), or German vor ('ahead, in front'), denoting points or time given in advance as a handicap.

форель.etymology: Borrowed in the eighteenth century from German Forelle ('trout'), from Middle High German forhele / Old High German forhana ('trout', literally 'speckled fish', from PIE *perk̂- 'speckled, spotted').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: форель

форма.etymology: Borrowed via Polish forma (and German Form) from Latin fōrma ('shape, figure, mould, stamp, last'). In Russian it means outer 'shape, form', a school or military 'uniform', and a culinary 'baking tin, cake mould'.

history.meaning: shape, form; baking tin, mould; uniform

формально.etymology: Adverb formed from формальный ('formal'), borrowed via Polish formalny from Latin formalis ('relating to form, formal'), from forma ('shape, form, rule').

формат.etymology: Borrowed via German Format or French format from Italian formato ('size and shape of a book'), from Latin (liber) formatus ('shaped book', from formare 'to form, shape').

формула.etymology: Borrowed from Latin formula ('small form, mold, rule, fixed form of words'), diminutive of forma ('form, shape').

форс-мажор.etymology: Borrowed from the French legal phrase force majeure ('superior or irresistible force'), from Latin fortia ('strength, force') + maior ('greater').

форточка.etymology: Borrowed from German Pfortchen ('little door', diminutive of Pforte 'gate, door'), or via Polish fortka from the same German word, ultimately from Latin porta 'gate, door'. In Russian homes it came to name the small hinged pane set into a larger window frame for airing a room in winter.
форточка.notes: Открыть форточку is the classic way to let fresh air into a warm room without opening the whole casement.

форум.etymology: Borrowed from Latin forum ('public square, marketplace, assembly place in ancient Rome'), akin to foris ('outside, out of doors').

фото.etymology: Clipped indeclinable noun from фотография ('photography, photograph'), formed from the international Greek-derived compound photo- (from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός 'light') + -graphia ('drawing, writing').
фото.notes: Indeclinable neuter noun in Russian: старое фото ('an old photo').

фотограф.etymology: Borrowed from German Photograph or French photographe, coined from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός (phôs, phōtós, 'light') + -γράφος (-gráphos, 'writer, drawer', from γράφω 'to write, draw').

фотографировать.etymology: Borrowed from German photographieren or formed in Russian from фотография ('photography') + the verbal suffix -ировать.

фоторобот.etymology: Borrowed from French portrait-robot (adapted in Russian with фото- 'photo-' + робот 'robot', coined by French police commissioner Pierre Chabot in the 1950s for a composite facial sketch assembled from photographic strips).

фотошоп.etymology: Borrowed from English Photoshop, the trademarked name of the raster graphics editor Adobe Photoshop (created in 1988 by Thomas and John Knoll from photo + shop).

фраза.etymology: Borrowed via French phrase or German Phrase from Late Latin phrasis, from Ancient Greek φράσις ('way of speaking, expression, phrase'), derived from φράζω ('to point out, declare, express').

фрак.etymology: Borrowed via French frac and German Frack from English frock ('men's coat, smock, tunic', from Old French froc).

француз.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–17th centuries via Polish Francuz (influenced by French François / Français and German Franzose), ultimately from Late Latin Francus ('Frank').

фреш.etymology: Borrowed in the late 20th century from English fresh (short for freshly squeezed juice), from Old French freis and Proto-Germanic *friskaz.

фрикасе.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French fricassée ('dish of white meat cut into pieces and stewed in a white sauce'), the feminine past participle of fricasser ('to cut up and cook in sauce'), traditionally explained in French etymology as a blend of frire ('to fry', from Latin frīgere) and casser ('to break into pieces', from Late Latin quassāre).

history.meaning: meat cut into pieces and braised in white sauce

фсб.etymology: Russian initialism for Федеральная служба безопасности ('Federal Security Service', established in 1995), combining федеральная ('federal') + служба ('service', from служить 'to serve') + безопасность ('security', from без- + опасный 'safe').

фуа-гра.etymology: Borrowed from French foie gras (literally 'fat liver'), from foie ('liver', from Late Latin ficatum 'fig-fattened liver') + gras ('fat', from Latin crassus).

фугу.etymology: Borrowed via English fugu from Japanese 河豚 (fugu, 'pufferfish, blowfish').

фуд-стилист.etymology: Borrowed in the 21st century from English food stylist (a compound of food + stylist, a specialist who arranges dishes for photography or film).

функция.etymology: Borrowed via Polish funkcja or German Funktion from Latin functio ('performance, execution, duty'), derived from fungi ('to perform, execute, discharge').

фура.etymology: Borrowed via Polish fura ('wagon, cartload') from Middle High German vuore / German Fuhre ('wagon, cartload, haul'), from the root of fahren ('to drive, travel').

фургон.etymology: Borrowed from French fourgon ('covered baggage wagon, delivery van'), a word of uncertain Romance/Germanic origin originally denoting a long-poled baggage cart following an army.

фуршет.etymology: Shortened from French (déjeuner) à la fourchette ('(meal eaten) with a fork', i.e. a standing reception where guests eat with forks without sitting at a table), from fourchette ('fork', diminutive of fourche, from Latin furca).

футбол.etymology: Borrowed in the late 19th century from English football, a compound of foot and ball.

футболист.etymology: Derived from футбол ('football, soccer', borrowed from English football, from foot + ball) + the personal agent suffix -ист.

футболка.etymology: Formed in Russian with the suffix -ка from футбол ('football, soccer', from English football), originally denoting a jersey worn by football players before generalizing to any T-shirt.

ха.etymology: Primary vocalic interjection imitating the open-mouthed exhalation of laughter or sudden exclamation, with parallels across Slavic and Indo-European languages (compare English ha!).

халат.etymology: Borrowed via Turkic (compare Turkish hilat, Tatar xalat) from Arabic خِلْعَة (ḵilʿa, 'robe of honor bestowed by a ruler'), from خَلَعَ (ḵalaʿa, 'to take off clothes to bestow as a gift').

хам.etymology: From the biblical name Хам ('Ham', son of Noah in Genesis 9:22, who mocked his father's nakedness), borrowed via Old Church Slavonic Хамъ and Greek Χάμ from Hebrew חָם (Ḥām), used in Russian first for serfs and later for any insolent boor.

хамить.etymology: Denominal verb derived in Russian from хам ('boor, insolent lout'), originally the biblical personal name Хам (Ham, son of Noah in Genesis 9, who mocked his father's nakedness and became a byword for impudent disrespect).

хан.etymology: Borrowed into Old East Slavic (ханъ / канъ) from Turkic and Mongolic khan / qan ('ruler, sovereign, prince').

хана.etymology: Colloquial slang word borrowed via criminal argot (Odessa/fenya), most likely from Yiddish חנה (khane) or Hebrew חֲנָה (ḥănā, 'encampment, stopping place, end of the road'), or Turkic xana ('house, shelter, final station').

характер.etymology: Borrowed via Polish charakter and German Charakter from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, 'engraved mark, stamp, distinctive nature'), from χαράσσω (kharássō, 'to sharpen, engrave').

хачапури.etymology: Borrowed from Georgian ხაჭაპური (xač̣ap̣uri, 'cheese bread'), a compound of ხაჭო (xač̣o, 'curd, cottage cheese') + პური (p̣uri, 'bread').

хачапурщик.etymology: Formed in Russian with the occupational agent suffix -щик from хачапури ('khachapuri, Georgian cheese bread').

хвататься.etymology: Reflexive of хватать ('to seize, snatch, grab', iterative of хватить, from Proto-Slavic *xvatati / *xvatiti) + -ся, meaning 'to grab hold of, clutch at'.

хватить.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatiti ('to snatch, seize, reach'). From the concrete sense 'to grasp, reach far enough' developed the common impersonal sense хватит ('it suffices, that is enough!').

хватка.etymology: Derived with the nominal suffix -ка from хватать ('to grasp, seize, snatch', inherited from Proto-Slavic *xvatati).

химчистка.etymology: Twentieth-century compound abbreviation of химическая чистка ('chemical cleaning, dry cleaning'), combining хим- (from химический 'chemical') + чистка ('cleaning', from чистить 'to clean', Proto-Slavic *čistiti).

хитрец.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хитрьць (originally 'craftsman, skilled artisan, wise man'), formed with the agent suffix -ец from хитрый ('clever, skillful, cunning', from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ).

хитро.etymology: Short neuter form and adverb from хитрый ('cunning, clever, artful', in Old East Slavic also 'skilled, ingenious'), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ (originally 'quick to grasp', related to *xytiti 'to seize, catch').

хитроумный.etymology: Compound adjective formed from хитрый ('cunning, clever, skillful') + connecting vowel -о- + ум ('mind, wit') + -ный, modeled as a calque of Ancient Greek πολύμητις / ἀγκυλομήτης ('of crooked/clever counsel').

хитрый.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хитрыи (and Old Church Slavonic хꙑтръ 'skillful, clever, ingenious, artful'), from Proto-Slavic *xytrъ, originally a *-ro- adjective derived from the same root as хватать / похитить ('to seize, snatch, grasp quickly', Proto-Slavic *xytiti). From 'quick to grasp, dexterous, skillful' (still preserved in нехитрый 'simple, uncomplicated'), the meaning shifted to 'crafty, cunning, sly'.

хлам.etymology: Connected by Vasmer with Proto-Slavic *xlamъ / *xolomъ ('heap, mound, debris'; compare dialectal холомить 'to heap up carelessly' and холм 'hill').

хлеб.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хлѣбъ, from Proto-Slavic *xlěbъ, widely regarded by Vasmer and modern Slavicists as an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz ('baked loaf', the ancestor of Gothic hlaifs and English loaf).

хлопать.etymology: Expressive Slavic onomatopoeic verb built on the sound-symbolic root *xlop- imitating a flat slap, clap of hands, or banging of a door (compare Polish chłapać and Ukrainian хлопати).

хлопковый.etymology: Relational adjective formed with the suffix -овый from хло́пок ('cotton'), which developed in Russian from dialectal охло́пок ('tuft, flock of tow or fibres'), reshaped under the influence of хлопать.

хлопнуть.etymology: Semelfactive verb formed with the suffix -нуть from хлопать ('to clap, slap, slam'), derived from the Proto-Slavic onomatopoeic root *xlop- imitating a sharp clapping or slamming sound.

хлопок.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ок from хлопать ('to clap, bang, pop'), denoting a single sharp clap, pop, or bang (stressed хлопо́к). (A homograph stressed хло́пок means 'cotton', reshaped from dialectal охлопок 'tuft of tow or fibres'.)

history.meaning: to clap, bang → a clap, pop, bang

хлопок.notes: Watch the stress difference: **хлопо́к** (genitive хлопка́) means 'a clap, pop, bang', whereas **хло́пок** (genitive хло́пка) means 'cotton'.

хлопоты.etymology: Plural-only noun (singular хлопота in older and dialectal Russian), derived from the expressive Slavic stem *xlopotъ ('bustling noise, clatter, busyness'), related to хлопать ('to bang, bustle about').

хм.etymology: Onomatopoeic vocal gesture imitating a closed-lip throat clearing or nasal hum expressing thoughtfulness, hesitation, or mild doubt (parallel to English hm / hmph).

history.meaning: hm, hmph (interjection of thought or doubt)

хмурый.etymology: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *xmurъ ('overcast, gloomy, frowning'), related by ablaut and consonant alternation to *xmara (Russian dialectal хмара 'dark cloud, gloom, mist') and смурый ('dark-gray, gloomy').

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: хмурый

хобби.etymology: Borrowed in the mid-20th century from English hobby ('leisure pastime'), shortened from hobbyhorse ('toy horse, favorite pastime'), itself from Hob / Robin (pet forms of Robert).

ход.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic ходъ ('walking, motion, procession, way'), from Proto-Slavic *xodъ, a deverbal noun associated with *xoditi ('to walk, go', Russian ходить; Vasmer compares Ancient Greek ὁδός hodós 'way, road, journey' from PIE *sod-o-).

history.meaning: motion, course; move/turn (in a game); entrance

хозяин.etymology: Recorded in Russian from the 15th–16th centuries (earlier хозя 'master, owner'), borrowed from a Kipchak / Volga Turkic title (compare Tatar хуҗа and Chuvash хуҫа 'master, owner, head of household'), which goes back to Persian khwāja (خواجه, 'lord, master, merchant').
хозяин.notes: Plural drops the singulative *-ин* and adds *-ева*: **хозя́ева**.

хозяйственный.etymology: Formed in Russian from хозяйство ('household, economy, farmstead', derived from хозяин 'master of the house, owner') + the adjectival suffix -енный.

хозяйство.etymology: Derived with the suffix -ство from хозяин ('master, host, owner'), a borrowing into Russian from a Turkic language (compare Kipchak/Tatar xojayin, ultimately from Persian خواجه xwāja 'master, lord').

хоккей.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century from English hockey, probably related to Middle French hoquet ('shepherd's crook, curved stick').

холестерин.etymology: Borrowed via German Cholesterin from French cholestérine (coined in 1815 by Michel Eugène Chevreul for the solid substance isolated from gallstones), from Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ 'bile, gall') + στερεός (stereós 'solid, stiff').

холл.etymology: Borrowed in the late nineteenth or twentieth century from English hall ('entrance hall, hotel lobby, lounge').

холм.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic хълмъ ('hill, mound'), from Proto-Slavic *xъlmъ, an early borrowing from Proto-Germanic *hulmaz ('rising ground, hill, small island', cognate with Old English holm and ultimately related to Latin collis 'hill').

холод.etymology: Inherited from Old East Slavic холодъ (with East Slavic pleophony -оло-), from Proto-Slavic *xoldъ ('cold, coolness'), cognate with Old Church Slavonic хладъ.

sources.title: M. Vasmer, Etymological Dictionary — Vinogradov Institute, Russian Academy of Sciences: холод

холодец.etymology: Formed with the noun suffix -ец from холодный ('cold') / холод ('cold', from Proto-Slavic *xoldъ), denoting meat broth chilled until it sets into a savory jelly.
